questions.title: Acute Trauma Following Sporting Injury
questions.vignette: A 22-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after getting hit on the temporal region with a baseball bat. Initially, he experienced a brief 2-minute loss of consciousness, but subsequently regained full alertness and conversational ability. Three hours later in the observation unit, he becomes acutely somnolent with an ipsilateral dilated, non-reactive right pupil and contralateral hemiparesis. An emergent non-contrast head CT demonstrates a lenticular, biconvex hyperdense extra-axial collection along the right temporoparietal convexity that does not cross the cranial sutures.
questions.imageAnnotation: Lenticular biconvex hyperdensity constrained by cranial suture lines in the temporoparietal region.
options: Rupture of bridging cortical veins
Laceration of the middle meningeal artery
Rupture of an anterior communicating artery berry aneurysm
Thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus
Diffuse axonal injury with petechial shear hemorrhages
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation (lucid interval following temporal bone trauma followed by acute neurological decline and uncal herniation with 'blown' pupil) combined with the classic biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdensity on non-contrast CT is pathognomonic for an Epidural Hematoma (EDH). EDH typically occurs following fracture of the pterion, leading to laceration of the middle meningeal artery (a branch of the maxillary artery). Because the dura mater is tightly bound to the inner calvarium at cranial sutures, the hematoma cannot cross suture lines.
questions.highYieldPearl: Middle meningeal artery laceration = Pterion fracture = Biconvex lens-shaped collection on CT = Does NOT cross suture lines. Requires emergent surgical craniotomy decompression.

questions.title: Sudden Dyspnea and Sharp Chest Pain in a Tall Smoker
questions.vignette: A 21-year-old tall, slender male with a 4 pack-year smoking history presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath that began while resting at home. Vital signs: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 104/min, RR 24/min, SpO2 93% on room air. Physical exam reveals hyperresonance to percussion and severely diminished vesicular breath sounds over the right hemithorax. Trachea is strictly midline. An erect chest radiograph shows a thin, sharp white line representing the visceral pleura with complete absence of peripheral pulmonary vascular markings beyond this margin.
questions.imageAnnotation: Right visceral pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings; lung partially collapsed toward hilum.
options: Rupture of apical subpleural blebs
Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Deep venous thrombosis embolization to pulmonary trunk
Bacterial consolidation with air bronchograms
Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension
questions.explanation: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically occurs in tall, thin young males in their 20s due to the rupture of subpleural apical blebs or bullae. Chest radiography demonstrates a visible visceral pleural line with absent lung markings lateral to it. Because the trachea is midline and the patient is hemodynamically stable without hypotension or JVD, this is a non-tension pneumothorax.
questions.highYieldPearl: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax: tall, thin young males, rupture of apical subpleural blebs. Absence of peripheral vascular markings. If tension develops (trachea shifts opposite side, hypotension), perform immediate needle decompression before imaging.

questions.title: Severe Abdominal Distension in a Nursing Home Resident
questions.vignette: A 78-year-old male with chronic Parkinson's disease and chronic constipation residing in a nursing facility presents with progressive abdominal distension, obstipation, and cramping abdominal pain over the past 48 hours. Abdominal examination reveals a massively distended, tympanitic abdomen with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination shows an empty rectal vault. An abdominal plain radiograph reveals a hugely dilated, inverted U-shaped loop of bowel without haustra originating from the pelvis and extending toward the right upper quadrant, forming a classic 'coffee bean' appearance.
questions.imageAnnotation: Massive coffee-bean shaped loop of distended large bowel apex pointing to right upper quadrant.
options: Emergency exploratory laparotomy with total colectomy
Sigmoidoscopy with rectal tube insertion for decompression
High-dose intravenous polyethylene glycol
Immediate percutaneous transhepatic drainage
Oral barium swallow study
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation and radiograph showing the 'coffee bean sign' or 'bent inner tube sign' (distended sigmoid colon originating in pelvis with apex pointed toward RUQ) are classic for Sigmoid Volvulus. In a stable patient without peritoneal signs, bowel ischemia, or perforation, the first-line treatment is flexible sigmoidoscopy to untwist the volvulus and place a rectal decompression tube, followed by elective resection during the same admission due to high recurrence rates.
questions.highYieldPearl: Sigmoid volvulus: Coffee bean sign pointing to RUQ, common in elderly/neuropsychiatric/constipated patients. Initial management = endoscopic detorsion/decompression. In contrast, Cecal volvulus points to LUQ.

questions.title: Stridor, High Fever, and Drooling in an Unvaccinated Child
questions.vignette: A 4-year-old boy whose parents declined routine childhood vaccinations is brought to the emergency department with high fever (39.8°C / 103.6°F), severe sore throat, difficulty breathing, and refusal to swallow secretions. The child is sitting upright, leaning forward with his neck extended and mouth open, actively drooling. An anxious physician orders a portable lateral soft tissue neck radiograph under careful monitoring, which reveals a rounded, swollen, thumb-like soft tissue mass projecting into the supraglottic airway.
questions.imageAnnotation: Swollen epiglottis producing the classic Thumbprint sign in the hypopharynx.
options: Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup)
Acute bacterial epiglottitis
Retropharyngeal abscess with widened prevertebral space
Foreign body aspiration into right main bronchus
Peritonsillar abscess with uvular deviation
questions.explanation: Acute epiglottitis is characterized by the 3 D's: Dysphagia, Drooling, and Distress with the 'tripod position' and high fever. The lateral neck radiograph demonstrates the pathognomonic 'Thumbprint sign' representing marked edema of the aryepiglottic folds and epiglottis. Most classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) in unvaccinated children. The priority is securing the airway in an operating room environment; never agitate the child or perform forceful tongue blade examination.
questions.highYieldPearl: Thumbprint sign on lateral neck X-ray = Acute Epiglottitis. Tripod position, drooling, high fever. Keep child calm, prepare surgical airway, treat with IV 3rd gen cephalosporin (Ceftriaxone) + Vancomycin.

questions.title: Barking Cough and Inspiratory Stridor in a 14-Month-Old
questions.vignette: A 14-month-old female is brought to urgent care at 2:00 AM due to a sudden harsh, 'seal-like' barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor that woke her from sleep. She has had a low-grade fever and clear rhinorrhea for the past 2 days. An anteroposterior (AP) neck radiograph shows symmetric tapering and subglottic tracheal narrowing.
questions.imageAnnotation: Subglottic tracheal narrowing creating the classic 'Steeple Sign' (wine bottle sign).
options: Steeple sign caused by Parainfluenza virus
Thumbprint sign caused by Haemophilus influenzae
Membranous tracheal casts caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae
Carotid sheath displacement caused by Streptococcus pyogenes
Deep sulcus sign caused by respiratory syncytial virus
questions.explanation: Laryngotracheobronchitis (Croup) most commonly affects children aged 6 months to 3 years and is caused by Parainfluenza virus (paramyxovirus family, enveloped -ssRNA). The subglottic tracheal mucosal edema causes narrowing on AP neck radiograph known as the 'Steeple sign' (or pencil-point / wine-bottle sign). Treatment includes a single dose of oral or IM dexamethasone, with nebulized racemic epinephrine for moderate-to-severe stridor at rest.
questions.highYieldPearl: Steeple sign on AP neck film = Croup (Parainfluenza virus). Seal-like barking cough, inspiratory stridor. Treat with Dexamethasone ± Nebulized Racemic Epinephrine.

questions.title: Intermittent Colicky Pain and 'Currant Jelly' Stools in an Infant
questions.vignette: An 8-month-old infant boy is brought to the clinic for severe episodes of inconsolable crying during which he draws his knees up to his chest. Between these episodic spasms, he appears lethargic and calm. His mother notes that his last diaper change contained dark red, mucus-laden stool ('currant jelly' appearance). Physical exam reveals a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrates concentric alternating hypoechoic and hyperechoic rings in transverse section resembling a donut or target.
questions.imageAnnotation: Target sign / Donut sign representing intussusceptum invaginating into intussuscipiens.
options: Diagnostic and therapeutic air or water-soluble contrast enema
Immediate open appendectomy and bowel resection
Intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone pulse therapy
Upper gastrointestinal series with barium follow-through
Oral erythromycin for gastrointestinal motility enhancement
questions.explanation: This infant presents with the classic triad of Intussusception: intermittent abdominal pain with knee flexion, sausage-shaped RUQ mass, and 'currant jelly' (blood and mucus) stools. The pathognomonic ultrasound finding is the 'Target sign' (or 'Donut sign' / 'Pseudokidney sign') showing telescoping of bowel. The initial step is air (pneumatic) or contrast hydrostatic enema, which is both diagnostic and curative in >85% of uncomplicated cases.
questions.highYieldPearl: Target/donut sign on ultrasound = Intussusception. Most common lead point in infants is hypertrophied Peyer patches (post-viral gastroenteritis or rotavirus). Air enema is both diagnostic & therapeutic.

questions.title: Microcytic Anemia and Narrowing of Bowel Caliber
questions.vignette: A 67-year-old male presents with worsening constipation, fatigue, and an unintentional 15-pound weight loss over 4 months. He notes that his stools have become remarkably thin ('pencil-caliber'). Laboratory evaluation demonstrates hemoglobin of 9.1 g/dL with MCV of 72 fL (microcytic hypochromic anemia) and positive fecal occult blood. A fluoroscopic barium enema examination demonstrates a short, sharply demarcated, circumferential constricting lesion in the sigmoid colon with shelf-like overhanging margins.
questions.imageAnnotation: Annular constriction with shouldered borders known as the classic Apple Core sign.
options: Apple-core lesion representing Colorectal Adenocarcinoma
Lead pipe colon representing Ulcerative Colitis
String sign representing terminal ileal Crohn's disease
Bird's beak sign representing primary Achalasia
Paucity of gas representing Hirschsprung disease
questions.explanation: The 'Apple Core lesion' (napkin-ring lesion) on barium enema or CT colonography is classic for annular, constricting Colorectal Adenocarcinoma, most commonly in the descending/sigmoid colon. Left-sided colon cancers tend to grow circumferentially, presenting with altered bowel habits, 'pencil-thin' stools, and partial colonic obstruction. Right-sided lesions present with occult bleeding and iron deficiency anemia.
questions.highYieldPearl: Apple-core sign = Left-sided Colorectal Adenocarcinoma (annular napkin-ring constriction, pencil-thin stools). Right-sided cancers bleed (iron deficiency anemia); left-sided cancers obstruct.

questions.title: Bilateral Hilar Prominence and Erythema Nodosum in a Young Female
questions.vignette: A 32-year-old African American female presents with painful, tender erythematous nodules over her bilateral pretibial shins, bilateral ankle arthralgias, and a mild dry cough. A routine posteroposterior chest radiograph demonstrates symmetric, well-defined enlargement of the right paratracheal, right hilar, and left hilar lymph nodes with clear lung parenchyma. Serum calcium is 11.2 mg/dL (elevated).
questions.imageAnnotation: Symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal lymphadenopathy (Garland triad / 1-2-3 sign).
options: Systemic Sarcoidosis (Löfgren Syndrome)
Small cell lung carcinoma with oat cell histology
Primary Mycobacterium avium complex infection
Goodpasture disease with anti-GBM antibodies
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Usual Interstitial Pneumonia)
questions.explanation: Löfgren syndrome is an acute, self-limiting form of Sarcoidosis characterized by the classic triad of: 1) Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL), 2) Erythema nodosum, and 3) Migratory polyarthralgias (typically ankles). Radiographically, this is the Garland triad ('1-2-3 sign': right paratracheal, right hilar, and left hilar nodes). Hypercalcemia occurs because activated epithelioid macrophages in non-caseating granulomas express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, synthesizing active 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3 independently of PTH control.
questions.highYieldPearl: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + erythema nodosum = Löfgren syndrome (Sarcoidosis). Non-caseating granulomas, elevated ACE, hypercalcemia from 1-alpha-hydroxylase in macrophages.

radbot_chats.response:
Hello, future doctor! ANSI 1.0 PRO here, your neural study assistant for Synapse. 

Whether you need a high-yield breakdown of a tough pathophysiology concept, a structured differential for a clinical vignette, help finding the right resource in our platform (`#fa`, `#mehlman`, `#sketchy`, `#ddx`, `#qbank`), or strategic advice on your Step prep—I've got you covered.

What are we tackling today?

To understand the heart for the USMLE, you must categorize it into three distinct "languages": **Physiology (Function), Pathology (Disease), and Pharmacology (Treatment).**

### 1. The Physiology (The "Engine")
The heart is a **dual-pump system** in series.
*   **The Wiggers Diagram:** This is the "Holy Grail" of Step 1 cardiology. You must be able to correlate the ECG, heart sounds, and pressure changes in the atria, ventricles, and aorta simultaneously.
*   **Starling’s Law:** Stroke Volume is proportional to End-Diastolic Volume (EDV). If you increase venous return (preload), the heart stretches and pumps harder.
*   **Pressure-Volume (PV) Loops:** You will be asked how drugs or diseases shift these loops. 
    *   *Example:* **Aortic Stenosis** increases the pressure the left ventricle must overcome, causing a massive increase in afterload and a shift to the right/up.

### 2. The Pathology (The "Breakdowns")
*   **Ischemic Heart Disease:** The balance of $O_2$ supply vs. demand.
    *   *Supply:* Coronary blood flow (diastolic filling time).
    *   *Demand:* Heart rate, contractility, afterload, and wall stress.
*   **Valvular Disease:** Memorize the **"Mnemonic of Location":**
    *   **Aortic:** Right 2nd intercostal space.
    *   **Pulmonic:** Left 2nd intercostal space.
    *   **Tricuspid:** Left 4th intercostal space.
    *   **Mitral:** Left 5th intercostal space (mid-clavicular line).

### 3. The Pharmacology (The "Modulators")
*   **Beta-Blockers:** Decrease $O_2$ demand by slowing HR and contractility.
*   **Nitrates:** Decrease preload (venous dilation), reducing wall stress.
*   **ACE Inhibitors:** Decrease afterload and prevent pathological remodeling (the "long-term survival" drugs).

---

### Your Synapse Study Path
To master this, I recommend the following sequence:

1.  **#fa (First Aid):** Go to **page 279**. Start with the **Cardiac Physiology** section. Use the **AnKing** flashcards to drill the Wiggers Diagram until you can draw it from memory.
2.  **#mehlman:** Open the **HY Cardiovascular PDF**. Focus on the "Arrows" section. This is the single most effective way to prepare for the "What happens to X when Y changes?" style of USMLE questions.
3.  **#sketchy:** Open **Sketchy Pharmacology**. Watch the *Heart Failure* and *Anti-arrhythmic* videos. The visual memory of the drug sites of action is far superior to rote memorization.
4.  **#qbank:** Once you have reviewed the physiology, take a **15-question block on "Cardiac Hemodynamics."** 

**Pro-Tip:** If you are struggling with a specific concept (like why a patient with Aortic Stenosis gets syncope during exercise), tell me, and I will break down the hemodynamic logic for you. 

**Are you currently focusing on Physiology or Pathology?**

To master the "heart" for the USMLE, you must move beyond anatomy and view it as a **hemodynamic engine**. On the boards, you are tested on how the heart responds to stress, drugs, and disease.

### 1. The High-Yield "Big Three" for Boards
*   **Physiology (The Pump):** Focus on the **Pressure-Volume Loop**. You must be able to predict how changes in Preload, Afterload, and Contractility shift the loop.
    *   *Example:* Increased Afterload (e.g., Hypertension) increases the "height" of the loop and the End-Systolic Volume.
*   **Pathology (The Failure):** Distinguish between **HFrEF** (Systolic: low ejection fraction, thin walls) and **HFpEF** (Diastolic: normal EF, stiff/thick walls).
*   **Pharmacology (The Modulation):** Master the "Big Four" for heart failure: **ACE inhibitors/ARBs, Beta-blockers, Aldosterone antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors.** These are the only drugs proven to improve mortality in HFrEF.

### 2. Clinical Correlation: The Murmur Cheat Sheet
If you hear a murmur on a question, use this hierarchy:
*   **Systolic:** Aortic Stenosis (crescendo-decrescendo), Mitral Regurgitation (holosystolic, radiates to axilla), VSD (holosystolic, harsh).
*   **Diastolic:** Aortic Regurgitation (early decrescendo), Mitral Stenosis (opening snap + mid-diastolic rumble).

### 3. Anatomical "Must-Knows"
*   **Coronary Dominance:** 85% of people are "right-dominant" (the RCA supplies the PDA).
*   **The "Widow-Maker":** The LAD artery. Occlusion here causes an anterior wall MI (leads V1–V4).
*   **Nodal Supply:** The SA and AV nodes are usually supplied by the RCA. This is why inferior MIs (RCA) often present with bradycardia or heart block.

---

### Your Synapse Study Plan

*   **#fa (First Aid):** Navigate to **pages 279–336**. Start with the "Cardiac Physiology" section. Use the **AnKing** flashcards to memorize the Wiggers Diagram—it is the most high-yield visual for Step 1.
*   **#mehlman:** Open the **HY Cardiovascular PDF**. Use this specifically for the "arrows" questions (e.g., "What happens to the stroke volume when preload decreases?"). His explanations are the gold standard for board logic.
*   **#sketchy:** Watch the **Pharmacology** videos on *Anti-arrhythmics* and *Heart Failure drugs*. The visual mnemonics are essential for remembering the side effects (e.g., Amiodarone's pulmonary fibrosis/thyroid issues).
*   **#qbank:** Set up a 10-question block on "Cardiovascular Physiology." Focus on the *explanations* for the questions you get wrong—that is where the real points are gained.

**Are you currently studying for Step 1 or Step 2?** I can tailor the depth of my explanations based on your exam phase.

In the context of the USMLE, the heart is not just a pump; it is a **dynamic pressure-volume system** that you must understand in terms of hemodynamics, electrical conduction, and pathology.

### 1. The Cardiac Cycle (Pressure-Volume Loop)
Understanding the **Pressure-Volume (PV) Loop** is essential for Step 1.
*   **Isovolumetric Contraction:** All valves closed; pressure rises rapidly.
*   **Systolic Ejection:** Aortic valve opens; volume decreases.
*   **Isovolumetric Relaxation:** All valves closed; pressure drops.
*   **Diastolic Filling:** Mitral valve opens; volume increases.
*   **Board Pearl:** Increased **preload** (venous return) shifts the loop to the right; increased **afterload** (TPR) increases the height of the loop; increased **contractility** increases the stroke volume and decreases end-systolic volume.

### 2. Electrical Conduction
The heart’s rhythm is governed by the conduction system.
*   **SA Node:** The pacemaker (intrinsic rate 60–100 bpm).
*   **AV Node:** The "gatekeeper" (delays signal to allow ventricular filling).
*   **Bundle of His/Purkinje System:** Rapid conduction for synchronized ventricular contraction.
*   **Clinical Correlation:** Know the **ECG intervals**:
    *   **PR Interval:** < 200 ms (AV node conduction time).
    *   **QRS Complex:** < 120 ms (Ventricular depolarization).
    *   **QT Interval:** Corrected for heart rate; prolonged QT is a major risk for *Torsades de Pointes*.

### 3. Key Pathophysiology
*   **Heart Failure (HFrEF vs. HFpEF):** HFrEF (systolic) is a problem of contractility; HFpEF (diastolic) is a problem of compliance.
*   **Valvular Disease:** Know the murmur associations (e.g., Aortic Stenosis = "Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right sternal border").
*   **Ischemic Heart Disease:** The balance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand.

### Anatomical & Functional Overview
The heart is a four-chambered muscular pump situated in the mediastinum, responsible for maintaining systemic and pulmonary circulation. 

*   **Right Side (Pulmonary Circulation):** Right atrium $\rightarrow$ Tricuspid valve $\rightarrow$ Right ventricle $\rightarrow$ Pulmonic valve $\rightarrow$ Pulmonary artery $\rightarrow$ Lungs.
*   **Left Side (Systemic Circulation):** Lungs $\rightarrow$ Pulmonary veins $\rightarrow$ Left atrium $\rightarrow$ Mitral (bicuspid) valve $\rightarrow$ Left ventricle $\rightarrow$ Aortic valve $\rightarrow$ Aorta $\rightarrow$ Body.

---

### High-Yield USMLE Board Concepts

#### 1. Blood Supply (Coronary Circulation)
*   **Right Coronary Artery (RCA):** Supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, and typically the **inferior wall** of the left ventricle (leads II, III, aVF) and the **SA/AV nodes** (determines coronary dominance).
*   **Left Anterior Descending (LAD):** Supplies the **anterior wall** of the left ventricle and the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum (leads V1–V4). *Most commonly occluded artery ("widow-maker").*
*   **Left Circumflex (LCx):** Supplies the **lateral wall** of the left ventricle (leads I, aVL, V5–V6).

#### 2. Heart Sounds
*   **S1:** Closure of mitral and tricuspid valves (onset of systole). Best heard at the apex.
*   **S2:** Closure of aortic and pulmonic valves (onset of diastole). Physiological splitting occurs during inspiration due to increased venous return to the right side, delaying P2 closure.
*   **S3:** Early diastolic filling sound; normal in youth/athletes, pathological in **heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)** or volume overload (mitral regurgitation).
*   **S4:** Late diastolic sound caused by atrial contraction against a stiff, non-compliant ventricle; associated with **left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)**, hypertension, or aortic stenosis.

---

To dive deeper into cardiovascular physiology, pathology, and pharmacology for the boards, check out these sections on Synapse:
*   **#fa (First Aid):** Cardiovascular section (pages 279–336) for core organ system review and integrated **AnKing flashcards** (click the "M" button on any heading).

*   **#qbank:** Test your knowledge with USMLE-style questions on coronary syndromes and murmurs.

### 🫀 High-Yield Cardiovascular Concepts for USMLE

#### 1. Autoregulation of Blood Flow
Autoregulation maintains constant perfusion pressure over mean arterial pressures between **60–160 mmHg**.
* **Brain:** Regulated by local tissue **$p	ext{CO}_2$** (hypercapnia → potent cerebral vasodilation).
* **Heart:** Regulated by **adenosine, nitric oxide (NO), and local hypoxia**.
* **Kidney:** Regulated via myogenic stretch mechanism and **tubuloglomerular feedback** (macula densa detects distal tubular NaCl).
* **Skeletal Muscle:** Regulated by local metabolites during exercise: **adenosine, $	ext{K}^+$, $	ext{H}^+$, lactate, and $	ext{CO}_2$**.

#### 2. Classic Murmurs Distinction
* **Aortic Stenosis:** Crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at right 2nd intercostal space; radiates to **carotids**; pulsus parvus et tardus.
* **Mitral Regurgitation:** Holosystolic blowing murmur at apex; radiates to **axilla**; loudest in left lateral decubitus.
* **Aortic Regurgitation:** Early high-pitched blowing diastolic decrescendo murmur at left sternal border; wide pulse pressure (water-hammer pulse).
* **Mitral Stenosis:** Opening snap followed by mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at apex; often secondary to rheumatic heart disease.

### 🧬 High-Yield USMLE: The Immune System

The human immune system is divided into two primary arms: **Innate Immunity** (rapid, non-specific, no memory) and **Adaptive Immunity** (slow onset, highly specific, long-term memory).

---

#### 1. Innate Immunity (Immediate: 0 to 12 Hours)
* **First Line of Defense:** Epithelial barriers (skin, mucosa), defensins, lysosomes.
* **Cellular Effectors:** 
  * **Neutrophils:** Primary responders to acute bacterial infection and tissue necrosis; recruited by **C5a, LTB4, and IL-8**.
  * **Macrophages:** Phagocytosis, antigen presentation via MHC II, secretion of **IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α** (acute phase response).
  * **Natural Killer (NK) Cells:** Large granular lymphocytes that destroy virus-infected and malignant cells. They recognize cells with **decreased MHC Class I expression** ("missing-self" signal).
* **Complement Cascade:**
  * **Opsonization:** **C3b** (primary opsonin for macrophage phagocytosis).
  * **Anaphylatoxins:** **C3a, C4a, C5a** (trigger mast cell histamine release).
  * **Membrane Attack Complex (MAC):** **C5b-C9** punches osmotic holes in Gram-negative bacteria (deficiency leads to recurrent *Neisseria meningitidis/gonorrhoeae*).

---

#### 2. Adaptive Immunity (Delayed: >4 Days)
##### A. Cell-Mediated Immunity (T-Lymphocytes)
* Mature in the **thymus**; express CD3 and TCRs.
* **CD4+ Helper T Cells:** Bind **MHC Class II** (Expressed on APCs: dendritic cells, macrophages, B-cells).
  * **Th1:** Secretes **IFN-γ** → activates macrophages to kill intracellular pathogens (*M. tuberculosis*).
  * **Th2:** Secretes **IL-4, IL-5, IL-13** → activates eosinophils and drives IgE class switching (allergies, helminths).
  * **Th17:** Secretes **IL-17** → recruits neutrophils for mucosal barrier protection.
  * **Treg:** Secretes **IL-10 & TGF-β** → immune tolerance and suppression.
* **CD8+ Cytotoxic T Cells:** Bind **MHC Class I** (Expressed on all nucleated cells); kill infected targets via **perforin and granzyme B** inducing apoptosis.
* **Mnemonic:** **The Rule of 8**: $	ext{CD4} 	imes 	ext{MHC II} = 8$ and $	ext{CD8} 	imes 	ext{MHC I} = 8$.

##### B. Humoral Immunity (B-Lymphocytes & Antibodies)
* Mature in **bone marrow**; differentiate into plasma cells that produce immunoglobulins.
* **IgG:** Most abundant; **crosses the placenta** (passive immunity to infant); secondary immune response.
* **IgA:** Secretory dimer in mucus, saliva, tears, and breast milk; protects mucosal surfaces.
* **IgM:** Pentamer; primary acute immune response; highest avidity; excellent complement activator.
* **IgE:** Binds to high-affinity receptors on mast cells and basophils; mediates **Type I hypersensitivity** and defense against helminthic parasites.

---

#### 3. High-Yield Immunodeficiencies on Boards
* **DiGeorge Syndrome (22q11.2 deletion):** Failed development of 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches → thymic aplasia → **severe T-cell deficiency** + hypocalcemia (parathyroid aplasia).
* **X-Linked (Bruton) Agammaglobulinemia:** Defect in **BTK (Bruton tyrosine kinase)** → failure of pre-B cells to mature → **absent B cells and low all Ig classes** (recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections after 6 months of age).
* **SCID (Severe Combined Immunodeficiency):** Defective IL-2R gamma chain or adenosine deaminase deficiency → **absent T cells and B cells**; infant presents with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, and thrush.
* **Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD):** NADPH oxidase defect → impaired respiratory burst → recurrent infections by catalase-positive organisms (*S. aureus, Serratia, Aspergillus*).

---

#### 📚 Where to Study This in Synapse:
* **First Aid 2024 (#fa):** Open **Immunology (pages 95–124)**. Click the **M** buttons on each heading to launch targeted AnKing practice cards.
* **Mehlman HY PDFs (#mehlman):** Review **HY Immunology** for high-yield diagnostic questions.
* **Sketchy (#sketchy):** Review **Sketchy Micro (Bacteria/Viruses)** for immune evasion mechanisms.

radbot_chats.message: High yield points from Mehlman HY Neurology
radbot_chats.response:
Here are the high-yield, most heavily tested concepts from **Mehlman HY Neurology** for USMLE Step 1 and Step 2:

### 1. Neurovascular Syndromes (Know Your Strokes)
*   **MCA Stroke:** Contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss of the **face and arm > leg**. 
    *   *Left MCA:* Aphasia (Broca or Wernicke).
    *   *Right MCA:* Neglect (parietal lobe).
*   **ACA Stroke:** Contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss of the **leg > face and arm**. Associated with urinary incontinence and abulia (apathy).
*   **Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome:** PICA occlusion. 
    *   *Key triad:* Ipsilateral Horner syndrome + ipsilateral cerebellar signs (ataxia) + contralateral pain/temperature loss in the body (spinothalamic). *Bonus:* Hoarseness and dysphagia (nucleus ambiguus).
*   **Lateral Pontine Syndrome:** AICA occlusion. 
    *   Similar to Wallenberg, but **ipsilateral facial paralysis** (CN VII) and **sensorineural hearing loss** (CN VIII - labyrinthine artery branch).

### 2. Spinal Cord Lesions
*   **Brown-Séquard Syndrome (Hemisection):**
    *   *Ipsilateral:* Loss of **motor** (corticospinal) and **fine touch/proprioception** (dorsal columns) *below* the lesion.
    *   *Contralateral:* Loss of **pain and temperature** (spinothalamic) starting 1-2 levels below the lesion.
*   **Syringomyelia:** Expansion of the central canal (usually C8-T1).
    *   Bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a **"cape-like" distribution** (crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure) with preserved vibration/proprioception.
*   **Vitamin B12 Deficiency (Subacute Combined Degeneration):**
    *   Demyelination of **dorsal columns** (loss of proprioception/vibration, positive Romberg), **lateral corticospinal tracts** (spastic paresis), and **spinocerebellar tracts**.

### 3. Neuromuscular Junction Disorders
*   **Myasthenia Gravis (Post-synaptic ACh receptors):**
    *   Worsens with use (fatigable weakness). Ptosis and diplopia that worsen throughout the day.
    *   *Association:* Thymoma or thymic hyperplasia. Diagnosed with anti-AChR antibodies and edrophonium (Tensilon) test.
*   **Lambert-Eaton Syndrome (Pre-synaptic voltage-gated calcium channels):**
    *   Improves with use! Proximal muscle weakness, dry mouth, autonomic dysfunction (impotence).
    *   *Association:* **Small cell lung cancer** (paraneoplastic).

### 4. Dementia & Neurodegeneration
*   **Alzheimer Disease:** Temporal lobe/hippocampal atrophy. Intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated **tau**) and extracellular amyloid-beta plaques. Associated with **ApoE4**.
*   **Frontotemporal Dementia (Pick Disease):** Early personality and behavioral changes, disinhibition, language impairment. Associated with tau-containing Pick bodies or TDP-43.
*   **Lewy Body Dementia:** Visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, **parkinsonism** early in the disease course (within 1 year of cognitive symptoms). Alpha-synuclein inclusions.
*   **Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus:** *Wet, wacky, and wobbly* (urinary incontinence, cognitive impairment, gait ataxia). Communicating hydrocephalus with "wet tap" improvement.

### 5. Movement Disorders
*   **Huntington Disease:** CAG repeat expansion on chromosome 4 (anticipation). Caudate nucleus atrophy with loss of GABAergic neurons (indirect pathway). Presents with chorea, psychiatric symptoms, and dementia.
*   **Parkinson Disease:** Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the **substantia nigra pars compacta**. Lewy bodies (alpha-synuclein). Resting tremor, rigidity, akinesia, postural instability.

---

Here are the high-yield, board-tested neurological concepts heavily emphasized in **Dr. Mehlman’s HY Neurology** PDF. 

### 1. Neurovascular Syndromes (Know Your Strokes)
*   **MCA Stroke:** Contralateral motor and sensory loss of the **face and arm > leg**, aphasia (if dominant hemisphere, usually left—Broca or Wernicke), and contralateral neglect (if non-dominant hemisphere, usually right).
*   **ACA Stroke:** Contralateral motor and sensory loss of the **leg > face and arm**, along with abulia (apathy/lack of willpower) and urinary incontinence.
*   **Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome:** PICA (or vertebral artery) stroke. 
    *   *Symptom triad:* **Ipsilateral Horners syndrome**, **contralateral pain/temperature loss** in the body, and **ipsilateral pain/temperature loss** in the face. Plus: dysphagia, hoarseness, vertigo, and nystagmus. (Remember: "Don't *pick* (PICA) a *wall* (Wallenberg) to *ice* (ipsilateral face) *contra* (contralateral body) the *horn* (Horner).")
*   **Medial Medullary Syndrome:** Anterior spinal artery stroke. Contralateral paralysis of arm/leg, contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception, and **ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) lesion** (tongue deviates toward the lesion).

### 2. Spinal Cord Syndromes
*   **Brown-Séquard Syndrome (Hemisection):** 
    *   *Ipsilateral:* Loss of motor, vibration, and proprioception **below the lesion**; plus an upper motor neuron (UMN) sign (Babinski) at the level of the lesion.
    *   *Contralateral:* Loss of pain and temperature starting **2-3 levels below** the lesion (spinothalamic tract crosses a few levels up).
*   **Syringomyelia:** Expansion of the central canal (usually C8-T1). Leads to a **bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a "cape-like" distribution** (crossing fibers of the spinothalamic tract are damaged first) with preserved vibration/touch. Often associated with Chiari I malformation.
*   **Subacute Combined Degeneration (Vitamin B12 Deficiency):** Demyelination of dorsal columns (vibration/proprioception), lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic paresis), and spinocerebellar tracts. Look for broad-based ataxia, loss of position sense, and + Romberg, **without** cranial nerve or visual symptoms (unlike Tabes Dorsalis).

### 3. Neurodegenerative Pearls
*   **Parkinson Disease:** Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the **pars compacta of the substantia nigra**. 
    *   *Tetrad:* TRAP (Tremor-rest, Rigidity, Akinesia/bradykinesia, Postural instability). 
    *   *Histology:* **Lewy bodies** (alpha-synuclein).
*   **Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS):** Combined **Upper Motor Neuron (UMN)** (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski) and **Lower Motor Neuron (LMN)** (fasciculations, atrophy, flaccidity) signs **without sensory loss**. 
    *   *Key rule:* Never forget that **bowel/bladder and extraocular movements are spared** in ALS.
*   **Huntington Disease:** Autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion on **Chromosome 4**. Anticipation occurs. Look for chorea, psychiatric changes, and caudate nucleus atrophy (leads to ex vacuo ventriculomegaly).

### 4. Neurocutaneous Disorders (The "Phakomatoses")
*   **Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1):** Chromosome **17**. Café-au-lait spots, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), neurofibromas, optic gliomas, and pheochromocytomas. (*Tip: 17 letters in "Neurofibromatosis"*).
*   **Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2):** Chromosome **22**. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas), cataracts, ependymomas, and meningiomas. (*Tip: 22 letters in "Type two neurofibroma"*).
*   **Tuberous Sclerosis:** Chromosome **9 and 16**. **A**ngiofibromas (facial), **L**eaf spots (ash-leaf hypopigmented macules), **R**habdomyomas (cardiac), **T**uberous sclerosis, **S**hagreen patches, subependymal giant cell astrocytomas. 
*   **Sturge-Weber Syndrome:** Congenital non-inherited vascular disorder affecting **CN V1/V2 distribution** (port-wine stain). Associated with **ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma**, seizures, intellectual disability, and early-onset glaucoma.

Here is a high-yield summary of the **Mehlman HY Neurology** essentials for the USMLE:

*   **Spinal Cord Syndromes:** 
    *   *Brown-Séquard (Hemisection):* Ipsilateral motor + vibration/proprioception loss; contralateral pain/temperature loss starting 1–2 segments below.
    *   *Syringomyelia:* Bilateral loss of pain/temperature in a "cape-like" distribution (spares vibration).
*   **Brainstem Strokes:**
    *   *Weber (Midbrain/PCA):* Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis.
    *   *Wallenberg (Lateral Medullary/PICA):* Ipsilateral face/Horner/ataxia + contralateral body pain/temp + dysphagia/hoarseness.
*   **Movement & Degenerative Disorders:**
    *   *Parkinson:* Substantia nigra pars compacta dopamine loss (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia).
    *   *Huntington:* Caudate nucleus atrophy, CAG repeats, chorea.
    *   *ALS:* Mixed UMN + LMN signs with **completely spared sensation**.
*   **Neuromuscular Junction:**
    *   *Myasthenia Gravis:* Postsynaptic AChR antibodies; worsens with use; associated with thymoma.
    *   *Lambert-Eaton:* Presynaptic Ca²⁺ channel antibodies; improves with use; associated with small cell lung cancer.
*   **Peripheral & Neurocutaneous:**
    *   *Guillain-Barré:* Ascending paralysis, albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF.
    *   *NF1 (Chr 17):* Café-au-lait spots, Lisch nodules, neurofibromas.

radbot_chats.message: High yield points from Mehlman HY Neurology
radbot_chats.response:
Here are the highest-yield, board-tested concepts from the **Mehlman HY Neurology** PDF, organized by clinical syndromes, neuro-anatomy, and pathologies to maximize your USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 scores.

---

### 1. Spinal Cord & Brainstem Lesions
*   **Brown-Séquard Syndrome (Hemisection of the Cord):**
    *   *Ipsilateral:* Loss of **motor** (corticospinal tract) + loss of **vibration/proprioception** (dorsal columns) *at and below* the lesion. Plus an ipsilateral Horner syndrome if lesion is above T1.
    *   *Contralateral:* Loss of **pain and temperature** (spinothalamic tract) starting **1–2 segments below** the lesion.
*   **Syringomyelia:**
    *   *Path:* Expansion of the central canal of the spinal cord (usually C8–T1).
    *   *Presentation:* Bilateral loss of **pain and temperature** in a "cape-like" distribution (crossing fibers of the spinothalamic tract in the anterior white commissure are damaged first). Spares vibration/proprioception initially.
*   **Weber Syndrome (Midbrain Stroke):**
    *   *Cause:* PCA/paramedian branch stroke affecting the midbrain.
    *   *Presentation:* **Ipsilateral CN III palsy** (down and out eye, ptosis, blown pupil) + **contralateral hemiparesis** (corticospinal tract).
*   **Wallenberg Syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome):**
    *   *Cause:* PICA (Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery) stroke.
    *   *Presentation:* **Ipsilateral** facial pain/temperature loss, Horner syndrome, ataxia, and nystagmus. **Contralateral** body pain/temperature loss. Plus **dysphagia and hoarseness** (nucleus ambiguus). *Mnemonic:* "Don't **PICA** **HOARSE** (horse) that has **WALL**-eyed **LAT**ERAL vision."

### 2. Neurodegenerative & Movement Disorders
*   **Parkinson Disease:**
    *   *Path:* Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the **pars compacta of the substantia nigra**.
    *   *Presentation:* Resting tremor, rigidity, akinesia/bradykinesia, postural instability, and a shuffling gait.
*   **Huntington Disease:**
    *   *Path:* Autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion on chromosome 4 (anticipation). Loss of GABAergic neurons in the **striatum** (caudate nucleus and putamen).
    *   *Presentation:* Chorea, psychiatric symptoms, dementia. Caudate atrophy with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly.
*   **Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS):**
    *   *Path:* Degeneration of both **Upper Motor Neurons (UMN)** in the cortex and **Lower Motor Neurons (LMN)** in the anterior horn of the spinal cord.
    *   *Presentation:* Mixed UMN (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski) and LMN (fasciculations, atrophy, flaccid paralysis) signs. **Sensation is completely spared.** *Crucial:* No sensory loss and no extraocular movement changes.

### 3. Peripheral Neuropathies & Neuromuscular Junction
*   **Guillain-Barré Syndrome (AIDP):**
    *   *Path:* Immune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves. Often follows *Campylobacter jejuni* or viral infections (molecular mimicry).
    *   *Presentation:* Ascending symmetric muscle weakness, hyporeflexia/areflexia, and autonomic instability. 
    *   *CSF finding:* **Albuminocytologic dissociation** (high protein, normal cell count).
*   **Myasthenia Gravis vs. Lambert-Eaton Syndrome:**
    *   *Myasthenia Gravis:* Antibodies against **postsynaptic ACh receptors**. Worse with repetitive use (fatigue). Associated with thymoma.
    *   *Lambert-Eaton:* Antibodies against **presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels**. *Improves* with repetitive use. Associated with small cell lung cancer (SCLC).

### 4. Neurocutaneous Disorders (Phakomatoses)
*   **Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1):**
    *   *Chromosome:* 17 (NF1 gene, neurofibromin).
    *   *Features:* Café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, **Lisch nodules** (iris hamartomas), optic gliomas, and axillary/inguinal freckling.
*   **Tuberous Sclerosis:**
    *   *Features:* **Hamartomas** in CNS and skin. Ash-leaf spots (hypopigmented), facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum), shagreen patches, subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, and cardiac rhabdomyomas.

---

### 🚀 Platform Navigation & Study Strategy
1.  **Read the full text:** Go to **#mehlman** and open the *HY Neurology* PDF (84 pages) for high-yield diagnostic algorithms and classic clinical vignettes.
2.  **Flashcards:** Head to **#fa**, open the **Neurology** chapter (pages 491–536), and click the **"M"** button on specific headings to launch targeted AnKing/Mehlman flashcards for spaced repetition.
3.  **Visuals:** Check out **#sketchy** (Pathology and Pharmacology sections) for visual memory hooks on neurodegenerative drugs and brain tumors.

radbot_chats.message: Give me high yield points from Mehlman HY Renal PDF
radbot_chats.response:
Here are the highest-yield, board-tested concepts from the **Mehlman HY Renal** PDF, organized by topic to maximize your USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 performance. 

---

### 1. Glomerular Diseases (The Big Four)
*   **Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN):** 
    *   *Timeline:* 1–3 weeks *after* group A beta-hemolytic *Streptococcus* pharyngitis or impetigo.
    *   *Biopsy:* **Subepithelial humps** on electron microscopy; IgG and C3 granular deposition ("starry sky" or "lumpy-bumpy").
    *   *Key Lab:* Decreased serum C3 levels (classic alternative complement pathway activation).
*   **Goodpasture Syndrome:** 
    *   *Path:* Anti-type IV collagen antibodies (specifically against the $\alpha$3 chain of glomerular and alveolar basement membranes).
    *   *Presentation:* Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) + hemoptysis.
    *   *Biopsy:* **Linear IgG** deposition along the GBM.
*   **Wegener Granulomatosis (GPA):** 
    *   *Presentation:* Upper respiratory tract symptoms (sinusitis, saddle nose), lower respiratory tract (cavitary lung lesions), and renal disease (RPGN).
    *   *Key Lab:* **c-ANCA** positive (anti-PR3).
*   **Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA) & Churg-Strauss (EGPA):**
    *   *Key Lab:* **p-ANCA** positive (anti-MPO). *Note:* Churg-Strauss also features asthma, eosinophilia, and neuropathy.

### 2. Tubular & Interstitial Pathology
*   **Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN):**
    *   *Causes:* Ischemia (shock, hypotension) or toxins (aminoglycosides, contrast, myoglobin).
    *   *Urinary findings:* **Muddy brown casts** and "renal tubular epithelial cells."
    *   *Labs:* Fractional excretion of sodium ($FENa$) **> 2%**; urine osmolarity $\le$ 350 mOsm/kg (tubules can't reabsorb sodium or concentrate urine).
*   **Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN):**
    *   *Causes:* Drugs (P-C-N: **P**enicillins/Cephalosporins, **C**iprofloxacin, **N**SAIDs), PPIs, and sulfonamides.
    *   *Presentation:* Fever, rash, arthralgias, and eosinophiluria 1–3 weeks after starting a drug.
    *   *Urinary findings:* **White blood cell casts** (eosinophils).

### 3. Renal Electrolyte & Acid-Base Disorders
*   **Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA) Summary:**
    *   *Type 1 (Distal RTA):* Failure to secrete $H^+$ in the collecting duct. Urine pH > 5.5. Associated with stones and **hypokalemia**. 
    *   *Type 2 (Proximal RTA):* Failure to reabsorb $HCO_3^-$ in the PCT. Associated with Fanconi syndrome and **hypokalemia**.
    *   *Type 4 (Hyperkalemic RTA):* Hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance. Associated with **hyperkalemia** (which inhibits renal ammoniagenesis).
*   **Bartter vs. Gitelman Syndromes:**
    *   *Bartter:* Defect in thick ascending limb ($Na^+/K^+/2Cl^-$ cotransporter). Mimics loop diuretic abuse. Presents with **hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and *hypocalcemia***.
    *   *Gitelman:* Defect in DCT ($NaCl$ cotransporter). Mimics thiazide diuretic abuse. Presents with **hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and *hypomagnesemia/hypocalciuria***.

### 4. Nephrolithiasis (Kidney Stones)
*   **Calcium Oxalate/Phosphate:** Most common. Radiolucent/Radiopaque? Radiopaque (seen on X-ray). Associated with Crohn disease (increased oxalate absorption).
*   **Struvite (Magnesium Ammonium Phosphate):** Associated with urease-positive organisms (*Proteus*, *Klebsiella*, *Serratia*). Forms **staghorn calculi**. Treat by removing the stone and treating the infection.
*   **Uric Acid:** Radiucolent (not seen on standard X-ray; use CT or US). Associated with gout and leukemia. Treatment includes alkalinizing the urine (potassium citrate).
*   **Cystine:** Genetic defect in dibasic amino acid transport (COLA: Cystine, Ornithine, Lysine, Arginine). Hexagonal crystals in urine. Sodium cyanide-nitroprusside test positive.

---

3.  **Practice Questions:** Test your application of these concepts in the **#qbank** section.

radbot_chats.message: What is autoregulation of blood flow? Brief answer.
radbot_chats.response:
**Autoregulation** is the intrinsic ability of an organ to maintain a constant blood flow despite changes in perfusion pressure (typically mean arterial pressure between 60–160 mmHg).

### Key Mechanisms:
1. **Myogenic Mechanism:** Vascular smooth muscle contracts in response to stretch (increased pressure) and relaxes when pressure drops.
2. **Metabolic Mechanism:** Local vasoactive metabolites (e.g., $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{H}^+$, adenosine, lactate, $\text{K}^+$) accumulate during high metabolic activity or low flow, causing vasodilation.

### Organ-Specific Highlights (High-Yield):
* **Brain:** Highly dependent on local $\text{CO}_2$ (potent vasodilator) and $\text{pH}$.
* **Heart:** Regulated primarily by **adenosine** (mediates coronary reactive hyperemia).
* **Kidney:** Utilizes the myogenic mechanism and **tubuloglomerular feedback** (macula densa sensing $\text{NaCl}$).
* **Lungs (Exception):** Unlike systemic circulation, pulmonary arterioles **hypoxic vasoconstriction**—shunting blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli to well-ventilated areas.

> 🔍 **Platform Tip:** For a deep dive into cardiovascular hemodynamics and organ-specific blood flow, head to **#fa** (Cardiovascular section, pages 279–336) or check out **#mehlman** (HY Cardiovascular PDF). Practice application questions in **#qbank**.

### 🩻 Systematic Approach: Chest Radiograph (ABCDE)

* **A - Airway:** Assess tracheal alignment (is it shifted away as in tension pneumothorax or towards as in atelectasis?). Check carina (<100°).
* **B - Bones & Soft Tissue:** Inspect clavicles, ribs (posterior rib fractures in abuse, flail chest), lytic/blastic lesions, and subcutaneous emphysema.
* **C - Cardiac Silhouette & Mediastinum:** Cardiothoracic ratio on PA view should be < 50%. Inspect aortic knob and mediastinal widening (>8cm = suspect aortic dissection/mediastinitis).
* **D - Diaphragms & Pleura:** Sharp costophrenic angles (blunting = >200-300 mL pleural effusion). Check for crescentic lucency under right hemidiaphragm (pneumoperitoneum).
* **E - Equal Lung Fields & Everything Else:** Compare bilateral symmetry, look for consolidations, air bronchograms, pneumothorax (absent lung markings laterally), and confirm endotracheal/nasogastric tube placements.

messages.text:
Hello, future doctor! ANSI 1.0 PRO here, your neural study assistant for Synapse. 

Whether you need a high-yield breakdown of a tough pathophysiology concept, a structured differential for a clinical vignette, help finding the right resource in our platform (`#fa`, `#mehlman`, `#sketchy`, `#ddx`, `#qbank`), or strategic advice on your Step prep—I've got you covered.

What are we tackling today?

To understand the heart for the USMLE, you must categorize it into three distinct "languages": **Physiology (Function), Pathology (Disease), and Pharmacology (Treatment).**

### 1. The Physiology (The "Engine")
The heart is a **dual-pump system** in series.
*   **The Wiggers Diagram:** This is the "Holy Grail" of Step 1 cardiology. You must be able to correlate the ECG, heart sounds, and pressure changes in the atria, ventricles, and aorta simultaneously.
*   **Starling’s Law:** Stroke Volume is proportional to End-Diastolic Volume (EDV). If you increase venous return (preload), the heart stretches and pumps harder.
*   **Pressure-Volume (PV) Loops:** You will be asked how drugs or diseases shift these loops. 
    *   *Example:* **Aortic Stenosis** increases the pressure the left ventricle must overcome, causing a massive increase in afterload and a shift to the right/up.

### 2. The Pathology (The "Breakdowns")
*   **Ischemic Heart Disease:** The balance of $O_2$ supply vs. demand.
    *   *Supply:* Coronary blood flow (diastolic filling time).
    *   *Demand:* Heart rate, contractility, afterload, and wall stress.
*   **Valvular Disease:** Memorize the **"Mnemonic of Location":**
    *   **Aortic:** Right 2nd intercostal space.
    *   **Pulmonic:** Left 2nd intercostal space.
    *   **Tricuspid:** Left 4th intercostal space.
    *   **Mitral:** Left 5th intercostal space (mid-clavicular line).

### 3. The Pharmacology (The "Modulators")
*   **Beta-Blockers:** Decrease $O_2$ demand by slowing HR and contractility.
*   **Nitrates:** Decrease preload (venous dilation), reducing wall stress.
*   **ACE Inhibitors:** Decrease afterload and prevent pathological remodeling (the "long-term survival" drugs).

---

### Your Synapse Study Path
To master this, I recommend the following sequence:

1.  **#fa (First Aid):** Go to **page 279**. Start with the **Cardiac Physiology** section. Use the **AnKing** flashcards to drill the Wiggers Diagram until you can draw it from memory.
2.  **#mehlman:** Open the **HY Cardiovascular PDF**. Focus on the "Arrows" section. This is the single most effective way to prepare for the "What happens to X when Y changes?" style of USMLE questions.
3.  **#sketchy:** Open **Sketchy Pharmacology**. Watch the *Heart Failure* and *Anti-arrhythmic* videos. The visual memory of the drug sites of action is far superior to rote memorization.
4.  **#qbank:** Once you have reviewed the physiology, take a **15-question block on "Cardiac Hemodynamics."** 

**Pro-Tip:** If you are struggling with a specific concept (like why a patient with Aortic Stenosis gets syncope during exercise), tell me, and I will break down the hemodynamic logic for you. 

**Are you currently focusing on Physiology or Pathology?**

To master the "heart" for the USMLE, you must move beyond anatomy and view it as a **hemodynamic engine**. On the boards, you are tested on how the heart responds to stress, drugs, and disease.

### 1. The High-Yield "Big Three" for Boards
*   **Physiology (The Pump):** Focus on the **Pressure-Volume Loop**. You must be able to predict how changes in Preload, Afterload, and Contractility shift the loop.
    *   *Example:* Increased Afterload (e.g., Hypertension) increases the "height" of the loop and the End-Systolic Volume.
*   **Pathology (The Failure):** Distinguish between **HFrEF** (Systolic: low ejection fraction, thin walls) and **HFpEF** (Diastolic: normal EF, stiff/thick walls).
*   **Pharmacology (The Modulation):** Master the "Big Four" for heart failure: **ACE inhibitors/ARBs, Beta-blockers, Aldosterone antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors.** These are the only drugs proven to improve mortality in HFrEF.

### 2. Clinical Correlation: The Murmur Cheat Sheet
If you hear a murmur on a question, use this hierarchy:
*   **Systolic:** Aortic Stenosis (crescendo-decrescendo), Mitral Regurgitation (holosystolic, radiates to axilla), VSD (holosystolic, harsh).
*   **Diastolic:** Aortic Regurgitation (early decrescendo), Mitral Stenosis (opening snap + mid-diastolic rumble).

### 3. Anatomical "Must-Knows"
*   **Coronary Dominance:** 85% of people are "right-dominant" (the RCA supplies the PDA).
*   **The "Widow-Maker":** The LAD artery. Occlusion here causes an anterior wall MI (leads V1–V4).
*   **Nodal Supply:** The SA and AV nodes are usually supplied by the RCA. This is why inferior MIs (RCA) often present with bradycardia or heart block.

---

### Your Synapse Study Plan

### 🫀 High-Yield Cardiovascular Concepts for USMLE

#### 1. Autoregulation of Blood Flow
Autoregulation maintains constant perfusion pressure over mean arterial pressures between **60–160 mmHg**.
* **Brain:** Regulated by local tissue **$p	ext{CO}_2$** (hypercapnia → potent cerebral vasodilation).
* **Heart:** Regulated by **adenosine, nitric oxide (NO), and local hypoxia**.
* **Kidney:** Regulated via myogenic stretch mechanism and **tubuloglomerular feedback** (macula densa detects distal tubular NaCl).
* **Skeletal Muscle:** Regulated by local metabolites during exercise: **adenosine, $	ext{K}^+$, $	ext{H}^+$, lactate, and $	ext{CO}_2$**.

#### 2. Classic Murmurs Distinction
* **Aortic Stenosis:** Crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at right 2nd intercostal space; radiates to **carotids**; pulsus parvus et tardus.
* **Mitral Regurgitation:** Holosystolic blowing murmur at apex; radiates to **axilla**; loudest in left lateral decubitus.
* **Aortic Regurgitation:** Early high-pitched blowing diastolic decrescendo murmur at left sternal border; wide pulse pressure (water-hammer pulse).
* **Mitral Stenosis:** Opening snap followed by mid-diastolic rumbling murmur at apex; often secondary to rheumatic heart disease.

Common causes of shoulder pain

Rotator cuff impingement or tendinopathy

  • Pain with abduction, external rotation
  • Subacromial tenderness
  • Normal range of motion with positive impingement tests (eg, Neer, Hawkins)

Rotator cuff tear

  • Similar to rotator cuff tendinopathy
  • Weakness with abduction & external rotation
  • Age >40

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)

  • Decreased passive & active range of motion
  • Initial painful phase followed by stiffness > pain

Biceps tendinopathy/rupture

  • Anterior shoulder pain
  • Pain with lifting, carrying, or overhead reaching
  • Weakness (less common)

Glenohumeral osteoarthritis

  • Uncommon & usually caused by trauma
  • Gradual onset of anterior or deep shoulder pain
  • Decreased active & passive abduction & external rotation

tables: Features of anterior cruciate ligament injury

Features of anterior cruciate ligament injury

Injury
mechanisms

  • Rapid deceleration or direction changes
  • Pivoting on lower extremity with foot planted

Symptoms

  • Pain: sudden onset, severe
  • Popping sensation at the time of injury
  • Significant swelling (effusion/hemarthrosis)
  • Joint instability

Examination
findings

  • Anterior laxity of the tibia relative to the femur (anterior
    drawer test, Lachman test)

Imaging

  • Plain x-rays usually normal, but fracture of tibial spine
    or anterolateral tibial plateau suggests ACL tear
  • MRI provides definitive diagnosis

Treatment

  • RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) measures
  • ± Surgery depending on age & activity level

ACL = anterior cruciate ligament.

tables: Meniscal tears

Meniscal tears

Etiology

  • Younger patients: rotational force on planted foot
  • Older patients: degeneration of meniscal cartilage

Symptoms

  • Acute popping sensation
  • Catching, locking, reduced range of motion
  • Slow-onset joint effusion

Examination

  • Joint line tenderness
  • Pain or catching in provocative tests (Thessaly, McMurray)

Diagnosis

  • MRI
  • Arthroscopy

Management

  • Surgery (knee arthroscopy): persistent symptoms &/or impaired activity
  • Conservative management:
    • Mild symptoms without impaired activity
    • Older patients with degenerative tears

tables: Meralgia paresthetica

Meralgia paresthetica

Etiology

Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment or injury due to:

  • Compression (eg, tight clothing, obesity, pregnancy)
  • Iatrogenic injury (eg, total hip arthroplasty)

Clinical
features

  • Paresthesia & ↓ sensation at lateral thigh
  • Normal motor & reflex examination

Management

  • Avoidance of tight garments, weight loss
  • Nonopioid analgesics (eg, NSAIDs)
  • Anticonvulsants (eg, gabapentin), nerve block, or surgical
    release for refractory cases

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Tarsal tunnel syndrome

Etiology

  • Trauma (fracture, dislocation)
  • Overuse injury (poor biomechanics)
  • Inflammatory disorder (eg, rheumatoid arthritis)

Pathology

  • Compression of posterior tibial nerve under flexor retinaculum in medial ankle

Presentation

  • Burning pain, numbness, or paresthesia
  • Medial ankle, heel, sole, and toes

Diagnosis

  • Clinical presentation
  • Nerve conduction studies

Management

  • Activity modification
  • Orthotics
  • NSAIDs/corticosteroid injection
  • Surgical release (refractory cases)

tables: Lateral epicondylitis

Lateral epicondylitis

Pathophysiology

  • Repetitive, forceful overuse of wrist & digit extensors
  • Angiofibroblastic tendinosis of extensor tendons at lateral epicondyle

Clinical
presentation

  • Insidious pain; onset weeks to months
  • Pain 1 cm distal to lateral epicondyle
  • Pain elicited by resisted wrist extension & passive wrist flexion

Management

  • Diagnosis based on clinical presentation
  • Musculoskeletal ultrasonography for doubtful cases
  • Initial treatment: activity modification, counterforce bracing/strap
  • Refractory symptoms: short-term NSAIDs, corticosteroid injection, surgery

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

directTables: Clenched-fist bite injury (fight bite)

Clenched-fist bite injury (fight bite)

Mechanism

  • Puncture through thin soft tissue overlying MCP joint
  • Enclosed bacterial proliferation under extensor tendon & within joint capsule

Pathogens

  • Oral flora (eg, Eikenella corrodens, beta-lactamase–producing anaerobes)
  • Skin flora (eg, streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus)

Clinical features

  • Small puncture wound appears minor initially; delay in care common
  • Septic arthritis: joint pain, swelling, erythema/warmth, restricted/painful ROM

Management

  • Urgent surgical irrigation & debridement
  • Antibiotics (eg, ampicillin-sulbactam [IV], amoxicillin-clavulanate [PO])

IV = intravenous; MCP = metacarpophalangeal; PO = orally; ROM = range of motion.

tables: Popliteal (Baker) cyst

Popliteal (Baker) cyst

Etiology

  • Extrusion of fluid from knee joint space into semimembranosus/gastrocnemius bursa

Risk factors

  • Trauma (eg, meniscal tear)
  • Underlying joint disease (eg, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis)

Clinical presentation

  • Asymptomatic bulge behind knee that diminishes with flexion
  • Posterior knee pain, swelling, stiffness

Complications

  • Venous compression (leg/ankle swelling)
  • Dissection into calf (erythema, edema, positive Homans sign)
  • Cyst rupture (acute calf pain, warmth, erythema, ecchymosis)

  • Tenderness at tendon insertion at inferior patellar margin
  • Common in jumping sports (eg, basketball, volleyball)

Prepatellar
bursitis

  • Anterior knee bogginess & tenderness
  • Propensity to secondary infection with Staphylococcus aureus
  • Common in patients who work on their knees ("housemaid's knee")
Popliteal (Baker) cyst

Popliteal (Baker) cyst

Etiology

  • Extrusion of fluid from knee joint space into semimembranosus/gastrocnemius bursa

Risk factors

  • Trauma (eg, meniscal tear)
  • Underlying joint disease (eg, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis)

Clinical presentation

  • Asymptomatic bulge behind knee that diminishes with flexion
  • Posterior knee pain, swelling, stiffness

Complications

  • Venous compression (leg/ankle swelling)
  • Dissection into calf (erythema, edema, positive Homans sign)
  • Cyst rupture (acute calf pain, warmth, erythema, ecchymosis)

topics.subject: path

subs.title: De Quervain tenosynovitis
subs.subject: path
tables: De Quervain tendinopathy

De Quervain tendinopathy

Pathogenesis

  • Myxoid degeneration of tendons/tendon sheaths
  • Involves abductor pollicis longus & extensor pollicis brevis

Symptoms

  • Lateral hand/wrist pain
  • Provoked by lifting objects, thumb or wrist movement

Diagnosis

  • Based on clinical features (eg, positive provocative testing)
  • Tenderness at radial styloid
  • Pain with thumb flexion + ulnar wrist deviation

Management

  • Thumb spica splint
  • Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
  • Persistent/severe cases: corticosteroid injection

subs.title: Dupuytren contracture
subs.subject: path
tables: Dupuytren contracture

Dupuytren contracture

Risk factors

  • Male sex, age >50, family history
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Tobacco & alcohol use

Clinical presentation

  • Thickening of palmar fascia at the 3rd, 4th & 5th digits
  • Discrete nodules along flexor tendons near distal palmar crease
  • Gradual decrease in extension of digits

Treatment

  • Modification of hand tools (eg, cushion tape, padded gloves)
  • Needle aponeurotomy, collagenase injection
  • Intralesional glucocorticoid injection
  • Surgery for contractures or advanced disease

subs.title: Ganglion cyst
subs.subject: path
tables: Ganglion cyst

Ganglion cyst

Pathophysiology

  • Mucoid degeneration of periarticular tissue
  • Herniation of connective tissue from joint capsule, tendon sheath, bursae
  • Filled with clear/gelatinous fluid

Presentation

  • Wrist (most common), dorsal foot, knee
  • Rubbery, round, well-circumscribed cystic nodule
  • Transillumination positive

Treatment

  • Observation for asymptomatic cysts
  • Needle aspiration (recurrence common)
  • Surgical excision

Prognosis

  • Most resolve spontaneously

subs.title: Limb compartment syndrome
subs.subject: path
tables: Clinical features of compartment syndrome

Clinical features of compartment syndrome

Common

  • Pain out of proportion to injury   
  • Pain ↑ on passive stretch
  • Rapidly increasing & tense swelling
  • Paresthesia (early)

Uncommon

  • ↓ Sensation
  • Motor weakness (within hours)
  • Paralysis (late)
  • ↓ Distal pulses
Acute compartment syndrome of the extremity

Acute compartment syndrome of the extremity

Pathophysiology

  • ↑ Pressure within enclosed fascial space
  • ↓ Blood flow & tissue perfusion

Common causes

  • Crush injury, long bone fracture, rhabdomyolysis
  • Reperfusion after prolonged ischemia
  • Massive fluid resuscitation

Clinical features

  • Early:
    • Progressive, severe pain
    • Rapidly ↑ & tense swelling
    • ↑ Pain with passive stretching
    • Paresthesia
  • Late:
    • ↓ Sensation
    • Weakness (within hours), paralysis (late)
    • Loss of pulses (uncommon)

Management

  • Compartment pressure measurement* can confirm diagnosis
  • Emergency fasciotomy

*Delta pressure (diastolic pressure − compartment pressure) ≤30 mm Hg is consistent with compartment syndrome.
Acute compartment syndrome of the extremity

Acute compartment syndrome of the extremity

subs.title: Plantar fasciitis
subs.subject: path
tables: Plantar fasciitis

Plantar fasciitis

Risk factors

  • Pes planus
  • Obesity
  • Working or exercising on hard surfaces

Symptoms

  • Pain at plantar aspect of heel & hindfoot
  • Worse with weight bearing (especially after prolonged rest)

Diagnosis

  • Tenderness at insertion of plantar fascia
  • Pain with dorsiflexion of toes
  • Presence of heel spurs on x-ray has low sensitivity & specificity

Treatment

  • Activity modification
  • Stretching exercises
  • Heel pads/orthotics
Common causes of subacute/chronic heel pain in adults

Common causes of subacute/chronic heel pain in adults

Condition

History

Physical Examination

Plantar fasciitis

  • Sharp, localized medial plantar heel pain
  • Worse with first steps in morning or after inactivity
  • Typically improves with movement
  • Tenderness at medial calcaneal tubercle
  • Pain with passive toe dorsiflexion

Achilles tendinopathy

  • Posterior heel pain and stiffness, typically 2-6 cm above insertion
  • Worsens with activity, improves with rest.
  • Tenderness, thickening, and possible crepitus along tendon

Retrocalcaneal bursitis

  • Posterior heel pain anterior to Achilles
  • Worsens with dorsiflexion or tight shoes
  • Swelling and tenderness over retrocalcaneal bursa
  • May have palpable bony prominence (Haglund deformity).

Calcaneal stress fracture

  • Gradual onset of deep heel pain
  • Worsens with weight-bearing & impact activity
  • Diffuse calcaneal tenderness
  • Pain with heel squeeze or hopping

Tarsal tunnel syndrome

  • Burning, tingling, or radiating heel/plantar foot pain or numbness
  • Typically worse at night & with prolonged standing
  • Tinel sign over tarsal tunnel
  • Sensory loss or paresthesia in tibial nerve distribution

Heel fat pad syndrome

  • Heel pain worsened by walking barefoot or on hard surfaces
  • Often in older adults
  • Tenderness on plantar heel
  • Diminished fat pad on palpation

topics.title: Childhood musculoskeletal conditions
topics.subject: path

subs.title: Radial head subluxation
subs.subject: path
tables: Radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow)

Radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow)

Mechanism

  • Pull injury in child age 1-4: axial traction on forearm with elbow extended (child pulled, lifted, or swung by arm)
  • Annular ligament slips past radial head & becomes trapped in radiohumeral joint

Physical findings

  • Arm held with elbow extended & forearm pronated
  • Pain with forearm/elbow movement
  • ± Mild tenderness over radial head
  • No swelling, deformity, or other tenderness

Management

  • Reduction: hyperpronation of forearm OR supination of forearm & flexion of elbow → symptom resolution within minutes
  • No postreduction imaging or care required

subs.title: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
subs.subject: path
tables: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

Developmental dysplasia of the hip

Pathophysiology

  • Abnormal development of acetabulum & femoral head → hip instability

Risk factors

  • Mechanical: breech positioning, excessively tight swaddling
  • Genetic: female sex, family history

Clinical
features

  • Infants
    • Hip instability (eg, positive Barlow &/or Ortolani maneuver)
    • Leg asymmetry (eg, positive Galeazzi sign, asymmetric gluteal/thigh folds)
  • Older children
    • Limited hip abduction
    • Leg-length discrepancy
    • Trendelenburg gait

Evaluation

  • Age ≤4 months: hip ultrasonography
  • Age >4 months: hip x-rays

subs.title: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
subs.subject: path
tables: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease

Pathogenesis

  • Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femur

Clinical
features

  • Boys age 3-12
  • Limp
  • Insidious hip, thigh, or knee pain
  • Restricted hip abduction & internal rotation
  • Positive Trendelenburg sign

Diagnosis

  • X-ray
    • Early stages: often normal
    • Later stages: femoral head flattening, fragmentation, sclerosis
  • MRI: avascular/necrotic femoral head

Treatment

  • Non–weight bearing
  • Splinting ± possible surgical repair

subs.title: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
subs.subject: path
tables: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

Risk factors

  • Obesity
  • Adolescence
  • Hypothyroidism

Clinical features

  • Hip pain
  • Referred groin, thigh, or knee pain
  • Altered gait
  • Limited internal rotation of hip

Diagnosis

  • X-ray:
    • Anterosuperior displacement of femoral neck relative to femoral head
    • Widened physis

Treatment

  • Non–weight bearing
  • Surgical pinning

Complications

  • Avascular necrosis of femoral head
  • Chondrolysis

directTables: Calcaneal apophysitis (Sever disease)

Calcaneal apophysitis (Sever disease)

Risk factors

  • Running/jumping sports
  • Growth spurts
  • Athletic cleat use or footwear without heel padding

Clinical features

  • Heel pain (50% bilateral)
  • Pain with calcaneal palpation or compression
  • Decreased gastrocnemius/soleus flexibility

Treatment

  • Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, ice
  • Activity limitation
Growing pains (idiopathic nocturnal pains of childhood)

Growing pains (idiopathic nocturnal pains of childhood)

Epidemiology

  • Children age 3-12

Clinical features

  • Episodic, bilateral lower extremity (eg, thighs, calves) pain
    • Occurs primarily at night
    • More likely to occur after increased physical exertion
  • No systemic symptoms, joint involvement, or activity limitations
  • Normal physical examination

Diagnosis & treatment

  • Clinical diagnosis based on characteristic history* & examination
  • Parental education & reassurance
  • Massage, heat, analgesics, or stretching exercises

Course

  • May wax/wane for months to years
  • Self-resolves by adolescence

*Unilateral pain can occur in growing pains but warrants evaluation (eg, x-ray) to exclude alternate diagnoses (eg, osteoid osteoma, osteosarcoma).

topics.title: Achondroplasia
topics.subject: path
directTables: Achondroplasia

Achondroplasia

Pathogenesis

De novo or autosomal dominant FGFR3 gain-of-function mutation → decreased endochondral ossification (skeletal dysplasia)

Clinical features

Short stature with rhizomelia (proximal limb shortening)

Craniofacial abnormalities:

  • Macrocephaly with frontal bossing
  • Midface hypoplasia

Normal cognition

Diagnosis

Molecular genetic testing

FGFR3 = fibroblast growth factor receptor 3.

topics.title: Osteoporosis
topics.subject: path
directTables: FRAX assessment tool

FRAX assessment tool

The FRAX risk calculator is an online assessment tool used to estimate the 10-year risk of fracture in patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis.  It is available at http://www.shef.ac.uk/FRAX/tool.jsp

The following variables are included in estimating fracture risk:

  • Age
  • Sex
  • Weight
  • Height
  • Previous fracture history
  • Smoking status
  • Glucocorticoid use
  • Rheumatoid arthritis history
  • Secondary causes of osteoporosis
  • Alcohol use
  • Bone mineral density at the femoral neck
Secondary causes of osteoporosis

Secondary causes of osteoporosis

Endocrine

  • Hyperthyroidism
  • Hyperparathyroidism
  • Hypercortisolism
  • Hypogonadism

Metabolic/nutritional

  • Calcium &/or vitamin D deficiency
  • Eating disorder

Gastrointestinal/hepatic

  • Malabsorption (eg, celiac disease, Crohn disease)
  • Chronic liver disease

Renal

  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Renal tubular acidosis

Medications

  • Glucocorticoids
  • Phenytoin, carbamazepine
  • Proton pump inhibitors

Other

  • Inflammatory disorder (eg, rheumatoid arthritis)
  • Multiple myeloma
  • Alcohol use disorder
  • Immobilization
Clinical features of vertebral compression fracture

Clinical features of vertebral compression fracture

Etiologies

  • Trauma (often trivial)
  • Osteoporosis, osteomalacia
  • Bone metastases
  • Metabolic (eg, hyperparathyroidism)
  • Paget disease

Clinical
presentation

Acute

  • Back pain & decreased spinal mobility
  • Pain increasing with standing, walking, lying on back
  • Referred pain to abdomen/flank
  • Spinal tenderness at affected level

Chronic/gradual

  • Painless
  • Progressive kyphosis
  • Loss of height

Complications

  • Increased risk for future fractures
  • Hyperkyphosis → protuberant abdomen, early satiety, weight loss, decreased respiratory capacity
Management of vertebral compression fracture

Management of vertebral compression fracture

Pain control

  • Analgesics: acetaminophen, NSAIDs, opioids/tramadol (avoid muscle relaxants)
  • Calcitonin (second line)

Activity
recommendations

  • Resume normal activity
  • Avoid excessive bed rest
  • Prescribe PT for gait training/core strengthening once pain improves

Adjunctive
measure

  • Vertebroplasty in selected patients

Secondary
prevention

  • Exercise & fall prevention
  • Treatment of underlying osteoporosis (eg, bisphosphonates)

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; PT = physical therapy.
Medications for osteoporosis

Medications for osteoporosis

Bisphosphonates
(eg, alendronate,
risedronate)

  • First-line treatment for most patients
  • Taken with water on an empty stomach an hour before food & other medications
  • Not recommended for patients with renal impairment
  • Atypical fractures possible with prolonged use
  • Oral & parenteral options available

Denosumab

  • Risk of infection & skin reactions
  • Close monitoring for hypocalcemia needed

Anabolic agents
(eg, teriparatide)

  • Useful in severe osteoporosis
  • Monitor serum calcium, uric acid & renal function

Nasal calcitonin

  • Modest reduction in fracture risk
  • Reduces pain from fracture

Selective estrogen
receptor modulators
(eg, raloxifene)

  • Less effective than bisphosphonates
  • May lower risk of breast cancer
  • Increased risk of DVT

DVT = deep vein thrombosis.

directImages: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
images: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
directTables: Avascular necrosis

Avascular necrosis

Etiology

  • Steroid use
  • Alcohol abuse
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Hemoglobinopathy (eg, sickle cell)
  • Infection (eg, osteomyelitis, HIV)
  • Kidney transplantation
  • Decompression sickness

Clinical manifestations

  • Groin pain on weight bearing
  • Pain on hip abduction & internal rotation
  • No erythema, swelling, or point tenderness

Laboratory findings

  • Normal white blood cell count
  • Normal ESR & CRP

Radiologic imaging

  • Crescent sign seen in advanced stage
  • MRI is most sensitive modality

CRP = C-reactive protein; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
Adult hip osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis)

Adult hip osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis)

Clinical presentation

  • Chronic/progressive groin, thigh, buttock pain
  • Decreased ROM: abduction, internal rotation

Pathogenesis

  • Macro- or microvascular occlusion, bone necrosis
  • Trabecular thinning & collapse of femoral head

Risk factors

  • Femoral head fracture (arterial disruption)
  • Glucocorticoids
  • Excessive alcohol use
  • Sickle cell disease
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus

Diagnosis

  • X-ray (low sensitivity): subchondral sclerosis,
    loss of sphericity
  • MRI: serpiginous low-intensity lines (T1 images); bone marrow edema

ROM = range of motion.

Avascular necrosis

Etiology

  • Steroid use

  • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Hemoglobinopathy (eg, sickle cell)

  • Normal white blood cell count
  • Normal ESR & CRP

  • Crescent sign seen in advanced stage
  • MRI is most sensitive modality

tables: Unicameral bone cyst

Unicameral bone cyst

Epidemiology &
pathophysiology

  • Skeletally immature children
  • Solitary, benign cyst with fibrous lining in medullary cavity of long bones (eg, humerus, femur)

Clinical features

  • Usually asymptomatic & found incidentally on imaging
  • ± Localized pain or pathologic fracture

Diagnosis

  • X-ray: well-defined lucent lesion arising from metaphysis with narrow transition zone & no periosteal reaction
  • MRI: homogeneous cyst with enhancing rim

Treatment &
prognosis

  • Observation with serial x-rays until spontaneous resolution (typically by the time of physeal closure)
Benign bone lesions

Benign bone lesions

Clinical features*

X-ray findings

Natural course

Osteochondroma (most common)

  • Hard, palpable nodule on long bone
  • Usually painless
  • Bony spur extending from metaphysis & away from joint
  • Contiguous with medullary cavity & cortex

Growth until physeal closure

Osteoid osteoma

  • Nocturnal pain in long bone or spine relieved by NSAID
  • Small, round radiolucency with sclerotic margins

Spontaneous resolution

Unicameral bone cyst

  • Asymptomatic or localized pain in long bone
  • Well-defined radiolucency with narrow transition zone in metaphysis

Chondroblastoma

  • Joint pain/swelling involving long bone
  • Well-defined radiolucency with thin sclerotic margin in epiphysis

Locally aggressive with extension into growth plate/soft tissue

  • Joint pain/swelling involving long bone
  • Age >20
  • Well-defined radiolucency with soap-bubble appearance in epiphysis

subs.title: Osteochondroma (exostosis)
subs.subject: path
tables: Osteochondroma

Osteochondroma

Epidemiology & pathophysiology

  • Most common benign bone tumor
  • Bony spur with cartilaginous cap
  • Can be a single, sporadic lesion or multiple lesions (hereditary)

Clinical features

  • Hard, palpable mass arising from long bone (eg, femur) near joint
  • Usually painless (may cause pain due to compression of local neurovascular structures)

X-ray findings

  • Bony spur (exostosis) at metaphysis pointing away from epiphysis
  • Medullary & cortical continuity with adjacent bone

Natural course

  • Growth until physeal closure (skeletal maturity)

tables: Osteoid osteoma

Osteoid osteoma

Pathogenesis

  • Benign nidus of unmineralized osteoid that produces prostaglandins

Clinical
features

  • Most common in adolescence
  • Proximal femur most frequent site
  • Pain
    • Worse at night
    • Unrelated to activity
    • Relieved by NSAIDs
  • No systemic symptoms

X-ray findings

  • Small (<2 cm), round lucency with sclerotic margin

Management
& prognosis

  • NSAIDs (prostaglandin inhibitor)
  • Serial monitoring for spontaneous resolution
