tables: Osteosarcoma vs Ewing sarcoma

Osteosarcoma vs Ewing sarcoma

Osteosarcoma

Ewing sarcoma

Epidemiology

  • Most common pediatric bone malignancy
  • Bimodal distribution (age <25 & >50)
  • Second-most common pediatric bone malignancy
  • Highest incidence between age 10-15

Clinical
features

  • Chronic, localized pain & swelling
  • Metaphyses of long bone (eg, femur, tibia, humerus)
  • Rare: systemic findings & metastases
  • Chronic, localized pain & swelling
  • Diaphyses of long bone; pelvis, axial skeleton (eg, spine, ribs)
  • Common: systemic findings (eg, fever, leukocytosis) & metastases (eg, lung)

X-ray
findings*

  • Ill-defined osteolytic/osteoblastic lesion
  • Sunburst periosteal reaction
  • Ill-defined lytic lesion (moth-eaten appearance)
  • Lamellated periosteal reaction ("onion skinning")

*Periosteal elevation (ie, Codman triangle) is a nonspecific finding related to aggressive bone growth but is most commonly associated with osteosarcoma.
Osteosarcoma

Osteosarcoma

Epidemiology

  • Most common primary bone malignancy in children
  • Bimodal distribution (age <25 and >50)

Risk factors

  • Prior radiation/chemotherapy
  • Inherited tumor suppressor gene mutations (eg, hereditary retinoblastoma)

Clinical
features

  • Chronic pain at long bone metaphyses (eg, femur, tibia, humerus)
  • Associated soft tissue mass common
  • Metastases & systemic findings rare

Evaluation

  • X-ray: ill-defined osteolytic/osteoblastic lesion with aggressive periosteal reaction (eg, sunburst pattern, Codman triangle)
  • ↑ ALP & LDH
  • MRI & biopsy (osteoid-producing, pleomorphic malignant cells)

ALP = alkaline phosphatase; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase.

subs.title: Rheumatoid arthritis
subs.subject: path
images: Rheumatoid arthritis of the cervical spine
tables: Clinical features of rheumatoid arthritis

Clinical features of rheumatoid arthritis

Clinical presentation

  • Pain, swelling & morning stiffness in multiple joints
  • Small joints (PIP, MCP, MTP); spares DIP joints
  • Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, anemia)
  • Cervical spine involvement: subluxation, cord compression

Laboratory/
imaging studies

  • Positive rheumatoid factor & anti-CCP antibodies
  • C-reactive protein & ESR correlate with disease activity
  • X-ray: soft tissue swelling, joint space narrowing, bony erosions

anti-CCP = anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide; DIP = distal interphalangeal; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; MCP = metacarpophalangeal; MTP = metatarsophalangeal; PIP = proximal interphalangeal.
Extraarticular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis

Extraarticular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis

Systemic

  • Fever
  • Weight loss
  • Fatigue

Pulmonary

  • Fibrotic lung disease
  • Pleural effusions
  • Lung nodules
  • Pulmonary hypertension

Cardiovascular

  • Atherosclerosis
  • Vasculitis

Musculoskeletal

  • Osteopenia/osteoporosis

Dermatologic

  • Rheumatoid nodules

Hematologic

  • Anemia

Neuropsychiatric

  • Depression
  • Neuropathy

Other

  • Sjögren syndrome
  • Raynaud phenomenon
  • Scleritis, episcleritis
Felty syndrome

Felty syndrome

Clinical
features

  • Rheumatoid arthritis
    • Severe erosive joint disease & deformity
    • Rheumatoid nodules
    • Vasculitis (mononeuritis multiplex, necrotizing skin lesions)
  • Neutropenia (ANC <2000/µL)
  • Splenomegaly

Diagnosis

  • Anti-CCP & RF are positive in >90% of patients
  • Markedly elevated ESR, often >85 mm/hr
  • Peripheral smear & bone marrow biopsy to rule out other causes of neutropenia

ANC = absolute neutrophil count; anti-CCP = anticyclic citrullinated peptide; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; RF = rheumatoid factor.

Gout & CPPD disease (pseudogout)*

Gout

Pseudogout

Risk factors

  • Hyperuricemia
  • Hypertension
  • Obesity
  • Alcohol
  • Diuretics

Affected joints

  • Ankle
  • Knee
  • Knee (most common)
  • Wrist
  • Ankle

Synovial fluid

Medications associated with gout

Medications associated with gout

Reduced uric acid excretion

  • Diuretics (eg, hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide)
  • Salicylates (eg, low-dose aspirin)
  • ACE inhibitors (eg, lisinopril)
  • Cyclosporine

Increased uric acid production

  • Cytotoxic chemotherapy agents (tumor lysis syndrome)

Rapid decline in uric acid levels

  • Xanthine oxidase inhibitors (eg, allopurinol)
  • Uricosuric drugs (eg, probenecid)

  • 50s-80s

Clinical
features

  • Mild to moderate mucosal dryness

features

tables: Clinical features of psoriatic arthritis

Clinical features of psoriatic arthritis

Arthritis

  • Affects peripheral and axial skeleton
  • Causes prolonged (≥30 min) morning stiffness
  • Varied patterns: oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis, spondylarthritis (eg, sacroiliitis), distal arthritis (eg, DIP joint)
  • Severe and deforming disease possible (eg, arthritis mutilans)

Soft tissue & nail involvement

  • Enthesitis (inflammation at tendon insertion site)
  • Dactylitis (sausage digits) of toe or finger
  • Nail pitting & onycholysis
  • Pitting edema of hands or feet

Skin lesions

  • Typically precedes onset of arthritis
  • May also occur with or after onset of arthritis

subs.title: Ankylosing spondylitis
subs.subject: path
tables: Treatment of ankylosing spondylitis

Treatment of ankylosing spondylitis

Nonpharmacologic
measures

  • Exercise (postural exercises, ROM/stretching exercises)
  • Physical therapy

Initial treatment

  • NSAIDs (eg, ibuprofen, naproxen)
  • COX-2 inhibitors (eg, celecoxib)

Treatment failure/
disease progression

  • TNF-α inhibitors (eg, etanercept, infliximab)
  • Anti–IL-17 antibodies (eg, secukinumab)

COX-2 = cyclooxygenase-2; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; ROM = range of motion; TNF-α = tumor necrosis factor-alpha.
Symptoms/signs of ankylosing spondylitis

Symptoms/signs of ankylosing spondylitis

  • Low back pain (onset age <40, insidious onset, improves with exercise but not with rest, pain at night)
  • Hip & buttock pain
  • Limited chest expansion & spinal mobility
  • Enthesitis (inflammation at the site of insertion of a tendon to the bone)
  • Systemic symptoms (eg, fever, chills, fatigue, weight loss)
  • Acute anterior uveitis (unilateral pain, photophobia, blurry vision)

Preceding infection

directTables: Manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus

Manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus

Clinical
symptoms

  • Constitutional: fever, fatigue & weight loss
  • Symmetric, migratory arthritis
  • Skin: butterfly rash & photosensitivity
  • Serositis: pleurisy, pericarditis & peritonitis
  • Thromboembolic events (due to vasculitis & antiphospholipid antibodies)
  • Neurologic: cognitive dysfunction & seizures

Laboratory
findings

  • Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia & leukopenia
  • Hypocomplementemia (C3 & C4)
  • Antibodies:
    • Antinuclear antibodies (sensitive)
    • Anti-dsDNA & anti-Smith (specific)
  • Renal involvement: proteinuria & elevated creatinine

dsDNA = double-stranded DNA.

topics.title: Antiphospholipid syndrome
topics.subject: path
directTables: Diagnostic criteria for antiphospholipid-antibody syndrome

Diagnostic criteria for antiphospholipid-antibody syndrome
(1 clinical & 1 laboratory criterion must be met)

Clinical

Vascular thrombosis

  • Arterial or venous

Pregnancy morbidity

  • ≥3 consecutive, unexplained fetal losses before 10th week
  • ≥1 unexplained fetal losses after 10th week
  • ≥1 premature births of normal neonates before 34th week due to preeclampsia, eclampsia, or placental insufficiency

Laboratory

  • Lupus anticoagulant
  • Anticardiolipin antibody
  • Anti–β2-glycoprotein I antibody
Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

Clinical features

Venous or arterial thromboembolic disease

  • Deep vein thrombosis
  • Pulmonary embolism
  • Ischemic stroke/transient ischemic attack
 

Adverse pregnancy outcomes

  • Unexplained embryonic or fetal loss
  • Premature birth due to placental insufficiency or preeclampsia

Laboratory findings

  • Lupus anticoagulant effect: paradoxical activated PTT prolongation not reversed on plasma mixing studies
  • Presence of specific antiphospholipid antibodies
    • Anticardiolipin antibody
    • Anti–β2-glycoprotein I antibody

Polymyalgia rheumatica

Clinical
features

  • Rapid-onset pain & stiffness in shoulders & hips ± neck involvement
  • Fatigue, weight loss, low-grade fever
  • ~10% associated with GCA (eg, headache, jaw claudication, visual symptoms)

Diagnostic

  • Elevated acute phase markers (eg, ESR, CRP)
  • Temporal artery biopsy if symptoms of GCA

Treatment

  • Very rapid response to oral glucocorticoids

  • Bilateral pain & morning stiffness >1 month
  • Involvement of 2 of the following:
    • Neck or torso
    • Shoulders or proximal arms
    • Proximal thigh or hip
    • Constitutional (fever, malaise, weight loss)

Physical examination

  • Decreased active ROM in shoulders, neck & hips

Laboratory studies

  • Elevated ESR
  • Elevated CRP
  • Normocytic anemia

Treatment

  • Oral glucocorticoids

CRP = C-reactive protein; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; ROM = range of motion.

topics.title: IgG4-related disease

directTables: IgG4-related disease

IgG4-related disease

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic generalized lymphadenopathy
  • Autoimmune pancreatitis, sclerosing cholangitis
  • Thyroid disease (eg, Riedel thyroiditis, fibrous Hashimoto)
  • Retroperitoneal fibrosis
  • Bilateral salivary &/or lacrimal gland involvement

Diagnosis

  • Elevated IgG4 levels (nonspecific, markers of disease severity)
  • Biopsy with characteristic triad: IgG4-positive lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis

Management

  • Immunosuppression with glucocorticoids (rapid improvement)

subs.title: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis
subs.subject: path
tables: Giant cell arteritis: clinical manifestations

Giant cell arteritis: clinical manifestations

Systemic symptoms

  • Fever, fatigue, malaise, weight loss

Localized symptoms

  • Headaches: located in temporal areas
  • Jaw claudication: most specific symptom of GCA
  • PMR
  • Arm claudication: associated bruits in subclavian or axillary areas
  • Aortic wall thickening or aneurysms
  • CNS: TIAs/stroke, vertigo, hearing loss

Visual symptoms

  • Amaurosis fugax: transient vision field defect progressing to monocular blindness
  • AION: most common ocular manifestation

Laboratory results

  • Normochromic anemia
  • Elevated ESR & CRP
  • Temporal artery biopsy

Treatment

  • PMR only: low-dose oral glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone 10-20 mg daily)
  • GCA: high-dose oral glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone 40-60 mg daily)
  • GCA with vision loss: pulse high-dose IV glucocorticoids (eg, methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily) for 3 days followed by intermediate- to high-dose oral glucocorticoids

AION = anterior ischemic optic neuropathy; CRP = C-reactive protein; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; GCA = giant cell arteritis; IV = intravenous; PMR = polymyalgia rheumatica; TIAs = transient ischemic attacks.

Takayasu arteritis

Risk factors

  • Female
  • Asian
  • Age 10-40

Symptoms

  • Constitutional (eg, fever, weight loss, fatigue)
  • Arterioocclusive (eg, claudication, ulcers) in upper extremities
  • Arthralgias/myalgias

Examination findings

  • Blood pressure discrepancies

subs.title: Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)
subs.subject: path
tables: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)

Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)

Etiology

  • Segmental small & medium-sized vessel vasculitis
  • Likely triggered by tobacco smoke

Clinical features

  • Age <45, predominantly men
  • Digital ischemic ulcerations, limb claudication
  • Raynaud phenomenon, superficial thrombophlebitis

Histopathology

  • Inflammatory intraluminal thrombi with vessel wall sparing
  • Extension into contiguous veins & nerves
Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)

Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease)

Clinical features

  • Age <45
  • Ongoing or recent smoking history
  • Distal limb ischemia, gangrene, ulceration due to nonatherosclerotic occlusion, thrombosis

Evaluation

  • Ischemia on vascular studies (eg, digital plethysmography)
  • Segmental occlusion of small- & medium-sized vessels on angiography

Treatment

  • Smoking cessation

subs.title: Kawasaki disease
subs.subject: path
images: Coronary artery aneurysms in Kawasaki disease
tables: Kawasaki disease

Kawasaki disease

Pathophysiology & epidemiology

  • Medium-vessel vasculitis
  • Usually affects children age <5
  • ↑ Incidence in East Asian ethnicity

Diagnostic criteria

  • Fever ≥5 days plus ≥4 of the following:
    • Conjunctivitis: bilateral, nonexudative
    • Mucositis: injected/fissured lips or pharynx, strawberry tongue
    • Cervical lymphadenopathy: ≥1 nodes >1.5 cm
    • Rash: perineal erythema & desquamation; polymorphous, generalized
    • Erythema & edema of the hands/feet, periungual desquamation

Laboratory findings

  • ↑ Platelets & white blood cells; ↓ hemoglobin
  • ↑ Acute-phase reactants (eg, C-reactive protein)
  • ↑ AST & ALT
  • Sterile pyuria

Treatment

  • Intravenous immunoglobulin & aspirin

Complications

  • Coronary artery aneurysm
  • Ventricular dysfunction

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase.

subs.title: Polyarteritis nodosa
subs.subject: path
tables: Polyarteritis nodosa

Polyarteritis nodosa

Pathophysiology

  • Correlation with underlying hepatitis B/C (immune complexes)
  • Fibrinoid necrosis of arterial wall → luminal narrowing & thrombosis → tissue ischemia
  • Internal/external elastic lamina damage → microaneurysm formation  → rupture & bleeding

Clinical
features

  • Constitutional: fever, weight loss, malaise
  • Skin: nodules, livedo reticularis, ulcers, purpura
  • Renal: hypertension, renal insufficiency, arterial aneurysms
  • Nervous: headache, seizures, mononeuritis multiplex
  • Gastrointestinal: mesenteric ischemia/infarction
  • Musculoskeletal: myalgias, arthritis

Diagnosis

  • Negative ANCA & ANA
  • Angiography: microaneurysms & segmental/distal narrowing
  • Tissue biopsy: nongranulomatous transmural inflammation

ANA = antinuclear antibodies; ANCA = antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies.

subs.title: Behçet syndrome
subs.subject: path
tables: Behçet disease

Behçet disease

Diagnosis

Recurrent, painful oral ulcers (>3 times in 1 year) & 2 of the following:

  • Recurrent genital ulcers, often with scarring
  • Ocular manifestations (eg, uveitis, retinal vasculitis)
  • Skin lesions (eg, erythema nodosum, superficial thrombophlebitis, papulopustular lesions, acneiform nodules)
  • Positive pathergy test*

Other manifestations

  • Superficial & deep venous thrombosis
  • Gastrointestinal ulceration
  • Pulmonary artery aneurysm
  • Asymmetric & nondeforming arthritis

*A pathergy test is positive when a papule ≥2 mm develops 24-48 hr after insertion of a needle 5 mm into the skin.
Behçet disease

Behçet disease

Epidemiology

  • Young adults
  • Turkish, Middle Eastern, or Asian descent

Clinical
findings

  • Recurrent, painful oral aphthous ulcers
  • Genital ulcers
  • Eye lesions (eg, uveitis)
  • Skin lesions (eg, erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions)
  • Thrombosis

Evaluation

  • Pathergy: Exaggerated skin ulceration with minor trauma (eg, needlestick)
  • Biopsy: Nonspecific vasculitis of different sized vessels

subs.title: Small-vessel vasculitis
subs.subject: path
tables: ANCA-associated vasculitis

ANCA-associated vasculitis

ANCA pattern

Histopathology

Organ involvement

 

GPA

  • Mainly c-ANCA (anti-proteinase-3)
  • Neutrophils, granulomas & fibrinoid necrosis
  • Necrotizing sinusitis
  • Cavitary lung lesions & DAH
  • RPGN
 

EGPA

  
  • Mainly p-ANCA (anti-myeloperoxidase)
  • Eosinophils, granulomas & fibrinoid necrosis
  • Allergic sinusitis & polyps
  • Asthma
  • Broadest involvement (eg, RPGN, myocarditis, cutaneous nodules, mononeuritis multiplex)

MPA

  • Neutrophils & fibrinoid necrosis (no granulomas)
  • RPGN
  • DAH

ANCA = antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies; DAH = diffuse alveolar hemorrhage; EGPA = eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis; GPA = granulomatosis with polyangiitis; MPA = microscopic polyangiitis; RPGN = rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

subs.title: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
subs.subject: path
tables: Clinical features of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis

Clinical features of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis

Prodromal phase
(2nd & 3rd decades
of life)

Atopic disease

  • Asthma
  • Allergic rhinitis
  • Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps

Eosinophilic phase
(>10% peripheral
blood eosinophilia)

Eosinophilic infiltration of multiple organs

  • Lungs: migratory pulmonary opacities
  • GI: eosinophilic enteritis (bleeding, obstruction, perforation)

Vasculitic phase
(3rd & 4th decades
of life)

Organ-threatening systemic vasculitis

  • Nervous system: mononeuritis multiplex (peripheral nerve ischemia)
  • Cardiovascular: myocarditis & conduction defects (leading cause of mortality)
  • Kidneys: necrotizing glomerulonephritis (usually pANCA)
  • Skin: tender subcutaneous nodules (granulomas)
  • Musculoskeletal: migratory polyarthritis

pANCA = positive antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody.

subs.title: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
subs.subject: path
tables: Granulomatosis with

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

Clinical manifestations

  • Upper respiratory: sinusitis/otitis, saddle nose
  • Lower respiratory: lung nodules/cavitation, interstitial lung disease, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
  • Renal: rapidly progressive GN
  • Skin: livedo reticularis, nonhealing ulcers

Diagnosis

  • ANCA: PR3 (~70%), MPO (~20%)
  • Biopsy:
    • Skin (leukocytoclastic vasculitis)
    • Kidney (pauci-immune GN)
    • Lung (granulomatous vasculitis)

Management

  • Corticosteroids & immunomodulators (eg, cyclophosphamide)

ANCA = antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; GN = glomerulonephritis; MPO = myeloperoxidase; PR3 = proteinase-3.

subs.title: Immunoglobulin A vasculitis
subs.subject: path
tables: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)

Pathogenesis

  • Perivenular leukocytoclastic (neutrophils & monocytes) vasculitis
  • Deposition of IgA, C3 & fibrin in small vessels

Clinical
manifestations

  • Classic findings*:
    • Palpable purpura/petechiae on lower extremities
    • Arthritis/arthralgia
    • Abdominal pain, intussusception
    • Renal disease (similar to IgA nephropathy)
  • Other findings: scrotal pain & swelling

Laboratory
findings

  • Normal platelet count & coagulation studies
  • Normal to ↑ creatinine
  • Hematuria ± RBC casts &/or proteinuria

Management

  • Supportive care (hydration & NSAIDs) for most patients
  • Hospitalization & systemic glucocorticoids for severe symptoms

*Clinical diagnosis requires purpuric rash plus ≥2 additional classic findings.

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; RBC = red blood cell.
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)

Pathogenesis

  • Deposition of IgA immune complexes in small vessels activates complement
  • Neutrophilic inflammation & vascular damage
  • Often follows an upper respiratory infection

Clinical
manifestations

  • Palpable purpura/petechiae on the lower extremities
  • Arthritis/arthralgia
  • Abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, intussusception
  • Renal disease (hematuria ± proteinuria)

Diagnosis

  • Usually clinical
  • Skin biopsy: leukocytoclastic vasculitis, IgA deposition in vessel walls

subs.title: Mixed cryoglobulinemia
subs.subject: path
tables: Cryoglobulinemia*

Cryoglobulinemia*

Type I

Mixed = type II or III

Associated
diseases

  • Plasma cell dyscrasias (eg, Waldenström, multiple myeloma)
  • Chronic viremia (eg, HCV, HIV)
  • Autoimmunity (eg, SLE, Sjögren syndrome)

Pathogenesis:
cryoglobulin

  • B-cell lineage malignancy: monoclonal IgM
  • B-cell hyperactivation: IgM RF** bound to polyclonal IgG

Clinical
findings

  • Cryoprecipitates → vascular occlusion (eg, livedo reticularis, retiform purpura, digital ischemia)
  • High cryocrit → hyperviscosity (eg, blurred vision, vertigo, ataxia)
  • Immune complexes → vasculitis (eg, palpable purpura, GN, arthralgia, neuropathy)
  • Viral hepatitis → hepatomegaly

Laboratory
findings

  • + Cryocrit, normal complement
  • ↑ Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
  • + Monoclonal spike on SPEP
  • + Cryocrit, ↓ C4
  • + RF autoantibodies
  • + Viral or antinuclear antibodies

*Immunoglobulins that precipitate at <37 C (98.6 F).

**Monoclonal RF (type II), polyclonal RF (type III).
GN = glomerulonephritis; HCV = hepatitis C virus; RF = rheumatoid factor; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus; SPEP = serum protein electrophoresis.

Medications to avoid in myasthenia gravis

  • Magnesium sulfate
  • Fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides
  • Neuromuscular blocking agents
  • CNS depressants
  • Muscle relaxants
  • Calcium channel blockers
  • Beta blockers
  • Opioids
  • Statins
Myasthenia gravis

Myasthenia gravis

Clinical
presentation

  • Fluctuating & fatigable proximal muscle weakness:
    • Ocular (eg, diplopia, ptosis)
    • Bulbar (eg, dysphagia, dysarthria)
    • Respiratory (myasthenic crisis)

Causes of
exacerbations

  • Medications: antibiotics (eg, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides), neuromuscular blocking agents, cardiac medications (eg, BBs), MgSO4, penicillamine
  • Physiologic stress: pregnancy/childbirth, surgery (especially thymectomy), infection

Diagnosis

  • Ice pack test (bedside), AChR-Ab (highly specific)
  • CT scan of chest (thymoma)

Treatment

  • AChE inhibitors (eg, pyridostigmine) ± immunotherapy (eg, corticosteroids, azathioprine)
  • Thymectomy

AChE = acetylcholinesterase; AChR-Ab = acetylcholine receptor antibodies; BBs = beta blockers; MgSO4 = magnesium sulfate.
Myasthenic crisis

Myasthenic crisis

Precipitating
factors

  • Infection or surgery
  • Pregnancy or childbirth
  • Tapering of immunosuppressive drugs
  • Medications (eg, aminoglycosides, beta blockers)

Signs/symptoms

  • ↑ Generalized & oropharyngeal weakness
  • Respiratory insufficiency/dyspnea

Treatment

  • Intubation for deteriorating respiratory status
  • Plasmapheresis or IVIG as well as corticosteroids

IVIG = intravenous immunoglobulin.

topics.title: Raynaud phenomenon
topics.subject: path
directTables: Raynaud phenomenon

Raynaud phenomenon

Primary

Secondary

Etiology

  • Idiopathic response to cold or stress
  • Risk factors include CVD, smoking
  • Vasoconstriction due to vascular pathology
  • Causes: autoimmune disease (eg, systemic sclerosis), drugs (eg, amphetamines), trauma (eg, frostbite)

Clinical
presentation

  • Young; predominantly female
  • Symmetric attacks
  • Normal examination & laboratory results
  • Older (>40); male & female
  • Asymmetric attacks
  • Examination/laboratory results: tissue injury (eg, digital ulcers), abnormal nail fold capillaries, autoimmune antibodies (eg, ANA)

Management

  • Nonpharmacologic: warming techniques, smoking cessation, stress reduction
  • Medication: CCB (first-line), PDE-5 inhibitor (second-line)
  • Evaluate & treat underlying disorder
  • Same medications as for primary RP
  • Consider aspirin if increased risk for digital ulceration

ANA = antinuclear antibody; CCB = calcium channel blocker; CVD = cardiovascular disease; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; PDE-5 = phosphodiesterase type 5; RP = Raynaud phenomenon.

topics.title: Scleroderma
topics.subject: path
directTables: Systemic sclerosis subtype characteristics

Systemic sclerosis subtype characteristics

Limited cutaneous

  • Scleroderma on head & distal upper extremities
  • Prominent vascular manifestations
    • Raynaud phenomenon
    • Cutaneous telangiectasia
    • Pulmonary arterial hypertension
  • CREST syndrome
  • Anticentromere antibodies
  • Better prognosis

Diffuse cutaneous

  • Scleroderma on trunk & upper extremities
  • Prominent internal organ involvement
    • Scleroderma renal crisis
    • Myocardial ischemia & fibrosis
    • Interstitial lung disease
  • Anti–Scl-70 (topoisomerase type I) antibodies
  • Anti–RNA polymerase III antibodies
  • Worse prognosis

CREST = Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly & Telangiectasia.
Scleroderma renal crisis

Scleroderma renal crisis

Risk factors

  • Diffuse, aggressive skin involvement, tendon friction rubs
  • High-dose glucocorticoid therapy
  • Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies (lower risk with anticentromere antibodies)

Clinical
presentation

  • Acute kidney injury
  • Moderate or severe hypertension/malignant hypertension
  • Proteinuria, normal urine sediment
  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

Management

  • Lower blood pressure to previous baseline in ≤72 hr
  • ACE inhibitors (preferred), dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
    (avoid beta blockers)

subs.title: Albinism
subs.subject: derm
tables: Oculocutaneous albinism

Oculocutaneous albinism

Pathophysiology

  • Autosomal recessive tyrosinase mutation
  • Impaired melanin synthesis
  • Abnormal optic nerve & foveal development

Eye findings

  • Photophobia
  • Reduced visual acuity
  • Strabismus, nystagmus
  • Light-colored, translucent iris
  • Hypopigmented retinal pigment epithelium

Skin findings

  • White/light skin & hair
  • ↑ Propensity for sunburn
  • ↑ Risk for skin cancer (eg, squamous cell)

subs.title: Vitiligo
subs.subject: derm
tables: Vitiligo

Vitiligo

 Manifestations

  • Depigmented macules due to melanocyte destruction
  • Distribution: acral/facial, mucosal (oral, genital), segmental (eg, dermatomal), universal (complete depigmentation)
  • Increased incidence of autoimmune disorders (eg, hypothyroidism)

Clinical course

  • Most cases progress gradually
  • Spontaneous repigmentation in 10%-20% of cases

Treatment

  • Limited disease: topical corticosteroid
  • Extensive or refractory disease: oral corticosteroid, topical calcineurin inhibitor, phototherapy

topics.title: Seborrheic dermatitis
topics.subject: derm
directImages: Seborrheic dermatitis distribution in an infant
images: Seborrheic dermatitis distribution in an infant
directTables: Seborrheic dermatitis in adults

Seborrheic dermatitis in adults

Pathogenesis

  • Possibly related to Malassezia colonization & associated inflammation

Clinical features

  • Erythematous, pruritic plaques with greasy scales
  • Scalp, central face, ears, chest

Risk factors

  • CNS disease (eg, Parkinson disease)
  • HIV

Treatment

  • Topical antifungals (eg, selenium sulfide, ketoconazole)
  • Topical glucocorticoids*
  • Maintenance treatment required to prevent recurrence

*Low-potency glucocorticoids should be used in areas with thin skin (eg, face).
Seborrheic dermatitis in infants

Seborrheic dermatitis in infants

Clinical features

  • Scalp (cradle cap), face (eg, eyebrows), retroauricular areas
    • Greasy, yellow scales ± erythematous plaques
  • Intertriginous regions (eg, neck folds, axillae, diaper area), umbilicus
    • Glistening, confluent erythema
  • ± Mild pruritus

Treatment

  • Emollients to soften scales (scalp)
  • Topical antifungal (eg, ketoconazole) &/or low-potency corticosteroid

Outcome

  • Symptoms wax/wane & resolve within months

images: Distribution of atopic dermatitis in infants
Distribution of atopic dermatitis in adults
tables: Atopic dermatitis (eczema)

Atopic dermatitis (eczema)

Risk factor

  • Family history of atopy (eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis)

Clinical features

  • Acute: pruritic, erythematous patches & papules
    • Infant: extensor surfaces, trunk & face
    • Child/adult: flexural creases
  • Chronic: lichenified plaques

Treatment

  • Topical emollients
  • First line: topical corticosteroids
  • Second line: topical calcineurin inhibitors

Complications

  • Secondary infection
    • Impetigo (eg, Staphylococcus aureus)
    • Eczema herpeticum (ie, herpes simplex virus)

Prognosis

  • Chronic with intermittent flares in early childhood
  • Usually resolves by adolescence

subs.title: Allergic contact dermatitis
subs.subject: derm
tables: Allergic contact dermatitis

Allergic contact dermatitis

Pathophysiology

  • Type IV hypersensitivity reaction
  • Common triggers: poison ivy/oak, nickel, dyes, topical medications, skin care products

Clinical
presentation

  • Acute: pruritic red, indurated plaques with vesicles/bullae
  • Chronic: lichenification, fissuring

Diagnosis

  • Clinical findings
  • Patch testing for persistent cases

Treatment

  • Avoidance of suspected allergen
  • Topical or systemic corticosteroid

Treatment of rosacea

General measures

subs.title: Bacillary angiomatosis
subs.subject: derm
tables: Bacillary angiomatosis

Bacillary angiomatosis

Epidemiology

  • Bartonella henselae/quintana
  • Cat exposure or homelessness (lice)
  • Severe immunocompromise
    • Advanced HIV (CD4 <100/mm3)

Manifestations

  • Vascular cutaneous lesions (papular, nodular, peduncular)
  • Systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, fatigue)
  • Organ involvement rarely (liver, bone, CNS)

Diagnosis

  • Lesional biopsy with microscopy/histopathology

Treatment

  • Doxycycline or erythromycin
  • Antiretroviral therapy

CNS = central nervous system.

subs.title: Kaposi sarcoma
subs.subject: derm
tables: Kaposi sarcoma

Kaposi sarcoma

Type

Risk group

Features

Classic

  • Mediterranean or Central/Eastern European
  • Age >60
  • Indolent
  • Visceral lesions rare

Endemic

  • Equatorial Africa
  • Indolent or aggressive
  • Visceral lesions can occur

Iatrogenic

  • Immunosuppression
  • Particularly after organ transplantation
  • Can be aggressive
  • Visceral lesions common
  • Usually improves when immunosuppressives reduced

AIDS

  • Men who have sex with men
  • CD4 <200/mm3
  • Can be aggressive
  • Visceral lesions common
  • Usually improves with antiretroviral therapy

subs.title: Infantile hemangioma
subs.subject: derm
tables: Infantile hemangioma

Infantile hemangioma

Natural history

  • Appears days to weeks after birth
  • Proliferation (age 0-12 months): growth of bright red, soft, raised plaque
  • Involution (age >12 months): deep red/violet lesion that regresses in size

Evaluation

  • Clinical diagnosis
  • Special considerations:
    • ≥5 cutaneous lesions → liver ultrasonography
    • Facial/segmental → echocardiography & MRI of the head (ie, PHACE)
    • Cervicofacial (beard distribution) → laryngoscopy
    • Lumbosacral → spinal ultrasonography

Management

  • Observation for most lesions
  • Beta blocker therapy (eg, propranolol) for high-risk features:
    • Large, facial, segmental, &/or rapidly growing (ulceration/scarring)
    • Periorbital (visual impairment)
    • Hepatic (high-output heart failure)
    • Subglottic (airway obstruction)

PHACE = Posterior fossa anomalies, Hemangioma, Arterial anomalies, Cardiac anomalies, Eye anomalies.

subs.title: Impetigo
subs.subject: derm
tables: Impetigo

Impetigo

Type

Nonbullous (more common)

Bullous

Microbiology

  • Staphylococcus aureus (most common)
  • Group A Streptococcus
  • S aureus

Mechanism

  • Skin disruption
  • Invasion & general inflammatory response
  • Intact skin
  • Exfoliative toxin destroys cell adhesion molecules (eg, desmoglein)

Clinical features

  • Papules → pustules → honey-colored crusts
  • Negative Nikolsky sign*
  • Vesicles → flaccid bullae → thin, brown crusts
  • Positive Nikolsky sign*

Complications

  • Group A Streptococcus: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
  • S aureus: staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome

*In conditions with impaired adherence between epidermal layers, rubbing gently (mechanical pressure) against the skin causes the upper & lower epidermal layers to separate, creating a blister (positive Nikolsky sign).

subs.title: Cellulitis
subs.subject: derm
tables: Risk factors for cellulitis

Risk factors for cellulitis

Immune suppression

  • Diabetes mellitus
  • HIV infection
  • Chronic glucocorticoid therapy

Breaches in
skin barrier

  • Dry skin
  • Chronic inflammation (eg, eczema, radiation therapy)
  • Chronic wounds (eg, pressure ulcer, venous ulcer)
  • Dermatophyte infection (eg, tinea pedis)

Chronic edema

  • Postsurgical lymphedema (eg, lymph node dissection)
  • Chronic venous insufficiency
  • Congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease
  • Prior cellulitis with lymphatic scarring

Other

  • Obesity

subs.title: Necrotizing fasciitis
subs.subject: derm
tables: Necrotizing fasciitis

Necrotizing fasciitis

Microbiology

  • Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus)
  • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Clostridiumperfringens
  • Polymicrobial

Pathogenesis

  • Bacteria spread rapidly through subcutaneous tissue & deep fascia, undermining the skin
  • Most commonly involves the extremities & perineal region

Clinical manifestations

  • Often antecedent history of minor trauma
  • Erythema of overlying skin
  • Swelling & edema
  • Pain out of proportion to examination findings
  • Systemic signs (eg, fever, hypotension)

Treatment

  • Requires surgical debridement & broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
Necrotizing fasciitis

Necrotizing fasciitis

Microbiology

  • Can be monomicrobial or polymicrobial
    • Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus)
    • Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)

Impetigo

Impetigo

Type

Nonbullous (more common)

Bullous

Microbiology

  • Staphylococcus aureus (most common)
  • Group A Streptococcus
  • S aureus

Mechanism

  • Skin disruption
  • Invasion & general inflammatory response
  • Intact skin
  • Exfoliative toxin destroys cell adhesion molecules (eg, desmoglein)

Clinical features

  • Papules → pustules → honey-colored crusts
  • Negative Nikolsky sign*
  • Vesicles → flaccid bullae → thin, brown crusts

  • S aureus: staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome

Bullous pemphigoid

features

  • Age >60

Erythema multiforme

Pathogenesis

  • Cell-mediated immune response
  • Commonly triggered by infection (eg, HSV, Mycoplasma pneumoniae)

  • Skin: acute onset of target lesions
    • Erythematous, well-defined border

tables: Chronic venous insufficiency

Chronic venous insufficiency

Risk factors

  • Advanced age, family history
  • Prolonged standing, obesity
  • Smoking, prior deep vein thrombosis or trauma

Clinical features

  • Leg discomfort/pain & heaviness, often improve with walking
  • Varicose veins & telangiectasia, edema
  • Stasis dermatitis (chronic): pruritus, scaling, brawny discoloration, woody induration
  • Ulceration: painful, irregular ulcers with shallow bases, most often near medial malleoli

Initial management

  • Leg elevation, when possible
  • Leg exercises (eg, ankle flexion, walking) to ↑ calf strength & venous return
  • Compression therapy (eg, graduated compression stockings)

Clinical characteristics of common lower extremity ulcers

Ulcer type

Common locations

Clinical features

Associated findings

Arterial (ischemic)

Tips of toes, lateral malleoli, heels

  • Painful (worse at night, with elevation)
  • Pale or necrotic base

Clinical characteristics of common lower extremity ulcers

Ulcer type

Common locations

Clinical features

Associated findings

Arterial (ischemic)

Tips of toes, lateral malleoli, heels

  • Painful (worse at night, with elevation)
  • Pale or necrotic base

  • Diminished or absent pulses

Medial lower leg  (above medial malleolus)

Neuropathic

Feet, under bony prominences (eg, metatarsal head)

  • Painless
  • Well-defined, punched-out edges
  • Surrounding callus
  • Intact pulses
  • Dry, cracked skin
  • Loss of protective sensation
Chronic venous insufficiency

Chronic venous insufficiency

Risk factors

  • Advanced age, family history
  • Prolonged standing, obesity
  • Smoking, prior deep vein thrombosis or trauma

Clinical features

  • Leg discomfort/pain & heaviness, often improve with walking
  • Varicose veins & telangiectasia, edema
  • Stasis dermatitis (chronic): pruritus, scaling, brawny discoloration, woody induration
  • Ulceration: painful, irregular ulcers with shallow bases, most often near medial malleoli

Initial management

  • Leg elevation, when possible
  • Leg exercises (eg, ankle flexion, walking) to ↑ calf strength & venous return
  • Compression therapy (eg, graduated compression stockings)

subs.title: Erythema nodosum
subs.subject: derm
tables: Erythema nodosum

Erythema nodosum

Clinical features

  • Tender, indurated, erythematous nodules
  • Most common on anterior legs

Pathogenesis

  • Delayed hypersensitivity reaction
  • Septal panniculitis without vasculitis

Associated conditions

  • Infections (eg, Streptococcus)
  • Inflammatory disorders (eg, IBD, sarcoidosis)
  • Medications (eg, antibiotics, oral contraceptive pills)
  • Pregnancy

Management

  • Evaluation (as appropriate): CBC, ESR, streptococcal testing, chest radiograph, tuberculin skin test
  • Symptomatic treatment: NSAIDs, KI, corticosteroids if symptoms are refractory

CBC = complete blood count; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; IBD = inflammatory bowel disease; KI = potassium iodide; NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.
Erythema nodosum: associated conditions*

Erythema nodosum: associated conditions*

Infection

30%-50%

  • Bacterial
    • Streptococcal pharyngitis (most common cause overall)
    • Gastroenteritis (eg, Yersinia, Salmonella, Campylobacter)
    • Mycobacteria (eg, tuberculosis, leprosy)
    • Others (eg, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma)
  • Fungal (eg, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, blastomycosis)
  • Viral (eg, Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis B virus, HIV)

Sarcoidosis

 10%-25%

  • Frequent extrapulmonary manifestation
  • Triad of EN, fever & hilar adenopathy = Löfgren syndrome

Drugs

5%-10%

  • Antibiotics (eg, sulfonamides, penicillins)
  • Oral contraceptives (lower-dose formulas have ↓ incidence)

Pregnancy

2%-5%

  • Affects ~5% of pregnancies

IBD

1%-4%

  • Crohn disease > ulcerative colitis

Other

<1%

  • Inflammatory disorders (eg, Behçet disease, Sweet syndrome)
  • Malignancy (eg, lymphoma, leukemia)

*Cause remains undetermined (ie, idiopathic) in 30%-50% of cases; percentage of each cause can vary based on population/geography (eg, ↑ mycobacteria in India & sub-Saharan Africa).

 EN = erythema nodosum; IBD = inflammatory bowel disease.
Erythema nodosum: characteristic nodule features

Erythema nodosum: characteristic nodule features

Color

  • Bright red at onset
  • Darken (eg, purplish, livid) over several days
  • Become bruise-like (eg, greenish-yellow) as they resolve

Appearance &
character

  • Round/ovoid; 2-6 cm diameter; no ulceration
  • Slightly raised; ↑ warmth; indistinct borders*
  • Tender to palpation; spontaneous pain ↑ with standing

Distribution

  • Sudden-onset; usually bilateral; roughly symmetric
  • Shins almost always involved (~98% of cases)**
  • May spread to other areas (eg, thighs, forearms, trunk)

*From subcutaneous location (ie, full extent of nodules often easier to palpate than visualize).
**Possibly explained by local anatomy (pretibial area lacks an underlying muscle pump to aid venous return → poor antigen clearance).

tables: Ichthyosis vulgaris

Ichthyosis vulgaris

Pathophysiology

  • Loss of function in filaggrin gene
    • Impaired epidermal barrier
    • Reduced skin moisturization

Clinical features

  • Onset in infancy/early childhood
  • Diffuse, scaly skin with mild pruritus
  • Worse on extensor extremities, spares intertriginous areas

Associated
conditions

  • Keratosis pilaris
  • Palmar hyperlinearity
  • Atopic disease

Diagnosis

  • Clinical findings
  • Biopsy if uncertain: reduced/absent granular layer in epidermis

Therapy

  • Long baths to remove scales
  • Moisturization
  • Keratolytics (eg, urea, α-hydroxy acid, salicylic acid)

tables: Sunburn

Sunburn

Clinical
manifestations

  • Symptoms begin hours after exposure, resolve by day 3-7
  • Mild-moderate: erythema, tenderness
  • Severe: as above + blistering, systemic symptoms (eg, fever, vomiting, headache)

Treatment

  • Mild-moderate
    • Topical: cool compresses, calamine lotion, aloe vera
    • Oral: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
  • Severe
    • Hospitalization
    • Intravenous fluids & analgesia
    • Wound care
Sun-protective measures

Sun-protective measures

Exposure

  • Sun avoidance, especially age <6 months
  • Reduce exposure from 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM

Sunscreen

  • SPF ≥30
  • Apply 15-30 minutes prior to sun exposure
  • Reapply every 2 hours & after swimming

Clothing

  • Long sleeves, broad-brim hats
  • Tight weave, dark color

SPF = sun protection factor.

subs.title: Inhalation injury
subs.subject: derm
tables: Inhalation injury

Inhalation injury

Pathophysiology

  • Upper airway thermal injury ± lower airway chemical injury
  • Concomitant CO & cyanide poisoning common

Concerning
features

  • Historical: smoke exposure in enclosed space
  • Physical: singed hair, facial burns, carbonaceous sputum, wheezing

Strong indicators
of airway injury

  • Oropharyngeal blistering or edema
  • Retractions, respiratory distress, hypoxia

Management

  • 100% oxygen to displace CO
  • Stable patients with concerning features but no strong indicators: bedside fiberoptic laryngoscopy
  • Unstable patients or patients with strong indicators: endotracheal intubation

CO = carbon monoxide.

topics.title: Burn classification
topics.subject: derm
directTables: Burn depth classification

Burn depth classification

First
degree

  • Superficial
  • Damage to epidermis
  • Blanchable redness
  • Dry, without vesicles or blisters

Second degree

  • Partial-thickness
  • Damage to epidermis & dermis
  • Red &/or mottled white base
  • Weeping blisters & vesicles
  • Edematous, moist
  • Very painful

Third
degree

  • Full-thickness
  • Damage to epidermis, dermis & subcutaneous tissue
  • Color varies from white, red &/or brown
  • Edematous, leathery or charred
  • Loss of sensation from nerve damage

Fourth
degree

  • Full-thickness
  • Damage extends into fascia, muscle &/or bone
Hypermetabolic response in burn injury

Hypermetabolic response in burn injury

Etiology

  • Moderate to severe burn injury (eg, inhalational, high-voltage electrical, TBSA >20%)
  • ↑ Inflammatory mediators, which result in ↑ catecholamines, glucocorticoids & glucagon

Clinical features

  • Hyperdynamic circulatory response: tachycardia, hypertension
  • ↑ Gluconeogenesis & insulin resistance: hyperglycemia
  • ↑ Basal metabolic rate: ↑ basal body temperature
  • ↑ Protein & lipid catabolism: ↑ lean muscle wasting

Treatment

  • Early burn excision & grafting
  • Beta blockade (eg, propranolol)
  • Glycemic control (eg, insulin)
  • Nutritional support & anabolic steroid therapy (eg, oxandrolone)

TBSA = total body surface area.

subs.subject: derm
tables: Actinic keratosis

Actinic keratosis

Clinical features

  • Erythematous, scaly papules; rough plaques
  • Sun-exposed areas

Diagnosis

  • Clinical appearance
  • Biopsy if features of possible SCC (eg, size ≥1 cm, rapid growth, ulceration, tenderness)

Prognosis

  • Chronic/persistent
  • Progression to SCC
  • Spontaneous resolution

Treatment

  • Isolated lesions: cryotherapy
  • Diffuse lesions: topical fluorouracil, imiquimod, tirbanibulin

SCC = squamous cell carcinoma.

directTables: Pre-transplant

Recommendations for reducing
 skin cancer risk in transplant recipients

Pre-transplant

  • Age-appropriate cancer screening as part of
    transplant candidate work-up

Post-transplant

  • Seek shade during peak sunlight hours (10 AM–4 PM)
  • Wear long-sleeve shirt (tightly woven fabrics are best)
  • Use broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF ≥ 30
    • Apply 15–30 minutes before sun exposure
    • Reapply every 2 hours
  • Wear a hat with ≥ 2" brim
  • Wear sunglasses to protect skin around the eyes
  • Have professional assess skin annually

tables: Management options for acute gout

Management options for acute gout

Agent

Patient selection

Adverse effects

NSAIDs

  • Effective for most patients
  • Contraindications: PUD, CKD, CHF
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Acute kidney injury

Colchicine

  • Effective alternate to NSAIDs
  • Use caution in patients with CKD
  • Diarrhea, abdominal cramps
  • Neuromyopathy

Intraarticular corticosteroids

  • 1-2 inflamed joints
  • Requires experienced provider
  • May accelerate undiagnosed septic arthritis

Systemic corticosteroids

  • >2 inflamed joints
  • Rebound attacks
  • Elevated blood pressure, hyperglycemia

CHF = congestive heart failure; CKD = chronic kidney disease; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; PUD = peptic ulcer disease.

directTables: Thyroglossal duct cyst

Thyroglossal duct cyst

Embryology

  • Forms along path of thyroid descent
  • Foramen cecum (base of tongue) to base of anterior neck

Clinical presentation

  • Midline cystic neck mass
  • Moves superiorly with swallowing or tongue protrusion
  • Often present after upper respiratory tract infection (secondary infection)
  • Associated with ectopic thyroid tissue

Management

  • Confirm presence of normal thyroid tissue
  • Surgical resection of cyst, associated tract & central portion of hyoid bone
Congenital neck masses

Congenital neck masses

Location (in the neck)

Clinical features

Thyroglossal duct cyst

Midline, near hyoid

  • Between foramen cecum & anterior neck
  • Moves with swallowing or tongue protrusion
  • Secondarily infected after URTI

Branchial cleft cyst

Lateral, anterior to SCM

  • Associated with sinus tract or fistula
  • Secondarily infected after URTI

Cystic hygroma

Posterior triangle

  • Associated with aneuploidy
  • Can cause compressive symptoms

Ectopic thymic cyst

Lateral, deep to SCM

  • Can cause compressive symptoms

SCM = sternocleidomastoid; URTI = upper respiratory tract infection.

directTables: Stimuli for secretion of antidiuretic hormone

Stimuli for secretion of antidiuretic hormone

Osmotic

  • Serum osmolality > ~285 mOsm/kg H2O

Nonosmotic

  • Nausea
  • Pain
  • Physical or emotional stress
  • Hypotension
  • Hypovolemia
  • Hypoxia
  • Hypoglycemia
Primary nocturnal enuresis

Primary nocturnal enuresis

Definition

  • Nighttime urinary incontinence age ≥5
  • No prior prolonged period of overnight dryness

Pathogenesis

  • Delayed maturation of bladder control
  • ↑ Nocturnal urine output (eg, ↑ evening fluids, ↓ ADH)
  • ↓ Bladder capacity

Risk factors

  • Family history
  • Boys age 5-8

Evaluation

  • Urinalysis (to exclude other causes)
  • Voiding diary

Management

  • Treatment of exacerbating factors (eg, constipation)
  • Behavioral modifications (eg, restrict evening fluids)
  • Enuresis alarm
  • Desmopressin therapy

ADH = antidiuretic hormone.
Serum osmolality

Serum osmolality

(normal: 275-295 mOsm/kg H2O)

Calculated serum osmolality

(2 × Na+) + (glucose / 18) + (BUN / 2.8) + (ethanol / 4.6)*

Serum osmolal gap

Laboratory-measured osmolality − calculated osmolality

(>10 suggests unmeasured substance)

*Ethanol is frequently measured in the laboratory & may be included in the calculated serum osmolality when appropriate.

BUN = blood urea nitrogen.

Causes of hyperprolactinemia

Physiologic

  • Pregnancy
  • Breastfeeding
  • Stress

Pathologic

  • Pituitary adenomas (eg, prolactinomas)
  • Hypothalamic disease with ↓ dopamine (eg, malignancy, sarcoidosis)
  • Drugs (eg, antipsychotics, metoclopramide)
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Chest wall injury (eg, burns, herpes zoster)
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Following generalized tonic-clonic or focal seizure

  • Hypothalamic disease with ↓ dopamine (eg, malignancy, sarcoidosis)
  • Drugs (eg, antipsychotics, metoclopramide)
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Chest wall injury (eg, burns, herpes zoster)
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Following generalized tonic-clonic or focal seizure

Thyroid changes in pregnancy

Physiologic
changes

  • Increased thyroid hormone demand
  • Estrogen increases thyroxine-binding globulin → increased total T4 & T3 levels
  • hCG stimulates thyroid follicles for increased T4 & T3 production with feedback suppression of TSH

Management

  • Use trimester-specific norms when interpreting TSH
    • First trimester: 0.1-2.5 µU/mL
    • Second trimester: 0.2-3.0 µU/mL
    • Third trimester: 0.3-3.0 µU/mL
  • Check free T4 or total T4/T3 levels if TSH significantly suppressed (<0.1 µU/mL)

tables: Nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia

Nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia

Pathophysiology

  • Autosomal recessive
  • ↓ 21-Hydroxylase activity
  • Normal glucocorticoids & mineralocorticoids  
  • ↑ Androgens

Clinical features

  • Early pubic/axillary hair growth
  • Severe acne
  • Hirsutism & oligomenorrhea in girls
  • ↑ Growth velocity & bone age
  • ↑ 17-Hydroxyprogesterone level

Treatment

  • Hydrocortisone
Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia

Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal recessive
  • 21-Hydroxylase deficiency → ↓ aldosterone, ↓ cortisol, ↑ androgens

Clinical presentation

  • Atypical (or ambiguous) genitalia (eg, clitoromegaly in 46,XX infant)
  • Adrenal crisis* (eg, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension)

Laboratory findings

  • ↓ Sodium, ↑ potassium & ↓ glucose*
  • ↑ 17-Hydroxyprogesterone

Treatment

  • Glucocorticoid & mineralocorticoid replacement
  • Sodium chloride supplementation

*Adrenal crisis & electrolyte abnormalities develop at age 1-3 weeks due to transient protective effects of maternal hormones at birth.

directTables: Classification of hyponatremia

Classification of hyponatremia

Serum osmolality

ECV

Urine findings

Causes

Hypotonic (<275 mOsm/kg)

Hypovolemic

UNa <40 mEq/L

  • Nonrenal salt loss (eg, vomiting, diarrhea)

UNa >40 mEq/L

  • Renal salt loss (eg, diuretics, primary adrenal insufficiency)

Euvolemic

UOsm <100 mOsm/kg

  • Primary polydipsia
  • Malnutrition (eg, beer potomania)

UOsm >100 mOsm/kg & UNa >40 mEq/L

  • SIADH*

Hypervolemic

Variable

  • Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome

Isotonic

Variable

  • Pseudohyponatremia (eg, paraproteinemia, hyperlipidemia)

Hypertonic (>295 mOsm/kg)

  • Translocational hyponatremia (eg, hyperglycemia, exogenous solutes such as mannitol)

*Hypothyroidism & secondary adrenal insufficiency should be ruled out.

ECV = extracellular volume; SIADH = syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; UNa = urine sodium; UOsm = urine osmolality.
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone

Etiologies

  • CNS disturbance (eg, stroke, hemorrhage, trauma)
  • Medications (eg, carbamazepine, SSRIs, NSAIDs)
  • Lung disease (eg, pneumonia)
  • Ectopic ADH secretion (eg, small cell lung cancer)
  • Pain &/or nausea

Clinical
features

  • Mild/moderate hyponatremia: nausea, forgetfulness
  • Severe hyponatremia: seizures, coma
  • Euvolemia (eg, moist mucous membranes, no edema, no JVD)

Laboratory
findings

  • Hyponatremia
  • Serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg H2O (hypotonic)
  • Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg H2O
  • Urine sodium >40 mEq/L

Management

  • Fluid restriction ± salt tablets
  • Hypertonic (3%) saline for severe hyponatremia

ADH = antidiuretic hormone; JVD = jugular venous distension; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
Common causes of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

Common causes of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

  • CNS disruptions (eg, stroke, infection, trauma, neurosurgery)
  • Malignancies (eg, small cell lung carcinoma)
  • Drugs (eg, desmopressin, chlorpropamide, carbamazepine)
  • Pulmonary disorders (eg, pneumonia, tuberculosis, ventilator use)
Thiazide-induced hyponatremia

Thiazide-induced hyponatremia

Pathogenesis

  • ↓ Water excretion (ADH-dependent & ADH-independent mechanisms)
  • ↑ Water intake (natural tendency to polydipsia)

Risk factors & presentation

  • Advanced age (mean age >75), female, low BMI
  • Typically within few weeks of therapy or after acute event (eg, diarrhea)
  • Patients often euvolemic with subtle symptoms (eg, confusion)

Treatment

  • Discontinue thiazide
  • Correct hyponatremia (eg, IV fluids)

ADH = antidiuretic hormone; IV = intravenous.

tables: Sheehan syndrome

Sheehan syndrome

Pathogenesis

  • Obstetric hemorrhage complicated by hypotension
  • Postpartum anterior pituitary infarction

Clinical
features

  • Spectrum of disease based on severity of pituitary infarction (immediate adrenal crisis → years after delivery)
  • Lactation failure (↓ prolactin)
  • Amenorrhea, hot flashes, vaginal atrophy (↓ FSH, LH)
  • Fatigue, bradycardia (↓ TSH)
  • Anorexia, weight loss, hypotension (↓ ACTH)
  • ↓ Lean body mass (↓ GH)

Diagnosis

  • Cortisol level (most important)
  • Thyroxine level
  • FSH level
  • Prolactin level

Treatment

  • Corticosteroids
  • Estrogen-progestin replacement therapy

directTables: Central hypothyroidism

Central hypothyroidism

Causes

  • Mass lesions (eg, pituitary adenoma)
  • Pituitary surgery, trauma, irradiation
  • Infiltrative disorders (eg, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis)
  • Pituitary infarction (eg, Sheehan syndrome)

Clinical features

  • Hypothyroid symptoms
  • Mass-effect symptoms (eg, headache, visual field defects) if due to mass

Hormone levels

  • Low free thyroxine (T4)
  • Low or inappropriately normal TSH
  • Other pituitary hormone deficiencies (eg, ACTH, prolactin, gonadotropins)

subs.title: Congenital hypothyroidism
subs.subject: path
tables: Congenital hypothyroidism

Congenital hypothyroidism

Pathophysiology

  • Thyroid dysgenesis most common (eg, agenesis, hypoplasia, ectopy)

Clinical
manifestations

  • Asymptomatic at birth*
  • Symptomatic weeks to months after birth (as maternal T4 wanes)
    • Hypometabolism: ↓ HR & temperature, lethargy/poor feeding, hypotonia, constipation, jaundice
    • Mucopolysaccharide accumulation: macroglossia, umbilical hernia
    • Delayed bone maturation: enlarged fontanelles

Diagnosis

  • Newborn screening
  • ↑ TSH & ↓ T4

Treatment

  • Levothyroxine

Prognosis

  • No deficits if treatment started in neonatal period
  • Untreated disease leads to intellectual disability, developmental delay & poor growth

*Can rarely present with delayed passage of meconium.

HR = heart rate.

subs.title: Other causes
subs.subject: path
tables: Euthyroid sick syndrome (low T3 syndrome)

Euthyroid sick syndrome (low T3 syndrome)

Risk factors

  • Severe acute illness
  • ICU admission
  • High-dose glucocorticoid therapy

Pathophysiology

  • High circulating levels of glucocorticoids and inflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor, interferon alpha)
  • Decreased peripheral conversion of T4 to T3

Diagnostic testing

  • Early:  Low T3, normal TSH & T4
  • Late:  Low T3, TSH & T4

Management

  • Observe without treatment
  • Follow-up testing when patient has returned to baseline health

ICU = intensive care unit.

directTables: Subclinical hypothyroidism

Subclinical hypothyroidism

Clinical features

  • Elevated TSH (verified on repeat measurement)
  • Normal free T4
  • Mild symptoms may or may not be present

Indications for treatment

  • TSH ≥10 µU/mL
  • TSH 7-9.9 µU/mL
    • Age <70: treat
    • Age ≥70: treat if convincing hypothyroid symptoms
  • TSH upper limit of normal - 6.9 µU/mL
    • Age <70: treat if convincing hypothyroid symptoms, enlarging goiter, or elevated anti-TPO titer
    • Age ≥70: do not treat (possible harm)

TPO = thyroid peroxidase.
Myxedema coma

Myxedema coma

Vital signs

  • Hypothermia
  • Bradycardia
  • Diastolic hypertension (narrow pulse pressure)
  • Hypoventilation

Examination findings

  • Decreased mental status
  • Nonpitting edema of face, hands & tongue
  • Psychosis, seizure, coma

Laboratory findings

  • Low free T4
  • Hyponatremia
  • Hypoglycemia

Associated conditions

  • Pericardial effusion
  • Concurrent adrenal insufficiency
  • Hypothalamic/pituitary dysfunction

Management

  • Parenteral levothyroxine (T4) & liothyronine (T3)
  • Glucocorticoids (eg, hydrocortisone)
Neuropsychiatric features of hypothyroidism

Neuropsychiatric features of hypothyroidism

Affective symptoms

  • Depression
  • Apathy

Cognitive symptoms

  • Impaired concentration & memory
  • Psychomotor slowing
  • Executive dysfunction

Severe symptoms

  • Delirium
  • Psychosis (myxedema madness)

    • Hypometabolism: ↓ HR & temperature, lethargy/poor feeding, hypotonia, constipation, jaundice
    • Mucopolysaccharide accumulation: macroglossia, umbilical hernia
    • Delayed bone maturation: enlarged fontanelles

Diagnosis

  • Newborn screening
  • ↑ TSH & ↓ T4

Treatment

  • Levothyroxine

Prognosis

  • No deficits if treatment started in neonatal period
  • Untreated disease leads to intellectual disability, developmental delay & poor growth

*Can rarely present with delayed passage of meconium.

HR = heart rate.
Euthyroid sick syndrome (low T3 syndrome)

Euthyroid sick syndrome (low T3 syndrome)

Risk factors

  • Severe acute illness
  • ICU admission
  • High-dose glucocorticoid therapy

Pathophysiology

  • High circulating levels of glucocorticoids and inflammatory cytokines (eg, tumor necrosis factor, interferon alpha)
  • Decreased peripheral conversion of T4 to T3

Diagnostic testing

  • Early:  Low T3, normal TSH & T4
  • Late:  Low T3, TSH & T4

Management

  • Observe without treatment
  • Follow-up testing when patient has returned to baseline health

ICU = intensive care unit.

images: Graves disease causes the overproduction of thyroid hormones
tables: Neonatal Graves disease

Neonatal Graves disease

Pathophysiology

  • Transplacental passage of maternal TSH receptor–stimulating antibodies (due to maternal Graves disease)
  • Antibodies bind to infant's TSH receptors & cause excessive thyroid hormone release → neonatal thyrotoxicosis

Clinical features

  • Tachycardia & irritability
  • Warm, moist skin
  • Low birth weight or preterm birth
  • ± Goiter, stare

Diagnosis

  • Maternal & neonatal TSH receptor–stimulating antibodies
  • ↓ TSH, ↑ free thyroxine

Treatment & outcome

  • Methimazole plus β blocker
  • Usually self-resolves within months (due to clearance of maternal antibodies)
Choice of treatment in Graves disease

Choice of treatment in Graves disease

Antithyroid drugs

  • Preferred in patients with limited life expectancy
  • May induce remission in mild hyperthyroidism
  • May be used as pretreatment prior to radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy (eg, high-risk patient, severe hyperthyroidism)

Radioactive iodine

  • Acceptable option for moderate hyperthyroidism
  • May initially worsen ophthalmopathy & hyperthyroid symptoms (increases TRAb)
  • Leads to permanent hypothyroidism over time

Thyroidectomy

  • Preferred in patients with very large goiter, obstructive symptoms, or ophthalmopathy
  • Potential complications from injury to parathyroids (eg, hypocalcemia, hypoparathyroidism) &/or laryngeal or vagus nerve (eg, hoarseness)

TRAb = thyrotropin receptor antibodies.

subs.title: Thyroid storm
subs.subject: path
tables: Clinical features of thyroid storm

Clinical features of thyroid storm

Precipitating factors

  • Thyroid or nonthyroidal surgery
  • Acute illness (eg, trauma, infection), childbirth
  • Acute iodine load (eg, iodine contrast)

Clinical presentation

  • Fever as high as 40-41.1 C (104-106 F)
  • Tachycardia, hypertension, congestive heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias (eg, atrial fibrillation)
  • Agitation, delirium, seizure, coma
  • Goiter, lid lag, tremor, warm & moist skin
  • Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice

Treatment

  • β Blocker (eg, propranolol) to ↓ adrenergic manifestations
  • PTU followed by iodine solution (SSKI) to ↓ hormone synthesis & release
  • Glucocorticoids (eg, hydrocortisone) to ↓ peripheral T4 to T3 conversion & improve vasomotor stability
  • Identify trigger & treat, provide supportive care

PTU = propylthiouracil; SSKI = potassium iodide.

Subclinical hyperthyroidism

Subclinical hyperthyroidism

Clinical characteristics

  • Suppressed TSH
  • Normal thyroid hormone levels
  • Hyperthyroid symptoms may or may not be present

Causes

  • Exogenous thyroid hormone
  • Graves disease
  • Nodular thyroid disease

Indications for treatment

  • TSH persistently <0.1 µU/mL
  • TSH 0.1-0.5 µU/mL plus additional risk factors:
    • Age ≥65
    • Heart disease
    • Osteoporosis
    • Nodular thyroid disease
Cardiovascular effects of thyrotoxicosis

Cardiovascular effects of thyrotoxicosis

Rhythm

  • Sinus tachycardia
  • Premature atrial & ventricular complexes
  • Atrial fibrillation/flutter

Hemodynamic effects

  • Systolic hypertension & ↑ pulse pressure
  • ↑ Contractility & cardiac output
  • ↓ Systemic vascular resistance
  • ↑ Myocardial oxygen demand

Heart failure

  • High-output failure
  • Exacerbation of preexisting low-output failure

Angina symptoms

  • Coronary vasospasm
  • Preexisting coronary atherosclerosis

  • Tremor (often absent)
  • Proximal muscle weakness/wasting

Endocrine

  • Proptosis, lid lag, thyromegaly (often absent)

Gastrointestinal

  • Decreased appetite
  • Constipation

topics.title: Thyroid adenoma

directTables: Toxic thyroid adenoma

Toxic thyroid adenoma

Clinical presentation

  • Hyperthyroid symptoms
  • Asymmetric thyroid gland or palpable nodule
  • Elevated T4, suppressed TSH

Diagnostic evaluation

  • Ultrasonography: well-circumscribed, hyperechoic nodule
  • Radioiodine uptake & scan: focal uptake in nodule ("hot" nodule), decreased uptake in surrounding thyroid gland
  • Biopsy not indicated

Initial management

  • ꞵ blockers
  • Antithyroid medication (eg, methimazole, propylthiouracil)

Definitive management

  • Radioactive iodine ablation
  • Surgical resection

directTables: Risk factors for malignant thyroid nodules

Risk factors for malignant thyroid nodules

Patient
characteristics

  • Exposure to ionizing radiation (especially in childhood)
  • Family history of thyroid cancer or thyroid cancer syndrome (eg, MEN2, familial polyposis coli, Cowden syndrome)
  • Age <30 or >60
  • Iodine deficiency
  • Elevated TSH

Nodule
characteristics

  • Rapid growth, hard/fixed nodule
  • Associated cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Obstructive symptoms (eg, hoarseness, dysphagia)
  • Ultrasound: size >1 cm, microcalcifications, hypoechoic, increased vascularity, infiltrative margins, length > width

MEN2 = multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.

tables: Primary hyperparathyroidism surgical indications

Primary hyperparathyroidism surgical indications

Parathyroidectomy is indicated for patients with ≥1 of the following*:

  • Symptoms of hypercalcemia
  • Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above upper limit of normal
  • Age <50
  • Bone mineral density T-score less than −2.5 or prior vertebral fracture on imaging
  • eGFR <60 mL/min
  • 24-hour urinary calcium >250-300 mg or evidence of nephrocalcinosis on imaging

*Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia should be excluded prior to surgery.

eGFR = estimated glomerular filtration rate.

topics.title: Diabetes mellitus
topics.subject: path
directTables: Gestational diabetes mellitus

Gestational diabetes mellitus

Pathophysiology

  • Human placental lactogen secretion

Screening

  • 24-28 weeks gestation
  • 1-hr 50-g GCT
  • 3-hr 100-g GTT

Management

  • 1st line: diet
  • 2nd line: insulin, glyburide, metformin

Target blood glucose goals

  • Fasting: ≤95 mg/dL
  • 1-hr postprandial: ≤140 mg/dL
  • 2-hr postprandial: ≤120 mg/dL

Postpartum management

  • Fasting glucose at 24-72 hr
  • 2-hr 75-g GTT at 6- to 12-week visit

GCT = glucose challenge test; GTT = glucose tolerance test.
Screening tests for diabetes mellitus

Screening tests for diabetes mellitus

Test

Interpretation

Hemoglobin A1c

  • Preferred test in nonfasting state
  • ≥6.5% = diabetes mellitus
  • 5.7%-6.4% = increased risk for diabetes
  • <5.7% = normal

Fasting blood
glucose

  • No caloric intake for >8 hr
  • ≥126 mg/dL = diabetes mellitus
  • 100-125 mg/dL = increased risk for diabetes
  • <100 mg/dL = normal

Random glucose
levels

  • ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms of hyperglycemia = diabetes mellitus
  • 140-199 mg/dL = increased risk for diabetes
  • <140 mg/dL = normal

Oral glucose
tolerance test

  • Most sensitive test
  • 75-g glucose load with glucose testing for 2 hr
  • ≥200 mg/dL = diabetes mellitus
  • 140-199 mg/dL= increased risk for diabetes
  • <140 mg/dL = normal
  • Testing may be repeated in cases of discordant or equivocal results.
  • If a patient is asymptomatic, a positive test should be reconfirmed with the same test on a different day.
Diabetic gastroparesis

Diabetic gastroparesis

Pathogenesis

  • Autonomic neuropathy
  • Destruction of enteric neurons
  • Failure of relaxation in fundus & uncoordinated peristalsis

Risk factors

  • Long-standing diabetes (especially type 1)
  • Chronic poor control
  • Labile blood glucose

Clinical presentation

  • Postprandial bloating & vomiting
  • Early satiety
  • Impaired nutrition & weight loss

Diagnosis

  • Nuclear gastric emptying study: delayed transit into duodenum

Treatment

  • Promotility drugs: metoclopramide, erythromycin
Health maintenance in diabetes mellitus

Health maintenance in diabetes mellitus

Glycemic control

  • Check A1c every 3-6 months
  • Goal A1c:
    • ≤7% (younger, otherwise healthy)
    • ≤8% (older, limited life expectancy, comorbidities)

Nephropathy
screening

  • Annual random urine albumin/creatinine ratio*
    • Normal value: <30 mg/g
  • Periodic serum creatinine level

Retinopathy
screening

  • Dilated eye examination every 1-2 years*

Neuropathy
screening

  • Visual inspection at each visit
  • Annual comprehensive foot examination

Cardiovascular
risk reduction

  • Address lifestyle factors (eg, tobacco, obesity, diet & exercise)
  • Annual lipid & BP screening
  • Aspirin and statin (depending on other risk factors)

*Begin at time of diagnosis for type 2 diabetes mellitus & within 5 years after diagnosis for type 1.

BP = blood pressure.
Clinical features of diabetic autonomic neuropathy

Clinical features of diabetic autonomic neuropathy

Cardiovascular

  • Tachycardia, impaired exercise tolerance
  • Postural hypotension with loss of diurnal blood pressure variation

Peripheral nerves

  • Dry skin, pruritus, callus formation
  • Foot ulcers & poor wound healing
  • Charcot arthropathy (increased fracture risk with resultant secondary ulceration)

Gastrointestinal

  • Gastroparesis with delayed gastric emptying
  • Esophageal dysmotility with possible dyspepsia
  • Intestinal involvement with possible diarrhea, constipation, or fecal incontinence

Genitourinary

  • Erectile dysfunction & retrograde ejaculation in men, decreased libido & dyspareunia in women
  • Decreased ability to sense full bladder, leading to incomplete emptying & decreased urination
  • Eventual recurrent urinary tract infections &/or overflow incontinence (eg, dribbling, poor urinary stream)

tables: Modifiable risk factors for development of T2DM

Modifiable risk factors for development of T2DM

Obesity

  • Visceral fat (central adiposity) appears to drive risk for insulin resistance
  • Decreases insulin sensitivity, increases circulation of inflammatory cytokines

Dietary factors

  • Sugary beverages and heavy consumption of foods high in saturated fat (eg, red meats) 
  • Low fruit, vegetable, and fiber intake

Sleep deprivation

  • Impairs insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism

Sedentary behavior

  • Associated with intramuscular lipid accumulation and insulin resistance

Mood disorders (eg, depression)

  • Associated with increased baseline cortisol, chronic inflammation, visceral fat 
  • Influences lifestyle behaviors associated with T2DM risk

T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Medical conditions associated with increased risk of T2DM

Medical conditions associated with increased risk of T2DM

Disorders increasing systemic inflammation or insulin resistance

  • Cardiovascular diseases 
  • Metabolic syndrome*
  • Polycystic ovarian syndrome
  • Cushing syndrome
  • Chronic kidney disease 

Disorders impairing pancreatic function

  • Hemochromatosis
  • Pancreatic insufficiency 

Diseases requiring chronic use of drugs, causing diabetes

  • HIV (antiretrovirals)
  • Psychosis (atypical antipsychotics)
  • Rheumatic disorders (glucocorticoids, certain immunosuppressants [eg, tacrolimus])
  • Certain cancers (immune checkpoint inhibitors)

*Drugs associated with treatment (eg, statins for hyperlipidemia, thiazides for hypertension) are also associated with increased risk for T2DM.

T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus.

subs.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis
subs.subject: path
tables: Diabetic ketoacidosis

Diabetic ketoacidosis

Patient characteristics

  • Young age
  • Brittle type 1 diabetes mellitus
  • May be initial manifestation of diabetes

Clinical symptoms

  • Acute to subacute onset
    • Initial: polydipsia/polyuria, blurred vision, weight loss
    • Later: altered mentation, hyperventilation, abdominal pain

Diagnosis

  • ↑Glucose (typically 300-800 mg/dL)
  • Metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate <18 mEq/L)
  • ↑ Anion gap
  • Positive serum ketones

Treatment

  • High-flow IV fluids (normal saline)
  • IV insulin
  • Follow & replace potassium

IV = intravenous.
Management of diabetic ketoacidosis

Management of diabetic ketoacidosis

Fluids

  • Initial: give isotonic intravenous fluids
  • Subsequent:
    • Continue isotonic fluids if serum Na+ <135 mEq/L
    • Switch to half normal saline if serum Na+ ≥135 mEq/L
    • Add dextrose when serum glucose <200 mg/dL

Insulin

  • Reduce insulin infusion rate when serum glucose <200 mg/dL
  • Hold insulin infusion if serum K+ <3.3 mEq/L
  • Switch to subcutaneous insulin on DKA resolution*

Potassium

  • Give replacement when serum K+ <5.3 mEq/L**

Bicarbonate

  • Consider replacement for severe DKA with blood pH ≤6.9

*Normalization of anion gap & patient able to eat.

**Due to total body potassium depletion and risk of insulin-induced hypokalemia.

DKA = diabetic ketoacidosis.
Diabetic ketoacidosis

Diabetic ketoacidosis

  • Type 1 diabetics usually
  • Younger age
  • Type 2 diabetics usually

  • Hyperventilation & abdominal pain common
  • More pronounced altered mentation

  • Hyperventilation & abdominal pain less common

presentation

subs.title: Secondary and tertiary adrenal insufficiency
subs.subject: path
tables: No risk

Risk of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal suppression with chronic glucocorticoid therapy

No risk
(No perioperative stress-dose steroids required)

  • Daily morning dose of prednisone <5 mg (or its equivalent) for any period
  • Any dose of any glucocorticoid for <3 weeks
  • Prednisone 10 mg (or its equivalent) every other day

Intermediate or unknown risk
(Preoperative evaluation of HPA axis recommended)

  • Daily morning dose of prednisone 5-20 mg (or its equivalent) for >3 weeks
  • Daily evening doses of prednisone <5 mg (may disrupt diurnal variation)
  • Prior longer duration or higher doses of glucocorticoids in the past year
  • Inhaled glucocorticoids for >3 weeks, or ≥3 intraarticular or spinal glucocorticoid injections within past 3 months

High risk
(Stress-dose glucocorticoids recommended during perioperative period)

  • Daily prednisone ≥20 mg (or its equivalent) for >3 weeks
  • Any patient taking glucocorticoids who has Cushingoid features (eg, buffalo hump, central obesity, moon face, weight gain)

directTables: Indications for diagnostic testing for pheochromocytoma

Indications for diagnostic testing for pheochromocytoma

Signs & symptoms

  • Episodic headaches, diaphoresis & tachycardia
  • Hyperadrenergic spells (eg, nonexertional palpitations, pallor)
  • Resistant hypertension or onset of hypertension at young age

Family history

  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Predisposing familial syndrome (eg, MEN2, NF1, VHL)

Other

  • Adrenal incidentaloma on imaging
  • Pressor response during surgery/anesthesia
  • Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy

MEN2 = multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2; NF1 = neurofibromatosis type 1; VHL = von Hippel-Lindau.
Surgical complications of adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma

Surgical complications of adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma

Complication

Mechanism

Hypertensive crisis

  • ↑ Catecholamine release during induction of anesthesia & adrenal gland manipulation (especially larger tumors)

Cardiac tachyarrhythmias

  • ↑ Catecholamine release

Hypotension

  • ↓ Catecholamines after tumor removal
  • Residual effects of preoperative alpha blocker (eg, phenoxybenzamine) therapy

Hypoglycemia

  • ↑ Insulin secretion following tumor removal (catecholamines suppress insulin secretion)
Pheochromocytoma

Pheochromocytoma

Indications for testing

  • Classic triad: episodic headache, sweating & tachycardia
  • Resistant HTN or HTN accompanied by unexplained ↑ glucose
  • Family history or familial syndrome (eg, MEN2, NF1, VHL)

Diagnostic approach

  • Urine or plasma metanephrine levels
  • Confirmatory abdominal imaging for ↑ metanephrines

Notable features

  • 10% bilateral, 10% extraadrenal, 10% malignant

Management

  • Preoperative alpha blockade prior to beta blockade
  • Laparoscopic or open surgical resection

HTN = hypertension; MEN2 = multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2; NF1 = neurofibromatosis type 1; VHL = von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.

subs.title: MEN1
subs.subject: path
tables: Multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1

Multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1

Manifestation

Clinical features

Pituitary adenomas
(10%-20%)

  • Secretion of prolactin, growth hormone, ACTH (or nonfunctioning tumors)
  • Mass effects (eg, headache, visual field defects)

Primary hyperparathyroidism
(>90%)

  • Multiple parathyroid adenomas or parathyroid hyperplasia
  • Hypercalcemia (eg, polyuria, kidney stones, decreased bone density)

Pancreatic/gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors
(60%-70%)

  • Gastrinoma: recurrent peptic ulcers
  • Insulinoma: hypoglycemia
  • VIPoma: secretory diarrhea, hypokalemia, hypochlorhydria
  • Glucagonoma: weight loss, necrolytic migratory erythema, hyperglycemia

directTables: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2

Inheritance

  • Autosomal dominant
  • Germ-line activating mutations of RET protooncogene

Type 2A

  • Medullary thyroid cancer (>95%)
  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Parathyroid hyperplasia

Type 2B

  • Medullary thyroid cancer (>95%)
  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus
Classification of multiple endocrine neoplasia

Classification of multiple endocrine neoplasia

Type 1

  • Primary hyperparathyroidism (parathyroid adenomas or hyperplasia)
  • Pituitary tumors (prolactin, visual defects)
  • Pancreatic tumors (especially gastrinomas)

Type 2A

  • Medullary thyroid cancer (calcitonin)
  • Pheochromocytoma

Weight

  • Metformin: primary prevention (reduced CVD events, mortality)

Heart failure

  • SGLT-2i: secondary prevention in patients with ASCVD (reduced heart failure hospitalizations, mortality)

Nephropathy & kidney disease

  • SGLT-2i: reduction in DKD progression (most benefits for GFR >45 mL/min/1.73 m2)

  • TZDs: reduction in progression of disease; may not be feasible due to adverse effects (eg, heart failure, fluid retention)

  • Sulfonylureas (short-acting), DPP-4 inhibitors, insulin & potentially GLP-1 RA: appropriate for safety & glycemic control (rather than organ-specific benefits)

subs.title: Metformin
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Biguanides (eg, metformin)

Biguanides (eg, metformin)

Mechanism of action

  • Reduce hepatic gluconeogenesis by inhibiting mitochondrial enzymes
  • Increase insulin sensitivity by upregulating AMPK
  • Reduce lipolysis & free fatty acid concentrations

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • Moderate-high A1c reduction (~1%-2%)
  • Mild weight loss
  • Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease & mortality
  • Lower cost, wide availability

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Diarrhea, bloating (avoid by titrating dose)
  • Lactic acidosis (rare risk), B12 deficiency (longstanding use)

Precautions & contraindications

  • Conditions predisposing to lactic acidosis:
    • Severe infection
    • Renal failure, decompensated heart failure
    • Alcohol use disorder
  • Decreased fluid intake (consider temporary discontinuation)

A1c = hemoglobin A1c; AMPK = AMP-activated protein kinase.

subs.title: Pioglitazone
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Thiazolidinediones

Thiazolidinediones

Mechanism of action

  • Increase insulin sensitivity by activating PPAR-γ
  • Upregulate genes involved in glucose transport & fatty acid oxidation

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • Low A1c reduction (~0.5%-1%)
  • Possible reduction in NASH progression
  • No risk for hypoglycemia

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Weight gain & fluid retention
  • Possible increase in CVD risk (eg, heart failure) in high-risk patients
  • Peripheral edema, macular edema
  • Fracture

Precautions & contraindications

  • Heart failure
  • Macular edema
  • Osteoporosis
  • Severe liver disease (not NASH)

CVD = cardiovascular disease; NASH = nonalcoholic steatohepatitis; PPAR = peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor.
