Sulfonylureas

Sulfonylureas

Mechanism of action

  • Directly stimulate pancreatic beta cells to produce insulin
  • Glucose-independent effect

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • Moderate-high A1c reduction (~1%-2%)
  • Rapid glucose-lowering effects
  • Low cost

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Hypoglycemia (older, frail populations)
  • Weight gain (due to increased insulin secretion)
  • Possible CVD risk (eg, increased heart failure)
  • No mortality benefits

Precautions & contraindications

  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Sulfonamide allergy
  • Hypoglycemia (more liberal A1c target advised)

A1c = hemoglobin A1c; CVD = cardiovascular disease.

subs.title: GLP-1 analogs
subs.subject: pharm
tables: GLP-1 receptor agonists

GLP-1 receptor agonists

Mechanism of action

  • Mimic incretin effects of GLP-1
  • Increases pancreatic insulin release in response to oral food intake (glucose-dependent effect)
  • Slow gut motility, increased satiety
  • Additive effects when combined with GIP RA

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • High A1c reduction (~2%)
  • Weight loss
  • No associated hypoglycemia
  • Secondary prevention of ASCVD, mortality, possible renoprotection
  • Potential alternative if insulin cannot be used (T2DM only)

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Significant gastrointestinal distress (gastroparesis, pancreatitis)
  • Possible retinopathy (eg, semaglutide)
  • Evidence of primary prevention of ASCVD/mortality lacking

Precautions & contraindications

  • Medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2A/2B
  • History of gastroparesis or pancreatitis
  • Severe kidney impairment (<30-45 mL/min/1.73 m2)

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; GIP RA = glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide receptor agonist; GLP-1 = glucagon-like peptide 1; MEN = multiple endocrine neoplasia; T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus.

subs.title: DPP-4 inhibitors
subs.subject: pharm
tables: DPP-4 inhibitors

DPP-4 inhibitors

Mechanism of action

  • Inhibit enzyme responsible for degradation of GLP-1
  • Indirectly potentiate GLP-1 effects
    • Decreased gut motility
    • Increased glucose-dependent pancreatic insulin secretion
  • Modest A1c reduction (~1%)

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • No risk for hypoglycemia

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Decreased effectiveness compared to GLP-1 RA due to indirect effects (weight neutral, no ASCVD benefits)
  • Possible increased risk for heart failure (saxagliptin)
  • Adverse effects (eg, nasopharyngitis, pancreatitis)

Precautions & contraindications

  • Pancreatitis

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; DPP-4 = dipeptidyl peptidase-4; GLP-1 RA = glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist.

subs.title: Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Adverse effects of SGLT-2 inhibitors

Adverse effects of SGLT-2 inhibitors

Genitourinary infections

  • Vulvovaginal candidiasis
  • Urinary tract infection
  • Fournier gangrene (rare)

Osmotic diuresis

  • Volume depletion, symptomatic hypotension
  • Acute kidney injury

Metabolic disturbance

  • Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis

Orthopedic complications

  • Low-trauma fracture
  • Foot ulcers that may increase amputation risk

SGLT-2 = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2.
SGLT-2 inhibitors

SGLT-2 inhibitors

Mechanism of action

  • Increase urinary excretion of glucose (block SGLT-2 in proximal tubule, reducing glucose reabsorption)
  • Induce osmotic diuresis, leading to weight loss
  • Induce natriuresis, leading to decreased extracellular volume, reduced cardiac preload/afterload

Advantages & physiologic effects

  • Reduced progression of proteinuria & nephropathy
  • Reduced cardiovascular morbidity & mortality
  • Reduced heart failure hospitalizations
  • Moderate weight loss

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Genitourinary infections
  • Euglycemic ketoacidosis in states that increase glucagon secretion (eg, fasting, illness)
  • Decreased effectiveness with impaired renal function
  • Orthostatic hypotension

Precautions & contraindications

  • Concomitant diuretic use (may require dose reduction or discontinuation)
  • Severely reduced GFR (<30-45 mL/min/1.73 m2)
  • DKA

DKA = diabetic ketoacidosis; GFR = glomerular filtration; SGLT-2 = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2.

directTables: Levothyroxine replacement therapy for hypothyroidism

Levothyroxine replacement therapy for hypothyroidism

Initial dose

  • Standard dose: 75-125 mcg/day
  • Elderly, heart disease: 25-50 mcg/day

Dose adjustments

  • Increase dose every 6 weeks until TSH is within normal range

Maintenance therapy

  • Monitor TSH every 6-12 months

Conditions requiring
higher doses

  • Malabsorption (eg, celiac disease)
  • Drugs that interfere with absorption (eg, iron, calcium)
  • Drugs that increase thyroxine metabolism (eg, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin)
  • Other: obesity, pregnancy, overt proteinuria

topics.title: Vesicoureteral reflux
topics.subject: embryo
directTables: Primary vesicoureteral reflux in children

Primary vesicoureteral reflux in children

Pathogenesis

  • Retrograde urine flow through a short intravesical ureter

Presentation

  • Febrile urinary tract infection

Diagnosis

  • Renal ultrasonography: hydronephrosis
  • Voiding cystourethrography: ureteral filling ± dilated collecting system

Management

  • Mild (grade I-II)*: observation ± prophylactic antibiotics
  • Severe (grade III-IV)*: prophylactic antibiotics ± surgery

Prognosis

  • Mild: spontaneous resolution with growth
  • Severe (without intervention): renal scarring and chronic kidney disease

*Plus screening/treatment of concomitant bladder & bowel dysfunction (eg, stool softeners/laxatives).
Vesicoureteral reflux

Vesicoureteral reflux

Pathophysiology

  • Retrograde flow of urine through ureter to kidneys

Primary cause

  • Congenitally shortened intravesical ureter → incomplete UVJ closure

Secondary causes

  • High pressure within bladder and/or ureter
    • Neurogenic bladder
    • Dysfunctional voiding (nonneurogenic)
    • Obstruction (eg, calculus)
  • Chronic inflammation (weakened UVJ)

Complications

  • Acute pyelonephritis
  • Reflux nephropathy (eg, interstitial scarring, tubular atrophy)

UVJ = ureterovesical junction.

Medication

Mechanism

subs.title: Metabolic alkalosis
subs.subject: phys
tables: Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis

Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis

Common etiologies

  • Gastric suction or severe vomiting
  • Loop or thiazide diuretic overuse

Pathophysiology

  • Gastric or renal H+ losses initiate alkalosis
  • Volume depletion activates RAAS
  • ↑ Renal K+ & H+ losses cause hypokalemia & worsen alkalosis
  • Relatively greater loss of Cl− than Na+ → profound Cl− depletion
  • ↓ Cl− impairs renal HCO3− excretion to perpetuate alkalosis

Management

  • Remove or treat initiating factor
  • Cl− replenishment with normal saline corrects alkalosis

RAAS = renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

Rare, usually normal (ie, isomorphic)

Proteinuria3

Often ≥1+ (>500 mg/day)

Usually negative or trace (<500 mg/day)

Color

Dark red or brown (cola, tea)

Bright red or pink

Clots

Absent

Possible1

subs.title: Infection-related glomerulonephritis

tables: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis

Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis

Pathophysiology

  • Several weeks after GAS infection (eg, pharyngitis, impetigo)
  • GBM immune complex deposition
  • Complement component C3 & CH50 accumulation

Clinical
features

  • Can be asymptomatic
  • If symptomatic:
    • Gross hematuria (tea- or cola-colored urine)
    • Edema (periorbital, generalized)
    • Hypertension

Laboratory
findings

  • Urinalysis: + protein, + blood, ± RBC casts
  • Serum:
    • ↑ Creatinine
    • ↓ C3 & CH50
    • Possible ↓ C4
    • Positive streptozyme test*

Management

  • Supportive care
  • Volume overload: loop diuretics
  • Hypertension: ± additional antihypertensives
  • Refractory cases: hemodialysis

Prognosis

  • Complete recovery in a few weeks in children
  • Adults more likely to develop chronic kidney disease

*Streptozyme tests: antistreptolysin O, anti-DNAse B, antihyaluronidase, anti–nicotinamide
adenine dinucleotidase, antistreptokinase.

GAS = group A Streptococcus; GBM = glomerular basement membrane; RBC = red blood cell.

subs.title: Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis
subs.subject: path
tables: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome)

Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome)

Pathogenesis

  • Alveolar capillary insult → exposed GBM epitopes
  • Autoantibodies form against α-3 chain of type IV collagen

Presentation

Autoantibodies bind to epitopes at:

  • Alveolar GBM → diffuse alveolar hemorrhage → dyspnea, hemoptysis
  • Renal GBM → RPGN → hypertension, hematuria

Pathology

  • Immunofluorescence: linear deposition of IgG & C3b on renal GBM

subs.title: Minimal change disease
subs.subject: path
tables: Minimal change disease

Minimal change disease

Epidemiology

  • Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children

Pathogenesis

  • T-cell–mediated injury to podocytes → ↑ molecular permeability to albumin

Clinical features

  • Edema (eg, periorbital, scrotal, generalized)
  • Fatigue
  • ± Abdominal pain

Diagnosis

  • Urine: nephrotic-range proteinuria
  • Serum: hypoalbuminemia ± hyperlipidemia
  • Kidney biopsy*: diffuse effacement of foot processes on EM

Treatment

  • Corticosteroids

Prognosis

  • Most achieve remission, but relapse is common
  • Low risk of chronic kidney disease if episodes are steroid responsive

*Indicated only for atypical cases.

EM = electron microscopy.

subs.title: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
subs.subject: path
tables: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

Pathogenesis

  • Primary FSGS: circulating factor causing immune injury to podocytes
  • Secondary FSGS: glomerular hyperfiltration (eg, obesity, solitary kidney, reflux nephropathy), podocyte toxin (eg, heroin), infection (eg, HIVAN)

Clinical features

  • Primary FSGS: usually nephrotic syndrome
  • Secondary FSGS: proteinuria ± nephrotic syndrome

Diagnosis

  • LM: segmental scarring in <50% of glomeruli*
  • IF: usually negative
  • EM: podocyte foot process effacement**

Treatment

  • Renin-angiotensin blockade, loop diuretics
  • Primary FSGS: immunosuppression
  • Secondary FSGS: risk factor modification (eg, weight loss, ART)

*Glomerular tuft collapse is also seen in HIVAN.

**Diffuse (≥80%) effacement in primary; segmental (<80%) effacement in secondary.

ART = antiretroviral therapy; EM = electron microscopy; FSGS = focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; HIVAN = HIV-associated nephropathy; IF = immunofluorescence microscopy; LM = light microscopy.

subs.title: Membranous nephropathy
subs.subject: path
tables: Membranous nephropathy

Membranous nephropathy

Etiology

  • Primary (most common): podocyte autoantibodies (eg, anti-PLA2R, anti-THSD7A [rare])
  • Secondary: solid tumors, NSAIDs, hepatitis B, lupus nephritis

Presentation

  • Nephrotic syndrome*

Diagnosis

  • Primary: testing for anti-PLA2R antibodies**
  • Secondary: testing for underlying disease (eg, cancer screening, virus testing, ANA testing); kidney biopsy

Management

  • Supportive measures for all (eg, ACE inhibitor, diuretic)
  • Primary:
    • Low risk: observation (spontaneous remission common)
    • Moderate to high risk: immunosuppression
  • Secondary: treatment of underlying disease, discontinuation of culprit medication

*Generalized edema, heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) & hypoalbuminemia.

**Kidney biopsy not needed when anti-PLA2R antibodies are present, kidney function is normal & evidence of secondary disease is absent.

ANA = antinuclear antibody; NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug; PLA2R = phospholipase A2 receptor; THSD7A = thrombospondin type-1 domain–containing 7A.

subs.title: Diabetic glomerulonephropathy
subs.subject: path
images: Prevention & management of diabetic kidney disease
tables: Typical features of diabetic kidney disease

Typical features of diabetic kidney disease

Major findings

  • Persistent albuminuria (>3 months duration)
  • Initial hyperfiltration followed by progressive decline in GFR
  • Hypertension usually present

Typical course

  • Gradual onset
    • ≥5 years after type 1 DM diagnosis
    • May be present at diagnosis in type 2 DM
  • Slow progression

Atypical features

Consider renal biopsy & additional evaluation if any of the following is present:

  • Early onset (<5 years after type 1 DM diagnosis)
  • Rapid progression:
    • >5-10× increase in albuminuria in <1-2 years
    • >5 mL/min/1.73 m2 decline in GFR per year
  • Active urinary sediment (eg, white or red blood cell casts)
  • Comorbid conditions associated with glomerulonephritis (eg, SLE)

DM = diabetes mellitus; GFR = glomerular filtration rate; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.
Characteristics warranting further work-up* in diagnosis of DKD

Characteristics warranting further work-up* in diagnosis of DKD

  • Active urinary sediment (eg, red blood cell casts, dysmorphic red blood cells, white blood cell casts)
  • Rapidly declining renal function and/or acute, severe rise in proteinuria (eg, over <1-2 years)
  • Initial presentation of severely increased albuminuria <5 years after onset of T1DM
  • Comorbid autoimmune disorder suggesting possible alternate etiology (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus)
  • Significant urinary symptoms (eg, postvoid dribbling, dysuria)

*Renal biopsy, ultrasonography.

DKD = diabetic kidney disease; T1DM = type 1 diabetes mellitus.

directImages: Major mechanisms of edema in nephrotic syndrome
images: Major mechanisms of edema in nephrotic syndrome
Prevention & management of diabetic kidney disease
directTables: Complications of nephrotic syndrome*

Complications of nephrotic syndrome*

Mechanism

Hypercoagulability
(↑ thromboembolism risk)

  • Urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins (eg, antithrombin III)
  • Hepatic synthesis of prothrombotic proteins (eg, fibrinogen)

Hyperlipidemia
(↑ atherosclerosis risk)

  • Hepatic synthesis of lipoproteins

Infection
(particularly encapsulated bacteria)

  • Urinary loss of immunoglobulins & opsonizing factors

Protein malnutrition

  • Negative nitrogen balance

Intravascular volume depletion

  • Low oncotic pressure

*Nephrotic syndrome results from glomerular filtration barrier (eg, podocyte) injury that leads to heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia & peripheral edema.

Risk & prevention of kidney stones

Stone type

Risk factors

Prevention

Calcium stones

(oxalate, phosphate)

  • Hypercalciuria (eg, hyperparathyroidism)
  • Hyperoxaluria (eg, malabsorption,
    low-calcium diet)
  • Hypocitraturia (eg, distal RTA)
  • Diet: ↑ sodium, ↑ protein, ↑ oxalate, 
    ↓ calcium
  • Reduce sodium, animal protein, oxalate intake
  • Increase potassium intake; moderate calcium intake

Uric acid

  • Gout

  • Urine alkalinization
  • Allopurinol

Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite)

  • Recurrent upper urinary infection
    (eg, Klebsiella, Proteus)
  • Stone removal
  • Suppressive antibiotics

All types

  • Dehydration
  • Increase fluid intake

topics.title: Hydronephrosis
topics.subject: path
directTables: Urinary tract obstruction

Urinary tract obstruction

Common
etiologies

  • Bladder: prostate disease, stones, tumors, neurogenic
  • Ureters: tumors/adenopathy, stones, retroperitoneal fibrosis
  • Urethra: posterior valves (in children)

Clinical
presentation

Site of obstruction

  • Bladder: bilateral hydronephrosis; high postvoid residual
  • Ureter: unilateral or bilateral hydronephrosis; low/no postvoid residual if bilateral

Complications

  • Renal function: AKI progressing to CKD (atrophy) if untreated
  • Other: infection & urosepsis (due to stasis)

Management

  • Decompression: PCNT/stenting (ureteral); urethral Foley catheterization (bladder)
  • Postobstructive polyuria: careful fluid & electrolyte management
  • Address underlying cause

AKI = acute kidney injury; CKD = chronic kidney disease; PCNT = percutaneous nephrostomy tube.

topics.title: Acute cystitis
topics.subject: path
directTables: Interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome)

Interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome)

Epidemiology

  • More common in women
  • Associated with psychiatric & pain disorders (eg, fibromyalgia)

Clinical presentation

  • Bladder pain with filling, relief with voiding
  • ↑ Urinary frequency, urgency
  • Dyspareunia

Diagnosis

  • Bladder pain with no other cause for ≥6 weeks
  • Normal urinalysis

Treatment

  • Not curative; focus is on improving quality of life
  • Behavioral modification, avoidance of triggers, physical therapy
  • Amitriptyline, pentosan polysulfate sodium
  • Analgesics for acute exacerbations
Urine dipstick results in

Urine dipstick results in urinary tract infection

Result

Pathophysiology

Clinical significance

Leukocyte esterase

  • Released by lysed neutrophils/macrophages
  • Marker of white blood cells

Nitrites*

  • Produced by conversion of urinary nitrate into nitrite by nitrate reductase
  • Marker of nitrate reductase–producing bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus mirabilis)

pH

  • Alkaline urine (pH >8) due to ammonia produced from hydrolysis of urea by urease
  • Marker of urease-producing bacteria (eg, Proteus mirabilis)

*The absence of nitrites does not exclude these bacteria.
Acute cystitis

Acute cystitis

Microbiology

  • Escherichia coli (most common)
  • Other gram-negative pathogens (eg, Proteus spp., Klebsiella spp.)
  • Staphylococcus saprophyticus

Clinical features

  • Dysuria
  • Increased urinary frequency and/or urgency
  • Suprapubic tenderness

Diagnosis

  • Urinalysis with pyuria (WBC > 10 cells/mm3), bacteria & positive leukocyte esterase and/or nitrites
  • Urine culture for organism identification & susceptibility

Empiric treatment

Oral antibiotics

  • Nitrofurantoin* 100 mg BID × 5 days
  • Fosfomycin 3 grams × 1 dose
  • Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim DS 1 tablet BID × 3 days (if no sulfa allergy)
*Contraindicated if creatinine clearance is < 60 mL/min.

DS = double-strength; WBC = white blood cells.

directTables: Laboratory features of rhabdomyolysis

Laboratory features of rhabdomyolysis

Muscle
enzymes

  • Elevated CK (often >10,000 U/L)

Urine tests

  • Red to brown urine with positive blood but no RBCs (myoglobinuria)

Electrolytes

  • Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia & hyperuricemia due to intracellular electrolyte release
  • Hypocalcemia & dehydration due to influx of calcium & intravascular fluid into injured muscles

Creatinine

  • AKI due to tubular injury from myoglobinuria
  • FENa can be falsely low

AKI = acute kidney injury; CK = creatine kinase; FENa = fractional excretion of sodium; RBCs = red blood cells.
Contrast-associated acute kidney injury

Contrast-associated acute kidney injury

Presentation

  • Highest risk with arterial iodinated contrast (eg, coronary angiogram)
  • Creatinine elevation 24-48 hr after contrast exposure, gradually returning to baseline within 3-7 days
  • Clinical diagnosis based on timing & trajectory above (ie, biopsy rarely needed)

Risk factors

  • Preexisting chronic kidney disease (especially diabetic nephropathy)
  • Decreased kidney perfusion (eg, NSAIDs, hypovolemia, venous congestion)
  • High contrast load

Pathophysiology

  • Prerenal vasoconstriction & direct tubular cytotoxicity
  • Prerenal state (eg, FeNa <1%) with concurrent necrosis (eg, muddy brown casts)

Prevention

  • Optimize kidney perfusion (eg, intravenous saline, avoidance of NSAIDs)
  • Minimize contrast load

FeNa = fractional excretion of sodium; NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug.
Rhabdomyolysis

Rhabdomyolysis

Etiology

Skeletal muscle lysis/necrosis due to:

  • Crush injury or prolonged immobilization
  • Intense muscle activity (eg, seizure, exertion)
  • Drug/medication toxicity (eg, statins)

Clinical features

  • Muscle pain & weakness
  • Dark urine (myoglobinuria/pigmenturia)
  • + Blood on urinalysis & no RBCs on microscopy
  • ↑ Serum K & PO4, ↓ serum Ca, ↑ AST > ALT
  • Acute kidney injury

Diagnosis

  • Serum creatine kinase >1,000 U/L
  • Consistent clinical features

Management

  • Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation
  • Sodium bicarbonate in some cases

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; RBCs = red blood cells.

directTables: Renal artery stenosis

Renal artery stenosis

Etiology

  • Atherosclerotic narrowing of the renal artery (>90% of cases)
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia (younger women)

Risk factors

  • Other atherosclerotic disease (eg, CAD, carotid stenosis)
  • Smoking, diabetes, hypertension

Presentation

  • Refractory hypertension
  • Recurrent flash pulmonary edema
  • Abdominal bruits
  • Acute kidney injury after initiation of ACE inhibitor

Pathology

  • Gross: Shrunken, atrophic kidney
  • Microscopic: Crowded glomeruli, tubular atrophy, interstitial
    fibrosis, focal inflammatory infiltrates

manifestations

treatment

directTables: Bladder cancer

Bladder cancer

Epidemiology

  • >90% urothelial carcinoma
  • ↑ Risk with smokers & exposure to industrial carcinogens

Manifestations

  • Painless hematuria throughout micturition
  • Irritative voiding symptoms (eg, frequency, urgency, dysuria)
  • Regional pain

Diagnosis

  • Flexible cystoscopy with biopsy (gold standard)
  • Urine cytology

Staging

  • TURBT
  • Upper urinary tract imaging (eg, IVP, MRI, CT scan)

Treatment

  • No muscle invasion: TURBT & intravesical immunotherapy
  • Muscle invasion: radical cystectomy & systemic chemotherapy
  • Metastatic: systemic chemotherapy & immunotherapy

IVP = intravenous pyelogram; TURBT = transurethral resection of bladder tumor.

topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Diuretic effects

Diuretic effects

 

Drug

Mechanism of action

Electrolyte abnormalities

Clinical indications

Loop diuretics

  • Furosemide
  • Torsemide
  • Bumetanide
  • Ethacrynic acid
  • Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
  • Hypokalemia
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Hypocalcemia
  • Volume-overloaded states (eg, congestive heart failure)

Thiazide diuretics

  • Hydrochlorothiazide
  • Chlorthalidone
  • Indapamide
  • Metolazone
  • Inhibits the Na-Cl cotransporter in the early distal convoluted tubule
  • Hyponatremia
  • Hypokalemia
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Hypertension
  • Calcium nephrolithiasis prophylaxis

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

  • Acetazolamide
  • Inhibits carbonic anhydrase enzyme in the proximal tubule
  • Hypokalemia
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Refractory metabolic alkalosis
  • Intracranial hypertension

Sodium channel blockers

  • Amiloride
  • Triamterene
  • Inhibits the apical ENaC channel in the cortical collecting duct
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Often used in synergy with loop & thiazide diuretics to limit potassium loss

Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists

  • Spironolactone
  • Eplerenone
  • Inhibits the apical ENaC channel & basolateral Na-K-ATPase pump in the cortical collecting tubules
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Metabolic acidosis

topics.title: Lung malformations
topics.subject: embryo
directTables: Congenital lung malformations

Congenital lung malformations

Pathogenesis

Clinical presentation

Bronchopulmonary anomalies

Bronchogenic cyst

Foregut duplication (embryonic stage)

  • Typically asymptomatic
  • Recurrent childhood respiratory infections (eg, postobstructive pneumonia)
  • Rare malignant transformation
  • Airway obstruction (eg, hyperinflation or atelectasis)

Congenital pulmonary airway malformation

Defective branching morphogenesis (pseudoglandular stage)

Pulmonary hypoplasia

Impaired alveolar development (any stage) due to compression (or oligohydramnios)

  • Severe respiratory failure
  • Persistent pulmonary hypertension (underdeveloped vasculature)

Congenital lobar emphysema

Bronchial "ball valve" obstruction from another developmental lesion

  • Increased work of breathing (eg, nasal flaring, retractions)
  • Unilateral hyperinflation (eg, hyperresonance)

Vascular anomalies

Bronchopulmonary sequestration

Systemically perfused region of lung tissue disconnected from the main respiratory tree

  • Typically asymptomatic
  • Recurrent respiratory infections due to lack of drainage

Pulmonary artery defects

Pulmonary artery atresia, stenosis, or slings

  • Atresia: Pulmonary hypertension (eg, atretic vascular bed)
  • Slings: Tracheal or esophageal compression

Anomalous pulmonary venous return

Anastomoses of pulmonary veins to right atrium or vena cavae (instead of left atrium)

  • Partial: Noncyanotic at birth but progression to right heart failure
  • Total: Cyanotic at birth

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations

Direct connection between pulmonary artery and vein, bypassing capillaries

  • Paradoxical emboli
  • Brain abscess
  • Hypoxia (right-to-left shunting)

Pulmonary artery defects

Pulmonary artery atresia, stenosis, or slings

  • Atresia: Pulmonary hypertension (eg, atretic vascular bed)
  • Slings: Tracheal or esophageal compression

Anomalous pulmonary venous return

Anastomoses of pulmonary veins to right atrium or vena cavae (instead of left atrium)

  • Partial: Noncyanotic at birth but progression to right heart failure
  • Total: Cyanotic at birth

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations

Direct connection between pulmonary artery and vein, bypassing capillaries

  • Paradoxical emboli
  • Brain abscess
  • Hypoxia (right-to-left shunting)

directTables: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia

Bronchopulmonary dysplasia

Pathogenesis

  • Premature arrest of pulmonary development
  • Alveolar hypoplasia with ↓ septation
  • Impaired vasculogenesis

Clinical diagnosis

  • Premature infant with continued supplemental oxygen requirement ≥28 days from birth*

Chest x-ray

  • Mild: diffuse hazy infiltrates, low/normal lung volumes
  • Severe: fibrocystic changes, hyperinflation

Treatment

  • Supportive (eg, oxygen, nutrition, fluid restriction/diuretics)

Complications

  • Pulmonary artery hypertension
  • Cardiovascular disease (eg, hypertension)
  • Recurrent respiratory infections

*Some definitions include an oxygen requirement at 36 weeks postmenstrual age (ie, gestational + chronologic age).
Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome

Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • Surfactant deficiency in premature infants
  • ↑ Alveolar surface tension → diffuse atelectasis
  • Ventilation/perfusion mismatch causes right-to-left intrapulmonary shunting

Clinical features

  • Tachypnea, retractions, grunting immediately after birth
  • Cyanosis & hypoxia
  • Decreased breath sounds

Chest x-ray

  • Diffuse, ground-glass appearance
  • Air bronchograms
  • ↓ Lung volumes

Management

  • Surfactant administration
  • Respiratory support (eg, continuous positive airway pressure)

Prevention

  • Antenatal corticosteroids (stimulate fetal surfactant production)

Complications

  • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (chronic lung disease)

topics.title: Alveolar gas equation
topics.subject: phys
directTables: Alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient calculation: worked example

Alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient calculation: worked example

48-year-old woman with emphysema
ABGs: pH 7.34, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, PaO2 50 mm Hg

Step 1

Calculate PiO2

  • PiO2 is the inspired oxygen that reaches the alveoli
  • Determined by atmospheric pressure (Patm), water vapor (PH2O) & FiO2 (21% at room air)

►Patient's PiO2 = (Patm − PH2O) × (FiO2) = (760 − 47) × (0.21) = 150 mm Hg

Step 2

Calculate PAO2

  • PAO2 is the oxygen in the alveolar airspace after admixture with CO2
  • Each molecule of O2 occupies the same space as 0.8 molecules of CO2

►Patient's PAO2 = PiO2 − PaCO2 / 0.8 = 150 − 60 / 0.8 = 150 − 75 = 75 mm Hg

Step 3

Calculate A-a gradient

  • Difference between PAO2 (calculated above) & PaO2 (from ABG analysis)
  • Elevated by a damaged alveolar membrane (eg, emphysema) or by right-to-left shunt

►Patient's A-a gradient = PAO2 − PaO2 = 75 − 50 = 25 mm Hg

Step 4

Compare to normal

  • Small A-a gradient is normal due to physiologic right-to-left shunting (eg, bronchial arteries)
  • Expected A-a gradient ~ age / 3 = 48 / 3 = 16 mm Hg

►Patient's A-a gradient is elevated (25 > 16)

ABG = arterial blood gas.

topics.title: Response to high altitude
topics.subject: phys
directTables: Physiologic responses to high altitude

Physiologic responses to high altitude

Lungs

  • Hypoxic vasoconstriction → ↑ PVR & PAP
  • ↑ Minute ventilation → ↑ PaO2 & ↓ PaCO2

Kidneys

  • ↑ Erythropoietin production
  • ↑ HCO3− excretion (compensatory metabolic acidosis)
  • Aldosterone suppression with diuresis & ↓ plasma volume

Blood

  • ↑ 2,3-biphosphoglycerate → ↑ O2 unloading in tissues
  • Upregulation of HIF → erythropoiesis & angiogenesis
  • ↑ Hemoglobin concentration (O2-carrying capacity)

Heart

  • ↑ Heart rate & slightly ↑ cardiac output

Brain

  • Vasodilation with ↑ cerebral blood flow

HIF = hypoxia inducible factor; PAP = pulmonary arterial pressure; PVR = pulmonary vascular resistance.

topics.title: Methemoglobin
topics.subject: phys
directTables: Clinical presentation of methemoglobinemia

Clinical presentation of methemoglobinemia

History

  • Exposure to oxidizing substances (eg, dapsone, nitrites,
    local/topical anesthetic)

Clinical examination

  • Cyanosis
  • Pulse oximetry saturation ~85%
  • Dark chocolate–colored blood

Laboratory findings

  • Saturation gap (>5% difference between oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry & ABG)
  • Normal PaO2

ABG = arterial blood gas.
Acquired methemoglobinemia

Acquired methemoglobinemia

Precipitating factors

  • Dapsone
  • Local/topical anesthetics (eg, benzocaine, teething medications)
  • Nitrates/nitrites (eg, drinking ground water)

Pathophysiology

  • Oxidation of heme iron from Fe2+ to Fe3+
  • Fe3+ unable to bind oxygen
  • Oxygen affinity of other hemes increased → left shift → decreased tissue oxygen delivery

Clinical manifestations

  • Cyanosis (not improved with supplemental O2)
  • Chocolate-brown blood (no color change on exposure to air/oxygen)
  • Pulse oximetry inaccurate → reads near 85% due to absorption wavelength

Management

  • Methylene blue

topics.subject: phys

subs.title: Cyanide
subs.subject: phys
tables: Manifestations of cyanide accumulation & toxicity

Manifestations of cyanide accumulation & toxicity

  • Skin: flushing (cherry-red color), cyanosis (occurs later)
  • CNS: headache, altered mental status, seizures, coma
  • Cardiovascular: arrhythmias
  • Respiratory: tachypnea followed by respiratory depression, pulmonary edema
  • Gastrointestinal: abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting
  • Renal: metabolic acidosis (from lactic acidosis), kidney failure
Treatment overview for suspected cyanide poisoning

Treatment overview for suspected cyanide poisoning

Decontamination

Dermal exposure

  • Removal of clothing
  • Skin decontamination

Ingestion

  • Activated charcoal

All exposures

  • Antidote
  • Hydroxocobalamin preferred
  • Sodium thiosulphate as alternate therapy
  • Antidote not available
  • Nitrites to induce methemoglobinemia

Respiratory support

  • No mouth-to-mouth resuscitation
  • Supplemental oxygen
  • Airway protection (intubation)

Cardiovascular support

  • Intravenous fluids for hypotension
Cyanide poisoning

Cyanide poisoning

Common etiologies

  • Structure fires (eg, combustion of plastics)
  • Occupational exposure (eg, mining)
  • Cyanide-containing medications (eg, sodium nitroprusside)

Pathophysiology

  • Inhibits oxidative phosphorylation & forces anaerobic metabolism
  • Rapidly lethal if untreated

Clinical features

  • Hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnea → circulatory collapse, death
  • Headache, confusion, anxiety → seizures, coma
  • Cherry-red skin
  • Elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis with ↑ lactic acid

Management

  • Decontamination
  • Supportive care (eg, 100% oxygen, intravenous fluids, vasopressors)
  • Empiric treatment with hydroxocobalamin ± sodium thiosulfate*

*Sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulfate is an alternate treatment but is contraindicated in carbon monoxide poisoning.

Upper extremity deep venous thrombosis

Epidemiology

  • Central catheter or PICC line

  • Thoracic outlet obstruction

Manifestations

  • Unilateral arm or forearm edema
  • Pain/heavy sensation
  • Erythema

Diagnosis

Treatment

Postthrombotic syndrome

Postthrombotic syndrome

Epidemiology

  • Chronic venous insufficiency following acute DVT
  • Most cases arise within 2 years of thrombus

Manifestations

  • Leg edema, fatigue, pain, superficial venous dilation, venous stasis ulcers
  • Often worse at the end of the day

Treatment

  • Exercise (eg, ankle flexion, walking)
  • Compression (eg, bandages, stockings)

directTables: +3 points

Modified Wells criteria for pretest probability
of pulmonary embolism

+3 points

  • Clinical signs of DVT
  • Alternate diagnosis less likely than PE

+1.5 points

  • Previous PE or DVT
  • Heart rate >100/min
  • Recent surgery or immobilization

+1 point

  • Hemoptysis
  • Cancer

Total score

  • ≤4 = PE unlikely
  • >4 = PE likely

DVT = deep vein thrombosis; PE = pulmonary embolism.
Pulmonary embolism management

Pulmonary embolism management

Classification

Definition

Typical management

Low risk

  • No RV dysfunction
 
  • No hypotension (SBP ≥90 mm Hg)
  • Anticoagulation unless contraindicated

Submassive

  • RV dysfunction (dilation &/or hypokinesis)
    • Higher risk: elevated biomarkers (troponin I &/or BNP)
 
  • No hypotension
  • Individualized strategies ranging from anticoagulation to tailored (eg, catheter-directed) thrombolysis if higher risk

Massive

  • RV dysfunction
 
  • Hypotension (SBP <90 mm Hg)
  • Systemic thrombolysis &/or embolectomy

BNP = B-type natriuretic peptide; RV = right ventricle; SBP = systolic blood pressure.

Acute postoperative mediastinitis

Etiology/epidemiology

  • Direct microbial contamination of operative site
  • Complicates 1%-2% of cardiothoracic operations involving sternotomy

Clinical presentation

  • 1-2 weeks after the operation

tables: Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Precipitants

  • Infectious (70%): respiratory viruses (eg, rhinovirus) & commensal bacteria (eg, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae)
  • Noninfectious (30%): sterile inflammation (underlying disease), pulmonary embolism, inhaled irritants

Pathophysiology
& presentation

  • Bronchial inflammation: systemic response (eg, fever, leukocytosis) usually absent
  • Cardinal symptoms: ↑ dyspnea, ↑ sputum volume, ↑ sputum purulence
  • ↑ WOB (hyperinflation) & impaired gas exchange (hypoxemia [↓ V/Q], hypercapnia [↑ VD])

Management

  • Maximize expiratory flow: inhaled bronchodilators
  • Reduce airway inflammation: systemic glucocorticoids
  • Treat underlying triggers: ± antibiotics* &/or antivirals (influenza, COVID-19)
  • Maintain adequate oxygenation: SpO2 target 88%-92%
  • Maintain adequate ventilation: NIPPV or invasive mechanical ventilation

*Antibiotics generally indicated if (1) there is increased sputum purulence + ≥1 other cardinal symptoms or (2) patient requires hospitalization.

NIPPV = noninvasive positive pressure ventilation; VD = alveolar dead space ventilation; V/Q = ventilation/perfusion ratio; WOB = work of breathing.
Management of stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Management of stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Nonpharmacologic

  • Smoking cessation*
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation*
  • Vaccination (influenza*, pneumococcal, COVID-19)
  • Long-term oxygen therapy* if SaO2 ≤88% at rest
  • Nocturnal noninvasive ventilation if daytime hypercapnia*

Surgical

  • Lung volume reduction or lung transplantation for advanced disease*

Medications

  • Bronchodilators (LAMA, LABA) ± ICS
  • Long-term macrolide (eg, azithromycin 3× weekly)**
  • PDE4 inhibitor (eg, roflumilast)**
  • Biologic therapy (eg, anti–IL-5 mAb) if eosinophilic/asthma overlap**

*Reduces mortality.

**Reduces hospitalizations for patients with frequent exacerbations.

ICS = inhaled corticosteroid; LABA = long-acting β2 agonist; LAMA = long-acting muscarinic antagonist; mAb = monoclonal antibody; PDE4 = phosphodiesterase 4.

Pathogenesis
& risk factors

  • Idiosyncratic (ie, not dose dependent) hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  • Risk factors: rheumatoid arthritis, parenchymal lung disease

Clinical

  • Onset 1-12 months: pneumonitis → fibrosis (restrictive PFTs)

topics.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
topics.subject: path
directTables: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

Pathophysiology
& risk factors

  • Microscopic alveolar epithelial injury (smoking, GERD, silent aspiration)
  • Inappropriate repair by fibrosis instead of epithelial regeneration
  • Risk factors/demographics: male, age >60, smoking, polymorphisms in genes regulating epithelial regeneration & health

Clinical presentation

  • Chronic progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, fatigue
  • Fine, Velcro-like inspiratory crackles; digital clubbing
  • HRCT: UIP (subpleural honeycombing, reticular opacities); PFTs: restrictive pattern

Management

  • Antifibrotic therapy (eg, pirfenidone, nintedanib)
  • Smoking cessation & treatment of GERD
  • Supplemental oxygen & pulmonary rehabilitation
  • Lung transplantation

GERD = gastroesophageal reflux disease; HRCT = high-resolution computed tomography; PFT = pulmonary function test; UIP = usual interstitial pneumonia.

topics.title: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

directTables: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

Etiology

  • Immunologic response to inhaled antigen (eg, mold, animal protein)

Clinical presentation

Acute

  • Abrupt-onset fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, fatigue, leukocytosis
  • Episodes often recurrent and self-resolving
  • Chest x-ray: scattered micronodular interstitial opacities
 

Chronic

  • Progressive cough, dyspnea, fatigue, weight loss
  • Hypoxemia that worsens with exertion
  • Chest x-ray: diffuse reticular interstitial opacities

Diagnosis

  • PFT: restrictive pattern, ↓ DLCO (chronic only)
  • BAL: high relative lymphocyte count
  • Lung biopsy: lymphocytic infiltrate, poorly formed noncaseating granulomas, interstitial inflammation or fibrosis (chronic only)

Treatment

  • Remove antigen exposure (resolves acute disease)
  • Glucocorticoids and/or lung transplantation (chronic only)

BAL = bronchoalveolar lavage; DLCO = diffusion capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide; PFT = pulmonary function testing.

Manifestations of sarcoidosis

Pulmonary

  • Bilateral hilar adenopathy
  • Interstitial infiltrates

Cutaneous

  • Papular, nodular, or plaquelike lesions
  • Erythema nodosum

Ophthalmologic

  • Anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis or iritis)
  • Posterior uveitis
  • Keratoconjunctivitis sicca

Reticuloendothelial

  • Peripheral lymphadenopathy
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Splenomegaly

Musculoskeletal

  • Acute polyarthritis (especially ankles)
  • Chronic arthritis

Cardiovascular

  • Atrioventricular block
  • Dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy

CNS/endocrine

  • Facial nerve palsy
  • Central diabetes insipidus
  • Hypercalcemia

Löfgren syndrome

  • Erythema nodosum
  • Hilar adenopathy
  • Migratory polyarthralgia
  • Fever
Sarcoidosis organ involvement & recommended treatment

Sarcoidosis organ involvement & recommended treatment

System

Indications for systemic corticosteroids

Indications for additional therapies

Lungs

  • Abnormal PFT
  • Dyspnea
  • Cough or wheezing (ICS)

Skin

  • Disfiguring plaques or nodules
  • Lupus pernio
  • Erythema nodosum (NSAIDs)

Musculoskeletal

  • Arthritis
  • Myositis & myopathy

Cardiac

  • Infiltrative cardiomyopathy
  • Conduction system disease
  • Dysrhythmias (ICD, pacemaker)

CNS

  • Encephalopathy
  • Hypopituitarism (hormone replacement)

Eyes

  • Uveitis

Other

  • Symptomatic hypercalcemia

Any organ-threatening disease unresponsive to corticosteroids

  • MTX, anti-TNF-α agents

Sarcoidosis organ involvement & recommended treatment

System

Indications for systemic corticosteroids

Lungs

Skin

  • Disfiguring plaques or nodules

directTables: Initial ventilator setup in ARDS

Initial ventilator setup in ARDS

Mode

  • Volume assist-control  

Tidal volume

  • Initial 8 mL/kg IBW
  • Reduce to 4-6 mL/kg over 1-3 hours

PEEP

  • 5-15 cm H2O
  • High PEEP for moderate/severe ARDS

Plateau pressure

  • ≤30 cm H2O

Rate

  • ≤35 breaths/min

Goal pH

  • ≥7.20

PaO2/SaO2

  • 55-80 mm Hg/88%-95%

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; IBW = ideal body weight; PEEP = positive end-expiratory pressure.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome: pathogenesis & diagnosis

Acute respiratory distress syndrome: pathogenesis & diagnosis

Risk factors &
pathogenesis

  • Direct (eg, pneumonia, inhalation) or indirect (eg, sepsis, pancreatitis, trauma) lung injury
  • Inflammatory cell activation & ↑ permeability ↔ fluid & cytokine leakage into alveoli

Pathophysiology

  • ↓ Lung compliance (alveolar flooding) → ↑ work of breathing
  • Severe V/Q mismatch (intrapulmonary shunt) → severe hypoxemia
  • ↑ Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → ↑ RV afterload & acute PHTN

Diagnosis

  • New bilateral alveolar opacities within 1 week of inciting insult
  • Edema not explained by cardiac failure or volume overload
  • Hypoxemia with PaO2/FiO2 ≤300
PHTN = pulmonary hypertension; RV = right ventricular; V/Q = ventilation/perfusion.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome: management & prognosis

Acute respiratory distress syndrome: management & prognosis

Mechanical ventilation

  • Lung protection: limit alveolar distending volume (VT 6 mL/kg) & pressure (Pplat ≤30 cm H2O)
  • Ventilation: tolerate permissive hypercapnia (ie, ↑ PaCO2 & ↓ pH acceptable) to avoid excessive VT
  • Oxygenation: set lowest feasible FiO2 (goal SpO2 92%-96%) to avoid O2 toxicity

Supportive care

  • Treat underlying etiology: source control (eg, sepsis)
  • Prevent iatrogenic harm: negative fluid balance, timely extubation (eg, minimize sedation)
  • ± Corticosteroids: select patients with moderate-to-severe early ARDS

Prognosis

  • Mortality rate: 40% in hospital, death mostly due to multiorgan failure
  • Morbidity rate: 50% with chronic cognitive impairment & physical debility, 25% with chronic pulmonary dysfunction (restriction & ↓ DLCO)

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; DLCO = diffusion capacity of lung for carbon monoxide; Pplat = plateau pressure; SpO2 = oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximetry; VT = tidal volume.
Diffuse airspace opacification

Diffuse airspace opacification

Definition: Alveolar filling processes that can involve multiple lobes

Fluid

  • Transudative edema: cardiogenic
  • Exudative edema: noncardiogenic (ARDS)

Cells

  • Neutrophils (pus): infectious pneumonia
  • Lymphocytes & macrophages: hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  • Eosinophils: acute eosinophilic pneumonia
  • Malignant cells: carcinomatosis

Blood

  • Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
  • Aspirated nonalveolar hemorrhage

Others

  • Fat: lipoid pneumonia (eg, vaping oils)
  • Protein: pulmonary alveolar proteinosis

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome.

subs.title: Obstructive sleep apnea
subs.subject: path
tables: STOP-Bang survey for obstructive sleep apnea

STOP-Bang survey for obstructive sleep apnea

1 point for each characteristic present

  • Snoring
  • Excessive daytime tiredness
  • Observed apneas or choking/gasping
  • High blood pressure
  • BMI >35 kg/m2
  • Age >50
  • Neck size: men >17 in (43.2 cm), women >16 in (40.6 cm)
  • Male gender

Scoring: 0-2 points: low risk; 3-4 points: intermediate risk; ≥5 points: high risk.
Clinical characteristics of obstructive sleep apnea

Clinical characteristics of obstructive sleep apnea

Symptoms/signs

  • Insomnia, nonrestorative sleep, daytime somnolence
  • Witnessed apneas ± snoring
  • Mood changes, cognitive deficits, impaired concentration, fatigue
  • Morning headaches
Potential sequelae
  • Resistant hypertension
  • Angina pectoris
  • Cardiac dysrhythmias
  • Pulmonary hypertension & cor pulmonale
  • Polycythemia
  • Decreased libido & impotence
Diagnosis
  • Polysomnography
Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea

Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea

Pathophysiology

  • Adenotonsillar hypertrophy

Clinical manifestations

  • Night symptoms
    • Loud snoring, pauses in breathing, gasping
    • Enuresis, parasomnias (eg, sleepwalking, sleep terrors)
  • Day symptoms
    • Inappropriate naps or falling asleep during school
    • Irritability, inattention, learning problems, behavioral problems
    • Mouth breathing, nasal speech

Complications

  • Poor growth (ie, failure to thrive)
  • Poor school performance
  • Cardiopulmonary (eg, hypertension, structural heart changes)

Management

  • Tonsillectomy & adenoidectomy
Obstructive sleep apnea

Obstructive sleep apnea

Pathophysiology

  • Relaxation of pharyngeal muscles, leading to closure of airway
  • Loud snoring with periods of apnea

Symptoms

  • Daytime somnolence
  • Nonrestorative sleep with frequent awakenings
  • Morning headaches
  • Affective & cognitive symptoms

Sequelae

  • Systemic hypertension
  • Pulmonary hypertension & right heart failure

subs.title: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
subs.subject: path
tables: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

Diagnostic criteria

  • Obesity with BMI ≥30 kg/m2
  • Awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mm Hg)
  • No alternate cause of hypoventilation

Work-up

  • ABG on room air (hypercapnia, normal A-a gradient)
  • No intrinsic pulmonary disease on chest x-ray
  • Restrictive pattern on PFTs
  • Normal TSH
  • Polysomnography

Treatment

  • Nocturnal positive pressure ventilation as first-line therapy
  • Weight loss (bariatric surgery in select cases)
  • Avoidance of sedative medications
  • Respiratory stimulants (eg, acetazolamide) as last resort

ABG = arterial blood gas; PFTs = pulmonary function tests.

topics.title: Pulmonary hypertension
topics.subject: path
directTables: Clinical features of pulmonary hypertension

Clinical features of pulmonary hypertension

Classification

  • Pulmonary arterial hypertension (WHO group 1)
  • Due to left heart disease (group 2)
  • Due to chronic lung disease or hypoxemia (eg, COPD, OSA) (group 3)
  • Due to chronic thromboembolic disease (group 4)
  • Due to other causes (eg, sarcoidosis) (group 5)

Symptoms

  • ↓ Cardiac output: exertional syncope/presyncope, fatigue, weakness
  • ↑ PA pressure: chest tightness, hemoptysis (rare)
  • RV demand ischemia: exertional angina/tightness
  • Venous congestion: abdominal distension (bowel edema), early satiety

Signs

  • Precordial heave due to RV hypertrophy
  • Loud P2, right-sided S3 &/or S4
  • Holosystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation
  • JVD, ascites, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly
COPD = chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; JVD = jugular venous distension; OSA = obstructive sleep apnea; PA = pulmonary artery; RV = right ventricular.
Classification of pulmonary hypertension

Classification of pulmonary hypertension

Pulmonary arterial
hypertension
(group 1)

  • Primary change in pulmonary arteries
    • Hereditary (eg, BMPR2 mutation)
    • Connective tissue disease (eg, RA, SS)
    • HIV infection
  • Treatment targeted at endothelial dysfunction

Pulmonary
hypertension
(groups 2-5)

  • Secondary to another disease process
    • Left-sided heart failure (group 2)
    • Chronic lung disease/hypoxia (group 3)
    • Chronic pulmonary thromboembolism (group 4)
    • Other (eg, sarcoidosis) (group 5)
  • Treatment aimed at underlying disease

RA = rheumatoid arthritis; SS = systemic sclerosis.
Management of pulmonary hypertension

Management of pulmonary hypertension

Group 1
PAH

  • Evaluate for autoimmune CTD, toxins (eg, amphetamines), HIV, schistosomiasis, etc.
  • Pulmonary vasodilator therapy, treat underlying (eg, autoimmune) cause

Group 2
Left-sided
heart disease

  • Echocardiography (± RHC if diagnosis unclear)
  • Optimize left ventricular function (eg, heart failure therapy), treat significant valve disease

Group 3
Lung disease &/or
chronic hypoxemia

  • Pulmonary function tests, chest imaging, polysomnography
  • Treat underlying respiratory condition (eg, obstructive sleep apnea)

Group 4
CTEPH

  • V/Q scan, pulmonary angiography
  • Pulmonary thromboendarterectomy surgery (curative), anticoagulation

General
measures

  • Refer to accredited PH center
  • Maintain normoxia, euvolemia & sinus rhythm
  • Contraceptive counseling, immunization, cardiac rehabilitation
  • Refractory PH: bilateral lung transplant

CTD = connective tissue disease (eg, scleroderma); CTEPH = chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension; PAH = pulmonary arterial hypertension; PH = pulmonary hypertension; RHC = right-sided heart catheterization; V/Q = ventilation-perfusion.

Acute opacified hemithorax (unilateral whiteout)

Trachea pulled toward
opacified side

Trachea midline

Trachea pushed away from
opacified side

Total lung atelectasis*
(eg, mainstem bronchial obstruction or intubation)

Extensive consolidation
(eg, pneumonia in all lobes
of 1 lung)

Massive pleural effusion
(eg, empyema, hemothorax)

  • Mainstem obstruction (eg, mucus plug) causes ipsilateral atelectasis
  • Mainstem intubation causes contralateral atelectasis
  • Alveoli fill with pus/debris, but no force is exerted on mediastinum
  • Pleural fluid displaces mediastinal structures to opposite side

*Trachea may remain midline early in the course of atelectasis.
Atelectasis

Atelectasis

Etiologies

Pathophysiology

Obstructive (resorptive)

  • Mucus plugging
  • Endobronchial mass
  • Hypoinflation

Obstruction or collapse of bronchus, leading to absent ventilation & resorption of alveolar gas

Compression

  • Pleural masses
  • Ascites or severe obesity
  • Chest wall trauma

Extrinsic compression of lung tissue by pleurae, chest wall, or abdomen

Relaxation (passive)

  • Pneumothorax
  • Pleural effusion

Separation of lung from chest wall, allowing natural inward recoil.

Adhesive

  • Neonatal RDS
  • ARDS
  • Drowning

Depletion or inactivation of surfactant, allowing alveolar walls to cling together due to surface tension

ARDS = adult respiratory distress syndrome; RDS = respiratory distress syndrome.

tables: Strategies to prevent aspiration pneumonia in hospitalized patients

Strategies to prevent aspiration pneumonia in hospitalized patients

Recommended

Not recommended

  • Elevation of head of bed to 30-45 degrees
  • Enteral feeding
  • Speech & swallow evaluation
  • Drainage of subglottal secretions*
  • Decontamination of oropharynx/digestive tract*
  • Prokinetic agents
  • Gastrostomy tube or nasogastric tube
  • Gastric volume measurement
  • Probiotic medications

*In intubated patients.
Aspiration: pneumonitis vs pneumonia

Aspiration: pneumonitis vs pneumonia

Chemical pneumonitis

Aspiration pneumonia

Cause

  • Inhalation of gastric acid leads to direct chemical injury of bronchial & alveolar epithelial cells
  • Inhalation of large inoculate of oropharyngeal or gastric microbes overwhelms host pulmonary defenses

Onset

  • Sudden: within min or hr
  • Indolent: a few days to weeks

Manifestations

  • Abrupt-onset dyspnea, cough, hypoxemia
  • Low-grade fever
  • Diffuse crackles/wheezes
  • Infiltrate in dependent portion of lung
  • Fever
  • Cough with putrid sputum
  • Infiltrate in dependent portion of lung

Management

  • Supportive care
  • Oropharyngeal suction if event is witnessed
  • Antibiotics (eg, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin) that target community-acquired pneumonia pathogens

Same
lung lobe*

Bronchial obstruction

Recurrent aspiration

Different
lung lobes

directTables: Pancoast (superior pulmonary sulcus) tumors

Pancoast (superior pulmonary sulcus) tumors

Anatomy

  • Lung apex: characteristic symptoms from invasion of nearby structures
  • Peripheral lung: pulmonary symptoms (eg, cough, hemoptysis) usually late findings

Clinical features (invaded structures)

  • Pancoast syndrome
    • Shoulder pain (brachial plexus, ribs &/or pleura)
    • Horner syndrome* (sympathetic chain)
    • Hand weakness/atrophy (brachial plexus)
  • Other findings
    • Potential emergencies**: paraplegia (spinal cord), face/arm edema (SVC)
    • Hoarseness (RLN), hemidiaphragm paresis (phrenic nerve), supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (metastasis)

Pathology

  • <5% of all lung cancers: non–small cell (95%), small cell (5%)

*Ptosis, miosis & anhidrosis.

**Typically require immediate evaluation/management.

RLN = recurrent laryngeal nerve; SVC = superior vena cava.

tables: Adverse effects of inhaled corticosteroids

Adverse effects of inhaled corticosteroids

Local

~75% of dose deposited in oropharynx

  • Dysphonia: steroid-induced laryngeal myopathy; common (50%) & usually minor
  • Thrush: affects tongue & pharynx (esophagus: very rarely); prevent by rinsing & gargling with water, using spacer (decrease local deposition)
  • Other: contact dermatitis (budesonide hypersensitivity); cough & reflex bronchoconstriction

Systemic*

~25% of dose deposited in peripheral lung & systemically absorbed

  • HPA axis: secondary adrenal insufficiency (usually subclinical); can coexist with ICS-induced Cushing syndrome
  • Skeletal: small ↑ osteoporosis & fracture risk
  • Other: dermal thinning (fragile skin, purpura), ocular effects (cataract formation, ↑ IOP), small ↑ CAP risk in COPD patients

*Uncommon. Typically seen only with prolonged (years) high-dose ICS use, superimposed oral glucocorticoid use, or concurrent administration of potent cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibitor.

CAP = community-acquired pneumonia; COPD = chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; HPA = hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal; ICS = inhaled corticosteroid; IOP = intraocular pressure.

directTables: Neonatal abstinence syndrome

Neonatal abstinence syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • In utero exposure to maternal substances (primarily opioids)

Clinical
manifestations

  • CNS: irritability, hypertonia, tremor, shortened sleep-wake cycles, uncoordinated swallowing
  • Autonomic nervous system: diaphoresis, sneezing, yawning
  • Gastrointestinal: feeding difficulty, vomiting, diarrhea

Diagnosis

  • Primarily clinical
  • Confirm: umbilical cord blood, urine, or meconium drug testing

Treatment

  • Mild withdrawal: nonpharmacologic
    • Minimize environmental stimuli, swaddling, frequent small feeds
  • Moderate to severe withdrawal: pharmacologic
    • Morphine, methadone

subs.subject: embryo
tables: Hypospadias

Hypospadias

Pathogenesis

  • Failure of urethral folds to fuse

Clinical features

  • Ventrally displaced urethral meatus
    • Mild: glans/shaft meatal location
    • Severe: scrotal/perineal meatal location, underdeveloped glans
  • Dorsal hooded foreskin
  • ± Penile curvature (chordee)

Evaluation

  • Mild & isolated: none
  • Severe or associated genital abnormalities (eg, cryptorchidism): karyotype & pelvic ultrasonography*
  • Associated nongenitourinary abnormalities (eg, cardiac or ocular defects): renal & bladder ultrasonography**

Management

  • Defer circumcision
  • Urologic evaluation for surgical repair
*To evaluate for underlying difference in sex development.
**To evaluate for underlying syndrome (eg, WAGR [Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, range of intellectual abilities], CHARGE [coloboma, heart defect, atresia choanae, retarded growth, genital anomalies, ear abnormalities]).

subs.title: Klinefelter syndrome
subs.subject: path
tables: Klinefelter syndrome

Klinefelter syndrome

Pathogenesis

  • Nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes, resulting in a 47,XXY male

Clinical features

  • Primary hypogonadism
  • Increased long bone length
  • Gynecomastia
  • Learning & socialization difficulties

Laboratory findings

  • ↓ Testosterone
  • ↑ LH & FSH (due to loss of feedback inhibition)
  • ↑ Estradiol

subs.title: Turner syndrome
subs.subject: path
images: Cystic hygroma on fetal ultrasound, Turner syndrome
tables: Turner syndrome

Turner syndrome

Etiology

  • Complete or partial loss of X chromosome

Presentation

  • Infancy:
    • Lymphedema, cystic hygroma
    • Renal & heart defects (eg, horseshoe kidney, aortic coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve)
  • Childhood:
    • Short stature
    • Dysmorphic features (eg, webbed neck, broad chest, high-arched palate, cubitus valgus, short 4th metacarpals)
  • Adolescence:
    • Delayed thelarche
    • Amenorrhea (primary or secondary)

Diagnosis & management

  • Karyotype (45,X)
  • Comorbidity screening (eg, cardiac & renal imaging)
  • Growth hormone & estrogen (± progestin) therapy
Comorbidity screening in Turner syndrome

Comorbidity screening in Turner syndrome

Cardiovascular

  • Congenital heart defects*: 4-extremity BP, ECG, echocardiography
  • Aortic dilation/dissection**: TTE or cardiac MRI
  • Metabolic syndrome: BP, HbA1c, lipid panel, LFT

Renal

  • Horseshoe kidney: renal ultrasonography

Musculoskeletal

  • Osteoporosis: 25-hydroxyvitamin D level, DXA scan

Vision & hearing

  • Strabismus, myopia: ophthalmology evaluation
  • Recurrent otitis media, hearing loss: audiology testing

Autoimmune

  • Celiac disease: tissue transglutaminase antibodies
  • Hypothyroidism: TSH, free T4

*Aortic coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve.

**High risk in pregnancy.

BP = blood pressure; HbA1c = glycosylated hemoglobin; LFT = liver function test; TTE = transthoracic echocardiography.

topics.subject: path
directTables: 5-α reductase deficiency

5-α reductase deficiency

Pathogenesis

  • 46,XY genotype
  • Impaired conversion of testosterone to DHT
  • Impaired virilization during embryogenesis
  • Normal male testosterone & estrogen levels

Clinical features

  • Male internal genitalia (eg, testes, vas deferens)
  • Female external genitalia (eg, blind-ending vagina)
  • Phenotypically female at birth
  • Virilization at puberty (↑ testosterone)
    • Clitoromegaly
    • Increased muscle mass
    • Male pattern hair development
    • Nodulocystic acne

DHT = dihydrotestosterone.

Placenta accreta

Definition

  • Morbidly adherent placental attachment to the myometrium

Risk factors

  • Placenta previa + prior uterine surgery (eg, cesarean delivery, D&C, myomectomy)

Clinical features

  • Prenatal diagnosis: US with placenta previa, numerous placental lacunae, myometrial thinning

  • Cesarean hysterectomy with placenta in situ

subs.title: Placenta previa
subs.subject: path
tables: Placenta previa

Placenta previa

Risk factors

  • Prior placenta previa
  • Prior cesarean delivery
  • Multiple gestation

Clinical
features

  • Painless vaginal bleeding at >20 weeks gestation

Diagnosis

  • Transabdominal followed by transvaginal sonography

Management

  • No intercourse
  • No digital cervical examination
  • Inpatient admission for bleeding episodes

subs.title: Vasa previa
subs.subject: path
tables: Vasa previa

Vasa previa

Definition

  • Fetal vessels overlying the cervix

Risk factors

  • Placenta previa
  • Multiple gestations
  • In vitro fertilization
  • Succenturiate placental lobe

Clinical presentation

  • Painless vaginal bleeding with ROM or contractions
  • FHR abnormalities (eg, bradycardia, sinusoidal pattern)
  • Fetal exsanguination & demise

Management

  • Emergency cesarean delivery

FHR = fetal heart rate; ROM = rupture of membranes.

  • Hypertension, preeclampsia
  • Abdominal trauma

subs.title: Preeclampsia
subs.subject: path
tables: Preeclampsia prevention

Preeclampsia prevention

Definition

  • New-onset hypertension & proteinuria &/or
    end-organ damage at >20 weeks gestation

High risk

  • Prior preeclampsia
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Chronic hypertension
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Multiple gestation
  • Autoimmune disease

Moderate risk

  • Obesity
  • Advanced maternal age
  • Nulliparity

Prevention

  • Low-dose aspirin at 12 weeks gestation
Preeclampsia

Preeclampsia

Risk factors

  • Nulliparity
  • Obesity
  • Preexisting medical condition (eg, SLE, chronic hypertension)
  • Multiple gestation
  • Advanced maternal age

Definition

  • New-onset hypertension* (SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 mm Hg)
    at ≥20 weeks

     AND

  • Proteinuria OR signs/symptoms of other end-organ damage

Severe features

  • Severe-range hypertension (SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110 mm Hg)
  • Platelets <100,000/mm3
  • Creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or 2x normal
  • Elevated transaminases >2x upper limit of normal
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Vision or cerebral symptoms (eg, headache)

Management

  • <37 weeks & no severe features: expectant
  • ≥37 weeks (or ≥34 weeks with severe features): delivery
  • Severe-range blood pressure: IV labetalol, IV hydralazine,
    PO nifedipine
  • Seizure prophylaxis: magnesium sulfate

*On 2 measurements ≥4 hr apart.

DBP = diastolic blood pressure; IV = intravenous; PO = by mouth; SBP = systolic blood pressure; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.
Treatment of preeclampsia

Treatment of preeclampsia

Drug

Indication

Hydralazine IV, labetalol IV, or nifedipine PO

Lower blood pressure acutely to decrease stroke risk

Magnesium sulfate IV or IM

Prevent or treat eclamptic seizures

IM = intramuscular; IV = intravenous; PO = by mouth.
Preeclampsia

Preeclampsia

Definition

  • New-onset hypertension & proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction after 20 weeks gestation

Hypertension

  • Systolic BP ≥140 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥90 mm Hg on 2 occasions at least 4 hours apart
    OR
  • Systolic BP ≥160 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥110 mm Hg confirmed on repeat check

Proteinuria

  • ≥300 mg (0.3 g) of protein in 24-hour urine collection
    OR
  • Protein/creatinine ratio of 0.3
    OR
  • Urine dipstick 1+ (when above are not available)

End-organ
dysfunction

  • Thrombocytopenia (<100,000/mm3 [100 × 109/L])
  • Renal insufficiency (serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL [97 mmol/L] or doubling creatinine)
  • Impaired liver function (ALT & AST twice normal)
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Cerebral or visual symptoms

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; BP = blood pressure.

options

  • Oral contraceptive pills for menstrual regulation
  • Letrozole for ovulation induction

Age <21

Lactational mastitis

Pathogenesis

  • Skin flora (eg, Staphylococcus aureus) enters ducts through nipple & multiplies in stagnant milk

Risk factors

  • History of mastitis
  • Engorgement & inadequate milk drainage due to
    • Sudden increase in sleep duration
    • Replacing nursing with formula or pumped breast milk

    • Poor latch

Clinical presentation

  • Fever
  • Firm, red, tender, swollen quadrant of unilateral breast
  • ± Myalgia, chills, malaise

Treatment

  • Analgesia
  • Frequent breastfeeding or pumping
  • Antibiotics

Breast abscess

Risk factors

  • First pregnancy
  • Tobacco use

Clinical features

  • Fever
  • Focal inflammation
  • Fluctuant, tender mass

Diagnosis

  • Breast ultrasonography

Management

  • Antibiotics
  • Drainage

Medication-induced gynecomastia*

Drug

Mechanism

Estrogens

Direct stimulation of ductal epithelial hyperplasia

Antiandrogens
(eg, flutamide, bicalutamide)

Competitive inhibition of testosterone receptor

5-alpha reductase
inhibitors (eg, finasteride)

↓ Conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone

Spironolactone

↓ Testosterone synthesis & inhibition of testosterone receptor

Ketoconazole

↓ Synthesis of steroid hormones (↓ androgen > ↓ estrogen)

Cimetidine

Inhibition of testosterone receptor

Androgen-anabolic
steroids

Aromatization of androgens to estrogen

*Drugs that increase the estrogen/testosterone ratio are associated with gynecomastia.
Causes of gynecomastia in adults

Causes of gynecomastia in adults

Physiologic gynecomastia

  • Decreased T synthesis with aging
  • Increased aromatization of androgens in adipose tissue

Hypogonadism

  • Low-circulating T levels
  • Uninterrupted adrenal production of E precursors (high E/T ratio)

Cirrhosis

  • Decreased hepatic clearance of Es

Medications

  • Spironolactone, antiandrogens (eg, flutamide) & cimetidine: androgen receptor antagonism
  • 5AR inhibitors (eg, finasteride): decreased conversion of T to DHT
  • Ketoconazole: decreased T synthesis
  • GnRH agonists: suppression of pituitary-gonadal axis
  • Androgenic steroids: increased aromatization to Es

Testicular tumors

  • hCG secretion by germ cell tumor
  • Impaired T production and increased aromatization in Leydig cells

Hyperthyroidism

  • Increased LH secretion
  • Increased aromatization of androgens
5AR = 5-alpha reductase; DHT = dihydrotestosterone; E = estrogen; T = testosterone.

tables: Priapism

Priapism

Pathogenesis

  • Impaired venous outflow from corpora cavernosa
  • Increased cavernosal pressure
  • Ischemia, hypoxia, acidosis

Causes/
risk factors

  • Autonomic dysfunction: spinal cord injury
  • Altered blood viscosity: sickle cell disease, blood dyscrasias

Testicular torsion

Pathogenesis

features

Imaging

  • No testicular blood flow on Doppler ultrasound

Management

  • Immediate surgical detorsion

topics.title: Varicocele
topics.subject: path
directTables: Varicocele

Varicocele

Clinical presentation

  • Soft scrotal mass ("bag of worms")
    • ↓ In supine position
    • ↑ With standing/Valsalva maneuvers
  • Subfertility
  • Testicular atrophy

Ultrasound findings

  • Retrograde venous flow
  • Tortuous, anechoic tubules adjacent to testis
  • Dilation of pampiniform plexus veins

Treatment

  • Reassurance & observation if asymptomatic
  • Gonadal vein ligation* for pain, testicular atrophy, or abnormal semen analysis

* Scrotal support and NSAIDs alone are recommended for older men not interested in fertility.

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Varicocele

Varicocele

Primary

Secondary

Pathophysiology

  • Compression of left renal vein between SMA and aorta
  • Incompetent venous valves
  • Extrinsic compression (renal or retroperitoneal mass) of IVC
  • Venous thrombus

Clinical features

  • "Bag of worms" mass
  • Pubertal onset
  • Left-sided
  • Decompresses when supine
  • "Bag of worms" mass
  • Prepubertal onset
  • Right-sided
  • Persists when supine

Initial management

  • Reassurance and observation if asymptomatic*
  • Abdominal ultrasonography

*Gonadal vein ligation may be indicated for pain, testicular atrophy, or abnormal semen analysis in adolescents and young men.
IVC = inferior vena cava; SMA = superior mesenteric artery.

topics.title: Prostatitis
topics.subject: path
directTables: Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome

Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome

Symptoms

  • Pain in pelvis, perineum, genitalia
  • Irritative voiding symptoms (eg, urgency, hesitancy)
  • Hematospermia, pain with ejaculation

Diagnosis

  • No or mild prostate tenderness
  • Sterile urine culture

Management

  • Alpha blockers (eg, tamsulosin)
  • Antibiotics (eg, ciprofloxacin), especially if history of UTI
  • 5-Alpha-reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride)

UTI = urinary tract infection.
Acute bacterial prostatitis

Acute bacterial prostatitis

Etiology

  • Reflux of urine & organisms from bladder & urethra
  • Mostly gram-negative bacilli (majority Escherichia coli)

Clinical presentation

  • Systemic symptoms (eg, fever, chills)
  • Lower urinary tract symptoms (eg, dysuria, urine retention, pelvic pain)
  • Examination: swollen, tender prostate

Diagnosis

  • Urine Gram stain & culture
Acute bacterial prostatitis

Acute bacterial prostatitis

Etiology

  • Intraprostatic reflux of pathogens in urine
  • Primarily gram-negative bacilli (Escherichia coli ~75%)

Manifestations

  • Flu-like illness (eg, fever, chills, malaise, myalgia)
  • Lower urinary symptoms (eg, dysuria, urine retention, pelvic pain)

Diagnosis

  • Digital rectal examination: tender, swollen prostate
  • Urine culture

Treatment

  • 6 weeks of TMP-SMX or fluoroquinolone

Complications

  • Bacteremia/systemic spread
  • Prostatic abscess
  • Chronic prostatitis

TMP-SMX = trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Chronic bacterial prostatitis

Chronic bacterial prostatitis

Epidemiology

  • Young & middle-aged men
  • ↑ Risk with diabetes mellitus, smoking, urinary tract procedure

Pathogens

  • Coliforms enter from urethra via intraprostatic reflux
  • Escherichia coli causes >75% of cases

Presentation

  • Recurrent urinary tract infection (with the same organism)
  • ± Prostatic tenderness & swelling (often absent)
  • Pain with ejaculation
  • History of antibiotic treatment → transient improvement

Diagnosis

  • Pyuria and bacteriuria on urinalysis
  • Bacteria in prostatic fluid > bacteria in urine

Treatment

  • Fluoroquinolones (eg, ciprofloxacin) for 6 weeks

Common associated conditions

Bite cell

  • "Bites" secondary to phagocytes extracting denatured hemoglobin (Heinz bodies) precipitates

  • G6PD deficiency

Schistocyte

Spherocyte

  • Autoimmune hemolysis

Target cell

  • Red blood cell with "bull's eye" extra hemoglobin drop in center

  • HbC disease
  • Postsplenectomy states
  • Liver disease (especially obstructive)

Teardrop cell

  • Teardrop shaped RBC
  • Extramedullary hematopoiesis (eg, myelofibrosis, major thalassemia)

Basophilic stippling

  • Blue granules of various sizes in RBC cytoplasm

  • Lead & heavy metal poisoning

Howell-Jolly bodies

  • Usually single, round, dark, purple-red & peripheral in location

tables: Iron deficiency anemia in young children

Iron deficiency anemia in young children

Risk factors

  • Prematurity
  • Lead exposure
  • Age <1
    • Delayed introduction of solids (ie, exclusive
      breastfeeding after 6 months)
    • Cow's, soy, or goat's milk
  • Age >1
    • >24 oz (>700 mL) per day of cow's milk
    • <3 servings/day of iron-rich foods

Diagnosis

  • Screening hemoglobin at age 1
  • Hemoglobin <11 g/dL (<6.83 mmol/L), ↓ MCV, ↑ RDW

Treatment

  • Empiric trial of iron supplementation

MCV = mean corpuscular volume; RDW = red blood cell distribution width.
Iron deficiency anemia in adults

Iron deficiency anemia in adults

Etiology

  • Blood loss (eg, menses, GI bleeding)
  • Decreased iron absorption (eg, celiac disease, bariatric surgery) or intake

Clinical
features

  • Fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, pallor
  • Pica, ice craving
  • Skin changes: angular cheilitis, koilonychia (nail spooning)

Laboratory
findings

  • Hypochromic, microcytic anemia
  • ↓ Serum iron
  • ↓ Serum ferritin
  • ↑ TIBC
  • ↓ Transferrin saturation

Management

  • Identify & treat underlying etiology
  • Prescribe iron supplementation

GI = gastrointestinal; TIBC = total iron-binding capacity.

tables: Causes

Vitamin B12 deficiency

Causes

  • Pernicious anemia (antibodies to intrinsic factor)
  • Drug-induced (eg, long-term metformin or PPI use)
  • Low intake or ↓ absorption (eg, gastric bypass, Crohn's disease)
  • Alcohol use disorder

Signs & symptoms

  • Fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, pallor, glossitis
  • Neurologic dysfunction
    • Peripheral neuropathy
    • Cognitive impairment
    • Psychiatric symptoms

Laboratory findings

  • ↓ Hgb, RBCs, reticulocyte count
  • ↑ MCV (> 100 fL), methylmalonic acid, homocysteine
  • ↓ Serum vitamin B12

Treatment

  • Cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12)
    • Parenteral (SC or IM injection)*
    • Nasal spray
    • Tablets

*Preferred for pernicious anemia, severe deficiency, or neurologic symptoms.

Hgb = hemoglobin; IM = intramuscular; MCV = mean corpuscular volume; PPI = proton pump inhibitor; RBC = red blood cell; SC = subcutaneous.

Pathogenesis of anemia of chronic kidney disease
tables: Anemia of chronic disease (inflammation)

Anemia of chronic disease (inflammation)

Pathogenesis

  • ↑ Inflammatory cytokines (eg, hepcidin)
  • Inhibition of ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages
  • ↓ Iron absorption and ↑ iron sequestration
  • Reduced circulating iron → impaired erythropoiesis

Common
etiologies

  • Malignancy
  • Chronic infection
  • Rheumatic disease
  • Obesity
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Heart failure

Laboratory
findings

  • Normocytic/slightly microcytic anemia
  • ↓ Serum iron, iron-binding capacity, reticulocyte count
  • ↑ Bone marrow iron
  • Lower than expected erythropoietin for degree of anemia

Treatment

  • Treat underlying condition causing inflammation

subs.title: Aplastic anemia
subs.subject: path
tables: Fanconi anemia

Fanconi anemia

Pathophysiology

  • Inherited DNA repair defect
  • Bone marrow failure

Clinical findings

                                          

  • Short stature
  • Hypo-/hyperpigmented macules
  • Abnormal thumbs
  • Genitourinary malformations

Laboratory findings

  • Pancytopenia
  • Positive chromosomal breakage testing

Treatment

  • Hematopoietic stem cell transplant
Aplastic anemia

Aplastic anemia

Pathogenesis

  • Multipotent hematopoietic stem cells are destroyed by cytotoxic T cells or direct cytotoxic injury → bone marrow aplasia/hypoplasia → lack of circulating peripheral blood cells

Common triggers

  • Autoimmune
  • Drugs: cytotoxic chemotherapy, immunosuppressants, idiosyncratic reactions
  • Ionizing radiation & toxins
  • Viral infections (eg, viral hepatitis, HIV)

Manifestations

  • Anemia (eg, fatigue, weakness, pallor)
  • Thrombocytopenia (eg, bleeding, bruising)
  • Leukopenia (eg, recurrent infections)

Diagnosis

  • Bone marrow biopsy: hypocellular marrow with abundance of stromal & fat cells

tables: Hereditary spherocytosis

Hereditary spherocytosis

Epidemiology

  • Usually autosomal dominant

Clinical presentation

  • Hemolytic anemia
  • Jaundice
  • Splenomegaly

Laboratory findings

  • ↑ MCHC
  • Negative Coombs test
  • Spherocytes on peripheral smear
  • ↑ Osmotic fragility on acidified glycerol lysis test
  • Abnormal eosin-5-maleimide binding test

Treatment

  • Folic acid supplementation
  • Blood transfusion
  • Splenectomy

MCHC = mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration.
Hereditary spherocytosis

Hereditary spherocytosis

Genetics

  • Autosomal dominant inheritance (most cases)

Pathogenesis

  • RBC membrane defect (eg, spectrin, ankyrin)
  • Spherocytes with ↓ deformability sequestered in spleen
  • Extravascular hemolysis

Clinical
presentation

  • Hemolytic anemia
  • Jaundice
  • Splenomegaly

Laboratory
findings

  • ↑ MCHC
  • Spherocytes on peripheral blood smear
  • Negative Coombs test
  • ↑ Osmotic fragility

Treatment

  • Splenectomy

Complications

  • Pigmented gallstones
  • Aplastic crisis (with parvovirus B19 infection)

RBC = red blood cell; MCHC = mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration.

subs.title: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

tables: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA)

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA)

Warm agglutinin AIHA

Cold agglutinin AIHA

Etiology

  • Drugs (eg, penicillin)
  • Viral infections
  • Autoimmune (eg, SLE)
  • Immunodeficiency states
    • Lymphoproliferative (eg, CLL)
  • Infections (eg, Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection & infectious mononucleosis)
  • Lymphoproliferative diseases

Clinical presentation

  • Asymptomatic to life-threatening anemia
  • Direct Coombs positive with anti-IgG, anti-C3, or both
  • Symptoms of anemia
  • Livedo reticularis & acral cyanosis with cold exposure that disappear with warming
  • Direct Coombs positive with anti-C3 or anti-IgM, but usually not IgG

Treatment

  • Corticosteroids
  • Splenectomy for refractory disease
  • Avoidance of cold temperatures
  • Rituximab ± fludarabine

Complications

  • Venous thromboembolism
  • Lymphoproliferative disorders
  • Ischemia & peripheral gangrene
  • Lymphoproliferative disorders

CLL = chronic lymphocytic leukemia; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.

subs.title: Drug-induced hemolytic anemia
subs.subject: path
tables: Drug-induced, immune-mediated hemolytic anemia

Drug-induced, immune-mediated hemolytic anemia

Pathogenesis

  • Drug coats erythrocytes → IgG binding → splenic destruction of RBCs (extravascular hemolysis)
  • Drug triggers immune complexes → complement-mediated destruction of RBCs (intravascular hemolysis)

Manifestations

  • Sudden onset (within hours of exposure)
  • Anemia: fatigue, pallor, dyspnea
  • Hemolysis: jaundice, dark urine, abdominal or back pain
    • ↑ Reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin & LDH
    • ↓ Haptoglobin
    • Spherocytes on peripheral blood smear
    • + Direct Coombs test (anti-IgG, anti-C3)

Treatment

  • Discontinue offending drug
  • Transfusion (if severe)
  • ± Glucocorticoids, IVIG

IVIG = intravenous immunoglobulin; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase; RBCs = red blood cells.

tables: Congenital causes of isolated* neutropenia

Congenital causes of isolated* neutropenia

Condition

Pathogenesis

Features

Benign familial neutropenia

  • Single nucleotide polymorphism
  • Asymptomatic (mild neutropenia)
  • Most commonly patients of African descent

Cyclic neutropenia

  • Mutations encoding neutrophil elastase
  • Episodic (q21 days) neutropenia → recurrent mucositis/fever starting in early childhood
  • Treatment: G-CSF

Severe congenital neutropenia**

  • Persistent/severe neutropenia → recurrent & severe infections starting in early infancy
  • Treatment: G-CSF

*Bone marrow disorders (eg, leukemia, aplastic anemia) & hypersplenism usually cause multiple cytopenia.

**Most cases due to elastase mutation but can be caused by other mutations.

G-CSF = granulocyte colony-stimulating factor.
