images: Knee radiograph in a patient with chronic lead exposure
tables: Lead poisoning

Lead poisoning

Risk
factors

  • Home built before 1978
  • Pica or mouthing behaviors (eg, infants, developmental delay)
  • Sibling with lead poisoning
  • Low socioeconomic status
  • Immigrant or international adoptee

Clinical
features

  • May be asymptomatic
  • Abdominal pain/constipation
  • Cognitive impairment/behavioral problems
  • Encephalopathy

Management

  • Obtain venous sample (if screening performed by capillary sample)
  • Environmental surveillance (identify & remove lead sources)
  • Notify public health department
  • Nutritional counseling
  • Chelation therapy if lead level ≥45 µg/dL

subs.title: Acute intermittent porphyria
subs.subject: path
tables: Acute intermittent porphyria

Acute intermittent porphyria

Etiology

  • Autosomal dominant disorder with low penetrance
  • Reduced activity of porphobilinogen deaminase

Exacerbating factors

  • Medications (eg, cytochrome P-450 inducers, progesterone)
  • Physiologic stress (eg, fasting, surgery, illness)
  • Alcohol, tobacco

Manifestations

  • Abdominal pain
  • Peripheral neuropathy most pronounced in the proximal upper extremities
  • Autonomic dysfunction (eg, tachycardia, diaphoresis, hypertension)
  • Neuropsychiatric (eg, hallucinations, anxiety, psychosis)
  • Red-tinged urine that oxidizes with light/air exposure

Laboratory findings

  • Elevated serum & urinary PBG, ALA, porphyrins
  • ± Hyponatremia, elevated transaminases

Management

  • Glucose & hemin (heme analogue)

ALA = aminolevulinic acid; PBG = porphobilinogen.

subs.title: Porphyria cutanea tarda
subs.subject: path
tables: Porphyria cutanea tarda

Porphyria cutanea tarda

Clinical presentation

  • Blisters, bullae, scarring, hypopigmentation/hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed skin (eg, back of hands, forearms, face)
  • Scarring & calcification similar to scleroderma

Associated conditions

  • Hepatitis C
  • HIV
  • Excessive alcohol consumption
  • Estrogen use
  • Smoking

Diagnostic testing

  • Mildly elevated liver enzymes & iron overload
  • Elevated plasma or urine porphyrin levels

Hemophilia A & B

Inheritance

features

  • Delayed/prolonged bleeding after mild trauma

subs.title: Immune thrombocytopenia
subs.subject: path
tables: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura

Epidemiology

  • Commonly acquired form of thrombocytopenia
  • Autoantibody formation
  • Often recent viral infection or comorbidity (eg, HIV, HCV, CLL)

Manifestations

  • Frequently asymptomatic
  • Mucocutaneous bleeding (eg, menorrhagia, epistaxis)
  • Ecchymoses, petechiae, purpura
  • Severe hemorrhage is rare

Diagnosis

  • Diagnosis of exclusion
  • Normal coagulation tests, platelet morphology (peripheral smear)
  • HIV, HCV testing (commonly induces ITP)

Treatment

  • Observation if no bleeding & platelets >30,000/mm3
  • Corticosteroids if platelets <30,000/mm3
  • IVIG & platelet transfusion if hemorrhage

CLL = chronic lymphocytic leukemia; HCV = hepatitis C virus; ITP = immune thrombocytopenic purpura; IVIG = intravenous immunoglobulin.

directTables: Common causes of thrombocytopenia

Common causes of thrombocytopenia

Decreased production

  • Bone marrow disorders
    • Infections (eg, EBV, hepatitis C, HIV)*
    • Bone marrow failure (eg, infiltrative neoplasms, aplastic anemia)
    • Therapy (eg, chemotherapy, radiation)
    • Nutritional deficiency (eg, folate, vitamin B12)
  • Inherited platelet disorders (eg, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, Fanconi anemia)
  • Liver disease (reduced TPO synthesis)

Increased destruction

  • Immune-mediated (eg, ITP, drug-induced thrombocytopenia, HIT)
  • Non–immune-mediated (eg, TTP, HUS, DIC, mechanical heart valves, ECMO)

Sequestration

  • Hypersplenism (eg, from portal hypertension, lymphoproliferation)
  • Placental sequestration during pregnancy

Dilution

  • Plasma expansion during pregnancy (ie, gestational thrombocytopenia)
  • Volume resuscitation, massive RBC transfusions
  • Postoperative

*Viral infections such as HIV may also contribute to autoantibody-induced platelet destruction.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura

Epidemiology

  • Commonly acquired form of thrombocytopenia
  • Autoantibody formation
  • Often recent viral infection or comorbidity (eg, HIV, HCV, CLL)

Manifestations

  • Frequently asymptomatic
  • Mucocutaneous bleeding (eg, menorrhagia, epistaxis)
  • Ecchymoses, petechiae, purpura
  • Severe hemorrhage is rare

Diagnosis

  • Diagnosis of exclusion
  • Normal coagulation tests, platelet morphology (peripheral smear)
  • HIV, HCV testing (commonly induces ITP)

Treatment

  • Observation if no bleeding & platelets >30,000/mm3
  • Corticosteroids if platelets <30,000/mm3
  • IVIG & platelet transfusion if hemorrhage

CLL = chronic lymphocytic leukemia; HCV = hepatitis C virus; ITP = immune thrombocytopenic purpura; IVIG = intravenous immunoglobulin.

tables: Thrombocytic thrombocytopenic purpura

Thrombocytic thrombocytopenic purpura

Pathophysiology

  • Plasma enzyme deficiency → disseminated microvascular
    thrombosis (clotting)
  • Increased use of clotting factors → bleeding
  • Acquired (autoantibody) or hereditary

Clinical
manifestations

  • Fever
  • Hemolytic anemia (eg, jaundice, pallor)
  • Thrombocytopenia (eg, petechial rash, purpura)
  • Renal failure
  • Neurologic impairment (coma, convulsions, paralysis)

Laboratory
abnormalities

  • Hemolytic anemia (↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin, schistocytes)
  • Thrombocytopenia

Management

  • Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis)
  • Bleeding precautions

LDH = lactate dehydrogenase.

tables: Hemolytic uremic syndrome

Hemolytic uremic syndrome

Pathogenesis

  • Escherichia coli serotype O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae
  • Vascular damage & microthrombi formation

Clinical features

  • Preceding bloody diarrhea
  • Fatigue, pallor
  • Bruising, petechiae
  • Oliguria, edema

Laboratory findings

  • Hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, ↑ bilirubin)
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Acute kidney injury (↑ BUN, ↑ creatinine)

Treatment

  • Fluid & electrolyte management
  • Blood transfusions
  • Dialysis

Disseminated intravascular coagulation

Major causes

  • Sepsis
  • Severe traumatic injury
  • Malignancy
  • Obstetric complications

Pathophysiology

  • Procoagulant excessively triggers coagulation cascade →
  • Formation of fibrin-/platelet-rich thrombi & fibrinolysis →
  • Bleeding & organ damage (eg, kidneys, lungs)

Laboratory findings

  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Prolonged PT & PTT
  • ↓ Fibrinogen
  • ↑ D-dimer
  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes)

Hereditary thrombophilias*

Factor V Leiden

  • Most common in white patients
  • Activated protein C resistance

Prothrombin mutation

  • 2nd most common in white patients
  • ↑ Prothrombin levels

Antithrombin deficiency

  • Inherited form is rare
  • Acquired: DIC, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome

Protein C or S deficiency

  • ↓ Inactivation of factors Va & VIIIa
  • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis (protein C only)

*Typically autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.

tables: Multiple myeloma

Multiple myeloma

Pathophysiology

  • Plasma cell neoplasm produces monoclonal paraprotein (immunoglobulin)

Manifestations

  • Bone pain, fractures
  • Constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fatigue)
  • Recurrent infections

Laboratory

  • Normocytic anemia
  • Renal insufficiency
  • Hypercalcemia (constipation, muscle weakness)
  • Monoclonal paraproteinemia (M-spike)

Radiology

  • Osteolytic lesions/osteopenia (osteoclast activation)
Diagnostic criteria for multiple myeloma

Diagnostic criteria for multiple myeloma

  • Monoclonal protein in serum or urine
  • ≥10% Clonal plasma cells in bone marrow or
    soft tissue/bone plasmacytoma
  • End-organ damage (CRAB)
    • Calcium elevation
    • Renal insufficiency
    • Anemia (usually normocytic)
    • Bone pain (usually due to lytic lesions)

topics.title: Myelodysplastic syndromes
topics.subject: path
directTables: Myelodysplastic syndromes

Myelodysplastic syndromes

Epidemiology

  • Hematopoietic stem cell neoplasm
  • Risk ↑: Older age, previous chemotherapy/radiation
  • May transform to acute leukemia

Manifestations

  • Cytopenias
    • Anemia: Weakness, fatigue
    • Leukopenia: Infections
    • Thrombocytopenia: Bruising/bleeding
  • Hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy are rare

Diagnosis

  • Dysplastic red & white blood cells* on peripheral smear
  • Bone marrow biopsy (hypercellular marrow)

Treatment

  • Transfusions for symptomatic cytopenias
  • Chemotherapy
  • Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

*Dysplastic changes include ovalomacrocytosis & neutrophil hyposegmentation/hypogranulation.

topics.title: Leukemias
topics.subject: path

subs.title: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma
subs.subject: path
tables: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia

Epidemiology

  • Most common childhood cancer
  • Peak age: 2-5 years

Clinical
features

  • Nonspecific systemic symptoms (eg, fever, weight loss)
  • Leukemic cells overcrowd bone marrow
    • Pallor/fatigue (anemia)
    • Easy bruising/petechiae (thrombocytopenia)
    • Bone pain
  • Extramedullary spread
    • Lymphadenopathy
    • Hepatosplenomegaly
    • Testicular enlargement
  • Mediastinal mass (T cell lineage): airway compression &/or superior vena cava syndrome
  • Leptomeningeal spread: neurologic symptoms (eg, cranial nerve deficits, meningismus)

Evaluation
& diagnosis

  • Complete blood count*
  • Bone marrow biopsy (>20% blasts is diagnostic) with flow cytometry
  • Lumbar puncture to evaluate for CNS involvement

*≥2 cytopenias (leukocytes may be ↓ or ↑), ± blasts on peripheral smear.

subs.title: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma
subs.subject: path
tables: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

Clinical features

  • Lymphadenopathy (cervical, supraclavicular, axillary)
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Mild thrombocytopenia & anemia
  • Often asymptomatic

Diagnosis

  • Severe lymphocytosis & smudge cells
  • Flow cytometry
  • Lymph node & bone marrow biopsy not generally needed

Prognosis

  • Median survival 10 years
  • Worse prognosis with:
    • Multiple chain lymphadenopathy
    • Hepatosplenomegaly
    • Anemia & thrombocytopenia

Complications

  • Infection
  • Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  • Secondary malignancies (eg, Richter syndrome)

subs.title: Hairy cell leukemia
subs.subject: path
tables: Hairy cell leukemia

Hairy cell leukemia

Features

  • Clonal B-cell neoplasm
  • Middle-aged/older adults
  • BRAF mutation

Manifestations

  • Pancytopenia due to bone marrow fibrosis
    • Granulocytopenia (infections)
    • Anemia (fatigue, weakness)
    • Thrombocytopenia (bleeding, bruising)
  • Splenomegaly (early satiety)
  • Hepatomegaly/lymphadenopathy rare

Diagnosis

  • Peripheral smear: "hairy" leukocyte cells
  • Bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometry

Treatment

  • Chemotherapy (for moderate/severe)
  • Life expectancy is often near-normal

subs.subject: path
tables: Polycythemia vera

Polycythemia vera

Manifestations

  • ↑ Blood viscosity
    • Hypertension
    • Erythromelalgia (burning cyanosis in hands/feet)
    • Transient visual disturbances
  • ↑ RBC turnover (gouty arthritis)
  • Aquagenic pruritus
  • Bleeding

Examination

  • Facial plethora (ruddy cyanosis)
  • Splenomegaly
 

Laboratory

findings

  • Elevated hemoglobin
  • Leukocytosis & thrombocytosis
  • Low erythropoietin level
  • JAK2 mutation positive

Complications

  • Thrombosis
  • Myelofibrosis & acute leukemia

Treatment

  • Phlebotomy
  • Hydroxyurea (if ↑ risk of thrombus)

RBC = red blood cell.

subs.title: Myelofibrosis
subs.subject: path
tables: Primary myelofibrosis

Primary myelofibrosis

Pathogenesis

Chronic myeloproliferative disorder with clonal megakaryocytes → secrete transforming growth factor-ß → stimulates fibroblasts in BM to produce collagen → BM fibrosis → hematopoietic stem cells migrate to liver & spleen → extramedullary hematopoiesis

Manifestations

  • Severe fatigue
  • Hepatomegaly + massive splenomegaly (can compress stomach)
  • ≥1 cytopenias
  • Dacrocytes (teardrop cells) on peripheral blood smear
  • BM aspiration – often dry tap due to fibrosis

BM = bone marrow.

topics.title: Polycythemia
topics.subject: path
directTables: Neonatal polycythemia

Neonatal polycythemia

Definition

  • Hematocrit >65% in term infants

Causes

  • Increased erythropoiesis from intrauterine hypoxia: maternal diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or smoking; intrauterine growth restriction
  • Erythrocyte transfusion: delayed cord clamping, twin-twin transfusion
  • Genetic/metabolic disease: hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism, genetic trisomy (13, 18, 21)

Clinical presentation

  • Asymptomatic (most common)
  • Ruddy skin
  • Hypoglycemia, hyperbilirubinemia
  • Respiratory distress, cyanosis, apnea
  • Irritability, jitteriness
  • Abdominal distension

Treatment

directTables: Chromosomal translocations associated with hematologic malignancies

Chromosomal translocations associated with hematologic malignancies

Malignancy

Pathogenesis

Acute promyelocytic
leukemia

t(15;17) involving PML & RARA → PML-RARα oncoprotein → myeloid differentiation inhibited

  • RARα: nuclear receptor involved in myeloid differentiation
  • PML: fusion forms receptor with dominant negative activity

Burkitt
lymphoma

t(8;14) involving MYC & IGH → MYC overexpression → cell growth

  • MYC: transcription factor regulating cell growth
  • IGH: immunoglobulin heavy chain (high expression in B cells)

Chronic myeloid
leukemia

t(9;22) involving ABL1 & BCR → BCR-ABL1 oncoprotein → cell proliferation

  • ABL1: nonreceptor tyrosine kinase
  • BCR: fusion leads to activation

Follicular
lymphoma

t(14;18) involving IGH & BCL2 → BCL2 overexpression → apoptosis evasion

  • BCL2: antiapoptotic protein

Mantle cell
lymphoma

t(11;14) involving CCND1 & IGH → cyclin D1 overexpression → cell cycle progression

  • Cyclin D1: regulates cell cycle

topics.title: Tumor lysis syndrome
topics.subject: path
directTables: Tumor lysis syndrome

Tumor lysis syndrome

Risk

  • Tumors with high cell burden or rapid turnover
  • Combination chemotherapy/immunotherapy

Manifestations

  • Severe electrolyte abnormalities
    • ↑ Phosphorus, potassium, uric acid
    • ↓ Calcium
  • Acute kidney injury
  • Cardiac arrhythmias
  • Seizures

Prophylaxis

  • Intravenous fluids
  • Xanthine oxidase inhibitor* or rasburicase

Treatment

  • Intravenous fluids + rasburicase
  • Continuous telemetry
  • Aggressive electrolyte monitoring & treatment

*Allopurinol or febuxostat.
Risk for tumor lysis syndrome

Risk for tumor lysis syndrome

Risk

Associated malignancies

Recommended prevention

High
(>5%)

  • ALL or AML with WBC count ≥100,000/mm3
  • Certain lymphomas (eg, high-grade Burkitt)
  • Intermediate-risk disease with ↑ creatinine, uric acid, phosphorus, or potassium
  • Intravenous hydration
  • Prophylactic rasburicase (except in G6PD-deficient patients)

Intermediate
(1%-5%)

  • Lower-grade lymphomas
  • Solid tumors sensitive to chemotherapy (eg, neuroblastoma, germ cell, small cell)
  • Intravenous hydration
  • Allopurinol (preferred)
  • Rasburicase (alternatively)

Low
(<1%)

  • Multiple myeloma
  • CML
  • Most solid tumors
  • Intravenous hydration
  • Close monitoring

ALL = acute lymphoblastic leukemia; AML = acute myelogenous leukemia; CML = chronic myelogenous leukemia; G6PD = glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase; WBC = white blood cell.

Oral factor Xa inhibitors

Warfarin

Mechanism

2-4 hr

5-7 days

or LMWH for ~5 days

No

Pretest probability of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Pretest probability of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

2 points

1 point

0 points

  • Platelet count drop 30%-50% or nadir 10,000-19,000/mm3

Timing of drop
in platelet count

thrombocytopenia

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Clinical features

Heparin exposure ≥5 days & any of the following:

  • Drop in platelet count by >50%
  • Arterial or venous thrombosis
  • Necrotic skin lesions at heparin injection site
  • Anaphylactoid reaction after heparin

Diagnosis

  • Serotonin release assay

Treatment

  • Stop all heparin products
  • Start nonheparin medication
Clinical features of type 2 heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Clinical features of type 2 heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Clinical signs

Suspected with heparin exposure >5 days & any of the following:

  • Platelet count reduction >50% from baseline
  • Arterial or venous thrombosis
  • Necrotic skin lesions at heparin injection sites
  • Acute systemic (anaphylactoid) reactions after heparin

Diagnostic evaluation

  • Serotonin release assay: gold standard confirmatory test
  • Start treatment in suspected cases prior to confirmatory tests

Therapy

  • Stop all heparin products
  • Start a direct thrombin inhibitor (eg, argatroban) or fondaparinux (synthetic pentasaccharide)
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Type 1
(non–immune- mediated)

Type 2
(immune-mediated)

Occurrence

  • 10%-20%
  • <3%

Timing

  • 1-4 days after heparin
  • 5-10 days after heparin or ≤1 day if prior heparin exposure within last 30 days

Platelets

  • Usually >100,000/mm3
  • Usually >20,000/mm3

Clinical
outcome

  • None
  • Increased risk of thrombosis
  • Necrotic skin lesions at heparin injection sites
  • Acute systemic reactions

Management

  • Continue heparin & observe
  • Stop heparin
  • Use alternate anticoagulant to prevent thrombosis

tables: Select adverse effects of cyclophosphamide & ifosfamide

Select adverse effects of cyclophosphamide & ifosfamide

Adverse effect

Monitoring

Prevention

Hemorrhagic cystitis

  • Evidence of hematuria (visual and/or RBCs on urinalysis)
  • Lower urinary tract symptoms (eg, urinary urgency, painful urination)
  • Adequate hydration
  • Mesna*

Myelosuppression

  • Anemia: Hgb/Hct & symptoms (eg, weakness)
  • Neutropenia: WBCs & symptoms (eg, fever)
  • Thrombocytopenia: platelets & symptoms (eg, bleeding)
  • G-CSF for neutropenia

Nausea & vomiting

  • Patient symptoms (eg, vomiting episodes, hydration status)
  • Electrolytes (eg, potassium, magnesium, sodium)
  • Antiemetics (eg, NK1 RA,
    5-HT3 RA, dexamethasone)
  • IV/PO hydration

Neurotoxicity
(ifosfamide only)

  • Symptoms (eg, encephalopathy, cerebellar dysfunction)
  • Methylene blue

*With high doses (eg, > 1 gram/m2) of cyclophosphamide & all doses of ifosfamide.

5-HT3 RA = serotonin receptor antagonist; G-CSF = granulocyte colony-stimulating factor; Hct = hematocrit; Hgb = hemoglobin; NK1 RA = neurokinin-1 receptor antagonist.

directTables: Extra (gallop) heart sounds

Extra (gallop) heart sounds

Features

Associated disorders*

S3

  • Heard just after S2
  • Caused by abrupt cessation of LV filling during early diastole
  • Generally indicative of elevated LV filling pressure
  • Heart failure
  • High-output states (eg, thyrotoxicosis)
  • Mitral or aortic regurgitation

S4

  • Heard just before S1
  • Caused by blood striking a stiff LV wall during atrial contraction
  • Concentric LV hypertrophy
  • Restrictive cardiomyopathy
  • Acute myocardial infarction

*S3 can be normal in children, young adults & pregnant patients.  S4 can be normal in older adults (eg, age >70).

LV = left ventricular.

tables: Aortic stenosis

Aortic stenosis

Causes

  • Age-related calcification of normal valve (age >70)*
  • Calcification of congenital bicuspid valve (younger patients)
  • Rheumatic (common worldwide, rare in resource-rich countries)

Clinical manifestations

Etiology

  • Myxomatous degeneration leading to mitral valve prolapse

  • Rheumatic heart disease

images: Normal heart Transposition of the great arteries
Parallel circulation in transposition of the great arteries
tables: Transposition of the great arteries

Transposition of the great arteries

Anatomy

  • Parallel (separate) systemic & pulmonary circuits
    • Right ventricle → aorta
    • Left ventricle → pulmonary artery
  • Deoxygenated blood is delivered to the systemic circulation
  • Mixing shunt (eg, VSD, PDA) must be present for viability

Clinical features

  • Cyanosis at or shortly after birth
  • Tachypnea & tachycardia
  • Murmur typically absent at birth due to low velocity shunting

Diagnosis

  • Chest x-ray: narrow mediastinum ± cardiomegaly ("egg on a string")
  • Hyperoxia test: little to no ↑ in arterial oxygenation with 100% O2
  • Echocardiography typically confirmatory

Initial management

  • Promote mixing of oxygenated & deoxygenated blood
    • Prostaglandin infusion (maintains PDA)
    • Atrial septostomy (maintains PFO)

PDA = patent ductus arteriosus; PFO = patent foramen ovale; VSD = ventricular septal defect.

tables: Tetralogy of Fallot

Tetralogy of Fallot

Pathophysiology

  • Embryonic deviation of infundibular septum creates 4 defects:
    • RVOT obstruction
    • Ventricular septal defect
    • Overriding aorta
    • Concentric RVH (secondary to RVOT obstruction)

Clinical presentation

  • Based on severity of RVOT obstruction:
    • Severe: profound neonatal cyanosis & hypoxemia
    • Moderate: tet spells in infancy/childhood
    • Mild: heart failure in childhood/adulthood
  • RVOT obstruction is dynamic (eg, worsens with feeding or crying)
  • Squatting can improve cyanosis via increased systemic afterload

Clinical findings

  • Harsh systolic ejection murmur at LUSB (RVOT obstruction)
  • Soft or absent pulmonic component of S2
  • Chest x-ray: boot-shaped heart caused by RVH

LUSB = left upper sternal border; RVH = right ventricular hypertrophy; RVOT = right ventricular outflow tract.

Function of ductus arteriosus

Peripheral

directTables: Coarctation of the aorta

Coarctation of the aorta

Pathology

  • Thickening of tunica media of aortic arch
  • Can be associated with Turner syndrome or bicuspid aortic valve

Clinical
features

  • ↑ BP & strong pulses in upper extremities
  • ↓ BP & weak pulses in lower extremities
  • Neonates (critical narrowing)
    • May have differential cyanosis affecting lower extremities*
    • Heart failure & shock after ductal closure
  • Children/adults (lesser degree of narrowing)
    • Lower extremity claudication
    • Palpable pulsations of intercostal vessels (collaterals)
    • Secondary hypertension (upper body)

*Open ductus arteriosus shunts deoxygenated blood into descending aorta.

BP = blood pressure.

directTables: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

Pathogenesis

  • Abnormal persistence of elevated fetal pulmonary vascular resistance
  • Right-to-left shunting across ductus arteriosus

Risk factors

  • Lung hypoplasia (eg, congenital diaphragmatic hernia)
  • Meconium aspiration syndrome
  • Infection (eg, neonatal pneumonia)

Examination

  • ↓ Postductal relative to preductal oxygen saturation
  • Respiratory distress & cyanosis
  • Prominent S2

Treatment

  • Oxygenation & ventilation
  • Inhaled nitric oxide (pulmonary vasodilator)

  • Meconium aspiration syndrome
  • Infection (eg, neonatal pneumonia)

Examination

  • ↓ Postductal relative to preductal oxygen saturation
  • Respiratory distress & cyanosis
  • Prominent S2

Treatment

  • Oxygenation & ventilation
  • Inhaled nitric oxide (pulmonary vasodilator)

directTables: Causes of secondary hypertension

Causes of secondary hypertension

Condition

Clinical clues/features

Renal parenchymal disease

  • Elevated serum creatinine
  • Urinalysis abnormalities (eg, proteinuria, RBC casts)

Renal artery stenosis

  • Systolic-diastolic abdominal bruit
  • Recurrent flash pulmonary edema
  • Marked AKI following initiation of ACE inhibition

Primary hyperaldosteronism

  • Hypokalemia (spontaneous or thiazide induced)
  • Metabolic alkalosis

Obstructive sleep apnea

  • Daytime somnolence
  • BMI >35 kg/m2, large neck circumference

Pheochromocytoma

  • Paroxysmal hypertension & tachycardia
  • Episodic headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis

Cushing syndrome

  • Cushingoid body habitus, proximal muscle weakness
  • Hyperglycemia

Thyroid dysfunction

  • Hyperthyroidism: anxiety, heat intolerance, weight loss, tachycardia
  • Hypothyroidism: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, bradycardia

Primary hyperparathyroidism

  • Mild-to-moderate hypercalcemia ± symptoms
  • Nephrolithiasis

Coarctation of the aorta

  • Headaches & epistaxis
  • Upper extremity hypertension with brachial-femoral pulse delay

AKI = acute kidney injury; RBC = red blood cell.
Severe hypertension

Severe hypertension

Clinical features

Treatment

Severe
asymptomatic
hypertension

  • Blood pressure ≥180/120 mm Hg*
  • No symptoms or evidence of end-organ damage
  • Oral antihypertensives

Hypertensive
emergency

  • Severe hypertension with end-organ damage:
    • Acute coronary syndrome
    • Encephalopathy
    • Pulmonary edema
    • Acute kidney injury
    • Intracranial or subarachnoid hemorrhage
    • Aortic dissection
    • Retinopathy: papilledema, hemorrhages, exudates
  • IV antihypertensives: labetalol, esmolol, nicardipine, fenoldopam
  • Acute pulmonary edema: nitroglycerin plus furosemide
  • Acute coronary syndrome: nitroglycerin
  • Aortic dissection: labetalol

*Some guidelines specify ≥180/110 mm Hg.
Laboratory evaluation of hypertension

Laboratory evaluation of hypertension

Renal function tests

  • Serum electrolytes (Na, K, Ca)
  • Serum creatinine
  • Urinalysis
  • Urine albumin/creatinine ratio (optional)

Endocrine tests

  • Fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c
  • Lipid profile
  • TSH

Cardiac tests

  • ECG
  • Echocardiography (optional)

Other tests

  • Complete blood count
  • Uric acid (optional)
Hypertensive crisis

Hypertensive crisis

Hypertensive
urgency

  • Severe hypertension (≥180/120 mm Hg)
  • No evidence of end-organ damage

Hypertensive
emergency

  • Severe hypertension with end-organ damage:
    • Cardiovascular: angina, myocardial infarction, aortic dissection
    • CNS: encephalopathy, cerebral infarct/hemorrhage
    • Kidney: acute hypertensive nephrosclerosis
    • Lung: pulmonary edema
    • Retina: papilledema, flame-shaped hemorrhages, exudates

Treatment of symptomatic peripheral artery disease

Step 1A

Risk factor management

  • Smoking cessation
  • Blood pressure & diabetes mellitus control
  • Antiplatelet & statin therapy

Step 1B

  • Supervised exercise therapy

Step 2

  • Cilostazol (preferred over pentoxifylline)

Step 3

Revascularization for persistent symptoms

  • Autogenous or synthetic bypass graft
GLP

Secondary prevention of cardiovascular events in patients
with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease

Lifestyle
modifications

  • Complete smoking cessation*
  • Dietary modification (eg, ↑ whole grains, vegetables, legumes)
  • Regular exercise (>150 min/week)

Medical
therapy

  • Blood pressure control <130/80 mm Hg**
  • High-intensity statin therapy to achieve LDL <70 mg/dL
  • Antiplatelet monotherapy
  • GLP-1 agonist or SGLT-2 inhibitor for type 2 DM

*Greatest risk reduction for a single intervention.

**ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blocker preferred.

DM = diabetes mellitus; GLP = glucagon-like peptide; SGLT = sodium glucose transporter.

tables: Thoracic aortic aneurysm

Thoracic aortic aneurysm

Risk factors

  • Advanced age (>60), smoking, HTN
  • Connective tissue disease (eg, Marfan syndrome)
  • Family history, bicuspid aortic valve

Clinical
presentation

  • Usually asymptomatic & discovered incidentally
  • Subacute symptoms due to expansion:
    • Vague chest/back pain
    • Compression of structures (eg, hoarseness, dysphagia)
  • Symptoms indicate imminent risk of dissection/rupture

Imaging

  • CXR may show widened mediastinum, enlarged aortic knob
  • Chest CT or MR angiography for diagnostic confirmation

CXR = chest x-ray; HTN = hypertension.

subs.subject: path
images: Endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm
Evaluation of suspected unstable abdominal aortic aneurysm
tables: Abdominal aortic aneurysm

Abdominal aortic aneurysm

Risk factors

  • Advanced age (eg, >60)
  • Smoking, male sex, hypertension
  • History of atherosclerosis or CTD

Clinical presentation

  • Mostly asymptomatic
  • Rapid expansion
    • Dull abdominal/back pain
    • Distal embolization
  • Rupture
    • Sudden, severe abdominal/back pain ± shock
    • Umbilical/flank hematoma

Management

  • Smoking cessation
  • Asymptomatic:
    • Serial imaging: size <5.5 cm*
    • Elective repair: size ≥5.5 cm or rapid expansion
  • Symptomatic:
    • Urgent repair: HD stable patients
    • Emergency repair: HD unstable patients

*A smaller repair cutoff of 5 cm is used for women.  Serial imaging frequency depends on aneurysm size & expansion rate.

CTD = connective tissue disease; HD = hemodynamically.

directTables: Complications due to extension of acute aortic dissection

Complications due to extension of acute aortic dissection

Complication

(involved structure)

  • Stroke (carotid artery)
  • Horner syndrome (carotid sympathetic plexus)
  • Acute aortic regurgitation (aortic root/valve)
  • Myocardial ischemia/infarction (coronary artery ostia)
  • Pericardial effusion/tamponade (pericardium)
  • Hemothorax (pleural cavity)
  • Renal infarction (renal arteries)
  • Intestinal ischemia (mesenteric arteries)
  • Lower extremity paralysis (spinal arteries)
Acute aortic dissection

Acute aortic dissection

Risk factors

  • Chronic hypertension (strongest overall risk factor)
  • Underlying aortopathy (eg, Marfan syndrome)
  • Cocaine use

Clinical presentation

  • Severe, tearing chest or back pain, maximal at onset
  • ± Variation in SBP between arms >20 mm Hg
  • Hypertension usually present*

Diagnosis

  • ECG: normal or nonspecific ST-segment & T-wave changes
  • Chest x-ray: mediastinal widening
  • CT angiography or TEE for definitive diagnosis

Treatment

  • Pain control (eg, morphine)
  • Intravenous beta blockers (eg, esmolol)
  • ± Sodium nitroprusside (if SBP >120 mm Hg despite beta blockers)
  • Emergency surgical repair for ascending dissection

*Hypotension on presentation suggests aortic rupture or other complication (eg, cardiac tamponade, acute aortic regurgitation).

SBP = systolic blood pressure; TEE = transesophageal echocardiography.
Acute aortic dissection

Acute aortic dissection

Pathophysiology

  • Intimal tear allows pressurized blood into aortic wall
  • Propagation of dissection creates false aortic lumen
  • Complications arise from extension into nearby structures

Risk factors

  • Chronic hypertension (strongest overall risk factor)
  • Underlying aortopathy (eg, Marfan syndrome)

Clinical presentation

  • Sudden-onset, severe chest and/or back pain
  • Hypertension usually present*
  • Often a >20 mm Hg variation in SBP between arms
  • Often a widened mediastinum on chest x-ray

*Hypotension on presentation suggests aortic rupture or other complication (eg, cardiac tamponade,
acute aortic regurgitation).

SBP = systolic blood pressure.

tables: Vasospastic angina

Vasospastic angina

Pathogenesis

  • Hyperreactivity of coronary smooth muscle

Clinical
presentation

  • Young patients (age <50)
  • Smoking (minimal other CAD risk factors)
  • Recurrent chest discomfort
    • Occurs at rest or during sleep
    • Spontaneous resolution ≤15 min

Diagnosis

  • Ambulatory ECG: ST-segment elevation
  • Coronary angiography: no CAD

Treatment

  • Calcium channel blocker (preventive)
  • Sublingual nitroglycerin (abortive)

CAD = coronary artery disease.
Vasospastic angina

Vasospastic angina

Pathogenesis

  • Hyperreactivity of coronary smooth muscle due to endothelial dysfunction & autonomic imbalance

Clinical presentation

  • Young age (<50)
  • Minimal CAD risk factors (other than smoking)
  • Recurrent chest discomfort
    • At rest or during sleep
    • Spontaneous resolution ≤15 min

Diagnosis

  • ECG: ST-segment elevation during episode
  • Coronary angiography: no CAD

CAD = coronary artery disease.
Differential diagnosis & features of chest pain

Differential diagnosis & features of chest pain

Coronary artery
disease

  • Substernal
  • Precipitated by exertion
  • Relieved by rest or nitroglycerin

Pulmonary/pleuritic
(pleurisy, pneumonia,
pericarditis, PE)

  • Sharp/stabbing pain
  • Worse with inspiration
  • Pericarditis: worse when lying flat

Aortic
(dissection,
intramural hematoma)

  • Abrupt (maximal at onset), severe "tearing" pain
  • May radiate to back
  • Hypertension and/or inherited aortopathy

Esophageal

  • Substernal, may refer to neck
  • Associated with regurgitation
  • Provoked by recumbent position
  • Nonexertional, relieved by antacids

Chest wall/
musculoskeletal

  • Persistent pain
  • Worse with movement or change in position
  • Often follows repetitive activity

PE = pulmonary embolism.
Classic features of stable anginal chest pain

Classic features of stable anginal chest pain

Location & associated symptoms

  • Substernal
  • May radiate to arms, neck, lower jaw, or epigastrium
  • Often with dyspnea, nausea, &/or diaphoresis

Quality

  • Pressure-like or tight
  • Gradual in onset and offset
  • Not reproducible on palpation

Exacerbating &

alleviating factors

  • Provoked by a certain level of exertion
  • Relieved by rest or nitroglycerin

Duration

  • Episodes last 2-10 min

Frequency of presenting symptoms
in acute coronary syndrome

Chest pain

80%-85%

Dyspnea

70%-75%

Nausea

40%-55%

Vomiting

15%-20%

Epigastric pain

10%-15%
Myocardial infarction presentation

Myocardial infarction presentation

Ischemic chest pain

  • Described as pressure, heaviness, tightness
  • May radiate to jaw, arm, back, or upper abdomen
  • Lasts >30 min
  • Not improved with rest or position change
  • Worsens with exertion

Associated symptoms

  • Shortness of breath
  • Nausea & vomiting
  • Sweating
  • Anxiety
  • Indigestion
  • Dizziness
  • Fatigue & weakness

Atypical presentation

  • Associated symptoms with no chest pain
  • More common in female sex, older adults & clients with neuropathy (eg, diabetes mellitus)

directTables: Acute coronary syndromes

Acute coronary syndromes

Primary diagnostic finding

Management

STEMI

ST-segment elevation in ≥2 contiguous ECG leads

Emergency reperfusion (eg, PCI)

Non-STEMI*

Serum troponin elevation

Medical management initially, revascularization within 24-48 hr

Unstable angina**

Consistent history (eg, rest angina)

Monomorphic nonsustained ventricular tachycardia

Identification

  • ≥3 consecutive ventricular beats (wide QRS complex)
  • Rate >100/min & duration <30 sec

Predisposing conditions

  • Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
  • Ischemic heart disease
  • Other cardiomyopathy (eg, HCM)

Precipitating factors

  • Serum electrolyte abnormalities (eg, ↓ K, ↓ Mg)
  • Hypoxemia or acute myocardial ischemia
  • Elevated sympathetic tone (eg, sepsis)

Management

  • Address precipitating factors (eg, replace electrolytes)
  • Consider adding (or increasing dose of) beta blockade

HCM = hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

topics.title: Acute coronary syndrome treatments
topics.subject: path
directTables: Acute management of acute coronary syndrome

Acute management of acute coronary syndrome

(STEMI, NSTEMI, or unstable angina)

Nitrates

  • Rapid chest pain relief
  • Caution with hypotension (eg, RV infarction)

Beta blocker

  • Cardioselective (eg, metoprolol, atenolol)
  • Decreases myocardial O2 demand to limit infarct size
  • Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock & bradycardia

Antiplatelet therapy

  • Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor (eg, prasugrel, clopidogrel)*
  • Reduces platelet activity

Anticoagulation

  • Unfractionated heparin, bivalirudin, or enoxaparin
  • Limits thrombus expansion

Statin therapy

  • High potency (eg, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin)
  • Stabilizes atherosclerotic plaque

Coronary reperfusion

STEMI

  • PCI <90 min from first medical contact
  • Fibrinolytics (eg, alteplase) if PCI is unavailable

NSTEMI or unstable angina

  • Coronary angiography often within 24 hr

*In patients with NSTEMI or unstable angina, P2Y12 inhibitor therapy is often held until after coronary angiography in case the atherosclerotic coronary anatomy indicates the need for coronary artery bypass grafting.

NSTEMI = non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction; PCI = percutaneous coronary intervention; RV = right ventricular; STEMI = ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction.
Medical management following myocardial infarction

Medical management following myocardial infarction

Medication

Indication

Dual antiplatelet therapy
(low-dose aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor)

  • All patients (regardless of stent placement)
  • Low-dose aspirin continued indefinitely
  • P2Y12 inhibitor continued for 12 months

Beta blocker
(eg, metoprolol, carvedilol)

Absolute contraindications

Contraindications to fibrinolytic therapy for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction

Absolute contraindications

  • History of intracranial hemorrhage
  • History of ischemic stroke within 3 months
  • Presence of cerebrovascular malformation or intracranial malignancy
  • Suspected aortic dissection
  • Bleeding diathesis or active bleeding (except menses)
  • Major closed head or facial trauma within past 3 months

Relative contraindications

  • Blood pressure >180/110 mm Hg
  • History of ischemic stroke >3 months prior
  • Prolonged CPR or major surgery within past 3 weeks
  • Internal bleeding within past 2-4 weeks
  • Current warfarin use with INR >1.7
CPR = cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

Acute management of acute coronary syndrome

(STEMI, NSTEMI, or unstable angina)

Nitrates

  • Rapid chest pain relief
  • Caution with hypotension (eg, RV infarction)

Beta blocker

  • Cardioselective (eg, metoprolol, atenolol)
  • Decreases myocardial O2 demand to limit infarct size
  • Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock & bradycardia

Antiplatelet therapy

  • Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor (eg, prasugrel, clopidogrel)*
  • Reduces platelet activity

Anticoagulation

  • Unfractionated heparin, bivalirudin, or enoxaparin
  • Limits thrombus expansion

Statin therapy

  • High potency (eg, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin)
  • Stabilizes atherosclerotic plaque

Coronary reperfusion

STEMI

  • PCI <90 min from first medical contact
  • Fibrinolytics (eg, alteplase) if PCI is unavailable

NSTEMI or unstable angina

  • Coronary angiography often within 24 hr

*In patients with NSTEMI or unstable angina, P2Y12 inhibitor therapy is often held until after coronary angiography in case the atherosclerotic coronary anatomy indicates the need for coronary artery bypass grafting.

tables: Alcohol-induced cardiomyopathy

Alcohol-induced cardiomyopathy

Pathophysiology

  • Direct toxicity of ethanol leads to contractile dysfunction
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy eventually develops

Clinical presentation

  • History of heavy & prolonged alcohol use
  • Symptomatic HFrEF (eg, dyspnea, volume overload)
  • Laboratory evidence of heavy alcohol use (eg, AST/ALT >2:1)

Diagnosis

  • Consistent clinical presentation
  • Exclusion of other causes of HFrEF (eg, ischemic heart disease)

Management

  • Complete alcohol abstinence (may reverse cardiomyopathy)
  • Standard treatment of persistent HFrEF (eg, ARNI, diuretic)

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; ARNI = angiotensin receptor blocker-neprilysin inhibitor; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; HFrEF = heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
Dilated cardiomyopathy

Dilated cardiomyopathy

Pathophysiology

  • Myocardial contractile dysfunction → ventricular dilation
  • Heart failure & myocardial fibrosis can eventually develop*
  • May be preceded by myocarditis (myocardial inflammation)

Notable causes

  • Infection (eg, viral, Chagas disease)
  • Toxins (eg, alcohol, cocaine)
  • Medications (eg, anthracyclines, anti-HER2 agents)
  • Inherited (eg, classic familial, Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
  • Rheumatologic/infiltrative (eg, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis)
  • Nutritional deficiency (eg, thiamine, selenium)
  • Other (eg, idiopathic, peripartum, tachycardia induced)

*Cardiomyopathy may be reversible if disease process is halted before substantial fibrosis develops.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Pathophysiology

  • Genetic mutations affecting cardiac sarcomere proteins
  • Autosomal dominant inheritance
  • Variable phenotypic penetrance

Clinical features

  • Many patients are asymptomatic
  • Exertional dyspnea, fatigue, angina, light-headedness, syncope
  • Systolic ejection murmur accentuated by ↓ LV blood volume
  • Diastolic dysfunction with audible S4
  • ↑ Risk of atrial fibrillation & ventricular tachycardia

Diagnosis

  • ECG: left axis deviation, abnormalities of depolarization (eg, Q waves) or repolarization (eg, inverted T waves)
  • Echocardiography: septal LV hypertrophy, dynamic LVOT obstruction, LA dilation

Management

  • Beta blocker or nondihydropyridine CCB (↑ LV blood volume)
  • Avoidance of dehydration & vasodilators (↓ LV blood volume)
  • ICD placement if substantially increased risk for SCD
  • Septal ablation, cardiac transplantation

CCB = calcium channel blocker; ICD = implantable cardiac defibrillator; LA = left atrial; LV = left ventricular; LVOT = LV outflow tract; SCD = sudden cardiac death.

directTables: Peripartum cardiomyopathy

Peripartum cardiomyopathy

Risk factors

  • Maternal age >30
  • Multiple gestation
  • Preeclampsia, eclampsia

Clinical features

  • LVEF <45%
  • Onset: 36 weeks gestation to 5 months postpartum 
  • No other cause of heart failure

Management

  • Deliver based on maternal hemodynamic stability 
  • Standard systolic heart failure regimen
  • Thromboembolism prophylaxis

Recurrence risk

  • LVEF <20% at diagnosis
  • Persistent left ventricular systolic dysfunction

LVEF = left ventricular ejection fraction.
Stress-induced (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy

Stress-induced (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy

Risk factors

  • Postmenopausal woman
  • Recent physical or emotional stressor

Clinical features

  • Chest pain mimicking myocardial infarction
  • Decompensated heart failure
  • Moderate troponin elevation
  • ECG: ischemic changes in precordial leads

Diagnosis

  • Catheterization: no obstructive CAD
  • Echo: LV apical hypokinesis, basilar hyperkinesis

Treatment

  • Resolves in several weeks with supportive care

CAD = coronary artery disease; LV = left ventricular.

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

Etiology

  • LV diastolic dysfunction due to impaired relaxation

Risk factors

  • Chronic hypertension (concentric LV hypertrophy)
  • Obesity & sedentary lifestyle (myocardial interstitial fibrosis)
  • CAD & related risk factors (eg, diabetes mellitus)

Management

  • Specific therapies to reduce hospitalization & possibly mortality:
    • SGLT-2 inhibitor (eg, empagliflozin) added first
    • MRA (eg, spironolactone) added secondarily
  • Loop diuretics as needed to treat volume overload
  • Antihypertensives as needed to reduce afterload
  • Treatment of exacerbating conditions (eg, CAD, OSA, A-fib)
  • Exercise training, weight loss & cardiac rehabilitation

A-fib = atrial fibrillation; CAD = coronary artery disease; LV = left ventricular; MRA = mineralocorticoid antagonist; OSA = obstructive sleep apnea; SGLT-2 = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2.

directTables: High-output heart failure

High-output heart failure

Pathophysiology

  • ↓ SVR leads to ↑ cardiac output & ↑ venous return

Causes

  • Morbid obesity (most common)
  • Arteriovenous fistula (congenital or acquired)
  • Hyperthyroidism, severe anemia, advanced cirrhosis
  • Paget disease, thiamine deficiency

Clinical presentation

  • Hyperdynamic circulation (↑ PP, warm extremities)
  • Peripheral & pulmonary edema
  • Laterally displaced PMI, systolic flow murmur

Echocardiographic findings

  • Dilated LV, RV & inferior vena cava
  • Elevated resting cardiac index

LV = left ventricle; PMI = point of maximal impulse; PP = pulse pressure; RV = right ventricle; SVR = systemic vascular resistance.

Common mechanisms of reduced systemic vascular resistance
leading to high-output heart failure

Bypass of systemic
arteriolar resistance

  • Acquired AV fistula (eg, trauma, HD)
  • Congenital AV malformation
  • Paget disease of bone

Peripheral vasodilation due to
unmet metabolic demand
in the tissues

  • Hyperthyroidism
  • Severe anemia
  • Thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi)
  • Myeloproliferative disease
  • Chronic lung disease

Peripheral vasodilation
due to other factors

  • Morbid obesity (vasodilatory adipokines)
  • Cirrhosis (splanchnic vasodilation)

tables: High-output heart failure

High-output heart failure

Pathophysiology

  • ↓ SVR leads to ↑ cardiac output & ↑ venous return

Causes

  • Morbid obesity (most common)
  • Arteriovenous fistula (congenital or acquired)
  • Hyperthyroidism, severe anemia, advanced cirrhosis
  • Paget disease, thiamine deficiency

Clinical presentation

  • Hyperdynamic circulation (↑ PP, warm extremities)
  • Peripheral & pulmonary edema
  • Laterally displaced PMI, systolic flow murmur

Echocardiographic findings

  • Dilated LV, RV & inferior vena cava
  • Elevated resting cardiac index

LV = left ventricle; PMI = point of maximal impulse; PP = pulse pressure; RV = right ventricle; SVR = systemic vascular resistance.

Common mechanisms of reduced systemic vascular resistance
leading to high-output heart failure

Bypass of systemic
arteriolar resistance

  • Acquired AV fistula (eg, trauma, HD)
  • Congenital AV malformation
  • Paget disease of bone

Peripheral vasodilation due to
unmet metabolic demand
in the tissues

  • Hyperthyroidism
  • Severe anemia
  • Thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi)
  • Myeloproliferative disease
  • Chronic lung disease

Peripheral vasodilation
due to other factors

  • Morbid obesity (vasodilatory adipokines)
  • Cirrhosis (splanchnic vasodilation)

AV = arteriovenous; HD = hemodialysis.

Sepsis & septic shock

Sepsis & septic shock

Definitions & pathophysiology

  • Sepsis: infection + ≥2 organ system dysfunction (eg, encephalopathy, ARDS, DIC)
  • Septic shock: sepsis + refractory hypotension (ie, vasopressors) + ↑ lactate (hypoperfusion)

Work-up &
management

  • First 1-3 hr: cultures, empiric antibiotics & crystalloid (eg, lactated Ringer) resuscitation
  • Evaluate: infection source, sequential organ dysfunction
  • Organ protection: MAP >65 mm Hg, low tidal volume ventilation, glucose control
 

Prognosis

  • Mortality predictors: sequential organ failure (~15%/system), ↑↑ lactic acidosis (≥4 mmol/L)
  • Late mortality: mainly nosocomial infections (postseptic immune paralysis)
  • PICS: cognitive, emotional & physical impairments in most survivors 

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; DIC = disseminated intravascular coagulation, MAP = mean arterial pressure; PICS = post–intensive care syndrome.

directTables: Cardiac tamponade

Cardiac tamponade

Etiology

  • Blood in pericardial space (eg, left ventricular rupture, cardiac surgery)
  • Pericardial effusion (eg, malignancy, infection, uremia)

Clinical signs

  • Beck triad: hypotension, JVD, ↓ heart sounds
  • Pulsus paradoxus: >10 mm Hg drop in SBP during inspiration

Diagnosis

  • ECG: low-voltage QRS complex, electrical alternans
  • Chest x-ray: enlarged cardiac silhouette,* clear lungs
  • Echocardiogram: right atrial & ventricular collapse, IVC plethora

Treatment

  • Intravenous fluids to increase right-sided preload
  • Drainage via pericardiocentesis or pericardial window

*Subacute but not acute tamponade.

IVC = inferior vena cava; JVD = jugular venous distension; SBP = systolic blood pressure.

directTables: Vasovagal & situational syncope

Vasovagal & situational syncope

Triggers

  • Pain,* anxiety,* emotional stress, heat, prolonged standing
  • Situational: cough,* micturition,* defecation, eating, hair-combing*

Clinical
presentation

  • Prodrome (eg, warmth, pallor, nausea, diaphoresis)
  • Rapid recovery of consciousness (eg, <1-2 min)

Diagnosis

  • Mainly based on clinical history of event
  • Upright tilt table testing sometimes indicated in uncertain cases

Treatment

  • Reassurance & avoidance of triggers
  • Counterpressure techniques for recurrent episodes

*Particularly common triggers in the pediatric population.
Clues to etiology of syncope

Clues to etiology of syncope

Reflex syncope

Vasovagal

  • Trigger (eg, emotional stress, prolonged standing)
  • Prodrome (eg, nausea, sweating, warmth)

Situational

  • Occurs with micturition, defecation, swallowing, or coughing

Carotid hypersensitivity

  • Tactile stimulation of carotid sinus while standing
  • Advanced age, carotid atherosclerosis

Orthostatic syncope

Medications

  • Vasodilators (eg, α-1 blockers, antihypertensives)
  • Inotropic/chronotropic blockade (eg, β blockers)

Hypovolemia

  • History consistent with volume loss

Autonomic dysfunction

  • Advanced age
  • Predisposing disease (eg, DM, Parkinson)

Cardiac syncope

LV outflow obstruction

  • Syncope with exertion
  • Systolic ejection murmur

Ventricular tachycardia

  • No warning symptoms
  • Cardiomyopathy or ischemic HD (monomorphic)
  • QT-interval prolongation (polymorphic)

Conduction impairment*

  • Preceding fatigue or lightheadedness
  • ECG abnormalities (eg, sinus pauses, dropped QRS complexes)

*Sick sinus syndrome or advanced atrioventricular block.

DM = diabetes mellitus; HD = heart disease; LV = left ventricular.
Medication-induced orthostasis

Medication-induced orthostasis

Mechanism

Examples

α1 blockade–mediated vasodilation

  • Terazosin, prazosin, doxazosin
  • Antipsychotics (eg, risperidone)
  • Antihistamines, TCAs

Other vasodilation

  • ACE inhibitors & ARBs
  • Dihydropyridine CCBs
  • Hydralazine, nitrates
  • Phosphodiesterase inhibitors

Volume depletion

  • Diuretics
  • SGLT-2 inhibitors

Sympathetic blockade

  • β blockers
  • Clonidine

ARBs = angiotensin II receptor blockers; CCBs = calcium channel blockers;
SGLT-2 = sodium-glucose cotransporter-2; TCAs = tricyclic antidepressants.
Diagnosis of orthostatic hypotension

Diagnosis of orthostatic hypotension

Within 2-5 min of standing
from a supine position

  • ≥20 mm Hg ↓ in systolic blood pressure
    OR
  • ≥10 mm Hg ↓ in diastolic blood pressure

topics.title: Infective endocarditis
topics.subject: path
directTables: Bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis

Bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis

High-risk cardiac
conditions

  • Prosthetic heart valve
  • Previous valve repair using prosthetic material
  • Previous infective endocarditis
  • Unrepaired cyanotic CHD
  • Repaired CHD with residual shunt or defect
  • Valvular disease in transplanted heart

Indicated
procedures

  • Dental work with gingival manipulation
  • Respiratory tract procedure with incision or biopsy

Antibiotic
choice*

  • Amoxicillin (first-line)
  • Cephalexin, azithromycin, or doxycycline (if PCN allergy)

*Antibiotics are targeted at viridans group Streptococcus coverage.

CHD = congenital heart disease; PCN = penicillin.
Common surgical indications in infectious endocarditis

Common surgical indications in infectious endocarditis

  • Acute heart failure (eg, aortic/mitral valve regurgitation)
  • Extension of infection (eg, abscess, fistula, heart block)
  • Difficult-to-eradicate organism (eg, fungus, MDR pathogen)
  • Persistent bacteremia on antibiotics
  • Large vegetation/persistent septic emboli

MDR = multidrug-resistant.

Antibiotic prophylaxis for secondary prevention of rheumatic fever

Severity

Duration of therapy following last attack

Uncomplicated rheumatic fever

5 years or until age 21*

With carditis but no valvular disease

10 years or until age 21*

With carditis & valvular disease

10 years or until age 40*

*Whichever duration is longer. Intramuscular penicillin G benzathine every 3-4 weeks is preferred.
Acute rheumatic fever

Acute rheumatic fever

Epidemiology

  • Peak incidence: age 5-15
  • Twice as common in girls

Clinical features

  
  • Major Jones criteria*
    • Joints (migratory arthritis)
    • ♥ (Carditis)
    • Nodules (subcutaneous)
    • Erythema marginatum
    • Sydenham chorea
 
  • Minor Jones criteria*
    • Fever
    • Arthralgia
    • Elevated ESR &/or CRP
    • Prolonged PR interval on ECG

Late sequela

 Valvular disease (particularly mitral stenosis)

Prevention

Penicillin for group A streptococcal
pharyngitis

*Diagnosis confirmed with 2 major criteria OR 1 major & 2 minor criteria.
CRP = C-reactive protein; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate.

topics.title: Acute pericarditis
topics.subject: path
directTables: Acute pericarditis

Acute pericarditis

Etiology

  • Viral or idiopathic
  • Autoimmune disease (eg, SLE)
  • Uremia (acute or chronic kidney failure)
  • Post myocardial infarction
    • Early: peri-infarction pericarditis
    • Late: Dressler syndrome

Clinical features & diagnosis

  • Pleuritic chest pain (↓ when sitting) ± fever
  • Pericardial friction rub (highly specific)
  • ECG: diffuse ST-segment elevation & PR-segment depression
  • Echocardiography: pericardial effusion

Treatment

  • NSAIDs & colchicine for viral or idiopathic etiology
  • Variable for other etiologies

NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.
Etiologies of pericarditis

Etiologies of pericarditis

Infection

Viral (most common), bacterial

Iatrogenic

Surgery, trauma, radiation & drug-related

Connective tissue disease

Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus

Cardiac

Dressler syndrome (post myocardial infarction), usually 1-6 weeks after myocardial infarction

Uremic

Serum BUN usually >60 mg/dL, but degree of pericarditis does not always correlate with degree of elevation

Malignancy

Can be due to cancer (eg, lung, breast, Hodgkin lymphoma) or treatment (eg, radiation, chemotherapy)

BUN = blood urea nitrogen.

directTables: Constrictive pericarditis

Constrictive pericarditis

Etiology

  • Recurrent idiopathic or viral pericarditis
  • Cardiac surgery or radiation therapy
  • Tuberculous pericarditis (endemic areas)

Clinical presentation

  • Fatigue, dyspnea on exertion
  • Peripheral edema, ascites, hepatic congestion
  • Pericardial knock in early diastole
  • Elevated JVP with Kussmaul sign*
  • Prominent y descent of JVP waveform

Diagnostic findings

  • Chest x-ray: pericardial calcification
  • Cardiac CT scan/MRI: pericardial thickening & calcification
  • Echocardiography: biatrial enlargement, normal ventricular wall thickness & cavity size, abnormal septal motion during respiration

*Absence of the expected fall in JVP during inspiration.

JVP = jugular venous pulse.

topics.subject: path
directImages: Cardiac MRI characteristic gadolinium enhancement patterns
images: Cardiac MRI characteristic gadolinium enhancement patterns
directTables: Viral myocarditis

Viral myocarditis

Clinical presentation

  • Commonly asymptomatic & resolves without detection
  • Heart failure that may progress to DCM*
  • Chest pain, ventricular arrhythmia with risk of SCD
  •  Relatively young adults usually affected (eg, age <55)
  • ± Viral prodrome (eg, fever, malaise, myalgia)

Diagnosis

  • ECG: nonspecific findings
  • Laboratory: mild to moderate serum troponin elevation
  • Echocardiography: 4-chamber dilation with diffuse hypokinesis
  • Cardiac MRI: epicardial or midwall enhancement
  • Biopsy: lymphocytic infiltration, viral DNA or RNA**

  • Supportive care to allow time for recovery
  • HFrEF medications (eg, diuretic, ACE inhibitor, β blocker)
  • Temporary ventricular assist device, if needed
  • Heart transplant if no recovery

**Endomyocardial biopsy is rarely required for diagnosis.

Causes of myocarditis*

Causes of myocarditis*

Infectious

  • Viral (eg, coxsackievirus, adenovirus)**
  • Protozoal (eg, Chagas disease)
  • Spirochetal (eg, Lyme disease)
  • Rickettsial (eg, RMSF)
  • Fungal (eg, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis)
  • Mycobacterial (ie, tuberculosis)
  • Helminthic (eg, strongyloidiasis, trichinosis)
  • Bacterial toxins (eg, diphtheria)

Noninfectious

  • Rheumatologic disorders (eg, sarcoidosis, SLE)
  • Medication hypersensitivity (eg, antibiotics, clozapine)

*Some etiologies may cause persistent contractile dysfunction that can progress to dilated cardiomyopathy.

**Most common cause.

directTables: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu)

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu)

Vascular bed

Sequelae

CNS

  • Hemorrhagic CVA
  • Brain abscess: paradoxical bacterial embolization across pulmonary AVM

Mucocutaneous

  • Oral & cutaneous telangiectasia
  • Recurrent epistaxis

Lung

  • Pulmonary AVM: hemoptysis
  • PAH: right-sided heart failure

GI

  • Chronic GI bleed
  • Liver: portal hypertension, high-output heart failure

AVM =arteriovenous malformation; CVA = cerebrovascular accident; GI = gastrointestinal; PAH = pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Pathogenesis

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia
(Rendu-Osler-Weber syndrome)

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal dominant mutations impairing TGF-β signaling
  • Disrupted angiogenesis & loss of vascular integrity

Clinical
features

  • Mucocutaneous (oral, skin) telangiectasia
  • Recurrent epistaxis
  • Visceral organ AVMs: gastrointestinal tract (bleeding), lung (hemoptysis), brain (hemorrhagic stroke), liver

Complications

  • High-output heart failure*
  • Pulmonary hypertension*
  • Paradoxic embolism**
  • Iron deficiency anemia

*Secondary to high-volume, systemic AVMs.

**Bacterial translocation or embolization through pulmonary AVMs.

AVMs = arteriovenous malformations; TGF-β = transforming growth factor-β.

Tumor characteristics

  • Benign neoplasm, 80% located in left atrium

directTables: Pharmacologic management of chronic stable angina

Pharmacologic management of chronic stable angina

Beta blockers

  • First-line therapy
  • ↓ Myocardial contractility & heart rate

Nondihydropyridine CCBs

  • Alternate to beta blocker
  • ↓ Myocardial contractility & heart rate

Dihydropyridine CCBs

  • Added to beta blocker when needed
  • ↓ Afterload via systemic arterial dilation

Nitrates

  • Short-acting to abort acute symptoms
  • Long-acting added for persistent angina
  • ↓ Preload via dilation of capacitance veins

Ranolazine

  • Alternate therapy for refractory angina
  • ↓ Myocardial calcium influx

Indications for statin therapy in the prevention of ASCVD

Secondary prevention

Established ASCVD

Ezetimibe

Ezetimibe

Mechanism of action

  • ↓ Dietary cholesterol absorption by blocking NPC1L1 enterocyte transporter
  • ↓ Cholesterol delivery to liver, which ↑ LDL-R expression

Physiologic effects

  • ↓ LDL cholesterol, synergistic effects with statins
  • Small effect on TGs
  • Possible ↓ ASCVD in high-risk patients (when used with statin); no clear primary prevention benefits

Indications

  • Treatment intensification in high-risk patients (eg, prior MI) with persistently elevated LDL despite statin

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Gastrointestinal distress
  • Hepatotoxicity, myopathy (eg, when used with statins)
  • Possible ↑ risk of gallstones (eg, when used with fibrates)

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; MI = myocardial infarction; NPC1L1 = Niemann-Pick C1-like 1; PCSK9i = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor; TG = triglycerides.
Appropriate lipid-lowering therapy based on primary lipid derangement

Appropriate lipid-lowering therapy based on primary lipid derangement

Elevated LDL

  • First-line: statin
  • Intensification/alternative: ezetimibe, PCSK9

Low HDL

  • First-line: exercise, dietary changes
  • Consider statin if accompanied by ↑ ASCVD risk (eg, ↑ LDL)
  • Otherwise, therapy specifically to raise HDL not recommended (lack of demonstrated benefit)

High TG

  • First-line (low ASCVD risk): fibrates & lifestyle changes (eg, diet, exercise, alcohol avoidance)
  • First line (high ASCVD risk): omega-3 acids (along with statin)
    • Intensification with fibrate
    • Niacin not usually recommended due to adverse effects

topics.title: Lipid-lowering agents (continued)
topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Statins (eg, simvastatin)

Statins (eg, simvastatin)

Mechanism of action

  • Inhibits HMG CoA reductase to ↓ cholesterol & VLDL synthesis
  • Results in ↑ LDL-R expression and ↑ LDL clearance

Effects

  • Main: ↓ LDL cholesterol
  • Secondary: ↑ HDL, ↓ TG (modest)
  • ↓ CVD events & mortality

Indications

  • First-line treatment for primary & secondary ASCVD prevention
  • ASCVD risk >20% & age <75: high-intensity statin
  • ASCVD risk 7.5-10% &/or age >75: moderate-intensity statin
  • Synergistic effects with PCSK9i (in high-risk patients)

Adverse effects

  • Myalgias, myopathy
  • Transaminitis/hepatic inflammation
  • Increase in risk of T2DM (small)
  • Possible cognitive effects (mild)

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; CVD = cardiovascular disease; HDL = high-density lipoprotein; HMG CoA = 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; PCSK9i = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor; T2DM = type 2 diabetes mellitus; TG = triglycerides.
PCSK9 inhibitors

PCSK9 inhibitors(eg, evolucumab)

Mechanism of action

  • Blocks binding of PCSK9 to LDL-R to ↓ LDL-R degradation
  • Net effect is ↑ LDL receptor availability & LDL clearance

Physiologic effects

  • ↓ LDL cholesterol, synergistic effects with statins
  • ↓ CVD events in high-risk patients

Indications

  • Adjunct treatment to statin if persistent dyslipidemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, or very high CVD risk

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • High cost; administered as injection
  • Side effects: rare myopathy, injection site reaction

CVD = cardiovascular disease; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; PCSK9 = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9.
Omega-3 fatty acids

Omega-3 fatty acids

Mechanism of action

  • ↓ Hepatic VLDL synthesis
  • ↑ LPL activity (increased metabolism of circulating TGs)
  • ↑ PPAR-α activity → beta-oxidation of FFAs

Physiologic effects

  • ↓ TG, ↑ HDL
  • Effective for secondary ASCVD prevention in patients with high TGs
  • No clear effect for primary ASCVD prevention

Indications

  • First-line treatment of moderate-to-severe hyperTG (eg, >500 mg/dL) with ↑ ASCVD risk

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Often requires very high dose for effectiveness
  • May raise LDL, risk of atrial fibrillation

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; FFA = free fatty acid;  HDL = high-density lipoprotein; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; PPAR-α = peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha; TG = triglycerides; VLDL = very low density lipoprotein.
Fibrates (eg, gemfibrozil)

Fibrates (eg, gemfibrozil)

Mechanism of action

  • Stimulate lipoprotein lipase activity (↑ TG lipolysis)
  • ↑ FFA uptake, ↓ TG levels
  • Also ↓ bile acid synthesis → reducing dietary cholesterol solubility

Physiologic effects

  • ↓ LDL cholesterol, synergistic effects with statins
  • ↑ HDL

Indications

  • Hypertriglyceridemia (>500 mg/dL) → reduce risk of pancreatitis
  • No clear evidence of ↓ ASCVD risk for primary prevention

Adverse effects & disadvantages

  • Myopathy (especially when used with statins)
  • Gallstone precipitation (due to ↓ bile acids)

ASCVD = atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; FFA = free fatty acid; HDL = high-density lipoprotein receptor; LDL = low-density lipoprotein; TG = triglyceride.

Digoxin toxicity

Signs & symptoms

topics.title: Antiarrhythmics—β-blockers (class II)
topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Beta blocker toxicity

Beta blocker toxicity

Mechanism

  • Excessive adrenergic blockade → ↓↓ intracellular cAMP

Clinical
presentation

  • Beta 1 blockade–mediated effects:
    • Cardiac suppression with bradycardia & hypotension*
    • Confusion due to cerebral hypoperfusion
  • Beta 2 blockade–mediated effects:
    • Bronchospasm
    • Hypoglycemia (impaired gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis)
    • Confusion & seizures due to hypoglycemia**

Diagnosis

  • ECG: sinus node dysfunction, atrioventricular block
  • Consistent clinical presentation (drug levels not useful)

Treatment

  • Intravenous fluids for hypotension & atropine for bradycardia
  • Glucagon to directly counteract toxicity (↑ intracellular cAMP)
  • Calcium gluconate sometimes given to ↑ blood pressure

*Beta 1 blockade–mediated effects are predominant with cardioselective beta blockers (eg, metoprolol), whereas all effects are seen with nonselective beta blockers (eg, propranolol).

**Lipid-soluble beta blockers (eg, propranolol) can also cause confusion & seizures via direct CNS effects.

tables: Gastroschisis

Gastroschisis

Clinical
features

  • Full-thickness abdominal wall defect lateral to umbilicus
  • Bowel herniation without covering membrane
  • Usually isolated (extraintestinal anomalies rare)

Prenatal
findings

  • ↑ Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein
  • Free-floating bowel on fetal ultrasonography

Management

  • Place lower body in plastic bag to minimize heat & fluid loss
  • Insert tube for gastric decompression
  • Start intravenous fluids & antibiotics
  • Perform surgical repair (primary or staged closure)

VACTERL association

V: vertebral anomaly

A: anorectal malformation

C: cardiovascular anomaly

T: tracheoesophageal fistula

E: esophageal atresia

R: renal &/or radial anomaly

L: limb defect
Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia

Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia

Pathogenesis

  • Defective division of foregut into esophagus & trachea
  • Most commonly results in proximal esophageal pouch & fistula between distal trachea & esophagus

Clinical
features

  • Coughing, choking, vomiting with feeding
  • Excessive oral secretions
  • Commonly part of VACTERL association

Diagnosis

  • Inability to pass enteric tube into stomach
  • X-ray: enteric tube coiled in proximal esophagus

Management

  • Surgical correction
  • VACTERL screening: echocardiography, renal ultrasound

VACTERL = Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, TracheoEsophageal, Renal, Limb defects.

topics.title: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
topics.subject: embryo
directTables: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

Pathogenesis

  • Hypertrophy of pylorus → gastric outlet obstruction
  • Risk factor: macrolide antibiotic exposure

Clinical features

  • Age 3-6 weeks
  • Nonbilious projectile emesis
    • Immediately postprandial
    • Usually followed by interest in refeeding ("hungry vomiter")

Examination

  • Often normal
    • ± Palpable, olive-shaped epigastric mass
    • ± Visible peristalsis
    • ± Signs of dehydration (eg, sunken fontanelle)

Laboratory/Imaging

  • Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis*
  • Ultrasonography: thickened, elongated pylorus

Management

  • Intravenous hydration & electrolyte correction
  • Surgical pyloromyotomy

*Laboratory results may be normal if obtained early in disease course.

tables: Anal fissures

Anal fissures

Etiology

  • Local trauma (eg, constipation, prolonged diarrhea, anal sex)
  • Inflammatory bowel disease (eg, Crohn disease)
  • Malignancy

Clinical
presentation

  • Pain with bowel movements
  • Bright red blood on toilet paper or stool surface
  • Most common at posterior anal midline
  • Chronic fissure may have skin tag at distal end

Treatment

  • High-fiber diet & adequate fluid intake
  • Stool softeners
  • Sitz baths
  • Topical anesthetics & vasodilators (eg, nifedipine, nitroglycerin)

Pathogenesis

  • Incomplete fusion of pleuroperitoneal folds

directImages: Direct inguinal hernia Indirect inguinal hernia
images: Direct inguinal hernia Indirect inguinal hernia
directTables: Groin hernias

Groin hernias

Type

Classic presentation

Pathophysiology

Anatomy

Indirect inguinal

Male infants

Patent processus vaginalis

  • Originates lateral to inferior epigastric vessels
  • Protrudes through the deep inguinal ring into inguinal canal
  • May extend into the scrotum (following spermatic cord)

Direct inguinal

Older men

Weakness of transversalis fascia

  • Protrudes medial to the inferior epigastric vessels into Hesselbach's triangle
  • May pass through superficial inguinal ring
  • No direct route into the scrotum

Femoral

Women

Widening of the femoral ring

  • Emerges inferior to inguinal ligament
  • Protrudes through the femoral ring into the femoral canal
Groin hernias

Groin hernias

Epidemiology

  • Inguinal: more common in male patients
  • Femoral: more common in female patients; more likely to become incarcerated/strangulated (~40%)

Clinical features

  • Uncomplicated (reducible): ↑ groin bulge with ↑ abdominal pressure (eg, cough) ± discomfort
  • Incarcerated (nonreducible): moderate to severe groin pain & swelling
  • Strangulated (nonreducible & ischemic): severe groin pain & swelling, vomiting, fever ± peritonitis

Diagnosis

  • Clinical diagnosis; confirmatory testing typically not required
  • If diagnosis unclear: ultrasonography (preferred), CT scan, or MRI of the groin

Management

  • Watchful waiting considered for male patients with asymptomatic inguinal hernias
  • Elective surgical repair: symptomatic groin hernias; femoral hernias
  • Urgent or immediate surgical repair: incarcerated or strangulated hernias

directTables: Achalasia

Achalasia

Pathophysiology

  • Inflammatory degeneration of inhibitory ganglions of the myenteric plexus

Clinical
presentation

  • Chronic dysphagia to solids & liquids, regurgitation
  • Heartburn, weight loss

Diagnosis

  • Manometry: incomplete LES relaxation, ↓ peristalsis of distal esophagus
  • Barium esophagography: smooth "bird-beak" narrowing at gastroesophageal junction
  • Upper endoscopy to exclude malignancy

Management

  • Myotomy or pneumatic balloon dilation
  • Botulinum toxin injection, nitrates & CCB

CCB = calcium channel blocker; LES = lower esophageal sphincter.

subs.title: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
subs.subject: path
images: Nissen fundoplication for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
tables: Gastroesophageal reflux disease

Gastroesophageal reflux disease

Pathophysiology

  • Decreased tone or excessive transient relaxations of LES
  • Anatomic disruption to gastroesophageal junction (eg, hiatal hernia)
  • ↑ Risk with obesity, pregnancy, smoking, alcohol intake

Manifestations

  • Regurgitation of acidic material in mouth
  • Heartburn
  • Odynophagia (often indicates reflux esophagitis)
  • Extraesophageal manifestations: cough, hoarseness, wheezing

Complications

  • Esophageal: erosive esophagitis, Barrett esophagus, strictures
  • Extraesophageal: asthma exacerbation, laryngitis

Initial treatment

  • Lifestyle (eg, weight loss) & dietary changes
  • H2R blocker or PPI

H2R = histamine 2 receptor; LES = lower esophageal sphincter; PPI = proton pump inhibitor.

subs.title: Esophagitis
subs.subject: path
tables: Eosinophilic esophagitis in adults

Eosinophilic esophagitis in adults

Pathogenesis &
epidemiology

  • Th2-mediated inflammatory response triggered primarily by food antigen exposure
  • Comorbid atopic disease (asthma, eczema, food allergies, allergic rhinitis) common

Clinical
features

  • Dysphagia
  • Heartburn & epigastric pain
  • Regurgitation
  • Food impaction

Diagnosis

  • Endoscopy & esophageal biopsy (eosinophils: ≥15/hpf)
  • Exclusion of alternate diagnoses (eg, achalasia, infection)

Treatment

  • Elimination diet
  • Proton pump inhibitors
  • Topical glucocorticoids

Th2 = T-helper cell type 2.
Caustic ingestion

Caustic ingestion

Clinical features

Chemical burn or liquefaction necrosis resulting in:

  • Laryngeal damage: hoarseness & stridor
  • Esophageal damage: dysphagia & odynophagia
  • Gastric damage: epigastric pain & bleeding

Management

  • Secure airway, breathing & circulation
  • Decontamination: remove contaminated clothing & visible chemicals; irrigate exposed skin
  • X-ray of chest if respiratory symptoms present
  • Endoscopy within 24 hr

Complications

  • Upper airway compromise
  • Perforation
  • Strictures/stenosis (2-3 weeks)
  • Ulcers

Esophageal perforation

Etiology

  • Instrumentation (eg, endoscopy), trauma
  • Effort rupture (Boerhaave syndrome)
  • Esophagitis (infectious/drug-induced/caustic)

Clinical presentation

  • Chest/back &/or epigastric pain, systemic signs (eg, fever)

  • Pleural effusion with atypical (eg, green) fluid

Diagnosis

  • X-ray or CT scan of chest: widened mediastinum, pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax, pleural effusion

  • NPO, IV antibiotics & proton pump inhibitors
  • Emergency surgical consultation

images: Nissen fundoplication for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
tables: Gastroesophageal reflux disease

Gastroesophageal reflux disease

Pathophysiology

  • Decreased tone or excessive transient relaxations of LES
  • Anatomic disruption to gastroesophageal junction (eg, hiatal hernia)
  • ↑ Risk with obesity, pregnancy, smoking, alcohol intake

Manifestations

  • Regurgitation of acidic material in mouth
  • Heartburn
  • Odynophagia (often indicates reflux esophagitis)
  • Extraesophageal manifestations: cough, hoarseness, wheezing

Complications

  • Esophageal: erosive esophagitis, Barrett esophagus, strictures
  • Extraesophageal: asthma exacerbation, laryngitis

Initial treatment

  • Lifestyle (eg, weight loss) & dietary changes
  • H2R blocker or PPI

H2R = histamine 2 receptor; LES = lower esophageal sphincter; PPI = proton pump inhibitor.

topics.title: Barrett esophagus
topics.subject: path
directTables: Barrett esophagus

Barrett esophagus

Definition

  • Intestinal metaplasia in distal esophagus (ie, replacement of stratified squamous epithelium with metaplastic columnar epithelium)

Risk
factors

  • Chronic GERD (eg, >5 years)
  • White patient
  • Family history
  • Age >50
  • Obesity
  • Smoking

Screening &
management

  • Consider screening patients with multiple risk factors
  • Lifelong PPI (reduces cancer risk, heals esophageal damage)
  • If dysplasia is present, offer endoscopic surveillance vs eradication

Prognosis

  • <1%/year risk for malignancy development, higher if dysplasia is present

GERD = gastroesophageal reflux disease; PPI = proton pump inhibitor.

Celiac disease

Risk factors

  • First-degree relative with celiac disease
  • Down syndrome
  • Autoimmune disorders (eg, type 1 diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroiditis)

Classic
symptoms

  • ± Abdominal pain, distension, bloating, diarrhea

Extraintestinal
manifestations
(may be sole
presentation)

  • General: failure to thrive/weight loss, short stature,* delayed puberty/menarche*
  • Oral: enamel hypoplasia, atrophic glossitis
  • Dermatologic: dermatitis herpetiformis
  • Hematologic: iron deficiency anemia (due to malabsorption)
  • Neuropsychiatric: peripheral neuropathy, mood disorders (eg, anxiety, depression)
  • Musculoskeletal: arthritis, osteomalacia/rickets* (due to vitamin D malabsorption),

Diagnosis

  • ↑ Tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody
  • Proximal intestinal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytosis)

Treatment

  • Gluten-free diet
  • Dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis

directImages: Evaluation of suspected irritable bowel syndrome
images: Evaluation of suspected irritable bowel syndrome
directTables: Clinical features of irritable bowel syndrome

Clinical features of irritable bowel syndrome

Rome IV diagnostic criteria

Recurrent abdominal pain/discomfort ≥1 days/week for past 3 months & ≥2 of the following:

  • Related to defecation (improves or worsens)
  • Change in stool frequency
  • Change in stool form

Alarm features

  • Older age of onset (≥50)
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding
  • Nocturnal diarrhea (ie, fasting state)
  • Worsening pain
  • Unintended weight loss
  • Iron deficiency anemia
  • Elevated C-reactive protein
  • Positive fecal lactoferrin or calprotectin
  • Family history of early colon cancer or IBD
IBD = inflammatory bowel disease.
Pharmacologic management

Pharmacologic management of IBS

Abdominal pain

  • First line: antispasmodic therapy (eg, hyoscyamine) as needed
  • Second line: tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline)*

Diarrhea

  • First line: soluble fiber (eg, psyllium), loperamide
  • Second line: bile acid sequestrants (eg, cholestyramine), serotonin-3 receptor antagonists (eg, alosetron)

Constipation

  • First line: soluble fiber (eg, psyllium), osmotic laxatives (eg, PEG)
  • Second line: lubiprostone, guanylate cyclase agonists (eg, linaclotide), sodium/hydrogen exchanger 3 inhibitor (eg, tenapanor) 

*Preferred for IBS with diarrhea; avoid with constipation.

IBS = irritable bowel syndrome; PEG = polyethylene glycol.
Rome IV criteria for functional constipation

Rome IV criteria for functional constipation

  • Symptoms present ≥6 months, with full criteria ≥3 months
  • ≥2 present for ≥25% of bowel movements
    • Straining with defecation
    • Lumpy or hard stool
    • Sensation of incomplete evacuation
    • Sensation of anorectal obstruction
    • Manual maneuvers required for defecation (eg, digital evacuation)
    • <3 bowel movements/week
  • Loose stools rare unless laxatives are used
  • Does not meet criteria for irritable bowel disorder

Acute appendicitis

Clinical
presentation

  • Nausea, vomiting, anorexia
  • Initially: diffuse abdominal pain (visceral pain)
  • Later: localized RLQ pain (somatic pain)
  • Mild leukocytosis

Examination

  • McBurney point tenderness
  • Psoas sign: pain with right hip extension
  • Obturator sign: pain with right hip internal rotation
  • Rovsing sign: RLQ pain with LLQ palpation

Diagnosis

  • Clinical presentation
  • CT scan or ultrasonography

Treatment

  • Surgical appendectomy

LLQ = left lower quadrant; RLQ = right lower quadrant.

Modified Alvarado score

(each)

Clinical feature

1

  • Migratory RLQ pain
  • Anorexia
  • Nausea or vomiting
  • Fever >37.5 C (>99.5 F)

2

  • RLQ tenderness
  • Leukocytes >10,000/mm3

9

Total possible score

0-3: appendicitis unlikely

  • Bowel rest
  • Antibiotics (eg, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole)

  • Abscess, obstruction, fistula, perforation

directTables: Diverticular disease

Diverticular disease

Etiology

  • Diverticulosis: ↑ intraluminal pressure causing herniation
    through points of weakness (vasa recta penetration)
  • Diverticular bleeding: injury to exposed vasa recta
  • Diverticulitis: trapped food particles & ↑ intraluminal pressure

  • Diverticulosis: none
  • Diverticular bleeding: painless hematochezia
  • Diverticulitis: left lower quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, fever

Risk
factors

  • Diet high in red meat & fat & low in fiber
  • Obesity, physical inactivity, smoking
