topics.title: Meckel diverticulum
topics.subject: path
directTables: Meckel diverticulum

Meckel diverticulum

Pathogenesis

  • Persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct
  • Often contains ectopic gastric mucosa → intestinal ulceration & bleeding

Epidemiology

Rule of 2s:

  • Presentation often by age 2 (but can occur at any age)
  • Usually <2 inches long
  • Location within 2 feet of ileocecal valve

Clinical presentation

  • May be asymptomatic (incidental finding)
  • Painless rectal bleeding ± iron deficiency anemia
  • Acute abdominal pain due to complications:
    • Intussusception (recurrent, atypical)
    • Diverticulitis (mimics appendicitis)
    • Bowel obstruction, perforation (peritoneal signs)

Diagnosis

  • Technetium-99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan detects gastric mucosa

topics.title: Hirschsprung disease
topics.subject: path
directImages: Evaluation of bilious emesis in the neonate
images: Evaluation of bilious emesis in the neonate
directTables: Hirschsprung disease

Hirschsprung disease

Pathophysiology

  • Failed neural crest cell migration to distal colon
  • Absent parasympathetic ganglia → chronic rectosigmoid contraction

Clinical presentation

  • Neonates: delayed passage of meconium, bilious emesis
  • Children: chronic constipation, failure to thrive

Examination findings

  • Distended abdomen
  • Tight anal sphincter & absent stool in rectal vault
  • Forceful stool expulsion on rectal examination (squirt sign)

Evaluation

  • Contrast enema: narrow rectosigmoid area with dilated proximal colon
  • Anorectal manometry: impaired relaxation of internal anal sphincter
  • Rectal suction biopsy (diagnostic): absent submucosal ganglion

Treatment

  • Surgical resection of aganglionic segment

topics.title: Malrotation
topics.subject: path
directTables: Malrotation with midgut volvulus

Malrotation with midgut volvulus

Pathogenesis

  • Failure of normal embryonic gut rotation
  • Narrow mesenteric base allows for ↑ small bowel mobility
  • Twisting of small bowel around superior mesenteric artery → gut ischemia & necrosis

Clinical
features

  • Most common in infancy (usually age <1 month)
  • Acute: bilious emesis, abdominal distension
  • Chronic: intermittent abdominal pain & vomiting, failure to thrive 
  • Untreated: hematochezia, peritonitis & shock

Diagnosis

  • Abdominal x-ray: ± dilated bowel, air-fluid levels, pneumoperitoneum
  • Upper gastrointestinal series (gold standard): ligament of Treitz on right; corkscrew, or bird's-beak, duodenum

Treatment

  • Emergency laparotomy (to relieve volvulus)
  • Ladd procedure (to reposition malrotated bowel)

topics.title: Intussusception
topics.subject: path
directTables: Intussusception

Intussusception

Pathogenesis &
epidemiology

  • Telescoping of one bowel segment into adjacent segment (most often ileocecal)
  • Bowel edema → ischemia & necrosis
  • Age 6 months to 3 years most common

Risk factors

  • Hypertrophy of intestinal Peyer patches (eg, recent viral illness)
  • Pathologic lead point (eg, Meckel diverticulum, HSP, intestinal tumor)

Clinical
presentation

  • Sudden, intermittent abdominal pain & vomiting
  • Sausage-shaped mass in right abdomen
  • Currant jelly stools
  • Lethargy or altered mental status

Diagnosis &
management

  • Ultrasonography: target sign 
  • Nonoperative enema reduction* (eg, air, saline, iodine-contrast)
  • Surgical intervention for failed enema reduction or signs of peritonitis
*Diagnostic & therapeutic.

HSP = Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

topics.title: Volvulus
topics.subject: path
directTables: Sigmoid volvulus

Sigmoid volvulus

Risk factors

  • Sigmoid colon redundancy (eg, dilation/elongation from chronic constipation)
  • Colonic dysmotility (eg, underlying neurologic disorder)

Presentation

  • Slowly progressive abdominal discomfort/distension ± obstructive symptoms (eg, nausea, emesis, obstipation)
  • Abdomen distended & tympanitic to percussion

Imaging

  • X-ray: dilated, inverted, U-shaped loop of colon (coffee bean sign)
  • CT scan: dilated sigmoid colon, mesenteric twisting (whirl sign)

Management

  • Endoscopic detorsion (eg, flexible sigmoidoscopy) & elective sigmoid colectomy
  • Emergency sigmoid colectomy if perforation/peritonitis present

subs.title: Acute mesenteric ischemia
subs.subject: path
tables: Acute mesenteric ischemia

Acute mesenteric ischemia

Presentation

  • Rapid onset of periumbilical pain (often severe)
  • Pain out of proportion to examination findings
  • Hematochezia (late complication)

Risk factors

  • Atherosclerosis (acute or chronic)
  • Embolic source (thrombus, cardiac vegetation)
  • Hypercoagulable disorder

Laboratory findings

  • Leukocytosis
  • Elevated amylase & phosphate levels
  • Metabolic acidosis (elevated lactate level)

Diagnosis

  • CT (preferred) or MR angiography
  • Mesenteric angiography if diagnosis is unclear
Clinical features of acute mesenteric ischemia

Clinical features of acute mesenteric ischemia

Etiology

  • Arterial occlusion of superior mesenteric artery (cardiac emboli or thrombotic)
  • Nonocclusive ischemia due to hypoperfusion to splanchnic circulation
  • Superior mesenteric vein occlusion

Clinical presentation

  • Sudden onset of severe periumbilical pain with nausea & vomiting
  • Pain out of proportion to examination (subjective pain but abdominal examination can be normal with mild distension or occult blood in stool)
  • Usually no peritoneal signs (eg, guarding, rebound tenderness)
  • Progression of small-bowel ischemia to infarction leads to grossly distended abdomen, absent bowel sounds & peritoneal signs

Diagnosis

  • Metabolic acidosis due to high lactate
  • Marked leukocytosis
  • Hemoconcentration (high hematocrit)
  • CT of abdomen (& CT angiography) can show focal or segmental bowel wall thickening, mesenteric stranding & porto-mesenteric thrombosis
Acute mesenteric ischemia

Acute mesenteric ischemia

Chronic mesenteric ischemia

Presentation

  • Rapid onset of periumbilical pain (often severe)
  • Hematochezia is a late complication
  • Dull postprandial epigastric pain, food aversion & weight loss (present in 80% of patients)

Risk factors

  • Advanced age
  • Atherosclerosis, atrial fibrillation, congestive heart failure
  • Hypercoagulable disorders
  • Cigarette smoking
  • Atherosclerosis

Laboratory

  • Leukocytosis; elevated serum lactate, amylase & phosphate levels; metabolic acidosis
  • None

Diagnosis

  • CT (preferred) or MR angiography
  • Mesenteric angiography, if diagnosis is unclear after initial imaging
  • CT or MR angiography
  • Duplex ultrasonography
  • Conventional angiography

Treatment

  • Resuscitative measures
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Nasogastric tube for decompression
  • Surgery for bowel infarction or perforation
  • Surgical reconstruction
  • Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty ± stent

subs.title: Necrotizing enterocolitis
subs.subject: path
tables: Necrotizing enterocolitis

Necrotizing enterocolitis

Pathogenesis

  • Gut mucosal wall invasion by gas-producing bacteria
  • Intestinal inflammation, necrosis

Risk
factors

  • Prematurity
  • Very low birth weight (<1.5 kg [3 lb 4 oz])
  • Enteral feeding

Clinical
findings

  • Nonspecific: apnea, lethargy, vital sign instability
  • Gastrointestinal
    • Abdominal distension
    • Feeding intolerance, bilious emesis
    • Bloody stools

X-ray
findings

  • Pneumatosis intestinalis (air in bowel wall)
  • Pneumoperitoneum (free air under diaphragm)

Complications

  • Sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Late: strictures, short-bowel syndrome
Management of necrotizing enterocolitis

Management of necrotizing enterocolitis

Immediate
interventions

  • Discontinuation of enteral feeds
  • Nasogastric decompression
  • Blood cultures & empiric antibiotics
  • Intravenous fluid repletion

Monitoring

  • Serial complete blood count & electrolytes
  • Serial abdominal examinations & imaging

Indications
for surgery

  • Bowel perforation (pneumoperitoneum)
  • Clinical deterioration despite medical management (suggestive of bowel necrosis)

subs.title: Proctitis
subs.subject: path
tables: Radiation proctitis

Radiation proctitis

Acute radiation proctitis

Chronic radiation proctitis

Postradiation onset

  • ≤8 weeks
  • >3 months to years

Pathogenesis

  • Direct mucosal damage
  • Obliterative endarteritis & chronic mucosal ischemia
  • Submucosal fibrosis

Manifestations

  • Diarrhea, mucus discharge, tenesmus
  • Minimal bleeding
  • Severe bleeding
  • ± Strictures with constipation & rectal pain

Endoscopic appearance

  • Severe erythema
  • Edema, ulcerations
  • Multiple telangiectasias
  • Mucosal pallor & friability

Management

  • Antidiarrheals (eg, loperamide)
  • Butyrate enemas
  • Endoscopic thermal coagulation
  • Sucralfate or glucocorticoid enemas
Gonococcal proctitis

Gonococcal proctitis

Transmission

  • Receptive anal intercourse
  • Direct spread from the vagina

Manifestations

  • Mucopurulent anal discharge, occasional rectal bleeding
  • Tenesmus, constipation
  • Pruritus, rectal pain, rectal fullness

Diagnosis

  • Nucleic acid amplification test of rectal swab

Treatment

  • Ceftriaxone + doxycycline (to cover Chlamydia)

subs.subject: path
images: Complicated small bowel obstruction with perforation
Small bowel obstruction on abdominal x-ray
tables: Small bowel obstruction

Small bowel obstruction

Clinical presentation

  • Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting
  • Inability to pass flatus or stool if complete (no obstipation if partial)
  • Hyperactive → absent bowel sounds
  • Distended & tympanitic abdomen

Diagnosis

  • Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels on plain film or CT scan
  • Partial: air in colon
  • Complete: transition point (abrupt cutoff), no air in colon

Complications

  • Ischemia/necrosis (strangulation)
  • Bowel perforation

Management

  • Bowel rest, nasogastric tube suction, intravenous fluids
  • Surgical exploration for signs of complications

Small bowel obstruction

  • Most commonly due to adhesions (scar tissue)

Clinical presentation

  • Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting
  • Inability to pass flatus or stool if complete (no obstipation if partial)
  • Hyperactive → absent bowel sounds
  • Distended & tympanitic abdomen

subs.title: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
subs.subject: path
tables: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

Pathogenesis

  • ↑ Colonic bacteria (eg, Bacteroides, Escherichia) in small intestine
  • ↑ Bacterial carbohydrate fermentation (eg, flatulence, bloating)
  • ↓ Vitamin B12 (bacterial consumption)
  • ↑ Folate, vitamin K (bacterial synthesis)
  • Mucosal injury/inflammation → malabsorption (eg, fat)

Risk factors

  • Anatomic abnormalities (eg, strictures, Roux-en-Y)
  • Motility disorders (eg, scleroderma)
  • Immunodeficiency (eg, IgA)
  • Gastric hypochlorhydria (PPI use)

Clinical manifestations

  • Diarrhea, bloating, flatulence, abdominal pain
  • Severe: steatorrhea, nutritional deficiencies (vitamins A, D, E, B12)

Treatment

  • Antibiotics (eg, rifaxmin), dietary changes (eg, low carbohydrate)

PPI= proton pump inhibitor.

Clinical presentation

  • Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting
  • Inability to pass flatus or stool if complete (no obstipation if partial)
  • Hyperactive → absent bowel sounds
  • Distended & tympanitic abdomen

Diagnosis

  • Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels on plain film or CT scan
  • Partial: air in colon
  • Complete: transition point (abrupt cutoff), no air in colon

Complications

  • Ischemia/necrosis (strangulation)
  • Bowel perforation

Management

  • Bowel rest, nasogastric tube suction, intravenous fluids
  • Surgical exploration for signs of complications

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

Pathogenesis

  • ↑ Colonic bacteria (eg, Bacteroides, Escherichia) in small intestine
  • ↑ Bacterial carbohydrate fermentation (eg, flatulence, bloating)
  • ↓ Vitamin B12 (bacterial consumption)
  • ↑ Folate, vitamin K (bacterial synthesis)
  • Mucosal injury/inflammation → malabsorption (eg, fat)

Risk factors

  • Anatomic abnormalities (eg, strictures, Roux-en-Y)
  • Motility disorders (eg, scleroderma)
  • Immunodeficiency (eg, IgA)
  • Gastric hypochlorhydria (PPI use)

Clinical manifestations

  • Diarrhea, bloating, flatulence, abdominal pain
  • Severe: steatorrhea, nutritional deficiencies (vitamins A, D, E, B12)

Treatment

  • Antibiotics (eg, rifaxmin), dietary changes (eg, low carbohydrate)

Surveillance after colon cancer resection

Surveillance after colon cancer resection

Stage I

  • Colonoscopy in 1 year & then every 3-5 years

Stages II & III

  • Colonoscopy in 1 year & then every 3-5 years

Risk factors for colon cancer

Risk factors for colon cancer

Lifestyle factors

  • Frequent consumption of red/processed meat
  • Tobacco, heavy alcohol use

Medical/family history

  • Inherited colon cancer syndromes (eg, familial adenomatous polyposis, Lynch syndrome)

Patients at
average risk

  • Start at age 45:
    • Colonoscopy every 10 years

topics.title: Budd-Chiari syndrome
topics.subject: path
directTables: Budd-Chiari syndrome

Budd-Chiari syndrome

Etiology

  • Hepatic venous outflow obstruction
  • Usually due to:
    • Myeloproliferative disorder (eg, PV)
    • Malignancy (eg, hepatocellular carcinoma)
    • Oral contraception use/pregnancy

Manifestations

  • Acute
    • Jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding
    • Prolonged INR/PTT; elevated transaminases
  • Subacute/chronic
    • Vague, progressive abdominal pain
    • Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites
    • Mild/moderate elevation in bilirubin, transaminases

Diagnosis

  • Abdominal Doppler ultrasonography: ↓ hepatic vein flow
  • Investigation for underlying disorders (eg, JAK2 testing for PV)

PV = polycythemia vera.

topics.title: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
topics.subject: path
directTables: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Clinical presentation

  • Ascites
  • Fever
  • Abdominal pain/tenderness
  • Altered mental status

Diagnosis

  • Paracentesis (ascitic fluid analysis):
    • PMNs1 ≥ 250 cells/mm3, protein < 1 g/dL
    • Positive culture: most commonly Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, streptococci

Treatment

  • 3rd-generation cephalosporin: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime
  • Critically ill or risk for MDR pathogens: piperacillin/tazobactam, carbapenem (eg, meropenem)
  • Duration: 5–7 days

Prevention

  • Criteria: ≥ 1 SBP episode or ascitic fluid protein < 1.5 g/dL PLUS impaired renal or hepatic function2
  • Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim or fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin)

1. Calculated using the white blood cell count & percentage of neutrophils & bands.

2. Impaired renal function: serum creatinine ≥ 1.2 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen ≥ 25 mg/dL, or serum sodium ≤ 130 mEq/L; impaired liver function: Child-Pugh score ≥ 9 & total bilirubin ≥ 3 mg/dL.

MDR = multidrug-resistant; PMNs = polymorphonuclear leukocytes; SBP = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

topics.title: Reye syndrome
topics.subject: path
directTables: Reye syndrome

Reye syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • Aspirin use in children during viral infection (eg, influenza, varicella)
  • Microvesicular fat deposits in the liver
  • Cerebral edema

Clinical features

  • Acute liver failure
    • Hepatomegaly without jaundice
  • Rapidly progressive encephalopathy
    • Vomiting, lethargy, seizure, coma

Laboratory findings

  • ↑ AST, ALT, ammonia
  • ↑ PT, INR, PTT
  • ↓ Glucose
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Normal bilirubin

Treatment

  • Supportive

ALT = alanine aminotransferase (SGPT); AST = aspartate aminotransferase (SGOT).

↑ Nitrogenous waste production

  • Upper GI bleeding
  • Hypokalemia & metabolic alkalosis
  • Muscle catabolism/wasting
  • Infections (especially SBP, urease-producing bacterial cystitis)

↓ Ammonia clearance

  • Renal insufficiency

  • Spontaneous
  • Iatrogenic (TIPS)

Other factors

  • CNS depressant drugs (eg, opioids, benzodiazepines)

directTables: Lactation failure jaundice vs breast milk jaundice

Lactation failure jaundice vs breast milk jaundice

Diagnosis

Timing

Pathophysiology

Clinical features

Lactation failure jaundice

Age <1 week

Insufficient intake of breast milk:

  • ↓ Bilirubin elimination
  • ↑ Enterohepatic circulation
  • Suboptimal breastfeeding
  • Signs of dehydration

Breast milk jaundice

Age >1 week

(peaks at 2 weeks)

↑ β-glucuronidase in breast milk:

  • ↑ Deconjugation of intestinal bilirubin
  • ↑ Enterohepatic circulation
  • Adequate breastfeeding
  • Well-hydrated
Bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction

Bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction

Pathophysiology

  • Excess free, unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier
  • Deposition of bilirubin in basal ganglia & brainstem nuclei
  • Neuronal damage, necrosis & atrophy

Risk factors

  • Prematurity
  • Hemolysis (eg, G6PD deficiency)
  • Birth trauma (eg, cephalohematoma)
  • Exclusive breastfeeding with excessive weight loss

Acute encephalopathy

  • ± Reversible (treatment: phototherapy, exchange transfusion)
  • Clinical findings
    • Lethargy or inconsolability
    • Hypotonia (early) or hypertonia (late)
    • Apnea/respiratory failure, feeding difficulties, seizures

Chronic encephalopathy

  • Irreversible
  • Clinical findings
    • Developmental delay
    • Sensorineural hearing loss
    • Choreoathetoid movements
    • Upward gaze palsy

directTables: Biliary atresia

Biliary atresia

Pathogenesis

  • Extrahepatic bile duct fibrosis → obstruction of bile (& bilirubin) flow from liver to intestines

Clinical
findings

  • Asymptomatic at birth
  • Infants age 2-8 weeks:
    • Jaundice, acholic stools, dark urine
    • Hepatomegaly

Diagnostic
evaluation

  • Direct hyperbilirubinemia
  • Ultrasonography:
    • Absent/abnormal gallbladder &/or CBD
  • Liver biopsy:
    • Intrahepatic bile duct proliferation
    • Portal tract inflammation & edema
    • Fibrosis
  • Intraoperative cholangiography (gold standard):
    • Biliary obstruction

Treatment

  • Surgical hepatoportoenterostomy (Kasai procedure)
  • Liver transplant

CBD = common bile duct.

tables: Gilbert

Gilbertsyndrome

Epidemiology

  • Most common inherited disorder of bilirubin metabolism

Pathogenesis

  • ↓ Hepatic UDP glucuronosyltransferase activity → ↓ conjugation of bilirubin

Clinical findings

  • Recurrent episodes of mild jaundice
  • Provoked by stress (eg, febrile illness, fasting, dehydration, vigorous exercise, menstruation, surgery)

Diagnosis

  • ↑ Unconjugated bilirubin (ie, indirect hyperbilirubinemia)
  • Normal CBC, blood smear, reticulocyte count
  • Normal AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase

Treatment

  • Benign; no treatment required

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; CBC = complete blood count.
Gilbert

Gilbertsyndrome

Epidemiology

  • Most common inherited disorder of bilirubin metabolism

Pathogenesis

  • ↓ Hepatic UDP glucuronosyltransferase activity → ↓ conjugation of bilirubin

Clinical findings

  • Recurrent episodes of mild jaundice
  • Provoked by stress (eg, febrile illness, fasting, dehydration, vigorous exercise, menstruation, surgery)

Diagnosis

  • ↑ Unconjugated bilirubin (ie, indirect hyperbilirubinemia)
  • Normal CBC, blood smear, reticulocyte count
  • Normal AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase

Treatment

  • Benign; no treatment required

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; CBC = complete blood count.

topics.title: Wilson disease
topics.subject: path
directTables: Wilson disease

Wilson disease

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal recessive mutation of ATP7B → hepatic copper accumulation → leak from damaged hepatocytes → deposits in tissues (eg, basal ganglia, cornea)

Clinical
findings

  • Hepatic (acute liver failure, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis)
  • Neurologic (parkinsonism, gait disturbance, dysarthria)
  • Psychiatric (depression, personality changes, psychosis)

Diagnosis

  • ↓ Ceruloplasmin & ↑ urinary copper excretion
  • Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination
  • ↑ Copper content on liver biopsy

Treatment

  • Chelators (eg, D-penicillamine, trientine)
  • Zinc (interferes with copper absorption)

Primary sclerosing cholangitis

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic initially; fatigue & pruritus with progressive disease
  • Associated with IBD, particularly ulcerative colitis

Laboratory & imaging results

  • Cholestasis (↑ ALP, GGT, bilirubin)
  • Multifocal strictures/dilation of bile ducts on MRCP

Complications

  • Cholangitis, cholangiocarcinoma, colon cancer
  • Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies

subs.subject: path
tables: Emphysematous cholecystitis

Emphysematous cholecystitis

Risk factors

  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Vascular compromise
  • Immunosuppression

Clinical
presentation

  • Fever, right upper quadrant pain, nausea/vomiting
  • Crepitus in abdominal wall adjacent to gallbladder

Diagnosis

  • Air-fluid levels in gallbladder, gas in gallbladder wall
  • Cultures with gas-forming Clostridium, Escherichia coli
  • Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, mildly elevated aminotransferases

Treatment

  • Emergency cholecystectomy
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics with Clostridium coverage
    (eg, piperacillin-tazobactam)
Acute calculous

Acute calculous cholecystitis

Risk factors

  • Obesity
  • Female sex
  • Age >40
  • Pregnancy

Clinical
features

  • Fever
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • RUQ/epigastric pain
  • Murphy sign (pain with gallbladder palpation)

Diagnosis

  • RUQ ultrasonography: thickened gallbladder,
    sludge, gallstones
  • HIDA scan: nonvisualization of gallbladder

Management

  • NPO, intravenous fluids
  • Antibiotics
  • Cholecystectomy (<72 hr)

RUQ = right upper quadrant.

tables: Acute cholangitis

Acute cholangitis

Etiology

  • Ascending infection due to biliary obstruction

Clinical
presentation

  • Fever, jaundice, RUQ pain (Charcot triad)
  • ± Hypotension, AMS (Reynolds pentad)

Diagnosis

  • Cholestatic liver function abnormalities
    • ↑ Direct bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase
    • Mildly ↑ aminotransferases
  • Biliary dilation on abdominal ultrasonography or CT scan

Treatment

  • Antibiotic coverage of enteric bacteria
  • Biliary drainage by ERCP within 24-48 hr

AMS = altered mental status; ERCP = endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography;
RUQ = right upper quadrant.

Gallstones without symptoms

Complicated gallstone disease*

  • Cholecystectomy within 72 hr

topics.title: Cholangiocarcinoma
topics.subject: path
directTables: Cholangiocarcinoma

Cholangiocarcinoma

Risk factors

  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis (90% of patients), cirrhosis, liver fluke infection (eg, southwest Asia)

Clinical & laboratory findings

  • Often clinically silent until advanced; may have jaundice, weight loss, RUQ pain
  • Cholestasis (↑↑ alkaline phosphatase, hyperbilirubinemia)
  • Elevated CA 19-9

Imaging

  • Unexplained extrahepatic bile duct obstruction (eg, ductal dilation but no gallstones or pancreatic mass on ultrasonography, CT scan)
  • Intrahepatic mass (~20% of cancers)

Histology

  • Adenocarcinoma with cuboidal or columnar cells with prominent nucleoli arranged in glandular structures
  • + Mucin production, + desmoplastic response
CA 19-9 = cancer-associated antigen 19-9; RUQ = right upper quadrant.

tables: Triglyceride-induced pancreatitis

Triglyceride-induced pancreatitis

Risk

Triglyceride levels (mg/dL)

  • <500: minimal risk
  • 500-999: mild risk
  • 1,000-1,999: moderate risk
  • ≥2,000: high risk

Other risk factors: pregnancy, alcoholism, obesity, uncontrolled diabetes

Clinical features

  • Acute epigastric pain radiating to back
  • ± Fever, nausea, vomiting
  • Elevated serum lipase (>3 times upper limit of normal)

Management

  • Intravenous fluid hydration, pain control
  • Triglycerides ≥500 mg/dL: consider insulin infusion
  • Triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL or severe pancreatitis (eg, lactic acidosis, hypocalcemia): consider apheresis (therapeutic plasma exchange)
Causes of acute pancreatitis

Causes of acute pancreatitis

G

  • Gallstones

E

  • Ethanol

T

  • Trauma

S

  • Steroids

M

  • Mumps

A

  • Autoimmune

S

  • Scorpion stings/spider bites

H

  • Hypertriglyceridemia

E

  • ERCP

D

  • Drugs

ERCP = endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography.
Clinical features of acute pancreatitis

Clinical features of acute pancreatitis

Etiology

  • Chronic alcohol use
  • Gallstones
  • Hyperlipidemia (types I, IV & V)
  • Drugs (eg, didanosine, azathioprine, valproic acid)
  • Infections (eg, cytomegalovirus, Legionella, Aspergillus)
  • Trauma
  • Iatrogenic (post-ERCP)

Clinical presentation

Diagnosis requires 2 of the following:

  • Acute epigastric abdominal pain often radiating to the back
  • ↑ Amylase/lipase >3 times normal limit
  • Abdominal imaging showing focal or diffuse pancreatic enlargement with heterogeneous enhancement with intravenous contrast (CT scan) or diffusely enlarged & hypoechoic pancreas (ultrasonography)
 

Other findings:

  • Nausea, vomiting, leukocytosis
  • Severe disease with possible abdominal tenderness, fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia & hypotension
  • ALT level >150 U/L → biliary pancreatitis

Complications

  • Pleural effusion
  • Ileus
  • Pancreatic pseudocyst/abscess/necrosis
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; ERCP = endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography.
Severe acute pancreatitis

Severe acute pancreatitis

Definition

  • Acute pancreatitis with organ failure (eg, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal) persisting >48 hr

Predictors

  • Patient factors:
    • Older age (eg, age >55)
    • Comorbidities, including obesity (BMI >30 kg/m2)
  • Clinical findings:
    • Altered mental status
    • SIRS (eg, leukocytes >12,000/mm3, temperature >38 C [100.4 F])
  • Laboratory findings of intravascular volume depletion:
    • ↑ BUN (>20 mg/dL) and/or ↑ creatinine (>1.8 mg/dL)
    • ↑ HCT (>44%)
  • Radiologic findings:
    • CXR: pulmonary infiltrates, pleural effusions
    • Abdominal CT scan: severe pancreatic necrosis

BUN = blood urea nitrogen; CXR = chest x-ray; HCT = hematocrit; SIRS = systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
Hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis

Hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis

Risk factors

  • Genetic predisposition (eg, familial dyslipidemia)
  • Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus

Clinical features

  • Meets 2 of 3 criteria for acute pancreatitis:
    • Characteristic abdominal pain
    • Lipase (or amylase) ≥3 times normal
    • Characteristic radiologic findings
  • Serum triglyceride >1,000 mg/dL
  • ± Eruptive xanthomas (eg, lipid deposits in skin)

Management

  • Supportive measures (eg, IV fluid, antiemetics, pain control)
  • Apheresis if severe (eg, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, lactic acidosis, hypocalcemia)
  • Insulin if not severe or if apheresis unavailable
  • Fibrates (eg, fenofibrate, gemfibrozil) to prevent recurrence

IV = intravenous.

tables: Overview of chronic pancreatitis

Overview of chronic pancreatitis

Etiology

  • Alcohol use
  • Cystic fibrosis (common in children)
  • Ductal obstruction (eg, malignancy, stones)
  • Autoimmune

Clinical presentation

  • Chronic epigastric pain with intermittent pain-free intervals
  • Malabsorption: steatorrhea, weight loss
  • Diabetes mellitus

Laboratory results/imaging

  • Amylase/lipase can be normal & nondiagnostic
  • CT scan or MRCP can show calcifications, dilated ducts & enlarged pancreas

Treatment

  • Pain management
  • Alcohol & smoking cessation
  • Frequent, small meals
  • Pancreatic enzyme supplements

MRCP = magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography.

directTables: Indications for stress ulcer prophylaxis

Indications for stress ulcer prophylaxis

Any 1 factor

  • Coagulopathy: platelets <50,000/mm3, INR >1.5,
    PTT >2x normal control
  • Mechanical ventilation >48 hr
  • GI bleeding or ulceration in last 12 months
  • Head trauma, spinal cord injury, major burn

≥2 factors

  • Glucocorticoid therapy
  • >1 week ICU stay
  • Occult GI bleeding >6 days
  • Sepsis

GI = gastrointestinal; ICU = intensive care unit.

directTables: Proton pump inhibitors

Proton pump inhibitors

Mechanism
of action

  • Irreversible inhibition of parietal cell hydrogen-potassium-ATPase

Common uses

  • Gastroesophageal reflux disease
  • Peptic ulcer disease

Adverse effects

  • Malabsorption of calcium, iron, magnesium & vitamin B12
    • Enhances fat absorption in patients given pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy
  • Increases risk of infection (eg, Clostridioidesdifficile, pneumonia)
  • Osteoporosis, chronic kidney disease, SIBO

SIBO = small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

tables: Milk-alkali syndrome

Milk-alkali syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • Excessive intake of calcium & absorbable alkali
  • Renal vasoconstriction & decreased GFR
  • Renal loss of sodium & water, reabsorption of bicarbonate

Symptoms

  • Nausea, vomiting, constipation
  • Polyuria, polydipsia
  • Neuropsychiatric symptoms

Laboratory
findings

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Acute kidney injury
  • Suppressed PTH

Treatment

  • Discontinuation of causative agent
  • Isotonic saline followed by furosemide

GFR = glomerular filtration rate; PTH = parathyroid hormone.

topics.title: Anticonstipation drugs
topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Anticonstipation agents

Anticonstipation agents

Bulk-forming laxatives
(eg, fiber supplements)

  • Binds luminal water to decrease consistency of stool
  • Adverse effects: flatulence, abdominal distension

Osmotic laxatives
(eg, polyethylene glycol, magnesium hydroxide, lactulose)

  • Osmotically active agent that draws water into the lumen
  • Adverse effects: electrolyte disturbances, bloating

Surfactant
(eg, docusate)

  • Decreases stool surface tension, enabling water to enter stool
  • Adverse effects: rare

Stimulant laxatives
(eg, bisacodyl, senna)

  • Activates enteric nerves in myenteric plexus to stimulate peristalsis
  • Adverse effects: abdominal cramping, electrolyte disturbances

Chloride channel agonist
(eg, lubiprostone)

  • Causes chloride efflux into intestinal lumen, which is followed by sodium and water
  • Adverse effects: headache, nausea

Peripherally acting µ-opioid
receptor antagonists
(eg, methylnaltrexone)

  • Counteracts inhibitory effect of opioids on peristalsis
  • Adverse effects: rare (does not cause opiate withdrawal)

*All constipation medications can cause diarrhea at high doses.
Opioid-induced constipation management

Opioid-induced constipation management

Nonpharmacologic
interventions

  • Increased fluids
  • Increased dietary fiber
  • Increased exercise
  • Early ambulation (postsurgical)

Pharmacotherapy

  • Osmotic laxatives (eg, polyethylene glycol, lactulose)
  • Contact cathartics or stimulant laxatives (eg, senna, bisacodyl)
  • Hard stools: stool softeners (eg, docusate)
  • Refractory: methylnaltrexone or lubiprostone

directTables: Danger signals (alarmins)

Danger signals (alarmins)

 

PAMPs

Septic inflammation

Foreign molecular motifs found on invading organisms

  • Bacteria: lipopolysaccharide, lipoteichoic acid
  • Fungi: β-glucan
  • Protozoa: profilin
  • Viruses: double-stranded RNA

DAMPs

Sterile inflammation (eg, pancreatitis)

Self motifs released from damaged host cells and tissues

  • Exposed intracellular contents: mitochondrial DNA, histones, uric acid
  • Fragmented extracellular matrix: fibrinogen, hyaluronic acid

DAMPs & PAMPs drive systemic inflammation by engaging immune cell pattern recognition receptors (eg, toll-like receptors)

DAMP = damage-associated molecular pattern; PAMP = pathogen-associated molecular pattern.
Innate & adaptive immunity

Innate & adaptive immunity

Innate
(eg, response to a dirty cut)

Adaptive
(eg, response to vaccination)

Function

  • Immediate general response to a broad range of pathogens
  • Same response with repeated exposures
  • Memory-based response to specific pathogens
  • Greater response with repeated exposures

Components

  • Natural barriers (eg, cilia)
  • Contact activation system (eg, local coagulation)
  • Neutrophils, NK cells, macrophages, dendritic cells
  • Inflammasome
  • Alternative complement pathway
  • Cell-mediated immunity: cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) & helper T cell (CD4+) response
  • Antibody-mediated (humoral) immunity: B cells, plasma cells, antibodies
  • Classical complement pathway

Activation

At site of invasion (eg, skin):

  • PAMPs & DAMPs activate innate immune receptors (eg, TLR)

In germinal centers of secondary lymphoid organs (eg, nodes, spleen):

  • APCs (eg, dendritic cells) process & display antigens on MHC, engaging TCRs
  • Affinity maturation (somatic hypermutation) of B cells to produce specific antibodies

APC = antigen-presenting cell; DAMP = damage-associated molecular pattern (eg, mitochondrial DNA); MHC = major histocompatibility complex; NK = natural killer; PAMP = pathogen-associated molecular pattern (eg, lipopolysaccharide); TCR = T-cell receptor; TLR = toll-like receptor.

tables: Clinical features of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

Clinical features of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

Clinical manifestations

  • Hemolysis → fatigue
  • Cytopenias (impaired hematopoiesis)
  • Venous thrombosis (intraabdominal, cerebral veins)

Work-up

  • Complete blood count (hypoplastic/aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia)
  • Elevated lactate dehydrogenase and low haptoglobin (hemolysis)
  • Indirect hyperbilirubinemia
  • Urinalysis (hemoglobinuria)
  • Flow cytometry (absence of CD55 & CD59)

Treatment

  • Iron & folate supplementation
  • Eculizumab (monoclonal antibody that inhibits complement activation)

Indications & contraindications for influenza vaccination

Live attenuated intranasal vaccine

Indications

  • Healthy individuals age 2-49 

Contraindications

  • Age <2 or ≥50
  • Immunosuppressed patients (eg, HIV with CD4+ cell count <200/mm3) & close contacts
  • Chronic cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, neuromuscular, or metabolic (eg, diabetes, renal insufficiency) diseases
  • History of Guillain-Barré syndrome following previous influenza immunization
  • Pregnant women
  • Children/adolescents receiving long-term aspirin therapy
  • Severe allergy to vaccine or its components 

Inactivated vaccine

Indications

  • Individuals age ≥6 months

Contraindications

  • Severe allergy to vaccine or its components

tables: Anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis

Triggers

  • Food (eg, nuts, shellfish)
  • Medications (eg, β-lactam antibiotics)
  • Insect stings

Clinical
manifestations

  • Cardiovascular
    • Vasodilation → hypotension & tissue edema
    • Tachycardia
  • Respiratory
    • Upper airway edema → stridor & hoarseness
    • Bronchospasm → wheezing
  • Cutaneous
    • Urticarial rash, pruritus, flushing
  • Gastrointestinal
    • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain

Treatment

  • Intramuscular epinephrine
  • Airway management & volume resuscitation
  • Adjunct therapy (eg, antihistamines, glucocorticoids)
Large local reactions

Large local reactions

Epidemiology & pathophysiology

  • Often due to bites from Hymenoptera species (eg, bees, ants, wasps)
  • Exaggerated, IgE-mediated, local allergic response (~10% of stung individuals)
  • Associated with possible increased risk for future systemic reactions

Manifestations

  • Significant (~10 cm or more) localized swelling, erythema & warmth
  • Swelling & erythema contiguous with site of the sting
  • Develop within 24 hr, peak within 24-48 hr, resolve in 5-10 days

Treatment

  • Cold compresses
  • Oral &/or topical steroids
  • Antihistamines
  • Anti-inflammatory medications
Diagnostic challenges in anaphylaxis

Diagnostic challenges in anaphylaxis

Nonclassic
presentation

  • No prior allergic reactions (ie, first episode)
  • Absence of hypotension, respiratory symptoms, or cutaneous signs
  • Protracted or biphasic presentation

Challenging
clinical situations

  • Preexisting conditions with similar symptoms (eg, asthma, COPD)
  • Ongoing physiologic shifts (eg, childbirth, hemodialysis)
  • Impaired communication (eg, sedation, severe psychiatric illness)

Medication
effects

  • Directly activate mast cells (eg, opiates, NSAIDs)
  • Interfere with epinephrine effect (eg, β-blockers,
    α-adrenergic blockers)

COPD = chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Clinical features of anaphylaxis

Clinical features of anaphylaxis

Cutaneous/
mucosal

  • Ocular: periorbital swelling, injected conjunctiva, tearing
  • Oral mucosa: swelling, tingling, or itching of tongue & lips; metallic taste
  • Skin: urticaria, flushing, pruritus

Respiratory

  • Nose: congestion, rhinorrhea
  • Upper airway: edema → hoarseness & stridor
  • Lower airway: bronchospasm → wheezing, dyspnea, tachypnea

Cardiovascular

  • Vasodilation → hypotension, light-headedness/syncope, tachycardia
  • Cardiac dysfunction, cardiac arrest

Gastrointestinal

  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea

Neurologic

  • Headache, confusion, anxiety, feeling of impending doom
Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis

Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis is likely if there is rapid symptom onset & any 1 of the following criteria:

1

Skin/mucosa involvement (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling) & either hypotension or respiratory distress

2

Involvement of ≥2 organ systems after exposure to a likely allergen

  • Skin/mucosa (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling)
  • Respiratory (eg, wheezing, stridor, dyspnea)
  • Cardiovascular (eg, hypotension, tachycardia, syncope)
  • Gastrointestinal (eg, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea)

3

Hypotension after exposure to a known allergen

IgE- & non–IgE-mediated food allergies

Example

Age

Symptom onset

Clinical
features

Anaphylaxis

(<1 hr)

  • Urticaria

Immunologic and nonimmunologic anaphylaxis

Immunologic and nonimmunologic anaphylaxis

Immunologic
(IgE-mediated)

Nonimmunologic
(Non-IgE-mediated)

Mechanism

Initial sensitization (priming) followed by mast cell degranulation upon reexposure (surface IgE crosslinking)

Non-IgE-mediated: Direct mast degranulation

Triggers

  • Foods (eg, peanut, shellfish)
  • Insect venom (eg, wasps)
  • Medications (eg, β-lactam antibiotics)
  • MRGPRX2 ligands (eg, vancomycin, radioiodine contrast)
  • Physical stimuli (eg, exercise, cold)
  • Idiopathic

Characteristics

  • Requires previous exposure (may be asymptomatic)
  • Idiosyncratic (not dose-dependent)
  • Can occur on first exposure
  • Dose-dependent

MRGPRX2 = mas-related G-protein coupled receptor-2.
Anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis

Triggers

  • Food (most common): nuts, shellfish, eggs
  • Medications (β-lactam antibiotics)
  • Insect stings

Diagnostic criteria

Acute onset (minutes to hours) of one of the following:

  • Criterion 1: skin/mucosal involvement (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling) PLUS hypotension OR respiratory distress
  • Criterion 2: involvement of ≥2 organ systems (skin/mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal)
  • Criterion 3: hypotension after exposure to known allergen

Treatment

  • Intramuscular epinephrine
  • Airway management & volume resuscitation (if needed)
  • Adjunctive therapy for severe or prolonged cases (steroids, H1 & H2 blockers)

Follow-up

  • Allergy testing & avoidance
  • Epinephrine autoinjector

  • Adjunct therapy (eg, antihistamines, glucocorticoids)
Large local reactions

Large local reactions

Epidemiology & pathophysiology

  • Often due to bites from Hymenoptera species (eg, bees, ants, wasps)
  • Exaggerated, IgE-mediated, local allergic response (~10% of stung individuals)
  • Associated with possible increased risk for future systemic reactions

Manifestations

  • Significant (~10 cm or more) localized swelling, erythema & warmth
  • Swelling & erythema contiguous with site of the sting
  • Develop within 24 hr, peak within 24-48 hr, resolve in 5-10 days

Treatment

  • Cold compresses
  • Oral &/or topical steroids
  • Antihistamines
  • Anti-inflammatory medications
Diagnostic challenges in anaphylaxis

Diagnostic challenges in anaphylaxis

Nonclassic
presentation

  • No prior allergic reactions (ie, first episode)
  • Absence of hypotension, respiratory symptoms, or cutaneous signs
  • Protracted or biphasic presentation

Challenging
clinical situations

  • Preexisting conditions with similar symptoms (eg, asthma, COPD)
  • Ongoing physiologic shifts (eg, childbirth, hemodialysis)
  • Impaired communication (eg, sedation, severe psychiatric illness)

Medication
effects

  • Directly activate mast cells (eg, opiates, NSAIDs)
  • Interfere with epinephrine effect (eg, β-blockers,
    α-adrenergic blockers)

COPD = chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Clinical features of anaphylaxis

Clinical features of anaphylaxis

Cutaneous/
mucosal

  • Ocular: periorbital swelling, injected conjunctiva, tearing
  • Oral mucosa: swelling, tingling, or itching of tongue & lips; metallic taste
  • Skin: urticaria, flushing, pruritus

Respiratory

  • Nose: congestion, rhinorrhea
  • Upper airway: edema → hoarseness & stridor
  • Lower airway: bronchospasm → wheezing, dyspnea, tachypnea

Cardiovascular

  • Vasodilation → hypotension, light-headedness/syncope, tachycardia
  • Cardiac dysfunction, cardiac arrest

Gastrointestinal

  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea

Neurologic

  • Headache, confusion, anxiety, feeling of impending doom
Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis

Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis is likely if there is rapid symptom onset & any 1 of the following criteria:

1

Skin/mucosa involvement (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling) & either hypotension or respiratory distress

2

Involvement of ≥2 organ systems after exposure to a likely allergen

  • Skin/mucosa (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling)
  • Respiratory (eg, wheezing, stridor, dyspnea)
  • Cardiovascular (eg, hypotension, tachycardia, syncope)
  • Gastrointestinal (eg, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea)

3

Hypotension after exposure to a known allergen
IgE- & non–IgE-mediated food allergies

IgE- & non–IgE-mediated food allergies

Example

Age

Symptom onset

Clinical
features

IgE-mediated

Anaphylaxis

Any

Immediate
(<1 hr)

  • Urticaria
  • Vomiting, wheezing
  • Angioedema, hypotension

Non–IgE-mediated

Immunologic and nonimmunologic anaphylaxis

Immunologic and nonimmunologic anaphylaxis

Immunologic
(IgE-mediated)

Nonimmunologic
(Non-IgE-mediated)

Mechanism

Initial sensitization (priming) followed by mast cell degranulation upon reexposure (surface IgE crosslinking)

Non-IgE-mediated: Direct mast degranulation

Triggers

  • Foods (eg, peanut, shellfish)
  • Insect venom (eg, wasps)
  • Medications (eg, β-lactam antibiotics)
  • MRGPRX2 ligands (eg, vancomycin, radioiodine contrast)
  • Physical stimuli (eg, exercise, cold)
  • Idiopathic

Characteristics

  • Requires previous exposure (may be asymptomatic)
  • Idiosyncratic (not dose-dependent)
  • Can occur on first exposure
  • Dose-dependent

MRGPRX2 = mas-related G-protein coupled receptor-2.
Anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis

Triggers

  • Food (most common): nuts, shellfish, eggs
  • Medications (β-lactam antibiotics)
  • Insect stings

Diagnostic criteria

Acute onset (minutes to hours) of one of the following:

  • Criterion 1: skin/mucosal involvement (eg, hives, lip/tongue swelling) PLUS hypotension OR respiratory distress
  • Criterion 2: involvement of ≥2 organ systems (skin/mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal)
  • Criterion 3: hypotension after exposure to known allergen

Treatment

  • Intramuscular epinephrine
  • Airway management & volume resuscitation (if needed)
  • Adjunctive therapy for severe or prolonged cases (steroids, H1 & H2 blockers)

Follow-up

  • Allergy testing & avoidance
  • Epinephrine autoinjector

subs.title: X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemia
subs.subject: resp
tables: X-linked agammaglobulinemia

X-linked agammaglobulinemia

Pathophysiology

  • BTK gene mutation resulting in defective Bruton tyrosine kinase
  • Impaired B-cell maturation & immunoglobulin production

Clinical manifestations

  • Recurrent sinopulmonary & gastrointestinal infections at age
    >3-6 months
  • Chronic enteroviral infection
  • Small or absent lymphoid tissue
    (eg, tonsils, adenoids)

Laboratory findings

  • ↓ Immunoglobulins & antibody response to vaccines
  • Flow cytometry: ↓ CD19+ B cells
    & normal T cells

Treatment

  • Immunoglobulin replacement therapy
  • Prophylactic antibiotics if severe

subs.title: Selective IgA deficiency
subs.subject: resp
tables: Selective IgA deficiency

Selective IgA deficiency

Epidemiology

  • Most common primary immune deficiency

Clinical features

  • Usually asymptomatic
  • Recurrent sinopulmonary & gastrointestinal infections
  • Associated with autoimmune disease (eg, celiac) & atopy (eg, asthma, eczema)
  • Anaphylaxis during transfusions

Diagnosis

  • Low or absent IgA
  • Normal IgG, IgM levels, B cells

Treatment

  • Supportive care
  • Medical alert bracelet for transfusion reactions (for severe deficiency)

subs.title: Common variable immunodeficiency
subs.subject: resp
tables: Common variable immunodeficiency

Common variable immunodeficiency

Pathophysiology

  • Abnormal differentiation of B cells into plasma cells → decreased immunoglobulin production

Clinical manifestations

  • Symptom onset classically age 20-40, as early as puberty
  • Recurrent respiratory infections (eg, pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis)
  • Recurrent GI infections (eg, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Giardia)
  • Chronic disease:
    • Autoimmune (eg, RA, thyroid disease)
    • Pulmonary (eg, bronchiectasis, fibrosis)
    • GI (eg, chronic diarrhea, IBD-like conditions)

Diagnosis

  • ↓↓ IgG, ↓ IgA/IgM
  • No response to vaccination

Management

  • Immunoglobulin replacement therapy

GI = gastrointestinal; IBD = inflammatory bowel disease; RA = rheumatoid arthritis.

tables: DiGeorge syndrome/velocardiofacial syndrome

DiGeorge syndrome/velocardiofacial syndrome

Pathogenesis

  • Chromosome 22q11.2 deletion
  • Defective development of pharyngeal pouches

Clinical

  • Conotruncal cardiac defects (tetralogy of Fallot,
    truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch)
  • Abnormal facies
  • Thymic hypoplasia/aplasia (T-cell deficiency)
  • Craniofacial deformities (cleft palate)
  • Hypocalcemia/Hypoparathyroidism

  • Chromosome 22q11.2 deletion

22q11.2 deletion syndromes

22q11.2 deletion syndromes

Phenotypes

  • DiGeorge syndrome, velocardiofacial syndrome*

Pathogenesis

  • Loss of genes that control embryonic tissue template transformation (eg, pharyngeal apparatus, secondary heart field) and migration of neural crest cells

Clinical features (CATCH)

  • Cardiac outflow tract anomalies (eg, tetralogy of Fallot, persistent truncus arteriosus)
  • Anomalous face (eg, prominent nasal bridge, low-set ears, micrognathia/retrognathia)
  • Thymic hypoplasia/aplasia → decreased T-cell immunity
  • Cleft palate
  • Hypoparathyroidism (hypoplastic/aplastic parathyroids) → hypocalcemia

*DiGeorge requires thymic involvement (CD3+ T-cell count <500/mm3); velocardiofacial syndrome requires facial abnormalities.

subs.title: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome
subs.subject: resp
tables: Hyper-IgE syndrome

Hyper-IgE syndrome

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal dominant
  • Defective JAK-STAT signaling → impaired Th17
  • ↓ Neutrophil proliferation/chemotaxis

Clinical features

  • Severe, chronic eczema
  • Noninflammatory (ie, "cold") abscesses (eg, Staphylococcus, Candida)
  • Recurrent sinopulmonary infections
  • Dysmorphic facies (eg, broad nose, prominent forehead)
  • Retained primary teeth

Laboratory findings

  • ↑ IgE
  • Eosinophilia
  • Normal leukocyte count with ↓ Th17

Management

  • Supportive skin care
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis & treatment

JAK-STAT = Janus activated kinase–signal transducer and activator of transcription; Th17 = T-helper cell type 17.

tables: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis

Pathogenesis

  • Autoimmune regulator gene (AIRE) deficiency
  • Impaired negative selection of T cells → T-cell immunodeficiency & autoimmunity

  • Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy
    • Hypoparathyroidism (eg, ↓ calcium, seizure)
    • Adrenal insufficiency
    • Type 1 diabetes mellitus
    • Thyroiditis

features

  • Chronic Candida infection (eg, skin, oropharynx, nails)
  • Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy
    • Hypoparathyroidism (eg, ↓ calcium, seizure)
    • Adrenal insufficiency
    • Type 1 diabetes mellitus
    • Thyroiditis

subs.title: Severe combined immunodeficiency
subs.subject: resp
tables: Severe combined immunodeficiency

Severe combined immunodeficiency

Etiology

  • Gene defect leading to failure of T-cell development
  • B-cell dysfunction due to absent T cells

Inheritance

  • X-linked recessive
  • Autosomal recessive

Clinical features

  • Recurrent, severe viral, fungal, or opportunistic (ie, Pneumocystis) infections
  • Failure to thrive
  • Chronic diarrhea

Treatment

  • Stem cell transplant

subs.title: Ataxia-telangiectasia
subs.subject: resp
tables: Ataxia-telangiectasia

Ataxia-telangiectasia

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal recessive
  • Defective DNA break repair

Clinical features

  • Presents in early childhood
  • Neurologic dysfunction
    • Progressive cerebellar ataxia
    • Uncoordinated head/eye movements
  • Telangiectasias: face & conjunctivae
  • Immune deficiency: recurrent sinopulmonary infections
  • ↑ Malignancy risk

Diagnosis

  • Mutation analysis

subs.title: Hyper-IgM syndrome
subs.subject: resp
tables: Hyper-IgM syndrome

Hyper-IgM syndrome

Genetics

  • Most commonly due to X-linked recessive CD40L deficiency

Pathophysiology

  • Impaired T-cell activation of B cells
    • Lack of immunoglobulin class switching
    • ↓ Memory B-cell production
  • Impaired T-cell interaction with APCs → lack of germinal centers

Clinical features

  • Sinopulmonary, gastrointestinal & opportunistic infections
  • Failure to thrive
  • Small lymphoid tissue

Diagnosis

  • ↑ IgM
  • ↓ IgG, IgA, IgE
  • Absent CD40L on CD4+ lymphocytes

APCs = antigen-presenting cells; CD40L = CD40 ligand.

subs.title: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
subs.subject: resp
tables: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome

Etiology

  • X-linked recessive defect in WAS protein gene
  • Impaired cytoskeleton changes in leukocytes, platelets

Clinical
features

  • Eczema
  • Microthrombocytopenia (small platelets, low platelet count)
  • Recurrent infections

Treatment

  • Stem cell transplant

subs.title: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (type 1)
subs.subject: resp
tables: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency

Pathophysiology

  • Defect in CD18-containing integrins
  • Impaired leukocyte adhesion & endothelial transmigration

Clinical features

  • Skin & mucosal infections (eg, cellulitis, periodontitis) without pus formation
  • Impaired wound healing
  • Delayed umbilical cord separation (age >3 weeks)

Laboratory findings

  • Leukocytosis & neutrophilia

subs.title: Chronic granulomatous disease
subs.subject: resp
tables: Chronic granulomatous disease

Chronic granulomatous disease

Pathogenesis

  • X-linked recessive mutation of NADPH oxidase
  • Impaired respiratory burst & ↓ reactive oxygen species → inhibition of phagocytic intracellular killing

Clinical features

  • Recurrent infections with catalase-positive* bacteria & fungi
  • Lungs, skin, liver, lymph node involvement
  • Diffuse granulomas (eg, gastrointestinal, genitourinary)

Diagnosis

  • Measurement of neutrophil superoxide production:
    • DHR flow cytometry (preferred)
    • NBT testing

Treatment

  • Prophylaxis: TMP-SMX, itraconazole, interferon gamma
  • Active infection: culture-based, antimicrobial therapy
  • Hematopoietic cell transplant is curative

*Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia (Pseudomonas) cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus.

DHR = dihydrorhodamine; NBT = nitroblue tetrazolium test; TMP-SMX = trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

topics.title: Transplant rejection
topics.subject: resp
directTables: Transplant rejection reactions

Transplant rejection reactions

Type of rejection

Onset time

Etiology

Morphology

Hyperacute

Minutes to hours

  • Preformed recipient antibodies against graft antigens
  • Gross mottling & cyanosis
  • Arterial fibrinoid necrosis & capillary thrombotic occlusion

Acute

Usually <6 months

  • Exposure to donor antigens induces activation of naive immune cells 
  • Predominantly cell-mediated
  • Cellular: lymphocytic interstitial infiltrate & endotheliitis
  • Humoral: C4d deposition, neutrophilic infiltrate, necrotizing vasculitis

Chronic

Months to years

  • Chronic low-grade immune response refractory to immunosuppression
  • Mixed cell-mediated and humoral
  • Vascular wall thickening & luminal narrowing
  • Interstitial fibrosis & parenchymal atrophy
Complications of solid organ transplantation

Complications of solid organ transplantation

Acute

<1 month

Postacute

Infectious

Nosocomial bacteria: blood stream infections, HAP, Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile

<12 months: opportunistic pathogens

  • Bacteria: mycobacteria
  • Viruses: CMV, HSV
  • Fungi: PCP, Candida, Aspergillus, Mucor spp.
 

≥12 months: community-acquired respiratory viruses & bacteria

Noninfectious

  • Surgical site: anastomotic dehiscence
  • Primary graft dysfunction: ARDS, ATN
  • Drug toxicity: nephrotoxicity (eg, calcineurin inhibitors), osteoporosis (eg, corticosteroids)
  • Malignancy: posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder (EBV)

Immunologic

  • Hyperacute rejection: ABO mismatch
  • Acute* rejection: cell or antibody mediated
  • Chronic rejection (>12 months): fibrosis of graft structures (eg, bronchiolitis obliterans of airways, sclerosis of glomeruli)

*Acute cellular rejection most common in first 90 days but can occur at any time after transplant.

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; ATN = acute tubular necrosis; CMV = cytomegalovirus; EBV = Epstein-Barr virus; HAP = hospital-acquired pneumonia; HSV = herpes simplex virus.

Common interactions of tacrolimus & cyclosporine

↑ Drug level

  • Macrolide antibiotics
  • Azole antifungals
  • Protease inhibitors
  • Diltiazem, verapamil, amiodarone
  • Grapefruit juice

↓ Drug level

  • Nafcillin, rifamycins
  • Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital
  • St. John's wort
Adverse effects of cyclosporine & tacrolimus

Adverse effects of cyclosporine & tacrolimus

Both medications

  • Electrolyte disturbances1
  • Hyperglycemia
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Hypertension
  • Infections
  • Nephrotoxicity
  • Neurotoxicity2
  • QT prolongation

Cyclosporine-specific

  • Gingival hyperplasia
  • Hirsutism (hair growth)

Tacrolimus-specific

  • Alopecia (hair loss)

1. Potassium, magnesium & phosphate.

2. Neurotoxicity may present as tremors, headaches, paresthesia &, in severe cases, seizures.

directTables: Mechanism of action of selected bacterial exotoxins

Mechanism of action of selected bacterial exotoxins

Organism

Toxin

Mechanism & effects

Bacillus anthracis

Anthrax exotoxin

Edema factor: Increases cyclic AMP concentration by acting as an adenylate cyclase, causing edema & phagocyte dysfunction

Lethal factor: Zinc-dependent protease that inhibits mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, causing apoptosis & multisystem physiologic disruption

Bordetella pertussis

Pertussis toxin

Disinhibits adenylate cyclase through Gi ADP-ribosylation, increasing cAMP levels; causes edema & phagocyte dysfunction

Adenylate cyclase toxin

Functions as an adenylate cyclase, increasing cAMP levels; causes edema & phagocyte dysfunction

Clostridium botulinum

Botulinum toxin

Blocks presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, resulting in flaccid paralysis

Clostridium difficile

Toxin A

Recruits & activates neutrophils, leading to release of cytokines that cause mucosal inflammation, fluid loss & diarrhea

Toxin B

Induces actin depolymerization, leading to mucosal cell death, bowel wall necrosis & pseudomembrane formation

Shigella dysenteriae

Shiga toxin

Halts protein synthesis by disabling the 60S ribosomal subunit, leading to intestinal epithelial cell death & diarrhea

Streptococcus pyogenes

Pyrogenic exotoxin

Acts as a superantigen, inducing fever & shock; associated with scarlet fever & streptococcal toxic shock syndrome

Streptolysin O&S

Damages erythrocyte membranes, causing beta hemolysis
Shiga toxin

Shiga toxin

Microbiology

  • Cytotoxin produced by Escherichia coli O157:H7* & Shigella dysenteriae

Mechanism
of action

  • Inactivates ribosomal subunit → halts protein synthesis → cell death

Clinical
manifestations

  • Inflammatory/bloody diarrhea (damage to enterocytes)
  • Hemolytic uremic syndrome (damage to renal endothelial cells)
    • Thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, renal insufficiency

*Also referred to as high-risk Shiga-toxin–producing or enterohemorrhagic E coli.

directTables: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome

Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome

Risks

  • Tampon use
  • Nasal packing
  • Surgical/postpartum wound infection

Pathogenesis

  • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Exotoxin release acting as superantigens

Clinical
features

  • Fever >38.9 C (102 F)
  • Hypotension
  • Diffuse macular rash involving palms & soles
  • Desquamation 1-3 weeks after disease onset
  • Vomiting, diarrhea
  • Altered mentation without focal neurologic signs

Treatment

  • Supportive therapy (fluid replacement)
  • Removal of foreign body (eg, tampon)
  • Antibiotic therapy (eg, vancomycin, cefepime, clindamycin)

directTables: Adult pneumococcal vaccination

Adult pneumococcal vaccination

Indications

  • Age ≥65
  • Age 19-64 with conditions that increase the risk for serious pneumococcal infection:
    • Diabetes mellitus; chronic heart, lung, liver, or kidney disease
    • Alcohol misuse, smoking
    • Asplenia, immune suppression
    • CSF leak, cochlear implant

Recommended vaccine

  • PCV20

OR

  • PCV15 followed by PPSV23

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid; PCV15 = 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine;

PCV20 = 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine; PPSV23 = 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine.

directTables: Antenatal screening

Preventing neonatal group B Streptococcus infection

Antenatal screening

  • Rectovaginal culture at 36-38 weeks gestation

Indications for intrapartum prophylaxis

  • GBS bacteriuria or GBS urinary tract infection in current pregnancy (regardless of treatment)
  • GBS-positive rectovaginal culture in current pregnancy
  • Unknown GBS status PLUS any of the following:
    • <37 weeks gestation
    • Intrapartum fever
    • Rupture of membranes for ≥18 hr
  • Prior infant with early-onset neonatal GBS infection 

Intrapartum prophylaxis

  • Intravenous penicillin

GBS = group B Streptococcus.
Intrapartum intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis for GBS colonization

Intrapartum intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis for GBS colonization

Penicillin, ampicillin

  • Preferred agents
  • No reported resistance
  • Penicillin favored due to narrow spectrum of activity

Cefazolin

  • Indicated for patients with mild penicillin allergy (maculopapular rash)

Clindamycin

  • Indicated for patients with severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis, respiratory distress, urticaria)

Vancomycin

  • Indicated for patients with severe penicillin allergy

     AND

  • Clindamycin-resistant GBS

GBS = group B Streptococcus.
Pathogenesis

Neonatal group B Streptococcus infection

Pathogenesis

  • Most common cause of neonatal sepsis, pneumonia & meningitis
  • Early onset (age <1 week)
    • Usually exposure to bacteria in maternal genital tract
  • Late onset (age >1 week)
    • Usually exposure to colonized contacts

Clinical findings

  • Sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis:
    • Temperature instability (eg, fever, hypothermia)
    • Irritability, lethargy, poor feeding
    • Tachycardia, hypotension
    • Respiratory distress (eg, tachypnea, grunting)
  • Focal infection (late onset):
    • Septic arthritis
    • Cellulitis

Prevention

  • Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for mothers with positive screening GBS culture at 36 weeks

GBS = group B Streptococcus.
Group B streptococcal infection in neonates & young infants

Group B streptococcal infection in neonates & young infants

Early onset (age <7 days)

Late onset (age ≥7 days)

Pathogenesis

  • Vertical transmission in utero or during vaginal delivery
  • Reduced transmission with maternal intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis
  • Horizontal transmission from colonized individuals

Clinical features

  • Typically presents within 24 hr
  • Sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis
  • Typically presents at age 4-5 weeks
  • Bacteremia, meningitis, focal infection (eg, cellulitis)

Diagnosis

  • Gram-positive cocci in pairs/chains on culture of blood, CSF, or body fluid

Treatment

  • Early initiation of empiric antibiotics
  • Definitive therapy with penicillin G

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid.

directTables: High CDAD risk

Antibiotics & Clostridioides difficile infection

High CDAD risk

Low CDAD risk

  • Fluoroquinolones
  • Clindamycin
  • 3rd-/4th-generation cephalosporins
  • Carbapenems
  • Monobactams
  • TMP-SMX
  • Macrolides
  • Tetracyclines
  • Aminoglycosides

CDAD = Clostridioides difficile–associated disease;
TMP-SMX = trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
First recurrence

Treatment of recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection

First recurrence

  • Preferred: fidaxomicin
  • Alternate: oral vancomycin in tapered & pulsed regimen
  • Consider adjunctive intravenous bezlotoxumab*

Second or
subsequent
recurrence

  • Preferred: fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin in tapered & pulsed regimen
  • Alternate: oral vancomycin followed by rifaximin
  • Consider adjunctive intravenous bezlotoxumab*
  • Consider suppressive therapy (eg, long-term oral vancomycin), fecal microbiota transplantation (eg, third or subsequent recurrence)
*Considered for patients with high recurrence risk (eg, age >65, immunocompromised, severe C difficile infection).
Isolation

Infection control measures for hospitalized patients with Clostridioides difficile

Hand
hygiene

Wash hands thoroughly with soap & water

Contact
precautions

Wear a gown & gloves to prevent spread

Isolation

Identify & isolate patients in a private room with a dedicated bathroom

Antibiotic
stewardship

Stop unnecessary and/or causative antibiotics if possible (eg, no suspicion for another concurrent bacterial infection)

tables: Tetanus prophylaxis

Tetanus prophylaxis

Clean/minor wound

Dirty/severe wound

≥3 tetanus toxoid doses

  • Tetanus toxoid–containing vaccine* only if last dose ≥10 years ago
  • No TIG
  • Tetanus toxoid–containing vaccine* only if last dose ≥5 years ago
  • No TIG

Unimmunized, uncertain, or
<3 tetanus toxoid doses

  • Tetanus toxoid–containing vaccine* only
  • No TIG
  • Tetanus toxoid–containing vaccine*

PLUS

  • TIG
*Booster given as tetanus/diphtheria (Td) toxoids adsorbed or tetanus toxoid/reduced diphtheria toxoid/acellular pertussis (Tdap).

TIG = tetanus immune globulin.
Tetanus

Tetanus

Cause

  • Clostridium tetani spores inoculate skin wound → germinate → produce tetanus toxin →  retrograde axonal transport to CNS → blocks inhibitory interneurons
  • Risk: incomplete childhood vaccines or lack of 10-year booster shot

Symptoms

  • Trismus (lockjaw) & difficulty swallowing
  • Intermittent intense muscular spasms
  • Opisthotonos (extremely arched back)
  • Risus sardonicus (facial muscle spasm while smiling)

Prevention

  • Tetanus toxoid vaccination

subs.subject: bact
tables: Infant botulism

Infant botulism

Pathogenesis

  • Ingestion of Clostridium botulinum spores (eg, environmental dust/soil, honey)
  • Spores colonize the immature gastrointestinal tract & produce toxin
  • Toxin inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release

Clinical presentation

  • Age <12 months
  • Constipation, poor feeding, hypotonia
  • Oculobulbar palsies (eg, absent gag reflex, ptosis)
  • Symmetric descending paralysis
  • Autonomic dysfunction (eg, decreased salivation, fluctuating HR/BP)

Diagnosis

  • Clinical; supported by abnormal EMG findings (eg, ↓ CMAP)
  • Confirmation by stool C botulinum spores or toxins

Treatment

  • Antitoxin therapy (botulism immunoglobulin)

BP = blood pressure; CMAP = compound muscle action potential; EMG = electromyography; HR = heart rate.
Foodborne botulism

Foodborne botulism

Pathogenesis

Clostridium botulinum toxin inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction

Sources

  • Improperly canned foods (eg, fruits, vegetables)
  • Aged seafood (eg, cured fish)

Clinical features

Acute onset within 36 hr of ingestion

  • Bilateral cranial neuropathies
    • Blurred vision, diplopia
    • Facial weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia
  • Symmetric descending muscle weakness
  • Diaphragmatic weakness with respiratory failure

Diagnosis

Serum analysis for toxin

Treatment

Equine serum heptavalent botulinum antitoxin

directTables: Diphtheria

Diphtheria

Epidemiology

  • Rare in resource-rich countries due to widespread vaccination
  • Risk: inadequate vaccination/10-year booster shot

Pathogenesis

  • Toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae colonizes respiratory tract → secretes diphtheria toxin → inhibits host protein synthesis (ADP-ribosylation of EF-2) → local & systemic toxin-mediated effects

Manifestations

  • Local: pseudomembranous pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Systemic: myocarditis/heart failure, neurologic toxicity
  • Pharyngeal edema/pseudomembrane spread can obstruct respiratory tract

Treatment

  • Diphtheria antitoxin (most important)
  • Antibiotics

EF-2 = elongation factor-2.

tables: Nocardiosis

Nocardiosis

Microbiology

  • Gram-positive rod (beaded or branching)
  • Partially acid-fast
  • Aerobic

Epidemiology

  • Endemic in soil
  • Inhaled in dust or skin inoculation
  • Immunocompromised at greatest risk

Clinical features

  • Cutaneous: ulcers/nodules, nodular lymphangitis
  • Lungs: pneumonia with nodules/cavities
  • CNS: brain abscess

Treatment

  • TMP-SMX for mild/moderate disease
  • Add amikacin or imipenem for severe/CNS disease
  • Surgical drainage of abscesses

TMP-SMX = trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

directTables: complex

Mycobacterium avium complex

Epidemiology

  • M avium, M intracellulare
  • Patients with advanced AIDS (CD4 <50/mm3)

Manifestations

  • Fever & weight loss
  • Abdominal pain & diarrhea
  • LAD & (often) hepatosplenomegaly
    • ↑ Alkaline phosphatase

Diagnosis

  • Blood/lymph node culture → nontuberculous mycobacteria

Treatment

  • Macrolide + ethambutol
  • Primary prophylaxis (azithromycin) no longer recommended

LAD = lymphadenopathy.
Pulmonary nontuberculous mycobacterial infection

Pulmonary nontuberculous mycobacterial infection

Nodulobronchiectatic

Cavitary

Risk factors

  • No preexisting lung disease
  • Thin body habitus
  • Elderly women
  • Underlying lung disease (eg, COPD)
  • Smoking, alcohol use disorder
  • Men age >50

Presentation

  • Indolent: chronic cough, fatigue, weight loss
  • AFB smear can be negative
  • More aggressive: fever, cough, weight loss, potential hemoptysis (similar to TB)
  • AFB smear usually positive

Chest imaging

  • Right middle lobe and lingula
  • Branching linear opacities with small nodules (tree in bud) and bronchiectasis
  • Upper lobes
  • Cavitary lesions with surrounding inflammatory infiltrates

AFB = acid-fast bacillus; COPD = chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; TB = tuberculosis.
Diagnostic criteria for MAC

Diagnostic criteria for MAC

Clinical

  • Pulmonary symptoms (eg, cough, fever, weight loss), chest x-ray showing nodular or cavitary opacities, or high-resolution CT scan with multifocal bronchiectasis and multiple small nodules

AND

  • Appropriate exclusion of other diagnoses

Microbiology

  • At least 2 positive sputum culture results

OR

  • One bronchial lavage (BAL) or wash with positive culture

OR

  • Transbronchial or other lung biopsy with histopathologic features of mycobacterial infection and positive culture for nontuberculosis mycobacterial lung disease

directTables: Tuberculin skin test (TST) thresholds

Tuberculin skin test (TST) thresholds

Induration size

Patient population

≥5 mm

  • Individuals with HIV infection
  • Recent contacts of patient with known TB
  • Persons with nodular or fibrotic changes on chest x-ray consistent with previously healed TB
  • Organ transplant recipients & other immunosuppressed persons

≥10 mm

  • Recent immigrants (<5 years) from TB-endemic areas
  • Injection drug users
  • Residents & employees in high-risk settings (eg, prisons, nursing homes, hospitals, homeless shelters)
  • Mycobacteriology laboratory personnel
  • Persons with conditions that result in higher risk for TB reactivation (eg, diabetes mellitus, leukemia, end-stage renal disease, chronic malabsorption syndromes, low body weight)
  • Children age <5 or those exposed to adults in high-risk categories

≥15 mm

  • All of the above plus healthy persons

TB = tuberculosis.
Transmission

Preventing the spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in health care settings

Transmission

  • Inhalation of airborne particles (droplets)
  • Occurs with active disease (pulmonary or laryngeal)

Prevention strategies

  • Single-occupancy room
  • Negative pressure room with a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter
  • N95 respirator mask or powered air-purifying respirator

directTables: Pertussis

Pertussis

Microbiology

  • Bordetella pertussis (gram-negative coccobacilli)

Clinical
phases

  • Catarrhal (weeks 1-2): mild cough, rhinitis
  • Paroxysmal (weeks 2-8): severe coughing spells
    • ± Inspiratory whoop, posttussive emesis, apnea/cyanosis (infants); posttussive syncope (older patients)
  • Convalescent (weeks 8+): symptoms resolve gradually

Diagnosis

  • Clinical: cough + paroxysmal symptoms &/or pertussis exposure
    • Supportive findings: low-grade/no fever, leukocytosis with lymphocytosis, normal/nonspecific chest x-ray
  • Confirmatory: pertussis PCR (sensitive) & culture (specific)

Treatment

  • Treat empirically with macrolide (eg, azithromycin)
  • Droplet precautions

Prevention

tables: Pertussis

Pertussis

Microbiology

  • Bordetella pertussis (gram-negative coccobacilli)

Clinical
phases

  • Catarrhal (weeks 1-2): mild cough, rhinitis
  • Paroxysmal (weeks 2-8): severe coughing spells
    • ± Inspiratory whoop, posttussive emesis, apnea/cyanosis (infants); posttussive syncope (older patients)
  • Convalescent (weeks 8+): symptoms resolve gradually

Diagnosis

  • Clinical: cough + paroxysmal symptoms &/or pertussis exposure
    • Supportive findings: low-grade/no fever, leukocytosis with lymphocytosis, normal/nonspecific chest x-ray
  • Confirmatory: pertussis PCR (sensitive) & culture (specific)

Treatment

  • Treat empirically with macrolide (eg, azithromycin)
  • Droplet precautions

Prevention

  • Acellular pertussis vaccine
  • Macrolides for close (home/health care) contacts regardless of vaccination status

Legionella pneumonia

Epidemiology

  • Contaminated water
    • Hospital
    • Travel (cruise, hotel)

  • Gastrointestinal: diarrhea, vomiting, cramps

infection

Legionella infection

Epidemiology

  • Species: Legionella pneumophilia (most common), Legionella longbeachae
  • Environmental reservoir: human-made water systems, soil
  • Transmission: inhalation of aerosolized particles

Clinical
manifestations

  • Legionnaires' disease (atypical CAP)
    • Fever, dyspnea, cough
    • GI symptoms (nausea/vomiting, diarrhea)
    • Hyponatremia
    • Relative bradycardia
    • Chest x-ray: lobar/multilobar patchy infiltrate
  • Pontiac fever (nonspecific, febrile illness)
    • Rapid onset (hours after transmission)
    • Fever, headache, chills, myalgia, GI symptoms
    • No lower respiratory manifestations

Diagnosis

  • PCR (sputum, BAL)
  • Urine Legionella antigen
  • Culture

Treatment

  • Respiratory fluoroquinolone
    OR
  • Azithromycin

BAL = bronchoalveolar lavage; CAP = community-acquired pneumonia; GI = gastrointestinal.

tables: gastroenteritis

Shigella gastroenteritis

Pathogenesis

  • Fecal-oral transmission, ingestion of contaminated food or water
  • Invasion of colonic mucosal cells → inflammation & ulceration
  • Often in outbreaks (eg, day care)

Clinical presentation

  • High fever, abdominal pain, tenesmus
  • Bloody/mucoid diarrhea (often watery initially)
  • Extraintestinal complications: seizure, bacteremia, HUS*

Evaluation

  • Stool microscopy: positive for WBCs & RBCs
  • Stool PCR testing
  • Stool & blood cultures with susceptibilities (due to antibiotic resistance)

Management

  • Fluid & electrolyte replacement
  • Antibiotics

*S dysenteriae infection only.

HUS = hemolytic uremic syndrome; RBC = red blood cell; WBC = white blood cell.

Campylobacter jejuni

Epidemiology

  • Motile, curved, gram-negative rod

topics.subject: bact
directTables: Test

Diagnosis of Helicobacter pylori

Test

Uses & limitations

Urea breath test

  • Confirms new infection or eradication
  • False-negative results with recent* use of PPI, antibiotics, bismuth

Stool antigen test

  • Confirms new infection or eradication
  • False-negative results with recent* use of PPI, antibiotics, bismuth

Serologic test (IgG)

  • Limited use
  • Cannot distinguish between past & current infection

Endoscopic biopsy urease test

  • Confirms new infection or eradication
  • False-negative results with recent* use of PPI, antibiotics, bismuth

*False-negative results possible with <2 weeks of PPI use or <4 weeks of bismuth or antibiotics.

PPI = proton pump inhibitor.
Preferred initial therapy

Treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection

Preferred initial therapy

Quadruple therapy: PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline for 10-14 days

Alternate therapy

Avoid if high risk of macrolide resistance*

Triple therapy: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole**) for 10-14 days

*In areas of endemic resistance (eg, United States), previous macrolide use.

**For patients with penicillin allergy.

PPI = proton pump inhibitor.
Regimen

Empiric Helicobacter pylori treatment regimens

Regimen

Medications included

Prescribing notes

Bismuth quadruple therapy (BQT)

  • Bismuth subsalicylate
  • Metronidazole
  • Tetracycline
  • PPI
  • Available also in fixed-dose capsule (with bismuth subcitrate)
  • Appropriate for patients with penicillin allergy
  • Avoid in pregnancy & small children

Rifabutin triple therapy

  • Rifabutin
  • Amoxicillin
  • PPI
  • More expensive, potential for drug-drug interactions
  • Alternative to BQT for patients without penicillin allergy

PCAB dual therapy

  • Amoxicillin
  • Vonoprazan
  • Simplest regimen, but more costly
  • May have less adverse effects than other regimens

PCAB = potassium-competitive acid blocker; PPI = proton pump inhibitor (eg, esomeprazole, rabeprazole).

directTables: Prophylaxis criteria for Lyme disease (must meet all 5)

Prophylaxis criteria for Lyme disease (must meet all 5)

  • Attached tick is an adult or nymphal Ixodes scapularis (deer tick)
  • Tick attached for ≥36 hr or engorged
  • Prophylaxis started within 72 hr of tick removal
  • Local Borrelia burgdorferi infection rate ≥20% (eg, New England area)
  • No contraindications to doxycycline (eg, age <8, pregnant, lactating)

topics.title: Leptospira interrogans
topics.subject: bact
directTables: Leptospirosis

Leptospirosis

Epidemiology

  • Spirochete from genus Leptospira
  • Endemic in tropical regions with poor sanitation
  • Reservoir is renal tubules of domestic/wild animals (eg, rodents)
  • Transmission occurs when contaminated soil/water contacts abraded skin, mucous membranes, conjunctiva

Manifestations

  • Mostly asymptomatic or mild/self-limited
  • Anicteric leptospirosis: acute febrile illness (fever, rigor, myalgia, headache), immune complications (uveitis, aseptic meningitis)
  • Icteric leptospirosis (Weil disease): fever, jaundice, end-organ complications (eg, renal failure, pulmonary hemorrhage)
  • Notable feature: conjunctival hyperemia with no purulence

Diagnosis

  • PCR
  • Serology

Treatment

  • Mild: oral doxycycline or azithromycin
  • Severe: intravenous penicillin, doxycycline, 3rd generation cephalosporin

tables: Syphilis in pregnancy

Syphilis in pregnancy

Screening

  • Universal at 1st prenatal visit
  • 3rd trimester & delivery (if high risk)

Serologic tests

  • Nontreponemal (RPR, VDRL)
  • Treponemal (FTA-ABS)

Treatment

  • Intramuscular penicillin G benzathine

Pregnancy effects

  • Intrauterine fetal demise
  • Preterm labor

Fetal effects

  • Hepatic (hepatomegaly, jaundice)
  • Hematologic (hemolytic anemia, ↓ platelets)
  • Musculoskeletal (long bone abnormalities)
  • Failure to thrive

FTA-ABS = fluorescent treponemal antibody-absorption; RPR = rapid plasma reagin .
Congenital syphilis

Congenital syphilis

Clinical
features

Early*

  • Snuffles: copious clear, purulent, or serosanguineous rhinorrhea
  • Maculopapular rash:
    • Palms, soles, buttocks, legs usually involved
    • Desquamation & hyperpigmentation
  • Long bone abnormalities (eg, metaphyseal lucencies)

Late

  • Saddle nose, notched (Hutchinson) teeth, saber shins, sensorineural hearing loss

Diagnosis

  • Serologic testing: VDRL, RPR
  • Darkfield microscopy: Treponema pallidum in infectious material (eg, nasal discharge, skin lesions, placenta)

Treatment

  • Penicillin

Prevention

  • 1st-trimester maternal screening; repeat if high risk (eg, other prenatal STI)
  • Prenatal penicillin

*Nonspecific findings: jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, growth restriction, "blueberry muffin" spots.

RPR = rapid plasma reagin; STI = sexually transmitted infection.

Cat scratch disease

Cat scratch disease

Etiology

  • Bartonella henselae (fastidious, gram-negative coccobacillus)
  • Transmitted by cat scratch/bite

Clinical manifestations

  • Skin lesion (eg, papule, vesicle) at inoculation site
  • Tender lymphadenopathy proximal to skin lesion
  • ± Fever, malaise, aches

Diagnosis

  • Usually clinical
  • ± Serology
  • Lymph node histopathology: necrotizing granulomas, stellate microabscesses

Treatment

  • Generally self-limiting
  • Azithromycin
Tularemia

Tularemia

Epidemiology

  • Transmission:
    • Wild animal (eg, hare, rabbit) hunting/skinning
    • Tick or mosquito bite
    • Bioterrorism agent

Common manifestations

  • Nonspecific systemic symptoms (fever, malaise)
  • Ulceroglandular disease
    • Single papuloulcerative lesion (sometimes absent)
    • Tender, suppurative regional lymphadenopathy
  • Pneumonia

Microbiology

  • Poorly staining, gram-negative coccobacillus
  • Most strains require cysteine for growth
  • Evades most immune defenses & replicates within macrophages/neutrophils

Plague

Microbiology

  • Yersinia pestis
  • Gram-negative coccobacillus

  • Zoonotic: Transmitted primarily by rodent fleas

  • Septicemic: High fever, hypotension, DIC, acral necrosis
