tables: Rocky Mountain spotted fever

Rocky Mountain spotted fever

Epidemiology

  • Rickettsia rickettsii infection
  • Transmitted by tick bite
  • Peaks in summer

Clinical features

  • Nonspecific fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia
  • Macular & petechial rash on wrists/ankles
  • Can develop complications of encephalitis, pulmonary edema, bleeding, shock

Laboratory findings

  • ↓ Platelets
  • ↓ Sodium
  • ↑ AST & ALT

Diagnosis

  • Rickettsia serology
  • Skin biopsy

Treatment

  • Doxycycline

ALT = alanine transaminase; AST = aspartate transaminase.

subs.title: Ehrlichiosis
subs.subject: bact
tables: Ehrlichiosis & Anaplasmosis

Ehrlichiosis & Anaplasmosis

Epidemiology

  • HGA (Anaplasma phagocytophilum):
    • Vector: Ixodes tick (same as Lyme disease/babesiosis)
    • Environmental reservoir: small mammals (eg, white-footed mouse)
    • Location: northeastern & midwestern United States
  • HME (Ehrlichia chaffeensis):
    • Vector: lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum)
    • Environmental reservoir: white-tailed deer
    • Location: southeast & south-central United States

Manifestations

  • Nonspecific flu-like syndrome
  • Nausea, vomiting, respiratory symptoms (in some patients)
  • Neurologic symptoms (HME)
  • Rash (HME) in a minority of patients; no central clearing

Laboratory findings

  • Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, &/or elevated transaminases
  • PCR, blood smear examination (intraleukocytic morulae), serology

Management

  • Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily

HGA = human granulocytic anaplasmosis; HME = human monocytic ehrlichiosis.

subs.title: Q fever
subs.subject: bact
tables: Q fever

Q fever

Epidemiology

  • Coxiella burnetii (obligate intracellular, gram-negative) is transmitted via aerosols from domestic animal products
  • Risk increased with certain occupations (farmer, abattoir/lab worker) or living near livestock
  • Low infectious dose; potential bioterrorism agent

Manifestations

  • Acute Q fever (self-limited): ~50% asymptomatic
    • Influenza-like febrile illness
    • Community-acquired pneumonia
    • Acute hepatitis
  • Chronic Q fever
    • Culture-negative endocarditis (prior valve disease)
    • Vascular infection (prior arterial disease/graft)
    • Bone/joint infection

Diagnosis

  • Serology (Coxiella LPS IgG)*
  • PCR (highest sensitivity in acute infection)

Treatment

  • Acute Q fever: oral doxycycline
  • Chronic Q fever: oral doxycycline + hydroxychloroquine × 18-24 months
  • Serial serology + clinical visits required to ensure resolution

*Phase I IgG (in vivo; weakly immunogenic) is elevated in chronic infection; phase II IgG (in vitro; strongly immunogenic) is elevated in acute infection.

LPS = lipopolysaccharide.

subs.title: Histoplasmosis
subs.subject: myco
tables: Disseminated histoplasmosis

Disseminated histoplasmosis

Epidemiology

  • Temperate regions worldwide
  • Soil contaminated by bird or bat droppings
  • ↑ Dose exposure or immunocompromised (eg, AIDS)

Symptoms

  • Systemic (fever, chills, malaise)
  • Weight loss & cachexia
  • Pulmonary (cough, dyspnea)
  • Mucocutaneous lesions (papules, nodules)
  • Reticuloendothelial (HSM, LAD)

Diagnosis

  • Laboratory findings:
    • Pancytopenia
    • Transaminase elevation
    • ↑ LDH & ferritin
  • Chest x-ray (reticulonodular or interstitial infiltrate)
  • Urine/serum histoplasma antigen (↑ sensitivity/rapid)
  • Serology
  • Culture (takes 4-6 weeks)

Treatment

  • Amphotericin B (moderate to severe disease &/or HIV positive)
  • Itraconazole (mild disease/maintenance)

HSM = hepatosplenomegaly; LAD = lymphadenopathy; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase.

subs.title: Blastomycosis
subs.subject: myco
tables: Blastomycosis

Blastomycosis

Epidemiology

  • South/South Central states, Mississippi & Ohio River valleys, Upper Midwest states, Great Lakes states & Canadian provinces
  • Disseminated disease may occur even in immunocompetent patients
  • Generally more severe in immunocompromised patients

Clinical features

  • Lung: acute & chronic pneumonia (usually mild to moderate but may be severe)
  • Skin: wart-like lesions, violaceous nodules, skin ulcers
  • Bone: osteomyelitis
  • Genitourinary: prostatitis, epididymo-orchitis
  • CNS: meningitis, epidural or brain abscesses

Diagnosis

  • Culture (blood, sputum, tissue specimens)
  • Microscopy (body fluids, sputum, tissue specimens)
  • Antigen testing (urine, blood)

Treatment

  • Mild pulmonary disease in immunocompetent patients: may consider not treating
  • Mild-to-moderate pulmonary disease, mild disseminated disease: oral itraconazole
  • Severe pulmonary disease, moderately severe to severe disseminated disease, immunocompromised patients: intravenous amphotericin B

tables: endophthalmitis

Candida endophthalmitis

Epidemiology

  • Transient/persistent fungemia → hematogenous dissemination to the choroid → invasion of the retina & fluid chambers
  • Risk factors: indwelling central catheter, TPN, broad-spectrum antibiotic use, gastrointestinal surgery & immunocompromise
  • Most cases arise in hospitalized patients or in those with recent eye surgery/trauma

Manifestations

  • Usually unilateral floaters & progressive vision loss
  • Pain rare until late in disease process
  • Fever may be absent & patient may otherwise feel well

Diagnosis

  • Blood cultures (often negative)
  • Vitreous fluid sampling & culture

Treatment

  • Systemic antifungal therapy
  • Vitrectomy + vitreous injection (when fluid chamber involved)

TPN = total parenteral nutrition.

subs.title: Aspergillus fumigatus
subs.subject: myco
tables: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis

Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis

Risk factors

  • Stem cell or solid organ transplantation
  • Prolonged neutropenia
  • Chronic corticosteroid use
  • Other immunosuppressive conditions (eg, AIDS)

Manifestations

  • Classic triad of:
    • Cough
    • Pleuritic chest pain
    • Hemoptysis

Diagnostic
workup

  • CT scan of the chest:  Nodules with ground-glass opacity (halo sign) &/or cavitations with air-fluid levels
  • Serum biomarkers: galactomannan, β-D-glucan
  • Sputum sampling for fungal stain and culture

Treatment

  • Voriconazole
  • Reduction of immunosuppressive regimen
  • Surgery (if needed)

subs.title: Cryptococcus neoformans
subs.subject: myco
tables: Clinical features of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis

Clinical features of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis

Presentation

  • Slowly progressive headache, fever & lethargy over 1-2 weeks
  • Patients with AIDS may present more acutely/severely

Diagnosis

  • Lumbar puncture: ↓ glucose & ↑ protein
  • India ink staining: transparent capsule
  • CSF shows positive cryptococcal antigen
  • Culture on Sabouraud agar

Treatment

  • Initial treatment: amphotericin B & flucytosine
  • Long-term maintenance therapy: fluconazole

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid.

subs.subject: myco
tables: Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis*

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis*

Risk factors

  • Diabetes mellitus (ketoacidosis)
  • Hematologic malignancy
  • Solid organ or stem cell transplant

Manifestations

  • Acute/aggressive
  • Fever, nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, headache, sinus pain
  • Necrotic invasion of palate, orbit, brain

Diagnosis

  • Sinus endoscopy with biopsy & culture

Treatment

  • Surgical debridement
  • Liposomal amphotericin B
  • Elimination of risk factors (eg, ↑ glucose, acidosis)

*Largely due to Rhizopus species.

topics.title: Pneumocystis jirovecii
topics.subject: myco
directTables: pneumonia

Pneumocystis pneumonia

Epidemiology

  • AIDS (CD4 <200/mm3)*
  • Immunosuppressive medications (eg, chronic glucocorticoids)

Manifestations

  • Indolent (AIDS) or acute respiratory failure (immunosuppressive treatment)
  • Dyspnea, hypoxia, dry cough, fever
  • ↑ Lactate dehydrogenase level
  • Diffuse bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates on pulmonary imaging

Diagnosis

  • Induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage

Treatment

  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole ± corticosteroids
  • Antiretroviral initiation (in AIDS)

*Patients with AIDS (CD4 <200/mm3) & those on chronic glucocorticoid therapy generally receive primary
prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Sporotrichosis

Epidemiology

  • Sporothrix schenckii (dimorphic fungus)
  • Decaying plant matter/soil
  • Gardeners, farmers & landscapers

Manifestations

  • Subacute/chronic manifestations
  • Inoculation → skin papule → ulceration → nonpurulent, odorless drainage
  • Proximal lesions form along lymphatic chain
  • Distant spread & systemic symptoms are rare

Diagnosis

  • Cultures (aspirate fluid or biopsy) → cigar-shaped yeast with narrow-based budding at 37 C (98.6 F)

Treatment

  • Prolonged course of itraconazole

subs.title: Giardia lamblia
subs.subject: para
tables: Giardiasis

Giardiasis

Risk factors

  • Contaminated food or water
  • Fecal incontinence & crowding (eg, day care, nursing home)
  • Immunodeficiency (eg, CVID, IgA deficiency, CF, HIV)

Pathogenesis

  • Villous blunting, disruption of epithelial tight junctions, loss of brush border enzymes → malabsorption

Clinical features

  • Subacute (<4 weeks) or chronic (months)
  • Loose, oily, nonbloody stools
  • Bloating, flatulence
  • Weight loss, decreased linear velocity (children), vitamin deficiencies

Diagnosis

  • Stool antigen or PCR testing (↑ sensitivity)
  • Stool microscopy (↓ sensitivity)

Treatment

  • First-line: tinidazole or nitazoxanide
  • Alternate: metronidazole
  • Pregnancy (first trimester): paromomycin
  • Refractory/recurrent symptoms: evaluation for immunodeficiency

CF = cystic fibrosis; CVID = common variable immunodeficiency.

subs.title: Entamoeba histolytica
subs.subject: para
tables: Risk factors

Entamoeba histolytica

Risk factors

  • Amoeba transmitted via the fecal-oral route
  • Ingestion of contaminated food/water
  • Resource-limited nations (travel/residence)

Manifestations

  • 90% of patients are asymptomatic
  • Colitis (diarrhea, bloody stool with mucus, abdominal pain)
  • Liver abscess (RUQ pain, fever)
  • Brain, lung, pleura abscess (less common)

Diagnosis

  • Stool ova & parasites: trophozoites/cysts
  • Colonoscopy: colonic ulcers (flask-shaped on biopsy)

RUQ = right upper quadrant.
Epidemiology

Entamoeba histolytica

Epidemiology

  • Tropical/subtropical regions with poor sanitation
  • Transmitted via ingestion of cysts in contaminated food/water

Manifestations

  • 90% of patients are asymptomatic
  • Colitis (diarrhea, bloody stool with mucus, abdominal pain)
  • Liver abscess (RUQ pain, fever)
  • Brain, lung, pleura abscess (less common)

Diagnosis

  • Intestinal:
    • Stool PCR/antigen testing (preferred)
    • Stool microscopy: cysts, trophozoites with ingested RBCs
    • Colonoscopy: flask-shaped ulcerations
  • Extraintestinal: serology + imaging

Treatment*

  • Tissue agent (eg, metronidazole) followed by:
  • Luminal agent (eg, paromomycin)

*Asymptomatic patients treated with luminal agent only.

RUQ = right upper quadrant.

subs.title: Cryptosporidium
subs.subject: para
tables: Cryptosporidiosis

Cryptosporidiosis

Epidemiology

  • Fecal-oral transmission (eg, contaminated water, animal contact)
  • Risk factors: immunosuppression (eg, AIDS, transplant recipient)

Clinical manifestations

  • Immunocompetent: self-resolving, watery (noninflammatory) diarrhea <2 weeks
  • Immunosuppressed:
    • Prolonged, severe diarrhea with weight loss/malabsorption
    • Biliary disease (eg, cholecystitis, cholangitis)

Diagnosis

  • Stool PCR testing
  • Stool microscopy: acid-fast staining oocysts or immunofluorescent assay
  • Intestinal biopsy: organisms on mucosal brush border

Treatment

  • Immunocompetent: supportive care only
  • Immunocompromised*: nitazoxanide

*Patients with HIV should be prescribed antiretroviral therapy first & treated with antimicrobial therapy only if symptoms persist.

subs.title: Toxoplasma gondii
subs.subject: para
tables: Congenital toxoplasmosis

Congenital toxoplasmosis

Maternal
risk factors

  • Raw or undercooked meat
  • Unwashed produce (ie, contaminated soil)
  • Handling of cat feces

Clinical
features

  • Classic triad:
    • Chorioretinitis
    • Diffuse intracranial calcifications
    • Hydrocephalus
  • Microcephaly (brain atrophy) or macrocephaly (severe hydrocephalus)
  • Seizures
  • Nonspecific findings: jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, growth restriction

Diagnosis

  • Toxoplasma serology or PCR

Treatment

  • Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, folinic acid
PCR = polymerase chain reaction.

subs.title: Plasmodium
subs.subject: para
tables: Malaria

Malaria

Epidemiology

  • Vector: female Anopheles mosquito
  • 4 major species of Plasmodium: P falciparum, P vivax, P ovale, P malariae
  • Highest burden of disease is in Africa but is found in most tropical/subtropical areas worldwide

Manifestations

  • Periodic febrile paroxysms
  • Nonspecific malaise, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, myalgia

Complications

  • Cerebral (eg, delirium, seizure), hypoglycemia, ARDS, acidosis, renal/hepatic failure, coagulopathy

Diagnosis

  • Thin & thick peripheral blood smears
  • Rapid testing

ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome.

subs.title: Babesia
subs.subject: para
tables: Babesiosis

Babesiosis

Epidemiology

  • Vector: Tick (Ixodes scapularis), blood transfusion
  • Location: Northeastern/Upper Midwestern United States
  • Risk factors for severe disease: splenectomy, HIV, immunosuppression

Manifestations

  • Mild: fevers, fatigue, myalgias, headache
  • Severe:  ARDS, CHF, DIC, AKI, liver failure, splenic rupture
  • Anemia & thrombocytopenia

Diagnosis

  • Thin blood smear: intraerythrocytic pleomorphic ring forms ("Maltese cross")
  • PCR: detection of Babesia DNA in the blood
  • Serology: may be negative in acute infection

AKI = acute kidney injury; ARDS = acute respiratory distress syndrome; CHF = congestive heart failure; DIC = disseminated intravascular coagulation

tables: Chagas disease

Chagas disease

Epidemiology

  • Caused by protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi
  • Vector: triatomine ("kissing") bug
  • Endemic in Central & South America

Cardiac
manifestations

  • Dilated cardiomyopathy with biventricular failure
  • Apical wall thinning with aneurysm ± mural thrombus
  • Ventricular arrhythmias

Gastrointestinal
manifestations

  • Megaesophagus (secondary achalasia)
  • Megacolon

subs.title: Leishmania spp
subs.subject: para
tables: Leishmaniasis

Leishmaniasis

Localized cutaneous

  • Painless, shallow, pink ulcer with indurated borders (± soft center) at sand fly bite site
  • Overlying eschar (Old World leishmaniasis) or fibrinous material (New World leishmaniasis)*
  • Spontaneous healing over months/years → atrophic scar/keloid

Mucocutaneous

  • Primarily in New World leishmaniasis, with or after cutaneous lesions
  • Mucosal erosions
    • Nasal: stuffiness, bleeding, facial disfigurement (cartilage destruction)
    • Larynx: hoarseness, brassy cough
    • Epiglottis/pharynx/palate: odynophagia

Visceral

(kala azar)

  • Often asymptomatic/subclinical (lifelong viable parasites, reactivation with immunosuppression)
  • Insidious clinical illness (2-6 months after transmission) from reticuloendothelial spread:
    • Constitutional (malaise, fever, weight loss)
    • Splenomegaly, left upper quadrant fullness
    • Skin darkening classic but uncommon (kala azar = "black fever")
  • Diagnosis: histopathology (amastigotes with kinetoplast)/culture, serology (resource-limited area)
  • >90% mortality without treatment

*Old World (Africa, Middle East, South Asia) vs New World (Central/South America) leishmaniasis reflects geographic & clinical differences.

topics.title: Nematodes (roundworms)
topics.subject: para

subs.title: Enterobius vermicularis
subs.subject: para
tables: Pathogenesis

Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm)

Pathogenesis

  • Transmission via ingestion of eggs
  • Larvae develop into adult worms in the intestines
  • Female worms migrate to the perianal region at night & deposit eggs

Findings

  • Nocturnal perianal pruritus → perianal erythema/excoriations*

Diagnosis

  • Mobile worms visualized near anal verge
  • Tape test: eggs visualized under microscopic examination

Treatment**

  • Albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate
  • Administered to patient & household contacts, then repeated in 2 weeks

*Worm migration to vulvar region may also cause symptoms of vulvovaginitis (eg, vulvar itching & erythema).

**Empiric treatment (ie, without visualization of eggs/worms) can be performed for those with classic findings.

subs.title: Strongyloides stercoralis
subs.subject: para
tables: Strongyloidiasis

Strongyloidiasis

Epidemiology

  • Tropical/subtropical climates worldwide
  • Poor sanitary practices
  • Warm, moist soil exposure (eg, barefoot)

Manifestations

  • Largely asymptomatic (immunocompetent)
  • Skin:
    • Acute: maculopapular rash
    • Chronic: pruritic urticaria or larva currens*
  • Respiratory:
    • Dry cough, dyspnea, hoarseness, wheezing
  • Gastrointestinal:
    • Nonspecific (eg, bloating, crampy pain, nausea, diarrhea, constipation, anorexia)
    • Severe cases: bleeding, ulceration, obstruction, enteropathy, or perforation
  • Hyperinfection/dissemination (immunocompromised)

Diagnosis

  • Serology
  • Stool microscopy (rhabditiform larvae) or PCR

Treatment

  • Ivermectin
  • Follow-up (symptom resolution, test improvement)

*Larva currens is a quickly-moving, pruritic, serpiginous rash.

subs.title: Ancylostoma spp, Necator americanus
subs.subject: para
tables: Cutaneous larva migrans

Cutaneous larva migrans

Epidemiology

  • Hookworm larvae
    • Dog (Ancylostoma caninum) or cat (Abraziliense)
  • Humans are incidental hosts
  • Barefoot contact with contaminated sand or soil

Clinical

  • Primarily lower extremity
  • Cutaneous (deeper infection rare)
  • Erythematous, pruritic papule at site of entry
  • Intensely pruritic, migrating, serpiginous, reddish-brown tracks

Diagnosis

  • History & clinical findings
  • Eosinophils usually normal

Treatment

  • Antihelmintic (eg, ivermectin)

subs.title: Toxocara canis
subs.subject: para
tables: Toxocariasis

Toxocariasis

Epidemiology

  • Toxocara canis or Toxocara cati eggs ingested in contaminated soil or food
  • Humans are dead-end hosts (larvae do not mature)
  • Young children at greatest risk

Manifestations

  • Often asymptomatic or mild/self-limited
  • VLM
    • Liver: hepatomegaly or nodules
    • Lung: dyspnea, wheezing, nonproductive cough
    • Gastrointestinal: abdominal pain
  • OLM
    • Unilateral vision loss, photophobia, floaters, leukocoria, strabismus
    • Lesions (white granuloma) in posterior pole/periphery

Diagnosis

  • Serology (excretory-secretory antigen ELISA)
  • Eosinophilia
  • Elevated IgE
  • Ophthalmologic consultation (for OLM)

Treatment

  • Albendazole
  • Corticosteroids added for OLM/severe symptoms

ELISA = enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay; OLM = ocular larva migrans; VLM = visceral larva migrans.

subs.title: Onchocerca volvulus
subs.subject: para
tables: Onchocerciasis (river blindness)

Onchocerciasis (river blindness)

Epidemiology

  • Leading cause of blindness in endemic areas (>99% of cases occur in Africa)
  • Black fly bite transmits filarial nematodes (Onchocerca volvulus) to skin → matures in subcutaneous nodules → microfilariae travel through lymph, skin, eyes

Manifestations

  • Subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas): over bony prominences: usually deep and asymptomatic
  • Cutaneous: intense pruritus, papular dermatitis, depigmentation
  • Ocular: keratitis, chorioretinitis, blindness

Diagnosis

  • Skin snip biopsy (gold standard)
  • Slit-lamp examination (visualize microfilariae)
  • Serologic testing (limited utility)

Treatment

  • Ivermectin
  • Doxycycline (kills endosymbiotic bacteria)
  • Vector control/mass treatment

subs.title: Loa loa
subs.subject: para
tables: Loiasis

Loiasis

Epidemiology

  • Caused by Loa loa (filarial nematode)
  • Transmitted by bite of Chrysops fly
  • Endemic to rainforests of Central/West Africa
  • Larvae, adult worms migrate through subcutaneous tissue/subconjunctiva, producing microfilariae

Manifestations

  • Calabar swellings: transient, focal areas of angioedema usually with localized pain/pruritic
  • Eye symptoms: transient tearing, foreign body sensation, conjunctival hyperemia (while worm passes through subconjunctiva)
  • Arterial thickening, nephropathy (chronic microfilaremia)
  • Encephalopathy (usually following treatment)

Diagnosis

  • Direct visualization of worms in eye or skin
  • Blood smear showing microfilaremia

Treatment

  • Must quantify microfilaremia and evaluate for onchocerciasis coinfection prior to starting treatment:
    • >20,000/mL: hospitalize + albendazole + recheck
    • 2,500-20,000/mL: ivermectin + recheck
    • <2,500/mL and no onchocerciasis: DEC
  • DEC is the definitive treatment

DEC = diethylcarbamazine.

subs.title: Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi
subs.subject: para
tables: Lymphatic filariasis

Lymphatic filariasis

Microbiology & risk factors

  • Parasitic nematode infection: Wuchereria bancrofti (~90%), Brugia malayi, Brugia timori
  • Mosquito vector
  • Endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, Pacific Islands, parts of Latin America & Caribbean

Pathogenesis

  • Third-stage larvae in mosquitoes infect host → mature to adult worms in lymphatics & reside in lymph nodes → adults release microfilariae into bloodstream → microfilariae ingested by mosquitoes  → third-stage larvae develop in mosquito GI tract

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic: most common
  • Acute: acute filarial lymphangitis, acute dermatolymphangioadenitis, filarial fever, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia
  • Chronic: severe lymphedema, hydrocele, elephantiasis

Diagnosis

  • Significant eosinophilia
  • Blood smear with Giemsa stain: circulating microfilariae
  • Circulating antigen detection (W bancrofti)

Treatment & prevention

  • Monoinfection: diethylcarbamazine
  • Coinfection*: combination regimen (eg, doxycycline, ivermectin, albendazole)
  • Prevention: mass drug administration

Prognosis

  • Chronic lymphedema, elephantiasis

*Coinfection with loiasis and/or onchocerciasis. Regimen dependent on type of coinfection and disease burden.

  • Larvae, adult worms migrate through subcutaneous tissue/subconjunctiva, producing microfilariae

Manifestations

  • Calabar swellings: transient, focal areas of angioedema usually with localized pain/pruritic
  • Eye symptoms: transient tearing, foreign body sensation, conjunctival hyperemia (while worm passes through subconjunctiva)
  • Arterial thickening, nephropathy (chronic microfilaremia)
  • Encephalopathy (usually following treatment)

Diagnosis

  • Direct visualization of worms in eye or skin
  • Blood smear showing microfilaremia

Treatment

  • Must quantify microfilaremia and evaluate for onchocerciasis coinfection prior to starting treatment:
    • >20,000/mL: hospitalize + albendazole + recheck
    • 2,500-20,000/mL: ivermectin + recheck
    • <2,500/mL and no onchocerciasis: DEC
  • DEC is the definitive treatment

DEC = diethylcarbamazine.
Lymphatic filariasis

Lymphatic filariasis

Microbiology & risk factors

  • Parasitic nematode infection: Wuchereria bancrofti (~90%), Brugia malayi, Brugia timori
  • Mosquito vector
  • Endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia, Pacific Islands, parts of Latin America & Caribbean

Pathogenesis

  • Third-stage larvae in mosquitoes infect host → mature to adult worms in lymphatics & reside in lymph nodes → adults release microfilariae into bloodstream → microfilariae ingested by mosquitoes  → third-stage larvae develop in mosquito GI tract

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic: most common
  • Acute: acute filarial lymphangitis, acute dermatolymphangioadenitis, filarial fever, tropical pulmonary eosinophilia
  • Chronic: severe lymphedema, hydrocele, elephantiasis

Diagnosis

  • Significant eosinophilia
  • Blood smear with Giemsa stain: circulating microfilariae
  • Circulating antigen detection (W bancrofti)

Treatment & prevention

  • Monoinfection: diethylcarbamazine
  • Coinfection*: combination regimen (eg, doxycycline, ivermectin, albendazole)
  • Prevention: mass drug administration

Prognosis

  • Chronic lymphedema, elephantiasis

*Coinfection with loiasis and/or onchocerciasis. Regimen dependent on type of coinfection and disease burden.

Neurocysticercosis

Epidemiology

  • Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) eggs
  • Fecal-oral human transmission
  • Central & South America, sub-Saharan Africa, Asia

Manifestations

  • Prolonged incubation (months to years)
  • Seizures
  • ICH (headache, vomiting, AMS)

Diagnosis

  • CT/MRI scans: cysts (hypodense, enhancement/edema, or calcified)
  • T solium serology

Treatment

  • Seizure/ICH management
  • Antiparasitic therapy (albendazole)
  • Corticosteroids

AMS = altered mental status; ICH = intracranial hypertension.

tables: Scabies

Scabies

Pathogenesis

  • Sarcoptes scabiei mite infestation
  • Spread by direct person-to-person contact

Clinical features

  • Extremely pruritic, small, erythematous papules
  • Distribution: interdigital web spaces, flexor wrists, extensor elbows, axillae, feet, umbilicus & genitalia
  • Burrows (thin serpiginous lines) may not be visible but pathognomonic if present

Diagnosis

  • Clinical
  • Skin scraping with microscopy is confirmatory

Treatment

  • Topical 5% permethrin OR oral ivermectin
  • Treat household members & close personal contacts
  • Environmental measures (eg, launder clothing/bedding)

directTables: Chigger bites

Chigger bites

Pathogenesis

  • Caused by trombiculid larval mites
    • Found on leaves & grass close to ground
    • Attach to exposed, accessible areas (eg, pant cuff)

Epidemiology

  • Most common in summer & fall
  • Found in areas with high humidity/moisture

Clinical features

  • Grouped papulovesicular rash, often involves waistline & ankles
  • Intense pruritus

Treatment

  • Supportive (eg, topical corticosteroids)

Prevention

  • Physical barriers to skin (eg, pants tucked into socks)
  • Insect repellants (eg, DEET)
DEET = N,N-diethyl-m-toluamide.

tables: Mpox

Mpox

Epidemiology

  • dsDNA orthopoxvirus similar to smallpox
  • Zoonotic spread in endemic areas (Central/West Africa)
  • Person-to-person spread in nonendemic areas during outbreaks (primarily MSM) 

Manifestations

  • Systemic symptoms: fever, headache, myalgia, LAD
  • Rash: macule → papule →  vesicle → pseudopustule → crusted lesion → scab → resolution
  • More rarely, pneumonitis, encephalitis, tonsillitis/pharyngitis, proctitis

Diagnosis

  • Clinical + PCR testing or serology

Management

  • Self-limited in most cases
  • Supportive care (eg, analgesics)
  • Antivirals if immunocompromised, severely ill, or young/pregnant
    • Techovirimat + brincidofovir
  • Vaccine available for preexposure or postexposure prophylaxis

dsDNA = double-stranded DNA; LAD = lymphadenopathy; MSM = men who have sex with men.

subs.subject: viro
tables: Human papillomavirus vaccine indications

Human papillomavirus vaccine indications

  • All girls & women* age 11-26 (but may be administered up to age 45)
  • Boys & men age 11-21 (up to age 26 for men who have sex with men)
  • Immunocompromised individuals (including HIV patients) age 11-26
  • Not indicated in pregnant women

*Including those with history of genital warts, abnormal cytology, or positive human papillomavirus DNA test.
Genital warts (condylomata acuminata)

Genital warts (condylomata acuminata)

Etiology

  • HPV 6, 11 & other low-risk strains

Clinical features

  • Pink, skin-colored, hyperpigmented lesions
  • Smooth or cauliflower-like papules/nodules

Treatment

  • Lesions <1 cm: imiquimod, cryotherapy, sinecatechins, podophyllotoxin, trichloroacetic acid
  • Lesions >1 cm: excision, laser therapy, electrosurgery
  • Screen for other STIs
  • Recurrence is common

Prevention

  • Vaccination
  • Barrier contraception

HPV = human papillomavirus; STIs = sexually transmitted infections.
Human papillomavirus

Human papillomavirus

Disease associations

  • Cervical cancer
  • Vulvar & vaginal cancers
  • Anal cancer
  • Penile cancer
  • Oropharyngeal cancer
  • Anogenital warts
  • Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis

Vaccine indications

  • All female and male patients* age 11-26
    (but may be given to those age 9-45)
  • Not indicated in pregnancy

*Including those with a history of genital warts, abnormal Pap cytology, or positive
human papillomavirus DNA test.

tables: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

Clinical presentation

  • Asymptomatic (most common)
  • Flu-like symptoms with rash
  • Acute, symmetric arthralgia/arthritis
  • Transient pure red cell aplasia, aplastic crisis  

Diagnosis

  • Acute infection
    • B19 IgM antibodies in immunocompetent
    • NAAT for B19 DNA in immunocompromised
  • Previous infection: B19 IgG antibodies
  • Fetus: PCR analysis of amniotic fluid for B19 DNA

Fetal sequelae

  • Fetal demise
  • Anemia
  • Hydrops fetalis

Prenatal management

  • Serial ultrasonography  
  • Middle cerebral artery Doppler measurements

Treatment

  • Severe anemia: Intrauterine blood transfusion 

NAAT = nucleic acid amplification testing; PCR = polymerase chain reaction.

tables: Neonatal varicella-zoster infection

Neonatal varicella-zoster infection

Clinical features

  • Fever
  • Vesicular eruption (chickenpox)
  • Systemic involvement (eg, pneumonia, hepatitis, meningoencephalitis)

Treatment

  • Acyclovir

Prevention

  • Isolate infant from varicella contact
  • Administer varicella-zoster immune globulin to infant if maternal infection developed 5 days before or 2 days after delivery
Classification of herpes zoster pain

Classification of herpes zoster pain

Pain

Timeframe

Treatment

Acute herpetic neuralgia

Persists ≤30 days from rash onset

NSAIDs, analgesics

Subacute herpetic neuralgia

Persists >30 days but resolves within 3 months of rash onset

NSAIDs, analgesics

Postherpetic neuralgia

Persists >3 months from rash onset

Gabapentin, pregabalin, TCAs

NSAID = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug; TCA = tricyclic antidepressant.
Primary varicella

Primary varicella

Epidemiology

  • Primary infection (chickenpox) with varicella-zoster virus
  • Transmission via direct contact or airborne respiratory particles
  • High risk: newborns, adolescents/adults, pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals

Clinical features

  • Prodrome (eg, fever, malaise)
  • Pruritic macules, papules & vesicles in different stages
  • Complications: skin infection, pneumonia, encephalitis

Management

  • Supportive care (eg, antihistamines)
  • Acyclovir for high-risk patients & complicated disease

subs.title: Epstein-Barr virus (HHV-4)
subs.subject: viro
tables: Infectious mononucleosis

Infectious mononucleosis

Etiology

  • Epstein-Barr virus (most common)

Clinical features

  • Fever
  • Tonsillitis/pharyngitis ± exudates
  • Posterior or diffuse cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Significant fatigue
  • ± Hepatosplenomegaly
  • ± Rash after amoxicillin

Diagnostic findings

  • Positive heterophile antibody (Monospot) test
    • 25% false-negative rate during 1st week of illness
  • Atypical lymphocytosis
  • Transient hepatitis

Management

  • Due to risk of splenic rupture:
    • Avoid sports for ≥3 weeks
    • Avoid contact sports for ≥4 weeks
Atraumatic splenic rupture

Atraumatic splenic rupture

Risk factors

  • Hematologic malignancy (eg, leukemia, lymphoma)
  • Infection (eg, CMV, EBV, malaria)
  • Inflammatory disease (eg, SLE, pancreatitis)
  • Splenic congestion (eg, cirrhosis, pregnancy)
  • Medications (eg, anticoagulation, G-CSF)

Clinical presentation

  • Diffuse or LUQ abdominal pain, peritonitis
  • Referred left shoulder pain (Kehr sign)
  • Hemodynamic instability

Diagnosis

  • Acute anemia
  • Intraperitoneal free fluid on imaging

Treatment

  • Catheter-based angioembolization (stable patients)
  • Emergency splenectomy (unstable patients)

CMV = cytomegalovirus; EBV = Epstein-Barr virus; G-CSF = granulocyte-stimulating colony factor; LUQ = left upper quadrant; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.

subs.title: Epstein-Barr virus (HHV-4)
subs.subject: viro
tables: Infectious mononucleosis

Infectious mononucleosis

Etiology

  • Epstein-Barr virus (most common)

Clinical features

  • Fever
  • Tonsillitis/pharyngitis ± exudates
  • Posterior or diffuse cervical lymphadenopathy
  • Significant fatigue
  • ± Hepatosplenomegaly
  • ± Rash after amoxicillin

Diagnostic findings

  • Positive heterophile antibody (Monospot) test
    • 25% false-negative rate during 1st week of illness
  • Atypical lymphocytosis
  • Transient hepatitis

Management

  • Due to risk of splenic rupture:
    • Avoid sports for ≥3 weeks
    • Avoid contact sports for ≥4 weeks
Atraumatic splenic rupture

Atraumatic splenic rupture

Risk factors

  • Hematologic malignancy (eg, leukemia, lymphoma)
  • Infection (eg, CMV, EBV, malaria)
  • Inflammatory disease (eg, SLE, pancreatitis)
  • Splenic congestion (eg, cirrhosis, pregnancy)
  • Medications (eg, anticoagulation, G-CSF)

Clinical presentation

  • Diffuse or LUQ abdominal pain, peritonitis
  • Referred left shoulder pain (Kehr sign)
  • Hemodynamic instability

Diagnosis

  • Acute anemia
  • Intraperitoneal free fluid on imaging

Treatment

  • Catheter-based angioembolization (stable patients)
  • Emergency splenectomy (unstable patients)

CMV = cytomegalovirus; EBV = Epstein-Barr virus; G-CSF = granulocyte-stimulating colony factor; LUQ = left upper quadrant; SLE = systemic lupus erythematosus.

West Nile virus

Clinical syndrome

  • West Nile fever: fever, headache, rash (maculopapular/morbilliform)
  • Neuroinvasive: meningitis, encephalitis, acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis
    • Parkinsonian symptoms (eg, rigidity, bradykinesia, tremor)

subs.subject: viro
tables: Bronchiolitis

Bronchiolitis

Pathophysiology

  • Viral-induced inflammation of small, distal airways
  • Bronchiolar obstruction from sloughed epithelial cells, leukocytes & mucus
  • RSV most common cause

Clinical presentation

  • Age <2
  • Antecedent nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, cough
  • Wheezing & crackles, tachypnea, retractions (peak severity days 3-5)
  • ± Hypoxia, fever

Radiographic findings

  • Bilateral hyperinflation, increased interstitial markings & peribronchial cuffing

Treatment

  • Supportive (eg, nasal suctioning, hydration, supplemental oxygen)

Complications

  • Apnea (age <2 months)
  • Respiratory failure

Prevention

  • Nirsevimab for all children age <8 months

RSV = respiratory syncytial virus.

Hand-foot-and-mouth disease

Pathogenesis & epidemiology

  • Coxsackievirus infection
  • Any age, usually age <7
  • Transmission: direct contact with respiratory, oral, vesicular secretions or fecal-oral spread

  • Myopericarditis
  • Aseptic meningitis
  • Nail dystrophy (1-2 months later)

Management

  • Supportive (eg, pain control, hydration)

subs.subject: viro
tables: Clinical features of dengue

Clinical features of dengue

Dengue without
warning signs

Following travel to a dengue-endemic area, fever with:

  • Flu-like febrile illness with marked myalgia &/or arthralgia
  • Diffuse maculopapular rash
  • Leukopenia
  • Positive tourniquet test (petechiae after sphygmomanometer cuff inflation for 5 min)

Dengue with
warning signs

Addition of any of the following:

  • Abdominal pain &/or persistent vomiting
  • Fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion)
  • Mucosal bleeding
  • Lethargy or restlessness
  • Hepatomegaly >2 cm
  • Increased hematocrit with rapidly decreasing platelet count

Severe dengue

Progression to:

  • Severe plasma leakage causing shock or respiratory distress
  • Severe bleeding
  • Severe organ involvement (AST or ALT ≥1,000 U/L, impaired conciousness, organ failure)

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase.
Manifestations of dengue

Manifestations of dengue

Nonhemorrhagic

  • Flu-like febrile illness with marked myalgia &/or arthralgia
  • Diffuse maculopapular rash
  • Retroorbital pain
  • Leukopenia

Hemorrhagic

  • Increased vascular permeability
  • Positive tourniquet test (petechiae after sphygmomanometer cuff inflation for 5 min)
  • Hemoconcentration & thrombocytopenia
  • Spontaneous bleeding → shock

topics.title: Rabies virus
topics.subject: viro
directTables: Human rabies

Human rabies

Pathogenesis

  • Transmission of rabies virus by a bite from an infected mammal

Reservoir

  • United States: bats (most common), raccoons, skunks, foxes
  • Resource-limited countries: dogs

Clinical

features

Encephalitic

  • Hydrophobia & aerophobia (due to pharyngeal spasm)
  • Autonomic instability
  • Spasticity
  • Agitation & altered mental status

Paralytic

  • Ascending flaccid paralysis

Postexposure
prophylaxis*

  • Rabies immunoglobulin
  • Rabies vaccine series

Prognosis

  • Coma, respiratory failure & death within weeks

*In cases of a high-risk animal that cannot be tested or observed.

directTables: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy

Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy

Definition

  • ≥100,000 CFU/mL bacteria

Risk
factors

  • Pregestational diabetes mellitus
  • History of urinary tract infection
  • Multiparity

Common
pathogens

  • Escherichia coli (most common)
  • Klebsiella
  • Enterobacter
  • Group B Streptococcus

Potential complications

  • Acute pyelonephritis
  • Preterm labor & delivery

Treatment

  • Cefpodoxime
  • Fosfomycin
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Nitrofurantoin*

*Avoided in first & third trimesters.

CFU = colony-forming units.
Urinary tract infection antibiotics in pregnancy

Urinary tract infection antibiotics in pregnancy

Recommended

Contraindicated

  • Nitrofurantoin*
  • Amoxicillin
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Cephalexin
  • Fosfomycin
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole*
  • Tetracyclines
  • Fluoroquinolones

*Avoid in 1st trimester & near term.
Recurrent urinary tract infection

Recurrent urinary tract infection

Definition

  • ≥2 infections in 6 months
  • ≥3 infections in 1 year

Risk factors

  • History of cystitis at age ≤15
  • Spermicide use
  • New sexual partner
  • Postmenopausal status

Evaluation

  • Urinalysis
  • Urine culture

Prevention

  • Behavior modification
  • Postcoital or daily antibiotic prophylaxis
  • Topical vaginal estrogen for postmenopausal patients
Urinary tract infection (UTI) in children

Urinary tract infection (UTI) in children

Risk factors

  • Female sex
  • Uncircumcised male infants
  • Urologic abnormalities (eg, vesicoureteral reflux)
  • Bowel/bladder dysfunction (eg, constipation)

Clinical features

  • Infants: fever, fussiness, poor feeding
  • Older children: dysuria, suprapubic/flank pain

Laboratory findings

  • Urinalysis: leukocyte esterase, nitrites, WBCs
  • Urine culture: bacteriuria

Management

  • Antibiotics (eg, cephalosporin)
  • First febrile UTI:
    • Age <2 years: RBUS, followed by VCUG if abnormal
    • Age ≥2 years: observation alone
  • Recurrent febrile UTIs: RBUS & VCUG

RBUS = renal & bladder ultrasonography; VCUG = voiding cystourethrogram; WBCs = white blood cells.
Catheter-associated urinary tract infection

Catheter-associated urinary tract infection

Clinical features

  • Fever, flank pain, suprapubic pain
  • ≥103 cfu/mL of uropathogenic organism (eg, Escherichia coli, Enterococcus, Klebsiella)
  • Current (or within 48 hr) use of urethral, suprapubic, or condom catheter

Risk factors

  • Duration of catheter use, especially >48 hr (most important)
  • Female sex
  • Advanced age
  • Diabetes mellitus

Prevention

  • Avoid unnecessary catheterization (eg, not indicated for incontinence)
  • Use sterile technique when placing catheter
  • Remove catheter promptly when no longer needed

cfu = colony-forming units.
Candiduria

Candiduria

Risk factors

  • Chronic colonization
  • Urinary tract drainage device (eg, Foley catheter)
  • Prior antibiotic use
  • Diabetes mellitus

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic UTI (most common)
  • Cystitis: suprapubic pain
  • Pyelonephritis: flank pain, CVA tenderness
  • Disseminated candidemia

Treatment

  • Asymptomatic: none indicated
  • Symptomatic UTI & disseminated infection: antifungal therapy*

Complications

  • Perinephric abscess
  • Fungus ball

*Fluconazole (amphotericin B if fluconazole resistant).

CVA = costovertebral angle; UTI = urinary tract infection.
Urinalysis interpretation in urinary tract infections

Urinalysis interpretation in urinary tract infections

Result

Pathophysiology

Clinical significance

White blood cells

  • Congregate in response to infection
  • Pyuria (WBC > 10 cells/mm3) indicates UTI

Red blood cells

  • Structural disruption caused by inflammation or infection
  • Not specific to infection, but often positive in UTIs

Bacteria

  • Bacteria ascend urinary tract to colonize and/or cause infection
  • Contamination (eg, improper sampling), colonization (eg, asymptomatic bacteriuria), or infection

Leukocyte esterase

  • Released by lysed neutrophils/macrophages
  • Marker of WBC & pyuria

Nitrites*

  • Urinary nitrate is converted to nitrite by nitrate reductase
  • Marker of nitrate reductase–producing bacteria (eg, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus mirabilis)

pH

  • Alkaline urine (pH > 8) due to ammonia produced from hydrolysis of urea by urease
  • Marker of urease-producing bacteria (eg, Proteus mirabilis)
*The absence of nitrites does not exclude these bacteria.

UTI = urinary tract infection; WBC = white blood cells.

Risk

Recurrent urinary tract infection

Definition

Risk factors

  • History of cystitis at age ≤15
  • Spermicide use
  • New sexual partner
  • Postmenopausal status

Evaluation

  • Urinalysis
  • Urine culture

Prevention

  • Behavior modification
  • Postcoital or daily antibiotic prophylaxis
  • Topical vaginal estrogen for postmenopausal patients

Risk factors

directTables: Acute cervicitis

Acute cervicitis

Etiology

  • Infectious: Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae
  • Noninfectious: foreign object, latex, douching 

Clinical presentation

  • Asymptomatic
  • Mucopurulent discharge  
  • Postcoital/intermenstrual bleeding
  • Friable cervix   

Evaluation

  • Nucleic acid amplification testing  
  • Wet mount microscopy

Management

  • Empiric treatment: ceftriaxone + doxycycline*

*Ceftriaxone + azithromycin in pregnancy.
Infectious genital ulcers

Infectious genital ulcers

Painful

Herpes simplex virus

  • Pustules, vesicles, or small ulcers on erythematous base
  • Tender lymphadenopathy
  • Systemic symptoms common

Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid)

  • Larger, deep ulcers with gray/yellow exudate
  • Well-demarcated borders & soft, friable base
  • Severe lymphadenopathy that may suppurate

Painless

Treponema pallidum (syphilis)

  • Usually single ulcer (chancre)
  • Indurated borders & hard, nonpurulent base

Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3 (lymphogranuloma venereum)

  • Initial small, shallow ulcers (often missed)
  • Then painful & fluctuant adenitis (buboes)
Infectious urethritis in men

Infectious urethritis in men

Etiology

  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae
  • Chlamydia trachomatis
  • Mycoplasma genitalium
  • Trichomonas vaginalis

  • Dysuria
  • Discharge

Diagnosis

  • Gram stain & culture
  • Nucleic acid amplification testing

  • GU alone: ceftriaxone
  • GU + Chlamydia*: ceftriaxone + doxycycline
  • Chlamydia/Mycoplasma: azithromycin
  • Trichomonas: metronidazole

directTables: Congenital TORCH infections

Congenital TORCH infections

Organism

Etiology

Clinical features

Toxoplasmosis

Obligate intracellular protozoan Toxoplasma gondii

Chorioretinitis, intracranial calcifications, hydrocephalus

Other (syphilis, VZV, parvovirus B19)

  • VZV: dsDNA virus
  • Parvovirus: ssDNA virus
  • Syphilis: spirochete Treponema pallidum
  • VZV: limb hypoplasia, cutaneous scarring, cataracts, chorioretinitis
  • Parvovirus: hydrops fetalis
  • Syphilis: rhinorrhea, hepatomegaly, skeletal anomalies

Rubella

ssRNA virus

Sensorineural deafness, cataracts, "blueberry muffin" rash, heart defects, hepatosplenomegaly

Cytomegalovirus

dsDNA virus

Sensorineural deafness, periventricular calcifications, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, chorioretinitis

Herpes simplex virus

dsDNA virus

Cutaneous vesicles, lesions, scarring

ds = double-stranded; ss = single-stranded; VZV = varicella zoster virus.
Key features of congenital infections

Key features of congenital infections*

Toxoplasmosis

  • Chorioretinitis
  • Hydrocephalus
  • Diffuse intracranial calcifications

Syphilis

  • Rhinorrhea
  • Skeletal anomalies
  • Desquamating rash (palms/soles)

Rubella

  • Cataracts
  • Heart defects (eg, PDA)
  • Sensorineural hearing loss

Cytomegalovirus

  • Periventricular calcifications
  • Microcephaly
  • Sensorineural hearing loss

Herpes simplex virus

  • Vesicular/ulcerative rash

*Nonspecific findings include growth restriction, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly & blueberry muffin rash.

PDA = patent ductus arteriosus.
Congenital toxoplasmosis vs congenital cytomegalovirus

Congenital toxoplasmosis vs congenital cytomegalovirus

Toxoplasmosis

CMV

Pathogenesis

  • Maternal consumption of undercooked meat or inadvertent ingestion of cat feces
  • Maternal contact with infected bodily fluids (eg, saliva)

Classic
features*

  • Chorioretinitis
  • Diffuse intracranial calcifications
  • Macrocephaly (ie, hydrocephalus) or microcephaly
  • Seizures
  • Chorioretinitis
  • Periventricular intracranial calcifications
  • Microcephaly
  • Sensorineural hearing loss

Diagnosis

  • Toxoplasma serology or PCR
  • Urine or saliva CMV PCR

Treatment

  • Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, folinic acid
  • Ganciclovir or valganciclovir if symptomatic

*Nonspecific features of congenital infections include jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, rash & growth restriction.

CMV = cytomegalovirus.

directTables: Pelvic inflammatory disease

Pelvic inflammatory disease

Symptoms

  • Lower abdominal pain
  • Abnormal bleeding

Risk
factors

  • Multiple sexual partners
  • Age 15-25
  • Previous pelvic inflammatory disease
  • Inconsistent barrier contraception use
  • Partner with sexually transmitted infection

Physical
examination

  • Fever >38.3 C (>100.9 F)
  • Cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness
  • Mucopurulent cervical discharge

Treatment

  • Inpatient: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Outpatient: PO broad-spectrum antibiotics

Complications

  • Tuboovarian abscess
  • Infertility
  • Ectopic pregnancy
  • Perihepatitis

Recommended treatment
for latent tuberculosis infection

  • Rifamycin-based therapy (preferred)
    • Rifampin daily for 4 months
    • Rifampin plus isoniazid daily for 3 months
    • Rifapentine plus isoniazid weekly for 3 months
  • Isoniazid monotherapy for 6-9 months*

Duration

Drugs

2 months

Continuation

≥ 4 months

  • Two drugs:

    • Isoniazid*

Malaria prevention

High-risk groups

  • Travelers new to endemic regions
  • Travelers returning to endemic region after long absence
  • Pregnant women

Mosquito bite
avoidance

  • Avoid being outside from dusk → dawn
  • Cover skin with clothing
  • Wear insect repellant
  • Use insecticide-treated bed nets
  • Sleep in screened/air-conditioned rooms

Chemoprophylaxis

  • Atovaquone-proguanil
  • Mefloquine
  • Doxycycline
  • Tafenoquine

directTables: HIV management during pregnancy

HIV management during pregnancy

Antepartum

  • Testing of HIV-1 viral load monthly until undetectable, then every 3 months
  • CD4 cell count every 3 months
  • Resistance testing if not previously performed
  • Initiation or continuation of HAART
  • Avoidance of amniocentesis if viral load is detectable

Intrapartum

  • Avoidance of artificial ROM, fetal scalp electrode, operative vaginal delivery
  • Viral load ≤50 copies/mL: ART + vaginal delivery
  • Viral load >50 copies/mL to ≤1,000 copies/mL: ART ± zidovudine + vaginal delivery
  • Viral load >1,000 copies/mL: ART + zidovudine + cesarean delivery

HAART = highly active antiretroviral therapy; ROM = rupture of membranes.
Mechanism of action of HIV antiretroviral medications

Mechanism of action of HIV antiretroviral medications

Class

Example(s)

Mechanism of action

NRTI

Tenofovir, emtricitabine, lamivudine, abacavir, zidovudine

Inhibits HIV DNA synthesis from RNA template by terminating DNA chain elongation

  • NRTI: Competitive nucleoside/nucleotide RT inhibitor
  • NNRTI: Allosteric RT inhibitor

NNRTI

Efavirenz, nevirapine

PI

Atazanavir, darunavir, indinavir, ritonavir

Inhibits HIV polyprotein cleavage

Integrase inhibitor

Dolutegravir, raltegravir

Inhibits HIV DNA integration into host genome

Fusion inhibitor

Enfuvirtide

Inhibits HIV fusion with target cell membrane by binding to HIV gp41

CCR5 antagonist

Maraviroc

Inhibits HIV entry by blocking the HIV gp120allosteric interaction with CCR5 (tropism testing required)

CCR5 = chemokine (C-C motif) receptor 5; NNRTI = non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor; NRTI = nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor; PI = protease inhibitor; RT = reverse transcriptase.
INSTI plus 2 NRTIs

Recommended initial HIV antiretroviral regimens for most patients1

INSTI plus 2 NRTIs

  • Bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (Biktarvy)
  • Dolutegravir (Tivicay) plus:
    • Emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Descovy)
    • Emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (Truvada)

INSTI plus 1 NRTI2

  • Dolutegravir/lamivudine (Dovato)
  1. A forward slash (/) indicates that the components are available in a combination pill.
  2. Do not use if pretreatment HIV RNA > 500,000 copies/mL, there is known hepatitis B coinfection, or HIV genotyping is not available.

INSTI =integrase strand transfer inhibitor; NRTI =nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor.

directTables: Neural tube defects

Neural tube defects

Types

  • Anencephaly
  • Encephalocele
  • Spina bifida, myelomeningocele

Risk

factors

  • Low folic acid intake
  • Methotrexate, antiepileptics
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Prior pregnancy with neural tube defect

Prenatal
screening

  • 2nd-trimester ultrasonography
  • Maternal serum α-fetoprotein

Prevention

  • Average risk: 0.4 mg folic acid daily
  • High risk: 4 mg folic acid daily
Spina bifida

Spina bifida

Pathogenesis

  • Failure of neural tube to close

Risk factors

  • Prenatal maternal folate deficiency (eg,
    inadequate supplementation, antifolate drugs)

Clinical features
& comorbidities

  • Motor/sensory dysfunction
  • Neurogenic bladder/bowel
  • Hydrocephalus
  • Scoliosis

Treatment

  • Surgical closure
  • Clean intermittent catheterization
  • Scheduled laxatives/enemas
  • Bracing; correction of deformities
Closed spinal dysraphism

Closed spinal dysraphism

Pathophysiology

  • Failure of posterior vertebral arch fusion
  • ± Spinal cord anomalies (eg, lipoma, cyst)
  • Stretch-induced distal spinal cord dysfunction (tethered cord)

Clinical features

  • May be asymptomatic
  • Cutaneous, lumbosacral anomalies (eg, hair tuft, mass)
  • Tethered cord syndrome*:
    • Neurologic: LMN signs (weakness, hyporeflexia)
    • Urologic: incontinence/retention; recurrent UTI
    • Orthopedic: back pain, scoliosis, foot deformities

Management

  • MRI of the spine
  • Surgical detethering of cord if symptomatic

*Age of onset & organ system involvement are variable.

LMN = lower motor neuron; UTI = urinary tract infection.

tables: Holoprosencephaly

Holoprosencephaly

Embryology

  • Incomplete forebrain (prosencephalon) division into 2 hemispheres

Etiologies

  • Genetic: trisomy 13, sonic hedgehog gene mutations
  • Environmental: maternal alcohol use, retinoic acid

Clinical features

  • CNS abnormalities
    • Range from asymptomatic to seizures, severe intellectual disability, death
  • Midface abnormalities
    • Range from mild hypotelorism and cleft lip/palate to cyclopia, primitive nose, facial cleft

directTables: Neurotransmitter systems of the CNS

Neurotransmitter systems of the CNS

Neurotransmitter & receptor pair

Functions in the CNS

Ionotropic: Ligand-gated ion channels
Transmembrane proteins that allow ions to cross the membrane

 Glutamate [E]
→ NMDA receptor: Ca2+ & Na+ influx

Long-term potentiation of learning & memory

GABA [I]
→ GABAA receptor*: Cl− & HCO3− influx

Sedation, anxiolytic & anticonvulsive

Glycine [I]
→ Glycine receptor: Cl− influx

Inhibits spinal interneurons (prevents spasticity)

Metabotropic: G protein–coupled receptors
Act through second messengers (eg, cAMP, PKA)

Dopamine
→ D1-5 receptors

Modulates attention, movement & reward

Serotonin
→ 5-HT receptors**

Modulates mood, nausea & trigeminovascular nociception (migraine)

Norepinephrine
→ α & β adrenoceptors

Promotes vigilance, attention & emotional memory

Histamine
→ H3 receptors

Promotes wakefulness

*GABAB is a G-coupled metabotropic receptor that increases K+ efflux (hyperpolarization).

**Except 5-HT3 receptor, an ionotropic receptor that primarily increases Na+ influx (depolarization).

 

[E] = excitatory (postsynaptic potential); [I] = inhibitory postsynaptic potential; PKA = protein kinase A.

directTables: Sleep stages

Sleep stages

EEG pattern & frequencies

Characteristics

Non-REM stage 1 (N1)

  • Theta waves (4-7.9 Hz)
  • Wakefulness-sleep transition
  • Easy to wake

Non-REM stage 2 (N2)

  • Theta waves (4-7.9 Hz)
  • Sleep spindles & K complexes
  • Largest percentage of sleep

Non-REM stage 3 (N3)

  • Delta waves (<4 Hz)
  • Prominent 1st half of night
  • Difficult to wake
  • Sleepwalking & night terrors

REM

  • EEG resembles wakefulness
  • Occasional sawtooth waves
  • Prominent 2nd half of night
  • Dreams, REMs, muscle atonia
  • REM sleep behavior disorder & nightmare disorder

EEG = electroencephalogram.

topics.title: REM sleep behavior disorder
topics.subject: anat
directTables: REM sleep behavior disorder

REM sleep behavior disorder

Clinical features

  • Recurrent episodes of arousal during REM sleep, exhibiting either one or both of the following:
    • Vocalizations (loud, coarse, emotion-laden)
    • Complex motor behaviors (eg, kicking, punching, flailing)
  • Fully alert upon awakening
  • Dreams are "acted out" with full recall of content
  • Occurs late in sleep period
  • Associated with some neurodegenerative disorders (eg, Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, multiple system atrophy)

Differential

diagnosis

  • Non-REM sleep arousal disorders (eg, sleep terrors, sleepwalking, confusional arousals)
  • Sleep-related seizures
  • Obstructive sleep apnea

directTables: Management of traumatic brain injury

Management of traumatic brain injury

Goal

Interventions

Maintain CPP
(= MAP − ICP)

  • Maintain MAP: isotonic fluids, vasopressor therapy
  • Reduce ICP: head elevation, sedation, osmotic therapy (eg, hypertonic saline, mannitol), decompressive interventions (eg, CSF removal, craniectomy)

Prevent ICH

  • Antifibrinolytic therapy (ie, tranexamic acid) within first 3 hr
  • Reversal of preexisting anticoagulation

Other
measures

  • Prevent seizures (eg, levetiracetam, phenytoin)
  • Control blood glucose (eg, insulin to target 140-180 mg/dL glucose)
  • Maintain normothermia (eg, antipyretics, surface-cooling devices)

CPP = cerebral perfusion pressure; CSF = cerebrospinal fluid; ICH = intracranial hemorrhage; ICP = intracranial pressure; MAP = mean arterial pressure.

directTables: Criteria for thrombolytics in stroke

Criteria for thrombolytics in stroke

Inclusion criteria

  • Ischemic stroke with disabling neurodeficits
  • Symptom onset <3-4.5 hr before treatment initiation

Strict exclusion criteria*

  • ICH on CT scan, history of ICH, suspected SAH
  • Ischemic stroke in the past 3 months
  • Intraaxial neoplasm, recent intracranial or intraspinal surgery
  • Blood pressure >185/110 mm Hg
  • Current anticoagulant use with INR >1.7, PT >15 sec, or ↑ active PTT
  • Glucose <60 mg/dL or platelets <100,000 mm3

*Careful consideration given for patients with recent major surgery, MI, or GI/GU bleeding.

GI/GU = gastrointestinal/genitourinary; ICH = intracranial hemorrhage; MI = myocardial infarction; SAH = subarachnoid hemorrhage.

topics.title: Fever vs heat stroke
topics.subject: path
directTables: Heat stroke

Heat stroke

Risk factors

  • Exertional heat stroke: strenuous activity in hot & humid weather
  • Nonexertional heat stroke: advanced age, impaired mobility, obesity, neuropsychiatric disease, recreational drugs (eg, cocaine, amphetamines), certain medications (eg, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, β blockers, diuretics)

Clinical manifestations

  • Core temperature >40 C (104 F), tachycardia, hypotension
  • Central nervous system dysfunction: confusion, weakness, dizziness, lethargy, ataxia, seizures
  • Rhabdomyolysis & acute kidney injury
  • Acute liver injury
  • Pulmonary edema & acute respiratory distress syndrome
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation

Management

  • Rapid cooling: misting systems, ice water immersion, ice packs
  • Fluid resuscitation
  • Electrolyte correction
Exertional heat stroke

Exertional heat stroke

Risk factors

  • Strenuous activity during hot & humid weather
  • Dehydration, poor acclimatization
  • Lack of physical fitness, obesity
  • Medications: anticholinergics, antihistamines, phenothiazines, tricyclics, antipsychotics

Clinical manifestations

  • Core temperature >40 C (104 F) with CNS dysfunction (eg, AMS, seizure)
  • Organ or tissue damage: renal or hepatic failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, acute respiratory distress syndrome

Management

  • Rapid cooling: ice water immersion preferred; can consider high-flow cold water dousing, ice-wet towel rotation, evaporative cooling
  • Fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction
  • Management of end-organ complications
  • No role for antipyretic therapy

AMS = altered mental status.
Heat exhaustion

Heat exhaustion

Risk factors

  • Strenuous activity during hot & humid weather
  • Dehydration, poor acclimatization
  • Lack of physical fitness, obesity
  • Acute illness
  • Medications: anticholinergics, antihistamines, phenothiazines, tricyclics, antipsychotics

Manifestations

  • Hyperthermia ≤40 C (104 F) with normal mental status
  • Profuse sweating
  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Headache, dizziness
  • Tachycardia, hypotension

Management

  • Cool patient (eg, air conditioning, cool water shower)
  • Salt-containing oral fluids
Nonexertional (classic) heat stroke

Nonexertional (classic) heat stroke

Risk factors

  • Elderly, obesity, poor physical fitness
  • Alcohol, medications (eg, diuretics, β blockers, anticholinergics, stimulants)
  • High temperatures, high humidity, lack of air conditioning

Manifestations

  • Temperature ≥40 C (104 F) with CNS dysfunction (eg, encephalopathy, seizure)
  • Tachycardia, tachypnea ± hypotension
  • Flushing ± diaphoresis
  • End-organ dysfunction (eg, DIC, pulmonary edema, renal/hepatic dysfunction)
  • Hemoconcentration (↑ hemoglobin, leukocytes, platelets, BUN)

Management

  • Stabilization (ie, airway, breathing, circulation)
  • Rapid cooling (evaporative techniques are best tolerated in the elderly)
    • Antipyretics/dantrolene are NOT indicated
  • Management of end-organ complications

BUN = blood urea nitrogen; DIC = disseminated intravascular coagulation.

subs.subject: path
images: Management of generalized convulsive status epilepticus
Management of generalized convulsive status epilepticus
directTables: Febrile seizure

Febrile seizure

Risk factors

  • Fever (typically with viral illness)
  • Family history of seizures

Clinical characteristics

  • Age 6 months to 5 years
  • No epilepsy history
  • No CNS infection or acute metabolic cause (eg, hypoglycemia)

Management

  • Antiepileptic (if seizure ≥5 min)
  • Symptomatic care (eg, antipyretics) & reassurance

Prognosis

  • No long-term complications
  • ↑ Risk for subsequent febrile seizure
  • Slight ↑ risk for epilepsy (~1%)

CNS = central nervous system.
Seizure types

Seizure types

Medication

Generalized onset (both hemispheres)

Tonic-clonic

  • LOC & postictal state
  • Diffuse contraction (tonic) → jerking (clonic)

Broad spectrum*: levetiracetam, valproic acid

Myoclonic

  • No LOC & no postictal state
  • Brief jerking movements

Atonic

  • Sudden loss of muscle control → drop to floor

Absence

  • Brief staring episodes
  • Automatisms may be present
  • No postictal state

Ethosuximide
(only for absence)

Focal onset (single hemisphere)

Aware

  • Aware during the event & no postictal state
  • Motor (eg, head turn) or sensory (eg, smell)

Narrow spectrum: phenytoin,** carbamazepine, gabapentin

Impaired awareness

  • Appears awake but consciousness is altered
  • Automatisms present (eg, lip smacking)
  • Postictal state

*Can be used for both generalized & focal seizures.

**Can be used for management of status epilepticus.

LOC = loss of consciousness.
Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures

Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures

Clinical features

  • Witnessed events during wakefulness
  • Long, fluctuating course
  • Asynchronous thrashing
  • Pelvic thrusting; rapid head turning
  • No loss of consciousness or postictal period

Comorbidities

  • Psychiatric conditions (depression, anxiety)
  • Physical/sexual abuse
  • Epilepsy

Diagnosis

  • Video electroencephalogram

Treatment

  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy
Seizure

Seizure

Syncope

Preceding symptoms

Aura (eg, smell, visual disturbance) or none

Prodrome (eg, nausea, diaphoresis) or none

Patient position

Any position

Often standing (vasovagal), but can occur in any position (cardiac)

Tongue biting

Common, often lateral

Rare, frontal if present

Convulsive movements

Common, typically start before or simultaneous with LOC

Less common but can occur after LOC*

Urinary incontinence

Common

Less common but can occur after LOC*

Post-episode recovery

Variable (minutes to hours or days), residual confusion is common

Rapid (1-2 min), no residual deficit

*Due to transient cerebral hypoperfusion & hypoxia.

LOC = loss of consciousness.
Febrile seizures vs meningitis

Febrile seizures vs meningitis

Febrile seizures

Meningitis

Clinical
features

  • Usually single episode, <15 min, rapid return to baseline (ie, simple febrile seizure)
  • No signs of intracranial infection
  • Age 6 months to 5 years
  • Associated seizures often prolonged or recurrent
  • Signs of intracranial infection
    • Headache, vomiting, bulging fontanelle (↑ ICP)
    • Nuchal rigidity
    • Altered mental status

Diagnosis

  • Clinical
  • No imaging or laboratory studies
  • Cerebrospinal fluid culture via lumbar puncture

Treatment

  • Supportive care (eg, acetaminophen)
  • Intravenous antibiotics

ICP = intracranial pressure.
Triggers of breakthrough seizures

Triggers of breakthrough seizures

Pharmacologic

●  Missed ASM doses (most common)

●  Changes in ASM formulation (eg, generic substitution)

Behavioral

●  Sleep deprivation

●  Anxiety, psychologic stress

●  Alcohol or recreational drug use/withdrawal

Physiologic

●  Fever, infection

●  Hormonal change (eg, menstruation, pregnancy)

●  Photosensitivity (eg, flashing lights, electronic devices)

●  Hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, hyponatremia

ASM = antiseizure medication.

tables: Migraine therapies

Migraine therapies

Abortives

  • Simple analgesics (eg, NSAIDs, acetaminophen)
  • Antiemetics (eg, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)
  • Triptans (eg, sumatriptan)
  • Ergotamine, dihydroergotamine
  • CGRP receptor antagonists (eg, rimegepant)

Preventives

  • Antiepileptics (eg, topiramate, divalproex sodium)
  • Tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline)
  • β Blockers (eg, propranolol)
  • CGRP monoclonal antibodies (eg, erenumab)

CGRP = calcitonin gene-related peptide; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

subs.title: Cluster
subs.subject: path
tables: Cluster headache

Cluster headache

Symptoms

  • Multiple short attacks (15-180 min) of severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain
  • Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea/nasal congestion)
  • Agitation or restlessness
  • Attacks occurring in clusters (6-12 weeks) separated by periods of remission

Acute treatment

  • 100% oxygen at 6-12 L/min for 15 min
  • Sumatriptan (subcutaneous)
  • Zolmitriptan nasal spray

Preventive treatment

  • Verapamil
  • Lithium
  • Topiramate

directTables: Headache red flags

Headache red flags

Red flag feature

Common diagnoses

Sudden onset, worst headache of life

  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Age ≥50

  • Mass lesion

Abortives

Cluster headache

Cluster headache

Symptoms

  • Multiple short attacks (15-180 min) of severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital, or temporal pain
  • Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea/nasal congestion)
  • Agitation or restlessness
  • Attacks occurring in clusters (6-12 weeks) separated by periods of remission

Acute treatment

  • 100% oxygen at 6-12 L/min for 15 min
  • Sumatriptan (subcutaneous)
  • Zolmitriptan nasal spray

Preventive treatment

  • Verapamil
  • Lithium
  • Topiramate

images: Trigeminal neuralgia secondary to multiple sclerosis
directTables: Trigeminal neuralgia

Trigeminal neuralgia

Pathophysiology

  • Compression of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) root (eg, vascular loop, multiple sclerosis plaque)

Clinical features

  • Paroxysmal attacks of unilateral, severe, stabbing pain lasting seconds to 2 min
  • Limited to CN V distribution (mainly V2 & V3)
  • Triggered by innocuous stimuli (eg, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, light touch)

Work-up

  • MRI/MRA of the brain with contrast
  • Nerve conduction (eg, trigeminal reflex) testing if unable to obtain MRI

Treatment

  • Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine
  • Surgery (eg, decompression) only for severe, medically refractory cases

MRA = MR angiography.

tables: Essential tremor

Essential tremor

Epidemiology

  • Family history often present
  • Up to 5% of population affected

Clinical
features

  • Action tremor (eg, hands outstretched)
  • Usually bilateral
  • Hands > arms > head >> legs
  • Worsens with stress, improves with alcohol

Treatment

  • Beta blockers: propranolol
  • Anticonvulsants: primidone

directTables: Clinical features of tremors

Clinical features of tremors

Essential

  • Bilateral action tremor of the hands
  • Head tremor without dystonia
  • No other neurologic signs
  • Improves with alcohol

Parkinson disease

  • Resting tremor; ↓ with voluntary movement
  • Pill-rolling
  • Asymmetric; hands & legs

Cerebellar

  • Usually associated with ataxia &/or dysmetria
  • ↑ Steadily as hand approaches target

Orthostatic

  • Legs & trunk
  • Occurs only when standing

Physiologic

  • Low amplitude, not visible under normal conditions
  • ↑ With sympathetic activity (eg, drugs, hyperthyroidism, anxiety, caffeine)
  • Worse with movement
  • Most common cause of action tremor
Tremor

Tremor

Clinical features

Essential

  • Action tremor
  • Bilateral hands &/or head
  • Improves with alcohol

Parkinson disease

  • Resting tremor (decreases with movement)
  • Hands & legs
  • "Pill-rolling"
  • Associated parkinsonian features (eg, rigidity, masked faces, short-stepped gait)

Cerebellar

  • Action tremor (increases as hand reaches target)
  • Associated ataxia, dysmetria, or gait disorder

Physiologic

  • Action & rest tremor
  • Low amplitude, high frequency (ie, "fine" tremor)
  • Not visible under normal circumstances
  • Enhanced with sympathetic activation (eg, anxiety, caffeine, hyperthyroidism)

directImages: Clinical features of restless legs syndrome (RLS)
images: Clinical features of restless legs syndrome (RLS)
directTables: Restless legs syndrome

Restless legs syndrome

Clinical features

  • Urge to move the legs
  • Unpleasant sensations in the legs  
    • Worse with inactivity
    • Relieved by movement  

Secondary causes

  • Iron deficiency
  • Uremia  
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease
  • Pregnancy
  • Drugs (eg, antidepressants, metoclopramide)

 Treatment

  • Iron supplement if serum ferritin ≤75 µg/L
  • Leg massage, heating pads, exercise
  • Dopamine agonists (eg, pramipexole)
  • Gabapentin/pregabalin
Restless legs syndrome

Restless legs syndrome

Manifestations

Uncomfortable urge to move legs with:

  • Unpleasant sensations in the legs
  • Onset with inactivity or at night
  • Relief with movement (eg, walking, stretching)

Risk factors &
associated conditions

  • Iron deficiency
  • Uremia
  • Pregnancy
  • Diabetes mellitus (especially with neuropathy)
  • Multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease
  • Drugs: antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiemetics

Nonpharmacologic therapy

  • Limit caffeine & alcohol
  • Regular, moderate exercise
  • Warm &/or cold soaks or compresses

Medications

  • Supplemental iron (if serum ferritin ≤75 ng/mL)
  • Mild intermittent symptoms: carbidopa-levodopa as needed
  • Frequent/daily symptoms: α2δ calcium channel ligand (eg, gabapentin, pregabalin)
  • Dopamine agonists (eg, pramipexole, ropinirole) not preferred

tables: Drug-induced parkinsonism

Drug-induced parkinsonism

Etiology

  • D2 receptor blockers
    • Antipsychotics (first-generation > second-generation)
    • Antiemetics/gastric motility agents (eg, prochlorperazine, metoclopramide)

Symptoms

  • Prominent rigidity & bradykinesia (eg, slowed movement, decreased arm swing)
  • Tremor (rest & postural)
  • Masked facies

Management

  • Decrease or discontinue offending medication
  • Anticholinergics (eg, trihexyphenidyl, benztropine)
Differential clinical features of parkinsonism

Differential clinical features of parkinsonism

(bradykinesia plus tremor or rigidity)

Idiopathic Parkinson disease

Parkinson-plus syndromes*

Progression

Slow

Rapid

Tremor

Common

Uncommon

Neurologic findings

Asymmetric

Symmetric

Postural instability/falls

Late

Early

Dysautonomia

Late

Early

Levodoparesponse

Excellent

Poor

*That is, atypical parkinsonism (eg, multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, dementia with Lewy bodies).
Parkinson-plus (atypical parkinsonism) syndromes*

Parkinson-plus (atypical parkinsonism) syndromes*

Characteristic "plus" features

Multiple system atrophy

  • Early autonomic failure (eg, severe orthostasis, urinary incontinence)
  • Early postural instability (eg, falls)
  • Cerebellar findings (eg, gait ataxia)

Progressive supranuclear palsy

  • Vertical gaze palsy
  • Early postural instability (eg, falls)
  • Akinesia (eg, early gait freezing)
  • Progressive aphasia

Dementia with Lewy bodies

  • Early dementia (executive dysfunction)
  • Visual hallucinations
  • Cognitive fluctuations
  • REM sleep behavior disorder

Corticobasal degeneration

  • Relatively rare
  • Myoclonus, dystonia
  • Alien limb phenomenon (ie, has a will of its own)
  • Cortical sensory loss

*Important findings suggesting Parkinson-plus syndromes instead of Parkinson disease include rapid progression, symmetric findings, absent tremor & poor levodopa response.
Differential diagnosis of idiopathic Parkinson disease

Differential diagnosis of idiopathic Parkinson disease

Atypical parkinsonism
(Parkinson-plus)

  • Multiple system atrophy
  • Progressive supranuclear palsy
  • Corticobasal degeneration
  • Dementia with Lewy bodies

Secondary parkinsonism

  • Drug induced (eg, antipsychotics)
  • Posttraumatic (eg, boxer)
  • Metabolic (eg, Wilson disease)
  • Toxic (eg, carbon monoxide)
  • Infectious (eg, prion disease)
  • Vascular (eg, lacunar strokes)

Mimics of parkinsonism

  • Normal pressure hydrocephalus
  • Essential tremor
  • Functional tremor
Diagnosis of idiopathic Parkinson disease

Diagnosis of idiopathic Parkinson disease*

Essential criterion

  • Motor parkinsonism = bradykinesia + either rest tremor or rigidity

Exclusion criteria

  • Vertical (supranuclear) gaze palsy
  • Cerebellar signs (eg, limb ataxia, evoked nystagmus)
  • Cortical sensory loss (eg, astereognosis)
  • Progressive aphasia
  • Antidopaminergic medication use (eg, haloperidol)

Supportive features

  • Excellent response to dopaminergic therapy (eg, levodopa)
  • Asymmetric limb findings (eg, tremor, rigidity)
  • Olfactory dysfunction
  • Abnormal dopaminergic function on neuroimaging

Red flags

  • Early postural instability (eg, recurrent falls or need for wheelchair)
  • Early bulbar dysfunction (eg, dysarthria, dysphagia)
  • Absence of nonmotor signs (eg, sleep disturbance, constipation)
  • Severe orthostatic hypotension (eg, ≥30 mm Hg systolic drop)
  • Symmetric symptoms, hyperreflexia

*Established Parkinson disease is parkinsonism + no exclusion criteria + 2 supportive criteria (no red flags).
Probable Parkinson disease is parkinsonism + no exclusion criteria + (supportive criteria ≥ red flags).
Pull (retropulsion) test of postural instability

Pull (retropulsion) test of postural instability*

Procedure

  • Patient in comfortable stance, eyes open, with examiner behind
  • Sudden, brief pull on patient's shoulders (ready to catch patient, if needed)
  • Scoring = number of steps to recover balance

Normal

  • 1-2 steps, recovers unaided

Slight

  • 3-5 steps, recovers unaided

Mild

  • >5 steps, recovers unaided

Moderate

  • Stands safely, falls during test if not caught by examiner

Severe

  • Loses balance spontaneously

*From the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale.

tables: Huntington disease

Huntington disease

Clinical features

  • Motor: chorea, delayed saccade
  • Psychiatric: depression, irritability, psychosis, obsessive-compulsive symptoms
  • Cognitive: executive dysfunction

Findings

  • Genetic: autosomal dominant CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion disorder
  • Neuropathology: loss of GABA-ergic neurons
  • Imaging: caudate nucleus & putamen atrophy

Management & prognosis

  • Treatment: supportive
  • Survival: 10-20 years

tables: Clinical features of Alzheimer disease

Clinical features of Alzheimer disease

Early
findings

  • Anterograde memory loss (ie, immediate recall affected, distant memories preserved)
  • Visuospatial deficits (eg, lost in own neighborhood)
  • Language difficulties (eg, difficulty finding words)
  • Cognitive impairment with progressive decline

Late
findings

  • Neuropsychiatric (eg, hallucinations, wandering)
  • Dyspraxia (eg, difficulty performing learned motor tasks)
  • Lack of insight regarding deficits
  • Noncognitive neurologic deficits (eg, pyramidal & extrapyramidal motor, myoclonus, seizures)
  • Urinary incontinence

Alzheimer disease risk factors

Modifiable risk factors

Genetic risk factors

  • Cerebrovascular disease
  • Obesity
  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus

directTables: Cognitive impairment in elderly patients

Cognitive impairment in elderly patients

Normal aging

  • Slight decrease in fluid intelligence (ability to process new information quickly)
  • Normal functioning in all activities of daily living

Mild neurocognitive disorder
(mild cognitive impairment)

  • Mild decline in ≥1 cognitive domains
  • Normal functioning in all activities of daily living with compensation

Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)

  • Significant decline in ≥1 cognitive domains
  • Irreversible global cognitive impairment
  • Marked functional impairment
  • Chronic & progressive, months to years

Major depression

  • Reversible mild-moderate cognitive impairment 
  • Features of depression (mood, interest, energy)
  • Episodic, weeks to months

findings

  • Anterograde memory loss (ie, immediate recall affected, distant memories preserved)
  • Visuospatial deficits (eg, lost in own neighborhood)
  • Language difficulties (eg, difficulty finding words)
  • Cognitive impairment with progressive decline

Late
findings

  • Neuropsychiatric (eg, hallucinations, wandering)
  • Dyspraxia (eg, difficulty performing learned motor tasks)
  • Lack of insight regarding deficits
  • Noncognitive neurologic deficits (eg, pyramidal & extrapyramidal motor, myoclonus, seizures)
  • Urinary incontinence
