subs.title: Frontotemporal dementia
subs.subject: path
tables: Comparison of frontotemporal dementia & Alzheimer disease

Comparison of frontotemporal dementia & Alzheimer disease

Criteria

Frontotemporal dementia

Alzheimer disease

Macroscopic examination

  • Pronounced atrophy of frontal & temporal lobes
  • Mild-to-moderate generalized brain atrophy

Onset

  • Early (50s & 60s)
  • 60s & 70s or older

Microscopic features

  • Initial neuronal loss in the frontotemporal lobes
  • Tau protein inclusions (eg, neurofibrillary tangles, Pick bodies)
  • TDP-43 protein inclusions
  • Initial neuronal loss in parietal & temporal lobes
  • Neurofibrillary tangles with tau protein
  • Amyloid plaques

Initial symptoms

  • Personality & behavioral changes (eg, apathy, socially inappropriate behavior)
  • Prominent memory impairment

Genetic basis

  • Autosomal dominant inheritance in 20%-40% of cases
  • Chromosome 21 (APP gene)
  • Apolipoprotein E4

TDP-43 = transactive response DNA-binding protein 43.
Frontotemporal dementia

Frontotemporal dementia

Pathogenesis

  • TDP-43 mutation
  • Tau protein inclusions (eg, Pick bodies)

Clinical features

  • Early onset (age 50s-60s)
  • Behavior &/or personality changes
    • Disinhibition
    • Apathy
    • Loss of empathy
    • Compulsions or rituals
    • Hyperorality
    • Executive dysfunction

Diagnosis

  • Primarily clinical
  • Neuroimaging (CT scan, MRI)
    • Asymmetric frontal/anterior temporal lobe atrophy
    • Functional imaging (eg, FDG-PET) may show hypometabolism

Management

  • Nonpharmacologic: behavior modification
  • Pharmacologic (symptomatic): SSRI, atypical antipsychotic agent

Prognosis

  • Progressive course; survival 8-10 years

FDG-PET = fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; TDP-43 = 43 kD transactive response (TAR) DNA-binding protein.

subs.title: Dementia with Lewy bodies
subs.subject: path
images: Parkinson disease vs dementia with Lewy bodies
tables: Diagnostic features of dementia with Lewy bodies

Diagnostic features of dementia with Lewy bodies

Central (required)

  • Progressive cognitive decline, dementia

Core

  • Fluctuating cognition
  • Visual hallucinations (detailed, recurrent)
  • Spontaneous parkinsonism features
  • REM sleep behavior disorder (eg, dream enactment)

Suggestive

  • Severe antipsychotic sensitivity
  • SPECT or PET showing low dopamine transporter uptake in basal ganglia

Supportive

  • Repeated falls
  • Syncope or near-syncope
  • Severe autonomic dysfunction
  • Delusions
  • Depression or anxiety

Conflicting
(make DLB less likely)

  • Neuroimaging showing cerebrovascular disease
  • Parkinsonism appearing first, with dementia later

DLB = dementia with Lewy bodies; PET = positron emission tomography; SPECT = single-photon emission computed tomography.
Dementia with Lewy bodies

Dementia with Lewy bodies

Clinical features

  • Visual hallucinations
  • Parkinsonism (eg, tremors, rigidity)
  • Cognitive impairment

Treatment

  • Cognition: cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Parkinsonism: carbidopa-levodopa
  • Hallucinations: 2nd-generation antipsychotic
Parkinson disease vs dementia with Lewy bodies

Parkinson disease vs dementia with Lewy bodies

Parkinson disease

DLB

Dementia

  • Late: >1 year after parkinsonism onset
  • Eventually develops in most patients (>10 years)
  • Early: <1 year of parkinsonism onset
  • Essential to diagnosis

Parkinsonism*

  • Prominent, typically asymmetric
  • 100% at dementia diagnosis
  • Usually mild (<50% at diagnosis), more symmetric

Visual
hallucinations

  • Usually mild in untreated disease
  • Often late sign, worsen with dopaminergic drugs
  • Usually well-formed & detailed
  • Prominent early sign

*Bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity & postural instability.

DLB = dementia with Lewy bodies.

subs.title: Vascular dementia
subs.subject: path
tables: Vascular dementia

Vascular dementia

Pathophysiology

Ischemia and/or infarcts due to:

  • Large-vessel atherosclerosis
  • Small-vessel disease (eg, arteriolosclerosis)
  • Cerebral amyloid angiopathy

Clinical
manifestations

  • Early, prominent executive dysfunction
  • Subtypes:
    • Multi-infarct: often with stepwise decline
    • Strategic infarct: associated with localizing cortical deficits
    • Subcortical vascular encephalopathy: associated with subcortical signs (eg, urinary incontinence, gait disturbances)

Imaging
findings

  • Cortical infarcts
  • Subcortical lacunar infarcts
  • White matter hyperintensities

Treatment

  • Risk factor modification (eg, hypertension, diabetes)
  • ± Antiplatelet therapy
  • Cholinesterase inhibitor

subs.title: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
subs.subject: path
tables: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

Clinical features

  • Rapidly progressive dementia
  • Myoclonus (provoked by startle)
  • Cerebellar signs (eg, ataxia)
  • Upper motor neuron signs (eg, hyperreflexia)
  • Extrapyramidal signs (eg, hypokinesia)
  • Mood &/or sleep disturbances

Findings

  • MRI: widespread atrophy (cerebrum & cerebellum), cortical enhancement (ie, cortical ribboning), enhancement of putamen & caudate head (hockey stick sign)
  • CSF: normal routine analysis, positive 14-3-3 protein titers, positive RT-QuIC test
  • EEG: sharp, triphasic, synchronous discharges
  • Neuropath: spongiform degeneration without inflammation

Management & prognosis

  • Symptomatic treatment, counseling, social services referral
  • No effective disease-modifying therapy, fatal in <12 months

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid; EEG = electroencephalography; RT-QuIC = real-time quaking-induced conversion.

topics.title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
topics.subject: path
directImages: Evaluation of suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension
images: Evaluation of suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension
directTables: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension

Risk factors

  • Women of childbearing age
  • Recent weight gain/obesity
  • Medications (eg, retinoids/vitamin A, tetracyclines, growth hormone)

Pathophysiology

  • Impaired CSF resorption & intracranial venous hypertension

Clinical
features

  • Headache/nausea/vomiting
  • Visual changes (transient obscurations; vision loss; diplopia due to abducens nerve [CN VI] palsy)
  • Pulsatile tinnitus
  • Retrobulbar pain/neck pain/back pain

Diagnosis

  • Papilledema & enlarged blind spots
  • MRI to rule out mass lesions/hydrocephalus
  • MR venography to rule out venous thrombosis
  • Lumbar puncture: elevated opening pressure

Treatment

  • Weight loss, including bariatric surgery
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (acetazolamide, topiramate)

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid.

topics.title: Multiple sclerosis
topics.subject: path
directTables: Multiple sclerosis

Multiple sclerosis

Common presenting symptoms

  • Sensory disturbances, motor weakness, bowel/bladder dysfunction
  • Ocular manifestations:  optic neuritis (painful eye movement), internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction on lateral gaze)
  • Lhermitte sign:  electrical sensation in limbs or back
  • Uhthoff phenomenon:  symptom worsening with increased body temperature

Risk factors

  • Female, HLA-DRB1
  • Environmental factors (United States, Europe, Australia)
  • Low vitamin D levels
  • Epstein-Barr infection

Diagnosis

  • Episodic/progressive symptoms disseminated over time & space
  • Hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted MRI
  • Oligoclonal IgG bands on cerebrospinal fluid analysis

subs.title: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
subs.subject: path
tables: Guillain-Barré syndrome

Guillain-Barré syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • Immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy
  • Preceding gastrointestinal (Campylobacter) or respiratory infection

Clinical features

  • Paresthesia, neuropathic pain
  • Symmetric, ascending weakness
  • Decreased/absent deep tendon reflexes
  • Autonomic dysfunction (eg, arrhythmia, ileus)
  • Respiratory compromise

Diagnosis

  • Clinical
  • Supportive findings
    • Cerebrospinal fluid: ↑ protein, normal leukocytes
    • Abnormal electromyography & nerve conduction
    • MRI: normal or enhancement of anterior nerve roots/cauda equina

Management

  • Monitoring of autonomic & respiratory function
  • Intravenous immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis

subs.title: Peripheral neuropathy
subs.subject: path
tables: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy

Distal symmetric polyneuropathy

Triggers

  • Diabetes mellitus (diabetic neuropathy)
  • Long-standing HIV infection
  • Uremia
  • Medications (eg, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole)
  • Chemotherapy (eg, cisplatin, paclitaxel)
  • Toxicity (eg, alcohol abuse, heavy metal exposure)

Pathophysiology

  • Damage to distal sensory peripheral nerve axons

Manifestations

  • Symptoms begin in toes/feet, progress proximally over time
  • Distal numbness, tingling, pins & needles sensation
  • ↓ Pain, temperature, touch & vibration sensation
  • ↓ Ankle/Babinski reflexes

Treatment

  • Treat underlying cause
  • Pain management: gabapentinoid, tricyclic antidepressant, duloxetine &/or capsaicin cream

Sturge-Weber syndrome

Pathophysiology

  • Mutation in GNAQ gene

Clinical features

  • Port-wine stain (trigeminal nerve [CN V1/V2] distribution)
  • Leptomeningeal capillary-venous malformation
  • Seizures ± hemiparesis
  • Intellectual disability
  • Visual field defects
  • Glaucoma

Diagnosis

  • MRI of the brain with contrast

Management

  • Laser therapy
  • Antiepileptic drugs
  • Intraocular pressure reduction

subs.title: Tuberous sclerosis complex
subs.subject: path
tables: Tuberous sclerosis complex

Tuberous sclerosis complex

Pathophysiology

  • Mutation (inherited or de novo) in TSC1 or TSC2 gene
  • Autosomal dominant

Clinical features

  • Dermatologic
    • Ash-leaf spots
    • Angiofibromas of the malar region
    • Shagreen patches
  • Neurologic
    • CNS lesions (eg, subependymal tumors)
    • Epilepsy (eg, infantile spasms)
    • Intellectual disability
    • Autism & behavioral disorders (eg, hyperactivity)
  • Cardiovascular: rhabdomyomas
  • Renal: angiomyolipomas

Surveillance

  • Tumor screening
    • Regular skin & eye examinations
    • Serial MRI of the brain & kidney
    • Baseline echocardiography & serial ECG
  • Baseline electroencephalography
  • Neuropsychiatric screening

Epidemiology

  • Autosomal dominantNF1 mutation
 

Manifestations

tables: related schwannomatosis*

NF2-related schwannomatosis*

Genetics

  • Autosomal dominant
  • NF2 gene on chromosome 22 encoding merlin (tumor suppressor)
  • Variable expressivity, usually at age 20-30

Clinical
manifestations

  • Bilateral vestibular schwannomas
  • Intracranial meningiomas
  • Spinal tumors (eg, schwannomas, ependymomas)
  • Cataracts
  • Cutaneous tumors or skin plaques

Tumor
surveillance

  • Audiography
  • Ophthalmologic evaluation
  • MRI of the brain & spine

*Previously known as neurofibromatosis type 2.

tables: Von Hippel-Lindau disease

Von Hippel-Lindau disease

Etiology

  • Mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3
  • Autosomal dominant inheritance

Manifestations

  • Cerebellar & retinal hemangioblastomas
  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell subtype)

Management

  • Surveillance for associated malignancies
    • Eye/retinal examination
    • Plasma or urine metanephrines
    • MRI of the brain & spine
    • MRI of the abdomen
  • Tumor resection

subs.title: Pituitary adenoma

tables: Complications of prolactinoma

Complications of prolactinoma

Hyperprolactinemia  

  • Premenopausal women: galactorrhea, estrogen deficiency (oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, decreased bone density, vaginal atrophy)
  • Men: infertility, decreased libido, impotence
  • Children/adolescents: delayed puberty, growth impairment

subs.title: Medulloblastoma
subs.subject: path
tables: Medulloblastoma

Medulloblastoma

Epidemiology

  • Most common malignant pediatric brain tumor
  • Posterior fossa tumor
    • Originates in cerebellum
    • Often compresses fourth ventricle

Clinical features

  • Cerebellar dysfunction
    • Truncal/gait ataxia (cerebellar vermis)
    • Dysmetria, intention tremor (cerebellar hemispheres)
  • Obstructive hydrocephalus (↑ ICP)
    • Headache, vomiting
    • Papilledema
    • Abducens nerve palsy

Treatment

  • Resection, craniospinal radiation, chemotherapy

ICP = intracranial pressure.

subs.title: Craniopharyngioma
subs.subject: path
tables: Craniopharyngioma

Craniopharyngioma

Epidemiology

  • Benign, slow growing
  • Derived from remnants of Rathke pouch
  • Bimodal age distribution (age 5-14 & 50-75)

Clinical features

  • Optic chiasm compression → bitemporal hemianopsia
  • Pituitary stalk compression → endocrinopathies
    • Growth failure in children (↓ TSH or ↓ GH)
    • Pubertal delay in children or sexual dysfunction in adults (↓ LH & FSH)
    • Diabetes insipidus (↓ ADH)

Diagnosis

  • MRI/CT scan: calcified &/or cystic suprasellar mass

Treatment

  • Surgical resection ± radiation therapy

ADH = antidiuretic hormone; GH = growth hormone.

directTables: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs

Upper vs lower motor neuron signs

UMN signs*

  • Spasticity (eg, ↑ tone, clasp-knife rigidity)
  • Hyperreflexia; pathologic reflexes (eg, Babinski, Hoffman)
  • Pseudobulbar affect (eg, inappropriate crying or laughing)

LMN signs**

  • Weakness (eg, flaccidity, ↓ tone)
  • Atrophy (amyotrophy)
  • Fasciculations (often with associated cramping)

*From loss of descending inhibition to anterior horn cells.

**From denervation.

LMN = lower motor neuron; UMN = upper motor neuron.

subs.title: Spinal muscular atrophy
subs.subject: path
tables: Spinal muscular atrophy

Spinal muscular atrophy

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal recessive deletion in SMN1 gene → deficiency of SMN protein
  • Degeneration of motor neurons (anterior horn cells & lower brainstem nuclei) → progressive muscle atrophy

Variants

  • Onset, severity, & presenting symptoms vary
    • Severe (infantile, most common): diffuse, flaccid paralysis
    • Moderate (toddler): delay/loss of motor skills
    • Mild (adolescent): symmetric proximal weakness (legs >arms)

Examination findings

  • Lower motor neuron signs (eg, hypotonia, hyporeflexia, weakness)
  • Tongue fasciculations

Diagnosis

  • SMN1 gene analysis
SMN = survival motor neuron.

subs.title: Tabes dorsalis
subs.subject: path
tables: Tabes dorsalis

Tabes dorsalis

Epidemiology

  • Years → decades after initial infection
  • Increased incidence/more rapid progression in those with HIV

Pathogenesis

  • Treponema pallidum directly damages dorsal sensory roots
  • Secondary degeneration of the dorsal columns

Clinical findings

  • Sensory ataxia
  • Lancinating pains
  • Neurogenic urinary incontinence
  • Associated with Argyll Robertson pupils

Treatment

  • 10-14 days of intravenous penicillin G

Blood supply of the spinal cord
directTables: Spinal cord compression

Spinal cord compression

Causes

  • Mechanical (eg, disc herniation, spinal stenosis)
  • Malignancy (eg, lung, breast, prostate cancers)
  • Infection (eg, epidural abscess)

Symptoms

  • Gradually worsening, severe back pain
  • Pain worse in recumbent position/at night

Physical examination

  • Early signs
    • Symmetric extremity weakness
    • ↓ Deep tendon reflexes
  • Late signs
    • ↓ Rectal tone
    • ↑ Deep tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski reflex
    • Paralysis

Management

  • Emergency MRI of the spine
  • Emergency surgical ± radiation oncology consultation
  • Intravenous glucocorticoids (eg, malignancy) or antibiotics (eg, infection)

subs.title: Friedreich ataxia
subs.subject: path
tables: Friedreich ataxia

Friedreich ataxia

Genetics

  • Autosomal recessive
  • Loss-of-function, trinucleotide repeat (GAA) in frataxin gene

Clinical features

  • Neurologic deficits
    • Cerebellar ataxia
    • Dysarthria
    • Loss of vibration and/or position sense
    • Absent deep tendon reflexes
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
  • Skeletal deformities (eg, scoliosis)
  • Diabetes mellitus

Prognosis

  • Mean survival age 30-40
  • Mortality due to cardiac dysfunction (eg, arrhythmia, congestive heart failure)

Cerebral palsy

Risk factors

  • Low birth weight

  • Permanent, nonprogressive deficits

topics.title: Common cranial nerve lesions
topics.subject: path
directTables: Cranial nerve lesions

Cranial nerve lesions

I (Olfactory)

  • Anosmia (loss of smell)

II (Optic)

  • Monocular blindness
  • Loss of pupillary reflex (afferent limb)

III (Oculomotor)

  • Diplopia, down & out eye deviation, ptosis
  • Mydriasis, loss of pupillary reflex (efferent limb)

IV (Trochlear)

  • Eye extorsion with head tilt to compensate
  • Vertical diplopia

V (Trigeminal)

  • Facial hemianesthesia, loss of corneal reflex (afferent limb)
  • Weakness of mastication muscles
  • Jaw deviation toward the side of lesion (unopposed action of opposite pterygoid)

VI (Abducens)

  • Horizontal diplopia with impaired eye abduction

VII (Facial)

  • Facial paralysis (nasolabial flattening, impaired eyelid closure)
  • Loss of taste in anterior two-thirds of tongue
  • Hyperacusis (stapedius paralysis),
  • Loss of corneal reflex (efferent limb)

VIII (Vestibulocochlear)

  • Sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo

IX (Glossopharyngeal)

  • Loss of sensation & taste in posterior one-third of tongue
  • Loss of gag reflex (afferent limb)

X (Vagus)

  • Dysphagia, hoarseness, impaired cough reflex
  • Loss of gag reflex (efferent limb)

XI (Accessory)

  • Impaired shoulder shrug (trapezius paralysis)
  • Impaired head turning (sternocleidomastoid paralysis)

XII (Hypoglossal)

  • Tongue weakness with deviation toward the side of lesion

topics.title: Otitis externa
topics.subject: oto
directTables: Otitis externa

Otitis externa

Risk factors

  • Water exposure
  • Trauma (eg, cotton swabs, ear candling)
  • Foreign material (eg, hearing aid, headphones)
  • Dermatologic conditions (eg, eczema, contact dermatitis)

Microbiology

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Staphylococcus aureus

Clinical
manifestations

  • Otalgia, pruritus, discharge, hearing loss
  • Pain with auricle manipulation
  • Ear canal erythema, edema, debris
  • Tympanic membrane spared (clear, not inflamed, no middle ear fluid)

Treatment

  • Remove debris
  • Topical antibiotic (eg, fluoroquinolone)
  • ± Topical glucocorticoid
  • Consider wick placement to facilitate medication delivery
Acute otitis externa

Acute otitis externa

Severity

Clinical features

Treatment

Mild*

  • Minor discomfort & pruritus
  • Minimal canal edema
  • Topical acidifying solution (eg, acetic acid)
 

Moderate/severe*

  
  • Moderate pain & pruritus
  • Partial or complete occlusion from edema
  • Clean the ear canal with wire loop
  • Topical antibiotics
    • Polymyxin B/neomycin
    • Colistin/neomycin
    • Fluoroquinolones (eg, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin)
  • Wick placement if canal is completely occluded
 

Invasive otitis (malignant otitis externa)

  • Risk factors: Diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression
  • Intense pain
  • Complete canal occlusion from edema
  • Periauricular erythema, lymphadenopathy & fever
  
  • Broad-spectrum systemic antibiotics (eg, ciprofloxacin)
  • ± Debridement

*Consider adding topical glucocorticoid (eg, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone) if significant pain or itching is present.
Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa

Necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa

Pathophysiology

  • Life-threatening infectious complication of acute otitis externa
  • Aggressive spread beyond external ear canal into skull base & adjacent tissues

Risk factors

  • Older age (>60)
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Ear irrigation (cerumen removal)

Microbiology

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Clinical features

  • Severe, unremitting ear pain (worse at night & with chewing)
  • Purulent otorrhea
  • Granulation tissue along floor of ear canal
  • ± Cranial nerve palsy (eg, facial droop from CN VII involvement)
  • Elevated ESR

Treatment

  • IV antipseudomonal antibiotic (eg, ciprofloxacin)

CN VII = facial nerve; ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate; IV = intravenous.

directTables: Acute otitis media

Acute otitis media

Microbiology

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae
  • Moraxellacatarrhalis

Clinical features

  • Ear pain ± fever
  • Otoscopy:
    • Bulging TM
      AND/OR
    • Middle ear effusion (eg, air-fluid level, impaired mobility) plus TM erythema

Treatment*

  • 1st-line: amoxicillin
  • 2nd-line: amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Penicillin-allergic: azithromycin or clindamycin

Complications

  • TM perforation
  • Conductive hearing loss
  • Local extension (eg, mastoiditis, meningitis, brain abscess)

*Observation can be considered for children age >6 months with unilateral disease, no/mild pain, and low-grade fever (<39 C [102.2 F]).

TM = tympanic membrane.
Mastoiditis

Mastoiditis

Pathophysiology

  • Infection of the mastoid air cells
  • Complication of acute otitis media
  • Most commonly due to Streptococcus pneumoniae

Clinical findings

  • Fever & otalgia
  • Inflammation of mastoid
  • Protrusion of the auricle
  • Opacification of mastoid air cells on CT scan or MRI

Management

  • Intravenous antibiotics
  • Drainage of purulent material (eg, tympanostomy, mastoidectomy)

Complications

  • Extracranial extension (subperiosteal abscess, facial nerve palsy, hearing loss, labyrinthitis)
  • Intracranial extension (brain abscess, meningitis)
Chronic suppurative otitis media

Chronic suppurative otitis media

Microbiology

  • Often polymicrobial
  • Staphylococcus aureus & Pseudomonas aeruginosa most common

Clinical features

  • Chronic (>6 weeks) otorrhea
  • ± Hearing loss

Examination

  • TM perforation with purulent middle ear drainage
  • Normal-appearing external auditory canal

Management

  • Otic fluoroquinolone drops (eg, ofloxacin)

Complications

  • Infectious spread (eg, mastoiditis, brain abscess)
  • Permanent hearing loss

TM = tympanic membrane.

  • Moraxellacatarrhalis

Clinical features

  • Ear pain ± fever
  • Otoscopy:
    • Bulging TM
      AND/OR
    • Middle ear effusion (eg, air-fluid level, impaired mobility) plus TM erythema

Treatment*

  • 1st-line: amoxicillin
  • 2nd-line: amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Penicillin-allergic: azithromycin or clindamycin

Complications

  • TM perforation
  • Conductive hearing loss
  • Local extension (eg, mastoiditis, meningitis, brain abscess)

*Observation can be considered for children age >6 months with unilateral disease, no/mild pain, and low-grade fever (<39 C [102.2 F]).

TM = tympanic membrane.
Mastoiditis

Mastoiditis

Pathophysiology

  • Infection of the mastoid air cells
  • Complication of acute otitis media
  • Most commonly due to Streptococcus pneumoniae

Clinical findings

  • Fever & otalgia
  • Inflammation of mastoid
  • Protrusion of the auricle
  • Opacification of mastoid air cells on CT scan or MRI

Management

  • Intravenous antibiotics
  • Drainage of purulent material (eg, tympanostomy, mastoidectomy)

Complications

  • Extracranial extension (subperiosteal abscess, facial nerve palsy, hearing loss, labyrinthitis)
  • Intracranial extension (brain abscess, meningitis)
Chronic suppurative otitis media

Chronic suppurative otitis media

Microbiology

  • Often polymicrobial
  • Staphylococcus aureus & Pseudomonas aeruginosa most common

Clinical features

  • Chronic (>6 weeks) otorrhea
  • ± Hearing loss

Examination

  • TM perforation with purulent middle ear drainage
  • Normal-appearing external auditory canal

Management

  • Otic fluoroquinolone drops (eg, ofloxacin)

Complications

  • Infectious spread (eg, mastoiditis, brain abscess)
  • Permanent hearing loss

TM = tympanic membrane.

tables: Presbycusis (age-related hearing loss)

Presbycusis (age-related hearing loss)

Etiology

  • Increasing incidence with age >60
  • Cochlear hair cell loss
  • Degeneration of spiral ganglion cells in the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)

Clinical features

  • Insidious, progressive, symmetric SNHL impacting high frequencies first
  • Difficulty hearing with background noise
  • Impaired speech discrimination
  • Tinnitus (nonpulsatile)
  • Can lead to social isolation &/or depression

Work-up

  • Bedside screening hearing tests (eg, finger rub, whisper, tuning fork)
  • Formal audiometry

Treatment

  • Hearing aids (amplification)
  • Education of patient & family

SNHL = sensorineural hearing loss.

directTables: Otosclerosis

Otosclerosis

Epidemiology

  • Younger (early- to mid-30s) White patients
  • More common in women
  • Autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance

Pathophysiology

  • Imbalance of bone resorption & deposition → stiffening of stapes

Clinical manifestations

  • Progressive conductive hearing loss
  • Paradoxic improvement in speech discrimination in noisy environments
  • ± Reddish hue behind tympanic membrane

Management

  • Amplification (eg, hearing aids)
  • Surgery (eg, stapes reconstruction)

Peripheral vertigo

Central vertigo

Etiologies

  • BPPV
  • Ménière disease
  • Vestibular neuritis
  • Stroke (eg, cerebellar)
  • Multiple sclerosis
  • Migraine

Nystagmus
characteristics

  • Never purely vertical
  • Inhibited by fixation of gaze
  • Fatigable (<1-min duration)
  • Latency period (2-40 sec)
  • May have any trajectory
  • Not inhibited by fixation of gaze
  • Not fatigable (>1-min duration)
  • No latency period

Other possible
neurologic signs

  • Hearing loss/tinnitus may be present
  • Walking usually preserved
  • No other CNS symptoms
  • Hearing loss/tinnitus absent
  • Severe postural instability
  • Other CNS symptoms (eg, headache, diplopia, weakness/numbness of face or limbs, dysarthria) often present

BPPV = benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
Common causes of vertigo

Common causes of vertigo

Ménière disease

  • Recurrent episodes lasting 20 minutes to several hours
  • Sensorineural hearing loss
  • Tinnitus &/or feeling of fullness in the ear

BPPV

  • Brief episodes triggered by head movement
  • Dix-Hallpike maneuver causes nystagmus

Vestibular neuritis

  • Acute, single episode that can last days
  • Often follows viral syndrome
  • Abnormal head thrust test

Migraine

  • Vertigo associated with headache or other migrainous phenomenon (eg, visual aura)
  • Symptoms resolve completely between episodes

Brainstem/
cerebellar stroke

  • Sudden-onset, persistent vertigo
  • Usually other neurologic symptoms

Dizziness type by symptoms

Dizziness type by symptoms

Category

Description

Potential causes

Vertigo

● Sense of motion (eg, "spinning," "whirling," "tilting")
● Worse with head movement
● Associated nausea & vomiting

● Peripheral (eg, BPPV, Ménière disease, vestibular neuritis)
● Central (eg, posterior circulation stroke or hemorrhage, migraine, MS)

Presyncope

● Lightheadedness (eg, "almost fainted," "nearly blacked out")
● Triggered by standing or exertion
● Associated diaphoresis, warmth

● Orthostatic (eg, hypovolemia, autonomic dysfunction)
● Cardiac (eg, dysrhythmia, valvular disease)
● Reflex (eg, vasovagal, situational)

Disequilibrium

● Imbalance (eg, "unsteady")
● Worse with walking or standing
● Associated falls without vertigo or presyncope

● Sensory input (eg, visual impairment, polyneuropathy, cervical spondylosis)
● Motor output (eg, Parkinson disease, MS, cerebellar disorder)

Nonspecific

● Vague symptom (eg, "giddiness," "floating") not fitting another description
● Associated psychiatric condition, polypharmacy, recreational drugs

● Psychiatric (eg, anxiety, depression, panic disorder)
● Other (eg, hyperventilation, medications, substance use disorder)

BPPV = benign paroxysmal positional vertigo; MS = multiple sclerosis.
Peripheral vs central vertigo

Peripheral vs central vertigo

Peripheral (labyrinth or CN VIII)

Central (cerebellum or brainstem)

CNS deficits

● Absent

● Common (eg, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia)

Auditory signs

● Common (↓ hearing &/or tinnitus)

● Absent

Imbalance

● One direction (sways toward lesion)

● Severe instability (often unable to walk)

Nystagmus

● One direction (never pure vertical)
● Same direction in all gazes
● Suppressed by visual fixation

● Any direction (pure vertical = central)
● May change direction with gaze
● Unsuppressed by visual fixation

Causes

● BPPV
● Ménière disease
● Vestibular neuritis (labyrinthitis)

● Vestibular migraine
● Multiple sclerosis
● Stroke or hemorrhage (eg, cerebellar)

BPPV = benign paroxysmal positional vertigo; CN = cranial nerve.
HINTS examination to distinguish peripheral from central vertigo*

HINTS examination to distinguish peripheral from central vertigo*

Peripheral
(vestibular nerve or labyrinth)

Central
(cerebellum or brainstem)

Head Impulse test
(rapid head movement
to each side)

●  Abnormal VOR: eyes dragged off
      target, followed by a corrective saccade
●  Peripheral structures trigger the VOR

●  Normal VOR:  eyes stay on target
●  Cerebellum is not involved in the
      VOR

Nystagmus
(observe in all gazes)

●  Unidirectional
●  Peripheral lesions cause unilateral
      imbalance of tonic vestibular inputs

●  Changes direction with gaze
●  Cerebellar and brainstem lesions
      can affect gaze-holding pathways

Test of Skew
(cover and uncover
each eye)

●  No vertical shift when eye uncovered
●  Peripheral lesions do not typically affect
      vertical eye alignment

●  Vertical shift when eye uncovered
●  Brainstem lesions can affect
      vertical eye alignment pathways

*Sustained vertigo with nystagmus must be present (ie, not useful for episodic vertigo).
 VOR = vestibulo-ocular reflex.

directTables: Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis

Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis

Transmission

  • Contact with infected genital secretions during delivery

Clinical presentation

  • Copious exudate & eyelid swelling (typically age 2-5 days)

Complications

  • Corneal ulceration & scarring → vision loss

Diagnosis

  • Nucleic acid amplification testing
  • Gram stain (gram-negative intracellular diplococci) & culture (Thayer-Martin medium)

Treatment

  • IM third-generation cephalosporin (eg, cefotaxime)

Prevention

  • Maternal screening (age <25 or with risk factors) & treatment
  • Ophthalmic erythromycin ointment at birth
IM = intramuscular.

Onset age

Findings

<24 hr

  • Uncommon adverse effect of topical medication (eg, erythromycin)

  • Marked conjunctival injection & eyelid edema

Cataracts

Pathogenesis

  • Oxidative damage & opacification of the lens

Risk factors

  • Age >60
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Chronic sunlight exposure
  • Tobacco use
  • Immunosuppression (eg, HIV, corticosteroids)

Clinical features

  • Loss of red reflex
  • Opacified lens

Treatment

  • Artificial lens implantation

tables: Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis)

Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis)

Pathogenesis

  • Detachment of lens from ciliary body
  • Blunt ocular trauma (forceful projectile)
  • Genetic condition (eg, Marfan syndrome)

Clinical features

  • Painless vision loss
  • Tremulous iris with eye movement
  • Lens displacement on slitlamp examination

Management

  • Glasses to correct refractive error
  • Surgical correction
  • Assessment for underlying condition if trauma is mild or absent

topics.title: Glaucoma
topics.subject: eye
directTables: Glaucoma in children

Glaucoma in children

Pathophysiology

  • Optic neuropathy ± ↑ IOP
  • Causes:
    • Impaired drainage of intraocular fluid
    • Primary anatomic abnormality (eg, angle dysgenesis)
    • Sturge-Weber syndrome
    • Tumor, trauma, infection involving the angle
    • Corticosteroid-induced

Key features

  • Tearing, photophobia, blepharospasm
  • Enlarged cornea and/or globe
  • Optic nerve cupping
  • Tonometry: ↑ IOP

Management

  • Surgery
  • ± Pressure-reducing eye drops  

IOP = intraocular pressure.

subs.title: Age-related macular degeneration
subs.subject: eye
images: Central vision loss in late-stage macular degeneration (AMD)
tables: Age-related macular degeneration

Age-related macular degeneration

Risk factors

  • Advancing age (exponentially after age 60)
  • Smoking

Clinical features

  • Gradual central vision loss
  • Impaired dark adaptation
  • May have acute-on-chronic vision loss*

Examination findings

Dry AMD

  • Drusen clustered around the macula
  • Retinal atrophy

Progression to wet AMD

  • Neovascularization
  • Subretinal fluid &/or hemorrhage

Treatment

  • Smoking cessation
  • Antioxidant supplement (vitamins C & E, zinc, copper, lutein)
  • Anti-VEGF intravitreal injections
  • ± Laser photocoagulation of neovascularization

*Due to subretinal fluid accumulation &/or hemorrhage.

AMD = age-related macular degeneration; VEGF = vascular endothelial growth factor.

subs.title: Diabetic retinopathy
subs.subject: eye
images: Vitreous hemorrhage in proliferative diabetic retinopathy
tables: Common ocular complications of diabetes mellitus

Common ocular complications of diabetes mellitus

Refractive
changes

  • Hyperglycemia, blurred vision
  • Acute myopia & ↓ acuity; no other examination findings

Cataract

  • Blurred vision, ↓ acuity, ↑ glare
  • Lens opacity, ↓ red reflex, ↓ fundus detail

Glaucoma

  • Open-angle: painless peripheral vision loss; ↑ IOP
  • Angle-closure: conjunctival redness, corneal edema, middilated pupil, ↑ IOP

Diabetic
retinopathy &
complications

  • Nonproliferative: cotton-wool spot, retinal hemorrhage, microaneurysm
  • Proliferative: neovascularization arising from the disc or retinal vessels
  • Macular edema: thickening/edema of macular retina
  • Vitreous hemorrhage: vitreous blood obscuring fundus
  • Tractional retinal detachment: detachment with fibrovascular bands & no tears

IOP = intraocular pressure.
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy

Clinical presentation

  • Decreased or fluctuating vision; sudden vision loss
  • Floaters (vitreous hemorrhage) or scotomas (blind spots)

Funduscopic findings

  • Neovascularization
  • Vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage
  • Fibrous tissue formation
  • Retinal ischemia

Management

  • Glucose optimization
  • Pars plana vitrectomy for nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment
  • Panretinal photocoagulation or anti-VEGF (ie, ranibizumab) injections to treat neovascularization

VEGF = vascular endothelial growth factor.

subs.title: Retinal artery occlusion
subs.subject: eye
tables: Amaurosis fugax

Amaurosis fugax

Definition

  • Painless, transient, monocular vision loss
  • "Curtain descending" over visual field

Etiologies

  • Ischemia from carotid artery disease (most common)
  • Giant cell arteritis
  • Retinal vein occlusion
  • Papilledema
Central retinal artery & vein occlusion

Central retinal artery & vein occlusion

Central retinal artery occlusion

Central retinal vein occlusion

Associated conditions

  • Embolism to retinal artery from carotid artery atherosclerosis (most common); giant cell arteritis
  • Mostly nonembolic (thrombosis)

Clinical findings

  • Painless, acute monocular vision loss (can be severe [ie, see only hand motion])
  • Painless (or painful if ischemia), acute or subacute monocular vision loss (cloudy haze)
  • History of amaurosis fugax (transient vision loss); more common in central retinal artery occlusion
  • Relative afferent pupillary defect

Funduscopy

  • Retinal whitening
  • Cherry-red spot (60%-90%)
  • Boxcar appearance of red blood cells
  • Tortuous, dilatedveins
  • Blood-&-thunder appearance due to diffuse hemorrhages
  • Disc swelling
  • Cotton-wool spots

subs.title: Retinitis pigmentosa
subs.subject: eye
tables: Retinitis pigmentosa

Retinitis pigmentosa

Etiology

  • Genetic dystrophy
  • Progressive retinal degeneration (photoreceptors, pigmented epithelium)

Clinical features

  • Loss of rods:
    • Night blindness
    • Peripheral visual field loss
  • Loss of cones:
    • Decreased central visual acuity (late finding)

Funduscopic changes

  • Retinal vessel attenuation (likely due to altered metabolic demand)
  • Optic disc pallor (optic nerve atrophy and gliosis)
  • Pigment accumulation (characteristic bone-spicule pattern around vessels)

subs.title: Retinoblastoma
subs.subject: eye
tables: Retinoblastoma

Retinoblastoma

Etiology

  • Mutation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene

Clinical presentation

  • Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex)
  • Most present prior to age 5 years

Diagnosis

  • Off-white mass seen on dilated funduscopic examination
  • May present with strabismus, nystagmus, or red, inflamed eye
  • Diagnosis confirmed using ultrasonography, CT scan, or MRI

Management

  • Mass removal via radiation, chemotherapy, or enucleation
  • Long-term follow-up due to recurrence and risk for other cancers (eg, osteosarcoma)

topics.title: Uveitis

directTables: Anterior uveitis

Anterior uveitis

Presentation

  • Symptoms: ocular pain, photophobia, decreased acuity
  • Examination: ciliary flush, pupillary constriction, hypopyon

Common causes/
associations

  • Infections: herpesviruses, toxoplasmosis, syphilis
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Spondylarthritis (eg, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis)
  • Inflammatory bowel disease

Evaluation/testing

  • Slit-lamp examination
  • As indicated: HLA-B27, pelvis/spine x-ray, chest x-ray, HIV, syphilis serology

Treatment

  • Dilating eye drops (eg, cyclopentolate)
  • Topical glucocorticoids

HLA-B27 = human leukocyte antigen B27.

topics.title: Strabismus
topics.subject: eye
directTables: Strabismus

Strabismus (ocular misalignment)

Clinical findings

  • Constant eye deviation at any age
  • Intermittent eye deviation at age >4 months
  • Eye deviation on cover test
  • Asymmetric corneal light reflexes
  • Asymmetric intensity of red reflexes
  • Torticollis or head tilt

Treatment

  • Strengthen deviated eye (eg, patch unaffected eye, cycloplegic drops to blur unaffected eye)
  • Correct refractive errors (ie, prescription glasses)
  • Surgery

Complications

  • Amblyopia (reduced visual acuity)
  • Diplopia
Amblyopia

Amblyopia

Definition

  • Functional reduction in visual acuity due to visual disturbances in early childhood
  • Unilateral (most common): ≥2-line difference in best-correct vision between eyes (eg, 20/30 & 20/50)
  • Bilateral: best-corrected vision worse than 20/40 at age ≥4

Etiology

  • Strabismus
  • Uncorrected refractive error
  • Vision deprivation (eg, cataracts, ptosis)

Management

  • Treat underlying condition (eg, corrective lenses for refractive error, surgery for cataract)
  • Encourage use of amblyopic eye (when unilateral)
    • Patching eye with better vision
    • Cycloplegic drops to blur normal eye

Common inflammatory eyelid conditions

Common inflammatory eyelid conditions

Etiology

Clinical findings

Blepharitis

Chalazion

  • Granulomatous reaction to obstructed meibomian gland

Hordeolum

  • External hordeolum (sty): focal infection of Zeis gland

  • Acute inflammation/infection of nasolacrimal sac
  • Painful swelling & redness around medial canthal region ± purulent discharge from punctum

Gabapentin and pregabalin

Common
uses

  • Focal onset seizures (adjunctive)
  • Neuropathic pain (eg, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia)
  • Postherpetic neuralgia
  • Restless legs syndrome
  • Anxiety
  • Alcohol withdrawal

Adverse
effects

  • CNS depression (eg, somnolence, ataxia)
  • Dizziness
  • Peripheral edema
  • Weight gain

Additional
notes

  • Structurally similar to GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter
  • Gabapentin enacarbil (Horizant) is an extended-release prodrug of gabapentin (Neurontin)
  • Lyrica (pregabalin) is more potent than gabapentin
  • Dosage adjustment required for CrCl < 60 mL/min

CNS = central nervous system; GABA = gamma-aminobutyric acid.

subs.title: Valproate
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Valproate

Valproate

Mechanism
 of action

  • Blocks sodium channels & ↑ GABA

Indications

  • Focal or generalized seizures (broad spectrum)
  • Bipolar disorder
  • Migraine prophylaxis

Boxed warnings

  • Hepatic failure
  • Fetal harm (neural tube defects & ↓ cognitive scores)
  • Pancreatitis

Adverse
effects

  • Alopecia
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Weight changes (gain more likely)
  • Nausea & vomiting
  • Hyperammonemia
  • CNS effects (eg, somnolence, dizziness)

Monitoring

  • Therapeutic range: 50–100 mcg/mL (total level)
  • LFTs
  • CBC with differential (especially platelets)

CBC = complete blood count; GABA = gamma-aminobutyric acid; LFTs = liver function tests.

directTables: Duration of action of common benzodiazepines

Duration of action of common benzodiazepines

Short
(half-life <6 hr)

Triazolam, midazolam

Intermediate
(half-life 6-50 hr)

Oxazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, clonazepam

Long
(half-life >50 hr)

Diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, flurazepam
Benzodiazepines

Benzodiazepines

Indications

  • Anxiety
  • Insomnia (short-term)
  • Agitation
  • Alcohol & sedative-hypnotic withdrawal
  • Preoperative sedation
  • Seizures

Adverse effects

  • Daytime sedation
  • Confusion/impaired attention
  • Memory impairment (anterograde amnesia)
  • Ataxia
  • Slowed psychomotor performance
  • Increased risk for falls, motor vehicle collisions & hip fractures in elderly patients
  • Respiratory depression (uncommon unless combined with alcohol)

Withdrawal

  • Tachycardia, ↑ blood pressure, hyperpyrexia
  • Restlessness, anxiety, panic attacks, irritability
  • Insomnia
  • Delirium
  • Tremor
  • Psychosis
  • Seizures, death (rare)

topics.title: Insomnia therapy
topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Nonpharmacological treatment of insomnia

Nonpharmacological treatment of insomnia

Sleep
hygiene

Encourage good sleeping habits

  • Maintain regular sleep schedule, avoid naps
  • Avoid caffeine after lunch
  • Avoid alcohol, smoking, large meals near bedtime
  • Keep bedroom quiet, dark & cool
  • Exercise regularly but not right before bedtime

Stimulus
control

Break link between bedroom & frustration/fear

  • Use bed only for sleep & sexual activity (no reading, television, eating)
  • Go to bed only when sleepy & leave bedroom if unable to sleep

Relaxation

Reduce tension/stress

  • Progressive muscle relaxation (contract & relax muscles in sequence)
  • Relaxation response (abdominal breathing, focus on peaceful image)

Sleep
restriction

Improve sleep efficiency (ratio of time asleep to time in bed)

  • Restrict time in bed to time of actual sleep (based on sleep diary)
  • Increase time in bed as efficiency improves

Cognitive
therapy

Change maladaptive beliefs

  • Manage catastrophic concern about effect of insomnia
  • Provide realistic expectations about the need for sleep
Chronic (≥3 months) insomnia

Chronic (≥3 months) insomnia

Etiologies

Primary
insomnia
(15%)

  • No comorbid psychiatric, medical, or intrinsic sleep conditions
  • Often triggered by stressful life event & perpetuated by conditioning

Secondary
insomnia
(85%)

  • Psychiatric (50%): anxiety, mood & substance use disorders
  • Medical (20%): cardiopulmonary (eg, COPD), neurologic (eg, dementia), medications (eg, corticosteroids)
  • Intrinsic sleep disorders (15%): OSA, RLS, circadian rhythm disorder

Management

  • Treat specific factors for secondary insomnia (eg, nocturnal hypoxemia with COPD)
  • Sleep hygiene (CBTi): most effective for psychiatric disorders & primary insomnia
  • Pharmacotherapy: melatonin- or orexin-based, then step up (eg, BZD as last resort)

BZD = benzodiazepine; CBTi = cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia; COPD = chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; OSA = obstructive sleep apnea; RLS = restless legs syndrome.

tables: Impulse control disorders in Parkinson disease

Impulse control disorders in Parkinson disease

General

  • Aberrant, reward-based, destructive behaviors (eg, pathologic gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping)
  • Primarily seen with dopamine agonists (reduce motor symptoms by D2 receptor stimulation)

Pathophysiology

  • Overstimulation of D3 receptor–mediated reward pathways

Risk factors

  • Dose and duration of treatment
  • Younger age, male sex
  • Comorbid depression and/or anxiety

Management

  • Gradual tapering of dopamine agonist
  • ± Increase levodopa dose to control motor symptoms
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy for persistent symptoms

tables: Drugs used for Alzheimer's disease

Drugs used for Alzheimer's disease

Drug class

Adverse effects

Key points

Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors
(eg, donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine)

  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Diarrhea
  • Titrate slowly (eg, every 6 weeks)
  • Take donepezil at bedtime
  • Bradycardia
  • Donepezil: QT prolongation
  • Use caution with drugs that decrease heart rate (eg, beta-blockers)
  • Insomnia
  • Change donepezil to morning administration

NMDA inhibitor
(eg, memantine)

  • Dizziness, confusion, headache
  • ER capsules can be opened & sprinkled on applesauce
  • Namzaric (donepezil/memantine): only for patients stabilized on donepezil 10 mg daily*

Amyloid beta monoclonal antibodies
(eg, aducanumab, lecanemab)

  • Infusion-related reactions
  • Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA)
  • IV only
  • Role in treatment not yet well defined

*All strengths of Namzaric contain donepezil 10 mg; donepezil requires titration from a starting dose of 5 mg to avoid gastrointestinal adverse effects.

ER = extended release; NMDA = N-methyl-D-aspartate.

topics.title: Malignant hyperthermia
topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Malignant hyperthermia

Malignant hyperthermia

Epidemiology

  • Genetic mutation alters control of intracellular calcium
  • Triggered by volatile anesthetics, succinylcholine, excessive heat

Manifestations

  • Masseter muscle/generalized rigidity
  • Sinus tachycardia
  • Hypercarbia resistant to increased minute ventilation
  • Rhabdomyolysis
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Hyperthermia (late manifestation)

Treatment

  • Respiratory/ventilatory support
  • Immediate cessation of causative anesthetic
  • Dantrolene

topics.title: Opioid analgesics
topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Strategies for safe opioid prescribing

Strategies for safe opioid prescribing

Optimize nonopioid interventions

  • Use acetaminophen/NSAIDs, supportive care (eg, heat/ice) for mild/moderate pain
  • Avoid routine opioid use for chronic pain

Optimize opioid dose and duration

  • Limit therapy to <5 days for acute pain
  • Use lowest dose resulting in adequate pain control
  • Avoid long-acting opioids

Optimize monitoring 

  • Counsel patients on safe use; arrange close follow-up 
  • Educate patients on safe disposal of unused opioids

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Opioid medications in patients with impaired kidney function

Opioid medications in patients with impaired kidney function

Recommended

Avoid

  • Fentanyl
  • Hydromorphone
  • Methadone
  • Buprenorphine
  • Morphine
  • Meperidine
  • Codeine
  • Tramadol

Strategies for safe opioid prescribing

Optimize nonopioid interventions

  • Use acetaminophen/NSAIDs, supportive care (eg, heat/ice) for mild/moderate pain
  • Avoid routine opioid use for chronic pain

Optimize opioid dose and duration

  • Limit therapy to <5 days for acute pain
  • Use lowest dose resulting in adequate pain control
  • Avoid long-acting opioids

Optimize monitoring 

  • Counsel patients on safe use; arrange close follow-up 
  • Educate patients on safe disposal of unused opioids

NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Opioid medications in patients with impaired kidney function

Opioid medications in patients with impaired kidney function

Avoid

  • Fentanyl
  • Hydromorphone
  • Methadone
  • Buprenorphine
  • Morphine
  • Meperidine
  • Codeine
  • Tramadol

topics.title: Ego defenses
topics.subject: psy
directTables: Key defense mechanisms

Key defense mechanisms

Immature

  • Acting out: expressing unacceptable feelings through actions
  • Denial: behaving as if an aspect of reality does not exist
  • Displacement: transferring feelings to less threatening object/person
  • Intellectualization: focusing on nonemotional aspects to avoid distressing feelings
  • Passive aggression: avoiding conflict by expressing hostility covertly
  • Projection: attributing one's own feelings to others
  • Rationalization: justifying behavior to avoid difficult truths
  • Reaction formation: transforming unacceptable feelings/impulses into the opposite
  • Regression: reverting to earlier developmental stage
  • Splitting: experiencing a person/situation as either all positive or all negative

Mature

  • Altruism: deriving pleasure from helping others, often at a personal cost
  • Humor: using humor to deflect anxiety or uncomfortable feelings
  • Sublimation: channeling impulses into socially acceptable behaviors
  • Suppression: putting unwanted feelings aside to cope with reality

tables: Nonaccidental trauma

Nonaccidental trauma

Red flags

  • Injury inconsistent with developmental stage
  • Delay in seeking care
  • Conflicting historical details

Clinical
features

  • Bruises: patterned appearance (eg, belt buckle), occurring in nonmobile child or over noninjury-prone area (eg, ear, trunk)
  • Burns: linear, well demarcated
  • Fractures:
    • Multiple & in various stages of healing
    • Femur fracture in nonambulatory child
    • Posterior rib fractures
    • Metaphyseal corner fractures
  • Head trauma: retinal & subdural hemorrhages

Management

  • Disposition: ensure immediate safety of the child (eg, inpatient management, child protective services)
  • Evaluation: skeletal survey, CT scan of the head, funduscopy

subs.subject: path
tables: Sexual abuse

Sexual abuse

Risk factors

  • Preadolescent girls
  • Unstable familial relationships
  • Perpetrator is often a trusted adult

Clinical features

  • Nonspecific behavioral changes
  • Developmentally inappropriate sexual play
  • Genitourinary concerns
  • Genital trauma
  • Laboratory evidence of STI

Management

  • Notify child protective services
  • STI treatment
  • ± Emergency contraception
  • Mental health referral

STI = sexually transmitted infection.

directTables: Features of possible child abuse

Features of possible child abuse

Risk
factors

Caregiver background

  • Young or single parents
  • Lower education levels
  • Substance use disorder
  • Psychiatric conditions (depression, impulse control disorders)
  • History of childhood abuse

Home environment

  • Unstable family situation (eg, divorce, conflict)
  • Financial difficulties, job loss
  • Lack of social support
  • Domestic violence

Children

  • Physical, intellectual, or emotional disabilities
  • Unplanned pregnancy/unwanted child

Clinical
presentation

  • Unexplained or implausible injuries
  • Injuries in different stages of healing
  • Malnutrition
  • Sudden behavioral or scholastic changes

Management

  • Document objective findings from evaluation
  • Report suspected abuse to child protective services
Medical child abuse

Medical child abuse

When to
suspect

  • Persistent or recurrent unexplainable illness
    • Nonphysiologic symptom clusters
    • Inconclusive diagnostic testing
    • Ineffective medical therapies
  • Reported signs/symptoms incongruous with clinical findings or seen only in presence of specific caregiver
  • Siblings who have died or have unexplained illness
  • Seeking care from multiple facilities or specialists
  • Reluctance to accept less severe diagnosis

Management

  • Report to child protective services
  • Case-specific medical evaluation for child abuse (eg, urine toxicology screen)

Communication
strategies

  • Focus on best interest/safety of child
  • Avoid assigning blame
  • Inform family of legal mandate to report
  • Use direct, honest & specific language (eg, "I suspect abuse")

subs.title: Autism spectrum disorder
subs.subject: path
tables: Autism spectrum disorder

Autism spectrum disorder

Clinical features

  • Social deficits with onset in early development
    • Difficulty sharing emotions or interests
    • Lack of nonverbal communication (eg, eye contact)
    • Difficulty developing/understanding relationships 
  • Restricted, repetitive behaviors & interests
    • Repetitive movements (eg, hand-flapping) or speech
    • Insistence on sameness/routines
    • Intense, fixated interests
    • Adverse responses to sensory input (eg, foods, textures)
  • ± Language delays & cognitive impairment 

Evaluation

  • Comprehensive clinical evaluation
  • Genetic testing (eg, chromosomal microarray, fragile X gene analysis)
  • ± Brain MRI (eg, macrocephaly, neurologic deficits)
   Management 
  • Behavioral, speech, occupational therapies

tables: Common causes of intellectual disability

Common causes of intellectual disability

Syndrome

Dysmorphic features

Comorbid conditions

Down syndrome

  • Upslanting palpebral fissures
  • Flat nasal bridge
  • Epicanthal folds
  • Single palmar crease
  • Heart disease (eg, AV canal defect)
  • Short stature, obesity
  • Hearing loss

Fragile X syndrome

  • Long face with prominent chin & forehead
  • Large, protruding ears
  • Macroorchidism
  • Macrocephaly
  • Self-injurious behavior (eg, hand biting)
  • Anxiety, autistic behaviors
  • Tall stature

Fetal alcohol syndrome

  • Smooth philtrum
  • Thin vermillion border
  • Small palpebral fissures
  • Seizures
  • Growth restriction

Secondary causes of behavioral change in patients with intellectual disability

Gastrointestinal disorders

  • Constipation, gastroesophageal reflux, bowel obstruction

Occult infection

  • Cellulitis, cystitis, otitis media, pneumonia

Unrecognized pain

  • Dental caries, menstrual pain, unreported trauma/fracture

  • Cerumen impaction, visual problems

subs.title: Oppositional defiant disorder
subs.subject: path
tables: Oppositional defiant disorder

Oppositional defiant disorder

Diagnosis

Pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness for ≥6 months

  • Argues with adults, defies authority figures, refuses to follow rules
  • Deliberately annoys others
  • Blames others for own mistakes or misbehavior
  • Easily annoyed, angry, resentful, or vindictive
  • Not due to another mental disorder

Treatment

  • Parent management training
  • Psychotherapy (anger management, social skills training)
  • No pharmacotherapy for ODD but assess for comorbid ADHD & treat if present

ADHD = attention deficit hyperactivity disorder; ODD = oppositional defiant disorder.

subs.title: Tourette syndrome
subs.subject: path
tables: Tourette syndrome

Tourette syndrome

Clinical
features

  • Both multiple motor & ≥1 vocal tics (not necessarily concurrent, >1 year) 
    • Motor: facial grimacing, blinking, head/neck jerking, shoulder shrugging, tongue protrusion
    • Vocal: grunting, sniffing/snorting, throat clearing, barking, yelling, coprolalia (obscenities)
  • Onset age <18

Comorbidity

  • Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
  • Obsessive-compulsive disorder

Treatment

  • Education/watchful waiting if mild & nondisabling
  • Behavioral therapy (habit reversal training)
  • Antidopaminergic agents
    • Tetrabenazine (VMAT2 inhibitor)
    • Antipsychotics (receptor blockers)
  • α2 Adrenergic receptor agonists

Prognosis

  • Severity peaks at age 10-12
  • Majority resolve or improve in adulthood; tics persist in one-third

VMAT2 = vesicular monoamine transporter type 2.

Oppositional defiant disorder

Oppositional defiant disorder

Diagnosis

Pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness for ≥6 months

  • Argues with adults, defies authority figures, refuses to follow rules
  • Deliberately annoys others
  • Blames others for own mistakes or misbehavior
  • Easily annoyed, angry, resentful, or vindictive
  • Not due to another mental disorder

Treatment

  • Parent management training
  • Psychotherapy (anger management, social skills training)
  • No pharmacotherapy for ODD but assess for comorbid ADHD & treat if present

ADHD = attention deficit hyperactivity disorder; ODD = oppositional defiant disorder.
Tourette syndrome

Tourette syndrome

Clinical
features

  • Both multiple motor & ≥1 vocal tics (not necessarily concurrent, >1 year) 
    • Motor: facial grimacing, blinking, head/neck jerking, shoulder shrugging, tongue protrusion
    • Vocal: grunting, sniffing/snorting, throat clearing, barking, yelling, coprolalia (obscenities)
  • Onset age <18

Comorbidity

  • Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
  • Obsessive-compulsive disorder

Treatment

  • Education/watchful waiting if mild & nondisabling
  • Behavioral therapy (habit reversal training)
  • Antidopaminergic agents
    • Tetrabenazine (VMAT2 inhibitor)
    • Antipsychotics (receptor blockers)
  • α2 Adrenergic receptor agonists

Prognosis

  • Severity peaks at age 10-12
  • Majority resolve or improve in adulthood; tics persist in one-third

VMAT2 = vesicular monoamine transporter type 2.

Korsakoff syndrome

Causes

  • Extreme thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency resulting from:
    • Chronic alcohol consumption (most common)
    • Eating disorders &/or chronic malnutrition

Characteristic findings

  • Retrograde & anterograde amnesia
  • Preserved long-term memory
  • Confabulation (memory fabrication without the intention to lie)
  • Lack of insight

  • Associated with severe trauma/abuse

tables: Schizophrenia symptoms

Schizophrenia symptoms

Positive

(pathologic excesses)

Negative

(pathologic deficits)

  • Hallucinations: false sensory perceptions in the absence of stimuli (eg, hearing voices)
  • Delusions: false beliefs despite evidence to the contrary (eg, "the neighbors are aliens")
  • Disorganized/incoherent speech
  • Disorganized/agitated behavior
  • Apathy: lack of motivation
  • Social withdrawal
  • Flat affect: emotional flattening/monotone speech
  • Poverty (lack) of speech
  • Anhedonia: inability to experience pleasure
Schizophrenia

Schizophrenia

Diagnosis

  • ≥2 of the following (at least 1 symptom from 1-3)
    1. Delusions
    2. Hallucinations
    3. Disorganized speech
    4. Disorganized or catatonic behavior
    5. Negative symptoms (eg, apathy, flat affect)
  • Continuous impairment ≥6 months
  • Significant functional decline

Treatment

  • Antipsychotic medication
  • Adjunctive psychosocial interventions (eg, social skills training,
    cognitive-behavioral therapy, family intervention)

Good

Poor

  • Predominantly negative symptoms

tables: Schizoaffective disorder

Schizoaffective disorder

DSM-5 criteria

  • Major depressive or manic episode concurrent with symptoms of schizophrenia
  • Lifetime history of delusions or hallucinations for ≥2 weeks in the absence of major depressive or manic episode
  • Mood episodes are prominent & recur throughout illness
  • Not due to substances or another medical condition

Differential diagnosis

  • Major depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features:  Psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during mood episodes
  • Schizophrenia:  Mood symptoms may be present for relatively brief periods

Delusional disorder

Clinical features

  • ≥1 delusions for ≥1 months
  • Other psychotic symptoms absent or not prominent
  • Behavior not obviously odd/bizarre; ability to function apart from delusion's impact
  • Subtypes: erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, persecutory & somatic

Treatment

  • Antipsychotics
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy

Differential diagnosis of DSM-5 psychotic disorders

Brief psychotic disorder

≥1 days & <1 month, sudden onset, full return to function

Schizophreniform disorder

≥1 months & <6 months, same symptoms as schizophrenia, functional decline not required

Schizophrenia

≥6 months (includes ≥1 months of active symptoms, can include prodromal & residual periods), requires functional decline

Brief psychotic disorder

Key features

  • Acute onset, typically associated with severe stressor
  • Psychotic symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech/behavior
  • Duration: ≥1 days & ≤1 month
  • Full return to premorbid functioning

Differential diagnosis

  • Mood disorders with psychotic features
  • Substance-induced psychotic disorder
  • Psychosis due to general medical conditions

    • Schizophrenia (≥6 months, functional decline)

Management

  • Hospitalization if safety issue &/or inability to care for self
  • Supportive care
  • Low-dose antipsychotic if necessary; discontinue once remitted

Manic episode

Clinical

directTables: Bipolar & related disorders

Bipolar & related disorders

Manic episode

  • Symptoms more severe
  • 1 week unless hospitalized
  • Marked impairment in social or occupational functioning or hospitalization necessary
  • May have psychotic features (makes episode manic by definition)

Hypomanic episode

  • Symptoms less severe
  • ≥4 consecutive days
  • Unequivocal, observable change in functioning from baseline
  • Symptoms not severe enough to cause marked impairment or necessitate hospitalization
  • No psychotic features

Bipolar I

  • Manic episode(s)
  • Depressive episodes common but not required for diagnosis

Bipolar II

  • Hypomanic episode(s)
  • ≥1 major depressive episodes

Cyclothymic disorder

  • ≥2 years of fluctuating, mild hypomanic & depressive symptoms that do not meet criteria for hypomanic or major depressive episodes
Mood stabilizers in bipolar disorder

Mood stabilizers in bipolar disorder

Indications

Adverse effects

Lithium

  • Manic & depressive features
  • Arginine vasopressin resistance
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Tremor
  • Ebstein anomaly (teratogenic)

Valproate

  • Manic features
  • Hepatotoxicity
  • Neural tube defects (teratogenic)

Carbamazepine

  • Manic features
  • Aplastic anemia
  • SIADH
  • Neural tube defects (teratogenic)

Lamotrigine

  • Depressive features
  • Benign rash
  • Stevens-Johnson syndrome

SIADH = syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion.
Treatment of bipolar disorder during pregnancy

Treatment of bipolar disorder during pregnancy

Treatment phase

Medications

Acute mania or hypomania

  • Typical antipsychotics (eg, haloperidol)
  • Atypical antipsychotics (eg, risperidone, olanzapine)

Acute depression

  • Lamotrigine
  • Quetiapine
  • Atypical antipsychotic + SSRI (except paroxetine)

Maintenance (relapse prevention)

  • Lamotrigine
  • Atypical antipsychotics (eg, quetiapine, risperidone)
  • Lithium*

Contraindicated (teratogenic risk)

  • Valproic acid, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental disorders)
  • Paroxetine (cardiac defects)

*Small, increased absolute risk of fetal cardiac defects (eg, Ebstein anomaly).

SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

tables: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia)

Clinical features

  • Chronic depressed mood ≥2 years (1 year in children/adolescents)
  • No symptom-free period for >2 months
  • Presence of ≥2 of the following:
    • Poor appetite or overeating
    • Insomnia or hypersomnia
    • Low energy or fatigue
    • Low self-esteem
    • Poor concentration or difficulty making decisions
    • Feelings of hopelessness

Specifiers

  • With pure dysthymic syndrome: criteria for major depressive episode never met
  • With intermittent major depressive episodes
  • With persistent major depressive episodes: criteria for major depressive episode met throughout previous 2 years

subs.title: MDD with seasonal pattern
subs.subject: path
tables: Seasonal affective disorder

Seasonal affective disorder

Clinical features

  • Recurrent episodes & remission of major depression, mania, or hypomania during certain times of year
  • Seasonal pattern: fall-winter onset, spring-summer onset
  • Symptoms similar to MDD (eg, depressed mood, anhedonia, loss of energy)
  • Atypical symptoms: increased appetite (especially to carbohydrates), weight gain, hypersomnia
  • Symptoms often improve with sunshine

Treatment

  • Antidepressants (eg, SSRIs, buproprion)
  • Light box therapy
  • Psychotherapy
  • Treatment resistance: ECT

ECT = electroconvulsive therapy; MDD = major depressive disorder; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

directTables: Major depressive episode & grief reaction

Major depressive episode & grief reaction

Major depressive episode

Grief reaction

  • ≥2 weeks; ≥5 of 9 symptoms: low mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, appetite change, low energy, psychomotor changes, guilt/worthlessness, concentration difficulty, suicidal ideation
  • May occur in response to a variety of stressors, including loss of a loved one
  • Marked social & occupational dysfunction
  • Suicidality related to hopelessness & worthlessness

topics.title: Risk factors for suicide death
topics.subject: path
directTables: Suicide risk assessment

Suicide risk assessment

Acute modifiable risk factors

  • Suicidal thoughts, plan & intent
  • Presence/severity of psychiatric illness
  • Impulsivity
  • Hopelessness
  • Psychosis/agitation
  • Intoxication (disinhibition)/active substance use
  • Recent psychosocial stressors
  • Medical illness/pain
  • Lack of social support/living alone
  • Access to means (eg, weapons, medications)

Static risk factors

  • Age (young adult & >70)
  • Sex
    • Attempts: female > male
    • Completion: male > female
  • Past suicide attempts
  • Family history of suicide/psychiatric illness
Suicide assessment: ideation, intent & plan

Suicide assessment: ideation, intent & plan

Evaluate ideation

  • Wish to die, not wake up (passive)
  • Thoughts of killing self (active)
  • Frequency, duration, intensity, controllability

Evaluate intent 

  • Strength of intent to attempt suicide; ability to control impulsivity
  • Determine how close patient has come to acting on a plan (rehearsal, aborted attempts)

Evaluate plan

  • Specific details: method, time, place, access to means (eg, weapons, pills), preparations
    (eg, gathering pills, changing will)
  • Lethality of method
  • Likelihood of rescue
Management of suicidality

Management of suicidality

Management

Imminent risk of suicide (voiced intent, high number of unmanaged risk factors, collateral concerns raised)

  • Ensure safety: hospitalize immediately (involuntary if necessary) & start 1:1 for constant observation
  • Remove personal belongings & objects in room that may present self-harm risk
  • Security may be required to hold against will
 

Nonimminent risk of suicide (no intent, strong social supports available, outpatient follow-up plan is reasonable)

  • Create safety plan (eg, coping skills, social supports, crisis numbers)
  • Ensure close follow-up (eg, psychiatry, therapy, intensive outpatient program)
  • Plan to address modifiable risk factors (eg, depression, psychosis, substance use, pain)
  • Ensure family or friends available to support patient
  • Remove access to potential means (eg, secure firearms & medications)

Suicide risk assessment: evaluate ideation, method, plan, intent

Suicidal
ideation

  • Wish to die, not wake up (passive)
  • Thoughts of killing self (active)

Method/
accessibility

  • Thoughts of specific method (eg, weapons, pills)
  • Accessibility of method (eg, medication, gun)
  • Lethality of method (eg, gunshot to head, jumping from high floor, potentially lethal overdose of pills)

Preparations/
planning

  • Steps taken toward making a suicide attempt: collecting pills, obtaining a gun, giving valuables away, writing a will or suicide note
  • Specific planning of time, place, details

Intent

  • Strength of intention to act on suicidal thoughts
  • Time frame (next 48 hr, weeks to months)

directTables: Panic disorder

Panic disorder

Clinical
features

  • Recurrent & unexpected panic attacks with ≥4 of the following:
    • Chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, choking
    • Trembling, sweating, nausea, chills
    • Dizziness, paresthesia
    • Derealization, depersonalization
    • Fear of losing control or dying
  • Worry about additional attacks, avoidance behavior

Treatment

  • Antidepressants (SSRI/SNRI)
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy

SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

directTables: Social anxiety disorder (social phobia)

Social anxiety disorder (social phobia)

Diagnosis

  • Marked anxiety about ≥1 social situations for ≥6 months
  • Fear of scrutiny by others, humiliation, embarrassment
  • Social situations avoided or endured with intense distress
  • Marked impairment (social, academic, occupational)
  • Subtype specifier: performance only

Treatment

  • SSRI/SNRI
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy
  • Beta blocker or benzodiazepine for performance-only subtype

SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.
Specific phobia

Specific phobia

Clinical
features

  • Marked anxiety about a specific object or situation for >6 months
  • Common types: flying, heights, animals, injections, blood
  • Avoidance behavior
  • Usually develops in childhood; can develop after traumatic event

Treatment

  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy using exposure techniques
  • Acutely: short-acting benzodiazepines (limited role)

topics.title: Obsessive-compulsive disorders
topics.subject: path
directTables: Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder)

Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder)

Features

  • Recurrent hair pulling resulting in hair loss
  • Repeated attempts to decrease/stop hair pulling
  • Not due to a medical/dermatological condition (eg, alopecia areata)
  • Not due to another mental disorder (eg, body dysmorphic disorder)

Examination
findings

  • Irregular patches of hair loss
  • Hair shafts of variable lengths
  • Noninflammatory, nonscarring

Treatment

  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy (habit reversal therapy)
Body dysmorphic disorder

Body dysmorphic disorder

Clinical features

  • Preoccupation with ≥1 perceived physical defects
  • Defects not observable or appear slight to others
  • Repetitive behavior or mental acts performed in response to the preoccupation
  • Significant distress or impairment
  • Variable insight (good, poor, absent/delusional beliefs)

Management

  • Antidepressants (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors)
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy
Obsessive-compulsive disorder

Obsessive-compulsive disorder

Clinical features

  • Obsessions
    • Recurrent, intrusive, anxiety-provoking thoughts, urges, or images (eg, contamination, symmetry, harm)
  • Compulsions
    • Responds to obsessions with repeated behaviors or mental acts (eg, cleaning, checking, counting)
    • Behaviors not connected realistically with preventing feared events (eg, counting to prevent harm to a loved one)
  • Time-consuming (>1 hr/day) or causing significant distress or impairment

Management

  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy (exposure & response prevention)

Comorbidities

  • Major depressive disorder/increased suicide risk
  • Anxiety disorders
  • Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
  • Tic disorders (eg, Tourette's)

Course & prognosis

  • Adolescent onset with chronic course
  • High rates of comorbid psychiatric disorders

topics.title: Trauma and stress-related disorders
topics.subject: path

subs.title: Adjustment disorder
subs.subject: path
tables: Adjustment disorder

Adjustment disorder

Clinical features

  • Mood & behavioral symptom onset within 3 months of identifiable stressor
  • Marked distress &/or functional impairment
  • Does not meet criteria for another DSM-5 disorder

Differential diagnosis

  • Normal stress response
    • Not excessive, no significant impairment
  • Acute stress disorder
    • Traumatic event, intrusive reexperiencing
  • Major depressive disorder
    • ≥2 weeks, 5/9 symptoms: depressed mood + SIGECAPS

Management

  • Psychotherapy is treatment of choice
  • Adjunctive pharmacotherapy
    • Short-term, reserved for rapid relief of impairing symptoms (eg, sleep aid, anxiolytic)

SIGECAPS = Sleep disturbance, loss of Interest, excessive Guilt, low Energy, impaired Concentration, Appetite disturbance, Psychomotor agitation/retardation, & Suicidal ideation.

subs.title: Post-traumatic stress disorder
subs.subject: path
tables: Posttraumatic stress disorder

Posttraumatic stress disorder

Risk factors

  • Military combat
  • Sexual trauma
  • Conflict & displacement
  • Physical injury
  • Medical illness (eg, MI, stroke, ICU stay)
  • Childhood abuse

Clinical features

  • Traumatic event exposure
  • Reexperiencing symptoms (eg, nightmares, flashbacks, intrusive memories)
  • Avoidance symptoms (eg, reminders of the trauma, amnesia to details of event)
  • Negative cognitions & mood (eg, emotional detachment, decreased interest in activities, negative worldview)
  • Hyperarousal symptoms (eg, sleep disturbance, hypervigilance, easy startle, irritability)
  • Duration ≥1 month

Treatment

  • Trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy
  • Antidepressants (eg, SNRIs, SSRIs)

Course

  • Onset typically within months of trauma; 25% delayed onset (≥6 months)
  • Commonly chronic (one-third remain symptomatic after 10 years)

ICU = intensive care unit; MI = myocardial infarction; SNRIs = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors; SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

directTables: Acute stress disorder

Acute stress disorder

Clinical features

  • Duration ≥3 days & ≤1 month
  • Exposure to actual or threatened trauma
  • Symptoms from following categories:
    • Avoidance of internal memories or external reminders
    • Intrusion (eg, nightmares, flashbacks)
    • Dissociation (eg, amnesia for event, derealization)
    • Arousal (eg, insomnia, hypervigilance, startle)
    • Negative mood

Management

  • Trauma-focused, brief CBT
  • Consider medication for insomnia, intense anxiety
  • Monitor for PTSD (symptom duration >1 month)

CBT = cognitive-behavioral therapy; PTSD = posttraumatic stress disorder.

topics.title: Personality disorders
topics.subject: path

subs.title: Paranoid
subs.subject: path
tables: Paranoid personality disorder

Paranoid personality disorder

Clinical features

  • Pervasive pattern of distrust & suspiciousness beginning in early adulthood & occurring in a variety of settings (no clear delusions)
    • Believes being exploited & deceived by others
    • Interprets benign comments & events as threats; reacts angrily
    • Bears grudges
    • Questions loyalty of partner without justification

Differential diagnosis

  • Delusional disorder (delusions only)
  • Schizophrenia (delusions, hallucinations, disorganization, negative symptoms)
  • Schizotypal personality disorder (eccentric behavior & thinking, unusual perceptual experiences)

subs.title: Borderline
subs.subject: path
tables: Borderline personality disorder

Borderline personality disorder

Diagnostic criteria

  • Pervasive pattern of unstable relationships, self-image & affects & marked impulsivity, with ≥5 of the following features:
    • Frantic efforts to avoid abandonment
    • Unstable & intense interpersonal relationships
    • Markedly & persistently unstable self-image
    • Impulsivity in ≥2 areas that are potentially self-damaging
    • Recurrent suicidal behaviors or threats of self-mutilation (eg, cutting)
    • Affective instability (marked mood reactivity)
    • Chronic feelings of emptiness
    • Inappropriate & intense anger
    • Transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation

Treatment

  • Primary treatment: psychotherapy (several types effective; best evidence for dialectical behavior therapy)
  • Adjunctive pharmacotherapy to target mood instability & transient psychosis (second-generation antipsychotics, mood stabilizers)
  • Antidepressants if comorbid mood or anxiety disorder

DSM-5 personality disorders

Cluster A
Odd/eccentric

  • Paranoid: suspicious, distrustful, hypervigilant
  • Schizoid: prefers to be a loner, detached, unemotional
  • Schizotypal: unusual thoughts, perceptions & behavior

Cluster B

  • Antisocial: disregard & violation of the rights of others
  • Borderline: chaotic relationships, abandonment fears, labile mood, impulsivity, inner emptiness, self-harm
  • Histrionic: superficial, theatrical, attention-seeking
  • Narcissistic: grandiosity, lack of empathy

Cluster C
Anxious/fearful

  • Avoidant: avoidance due to fears of criticism & rejection
  • Dependent: submissive, clingy, needs to be taken care of
  • Obsessive-compulsive: rigid, controlling, perfectionistic

directTables: Malingering

Malingering

Key feature

  • Falsification or exaggeration of symptoms to obtain external reward (eg, financial gain, avoidance of work or criminal prosecution)

Associated findings suggestive of malingering

  • Discrepancy between subjective distress & objective findings
  • Symptoms present only while observed
  • Inconsistencies in history/reluctance to provide information
  • Nonadherence/refusal of invasive procedures
  • Antisocial personality disorder
  • Analgesic, sedative medication misuse/abuse

Factitious disorder (imposed on self)

Behavioral
characteristics

  • Intentional falsification of illness:
    • Feigning illness
    • Self-induced illness
    • Exacerbation of preexisting illness
  • Motivation by internal factors rather than external gain (eg, financial compensation)

Clinical
presentation

  • Overt/dramatic symptoms
  • Frequent visits for medical care
  • Patient possibly refusing consent to release records or tampering with test samples
  • More common in health care workers

Diagnostic
confirmation

  • Direct observation or discovery of medical supplies (eg, medications, syringes)
  • Confirmatory testing (eg, sulfonylurea screen, stool laxative screen)
  • Medical record review

subs.title: Factitious disorder imposed on another
subs.subject: path
tables: Factitious disorder (imposed on another)

Factitious disorder (imposed on another)

Definition

  • Intentional falsification of symptoms or induction of illness in another person (eg, child, older person)

Characteristics of caregiver (offender)

  • Motivated by desire to assume caregiver role (no external gain)
  • Female > male (95% are female, often primary caretaker)

Clinical presentation

  • Frequent visits
  • History is incongruent with clinical findings
  • Unexplained illness persists despite comprehensive evaluation
  • Caregiver seeks multiple opinions (eg, doctor shopping)
  • Symptoms improve when caregiver is absent

Intervention

  • Seek information from other observers (eg, teacher, other family members)
  • Review previous medical records from all available sources
  • Create a multidisciplinary team of specialists for case analysis
  • Involve child/adult protective services

subs.title: Somatic symptom disorder
