tables: Management of somatic symptom disorder

Management of somatic symptom disorder

  • Schedule regular visits with same provider
  • Limit unnecessary workup & referral to specialists
  • Reassure that serious illness has been ruled out
  • Legitimize symptoms but make functional improvement the treatment goal
    • Decrease stress
    • Improve coping strategies
  • Mental health referral only once physician-patient relationship is well established
Somatic symptom disorder

Somatic symptom disorder

Clinical features

  • ≥1 somatic symptom(s) causing distress & functional impairment
  • Excessive thoughts or behaviors related to somatic symptoms
    • Unwarranted, persistent thoughts about seriousness of symptoms
    • Persistent anxiety about health or symptoms
    • Excessive time & energy devoted to symptoms
  • ≥6 months duration

Management

  • Regularly scheduled visits with same provider
  • Limit unnecessary workup & specialist referrals
  • Legitimize symptoms but make functional improvement the goal
  • Focus on stress reduction & improving coping strategies
  • Mental health referral if patient will accept

tables: Functional neurologic symptom disorder (conversion disorder)

Functional neurologic symptom disorder (conversion disorder)

Clinical

features

  • Neurologic symptoms (eg, weakness/paralysis, nonepileptic seizures, sensory disturbances)
  • Not intentionally produced (contrary to factitious disorder or malingering)
  • Findings incompatible with recognized neurologic conditions
  • Symptoms cause significant functional impairment

options

  • Physical therapy for motor symptoms

directTables: Key features of somatic symptom disorder & related conditions

Key features of somatic symptom disorder & related conditions

Somatic symptom disorder

≥1 unexplained symptoms; excessive thoughts, anxiety & behaviors in response to symptoms

Illness anxiety disorder

Minimal to no symptoms; preoccupation with idea of having a serious illness

Functional neurological symptom disorder
(conversion disorder)

Neurologic symptom(s) incompatible with anatomy or pathophysiology

Factitious disorder

Falsification of symptoms/inducing injury in the absence of obvious external rewards

Malingering

Falsification of illness for obvious external rewards
Factitious disorder—key features & differential diagnosis

Factitious disorder—key features & differential diagnosis

Factitious disorder

  • Intentional falsification of symptoms/inducing injury
  • External rewards absent; goal is to assume the patient role

Malingering

  • Intentional falsification with obvious external rewards (financial benefits, housing, medications)

Personality disorders

  • Enduring patterns of maladaptive interpersonal behavior that may include deliberate self-harm (borderline) & desire to be taken care of (dependent) but do not involve intentional deception

Somatic symptom disorders

  • Excessive illness anxiety/preoccupation with somatic symptoms & treatment seeking; no intention to deceive
Psychosomatic disorders

Psychosomatic disorders

Malingering

  • Intentional falsification or exaggeration of illness
  • Goal: secondary gain (eg, narcotics, shelter)

Factitious disorder

  • Intentional fabrication of symptoms or self-imposed injury or illness
  • Goal: assume sick role (no tangible secondary gain)

Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder)

  • Unintentional neurologic symptom(s) incompatible with anatomy or pathophysiology
  • Goal: no specific goal (often associated with comorbid psychiatric illness)

subs.title: Anorexia nervosa
subs.subject: path
tables: Anorexia nervosa

Anorexia nervosa

Clinical features

  • Underweight (BMI <18.5 kg/m2)
  • Fear of weight gain, distorted body image

Treatment

  • Psychotherapy (individual, family, group)
  • Nutritional rehabilitation
  • Olanzapine if severe/refractory

Indications for hospitalization

  • Bradycardia (<40/min), dysrhythmia
  • Hypotension (<80/60 mm Hg), orthostasis
  • Hypothermia (<35 C [95 F])
  • Electrolyte disturbance, marked dehydration
  • Organ compromise (renal, hepatic, cardiac)
  • <70% expected weight (BMI <15 kg/m2)
Cardiovascular manifestations of anorexia nervosa

Cardiovascular manifestations of anorexia nervosa

Structural

  • Myocardial atrophy ± fibrosis
  • Decreased wall thickness & chamber volume
  • Mitral valve prolapse*

Conduction

  • Increased vagal tone leading to bradycardia
  • Impaired chronotropic response

Vascular

  • Decreased sympathetic tone
  • Impaired vasoconstrictive response

Functional

  • Reduced cardiac output & blood pressure
  • Diminished exertional & orthostatic response

*Occurs secondary to reduced chamber volume.

subs.title: Bulimia nervosa
subs.subject: path
tables: Bulimia nervosa

Bulimia nervosa

Clinical features

  • Recurrent episodes of binge eating & inappropriate compensatory behavior (eg, vomiting, laxatives, excessive exercise)
  • Excessive preoccupation with body weight & shape
  • Body weight within or above normal range
  • Symptoms: abdominal pain, bloating, constipation, lethargy, irregular menses

Physical examination

  • Hypotension, tachycardia
  • Dental enamel erosion, caries
  • Dorsal hand calluses
  • Parotid gland swelling

Laboratory findings

  • Hypokalemia
  • Metabolic alkalosis

directTables: Type 1 diabetes mellitus & disordered eating

Type 1 diabetes mellitus & disordered eating

Etiology & risk factors

  • Sense of lack of control related to food intake & weight
  • Comorbid anxiety & depression
  • Body image dissatisfaction
  • Adolescent girls, overweight/obese

Presentation

  • Insulin restriction (diabulimia)
    • Poorly controlled hyperglycemia (rising hemoglobin A1c)
    • Recurrent DKA
  • Food restriction or purging
    • Episodic hypoglycemia

Screening

  • Diabetes-specific screening questionnaire starting at age 10

DKA = diabetic ketoacidosis.
SCOFF questionnaire

SCOFF questionnaire

  1. Do you make yourself Sick because you feel uncomfortably full?
  2. Do you worry that you have lost Control over how much you eat?
  3. Have you recently lost more than One stone (14 lb) in a 3-month period?
  4. Do you believe yourself to be Fat when others say you are too thin?
  5. Would you say that Food dominates your life?

topics.title: Sexual dysfunction
topics.subject: path
directTables: Common causes of erectile dysfunction

Common causes of erectile dysfunction

Clinical features

Vascular  

  • Cardiovascular risk factors (eg, hypertension, smoking, diabetes)
  • Abnormal vascular examination (eg, bruits, decreased pulses)

Neurologic

  • Neurologic comorbidity (eg, diabetic neuropathy, multiple sclerosis, spinal injury/surgery)
  • Gradual onset, loss of bulbocavernosus reflex

Psychogenic

  • Sudden onset
  • Situational (eg, ED with partner, normal erection during masturbation)
  • Normal nonsexual nocturnal erections

Endocrine

  • Additional symptoms due to underlying disorder
  • Abnormal hormone levels (eg, TSH, prolactin)

Medications

  • Onset related to starting medication
  • Antihypertensives, SSRIs, antiandrogenic medications

Hypogonadism

  • Gradual onset
  • Decreased libido, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy
  • Low serum testosterone

ED = erectile dysfunction; SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.
Sexual performance anxiety/psychogenic ED

Sexual performance anxiety/psychogenic ED

Causes & risk factors

  • Marital/relational stress, conflict
  • Major psychosocial trauma (loss of job or loved one)
  • Severe medical illness (stroke, myocardial infarction)
  • Mood, anxiety disorders

Features

  • Abrupt onset, clear precipitating event or stressor
  • Situational ED (normal nocturnal/nonsexual erections)
  • Impaired or premature orgasm

Management

  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy
  • Couples/relational therapy

ED = erectile dysfunction.
Premature ejaculation

Premature ejaculation

Clinical features

  • Decreased ejaculatory latency (<1 min)
  • Uncontrolled orgasm
  • Distress to patient &/or partner

Treatment

  • SSRIs
  • Topical anesthetics (lidocaine)
  • Psychotherapy, joint/couples therapy

SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

DSM-5 diagnostic criteria

  • Recurrent lapses into sleep or naps (≥3 times/week for 3 months)

  • Hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations
  • Sleep paralysis

directTables: Stages of change model

Stages of change model

Stage

Motivational interviewing

Precontemplation

Not ready to change: patient does not acknowledge negative consequences

  • Encourage patient to evaluate consequences of current behavior
  • Explain & personalize the risk
  • Recommending action is premature

Contemplation

Thinking of changing: patient acknowledges consequences but is ambivalent

  • Encourage evaluation of pros & cons of behavior change
  • Promote new, positive behaviors

Preparation

Ready to change: patient decides to change

  • Encourage small initial steps
  • Reinforce positive outcome expectations 

Action

Making change: patient makes specific, overt changes

  • Help identify appropriate change strategies & enlist social support
  • Promote self-efficacy for dealing with obstacles

Maintenance

Changes integrated into patient’s life; focus on relapse prevention

  • Follow-up support; reinforce intrinsic rewards
  • Develop relapse prevention strategies
IdentificationBehavior is automatic: changes incorporated into sense of self
  • Praise changes

subs.title: Serotonin syndrome
subs.subject: path
tables: Serotonin toxicity

Serotonin toxicity

Causes

  • Serotonergic medications, especially in combination (eg, SSRI/SNRI, TCA, tramadol)
  • Drug interactions: serotonergic medication & MAOI or linezolid
  • Intentional overdose of serotonergic medications
  • Serotonergic substances (eg, MDMA, dextromethorphan, amphetamines)

Clinical
features

  • Mental status changes (eg, anxiety, agitation, delirium)
  • Autonomic dysregulation (eg, diaphoresis, hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, vomiting, diarrhea)
  • Neuromuscular hyperactivity (eg, tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia)

Management

  • Discontinuation of all serotonergic medications
  • Supportive care, sedation with benzodiazepines
  • Serotonin antagonist (cyproheptadine) if supportive measures fail
  • Immediate sedation, paralysis & tracheal intubation if temperature >41.1 C (106 F)

MAOI = monoamine oxidase inhibitor; SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; TCA = tricyclic antidepressant.
Commonly implicated medications in serotonin toxicity

Commonly implicated medications in serotonin toxicity

↓ Serotonin reuptake
or
↑ Serotonin release

  • Antidepressants: SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs

Medication-induced dystonia

Precipitating medications
(dopamine antagonists)

  • Antipsychotics (eg, haloperidol)
  • Antiemetics (eg, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)

Clinical features

  • Onset minutes to 24 hours after starting medication
  • Sudden, sustained contraction of muscles, most often impacting the neck, mouth, tongue, & extraocular muscles
  • Painful, distressing, often with tachycardia &/or hypertension
  • Preserved mental status
  • ± Other extrapyramidal effects (eg, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia)

Treatment

  • Cessation (or ↓ dose) of offending medication (if possible)
  • Anticholinergics (eg, diphenhydramine, benztropine)

subs.title: Lithium toxicity
subs.subject: path
tables: Lithium toxicity

Lithium toxicity

Etiology

  • Overdose
  • Volume depletion
  • Reduced glomerular filtration
  • Drug interactions
    • Thiazide diuretics
    • NSAIDs (not aspirin)
    • ACE inhibitors

Features

Acute

  • GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
  • Neurologic findings occur much later

Chronic

  • Neurologic: ataxia, confusion, agitation, neuromuscular excitability (tremor)

Management

  • Bowel irrigation (asymptomatic acute overdose)
  • Intravenous hydration
  • Hemodialysis
    • Severe toxicity (seizures, encephalopathy)
    • >5 mEq/L
    • >4 mEq/L in patients with impaired kidney function
  • Lithium level every 4-6 hr

GI = gastrointestinal; NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Clinical features of tricyclic antidepressant overdose

CNS

  • Mental status changes (eg, drowsiness, delirium, coma)
  • Seizures, respiratory depression

Cardiovascular

  • Sinus tachycardia, hypotension
  • Prolonged PR/QRS/QT intervals
  • Arrhythmias (eg, ventricular tachycardia, fibrillation)

Anticholinergic

  • Dry mouth, blurred vision, dilated pupils
  • Urinary retention, flushing, hyperthermia
Serotonin toxicity

Serotonin toxicity

Causes

  • Serotonergic medications, especially in combination (eg, SSRI/SNRI, TCA, tramadol)
  • Drug interactions: serotonergic medication & MAOI or linezolid
  • Intentional overdose of serotonergic medications
  • Serotonergic substances (eg, MDMA, dextromethorphan, amphetamines)

Clinical
features

  • Mental status changes (eg, anxiety, agitation, delirium)
  • Autonomic dysregulation (eg, diaphoresis, hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, vomiting, diarrhea)
  • Neuromuscular hyperactivity (eg, tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia)

Management

  • Discontinuation of all serotonergic medications
  • Supportive care, sedation with benzodiazepines
  • Serotonin antagonist (cyproheptadine) if supportive measures fail
  • Immediate sedation, paralysis & tracheal intubation if temperature >41.1 C (106 F)

MAOI = monoamine oxidase inhibitor; SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; TCA = tricyclic antidepressant.

tables: Clinical features of acute opioid intoxication

Clinical features of acute opioid intoxication

Risk factors

  • Substance use disorder
  • Chronic opioid use
  • Hospitalization (especially postoperative)
  • Hepatic or renal insufficiency

Clinical findings

  • Somnolence, AMS
  • Pinpoint pupils (miosis)
  • Shallow breathing & ↓ respiratory rate
  • Bradycardia, hypothermia, ↓ bowel sounds
  • Respiratory acidosis on ABG analysis

Management

  • Naloxone (may need repeated administration)
  • Airway management & ventilation
  • Exclude other AMS causes (eg, hypoglycemia)

ABG = arterial blood gas; AMS = altered mental status.
Opioid withdrawal

Opioid withdrawal

Time course

  • 4 to 48 hr after opioid cessation
  • Immediately after opioid antagonist (life-threatening)

Clinical
presentation

  • Gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting, cramping, diarrhea, ↑ bowel sounds
  • Cardiac:↑ pulse, ↑ blood pressure, diaphoresis
  • Psychologic: insomnia, yawning, dysphoric mood
  • Other: myalgia, arthralgia, mydriasis, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, piloerection

Diagnosis

  • History & examination alone (clinical diagnosis)

Management

  • Opioid agonist: methadone or buprenorphine
  • Nonopioid: clonidine or adjunctive medications (antiemetics, antidiarrheals, benzodiazepines)

subs.title: Nicotine
subs.subject: path
tables: Nicotine poisoning

Nicotine poisoning

Epidemiology

  • Children age <6 are particularly susceptible
  • Toxicity dependent on amount & type of exposure*:
    • Ingested (eg, cigarette ends, nicotine gum, concentrated liquid nicotine)
    • Cutaneous (eg, green tobacco sickness from tobacco leaves)
    • Inhaled (eg, e-cigarettes)

Clinical features

  • Biphasic response due to action of nicotine at acetylcholine receptors:
    • Stimulatory phase (eg, hypertension, tachycardia, seizures, myoclonus)
    • Inhibitory phase (eg, hypotension, bradycardia, coma)
  • Muscarinic symptoms (eg, vomiting, diarrhea, bronchorrhea, salivation, wheezing)

Treatment

  • Primarily supportive
  • Decontamination if transdermal exposure
  • Benzodiazepines for seizures
  • Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia & muscarinic symptoms

*Highly concentrated nicotine liquid used in e-cigarettes can be toxic in small amounts.

tables: Adverse effects of cannabis use

Adverse effects of cannabis use

General

  • ↑ Increased injury & death from motor vehicle collision
  • ↑ Use of other drugs
  • ↓ Educational attainment*

Ophthalmologic

  • Conjunctival vasodilation 

Dental

  • Dry mouth
  • Leukoplakia, gingivitis & candidiasis*

Pulmonary

  • Wheezing & cough

Cardiovascular

  • ↑ Sympathetic activity (eg, tachycardia)

Gastrointestinal

  • Hyperemesis syndrome*

Reproductive

  • ↓ Spermatogenesis*

Neuropsychiatric

  • ↓ Short-term memory, coordination & judgment
  • Anxiety, paranoia & psychosis (high dose)
  • ↓ Hippocampal volume*
  • ↑ Risk of psychiatric disease* (eg, depression, bipolar disease)

*Associated only with chronic or heavy use.
Cannabis withdrawal

Cannabis withdrawal

Clinical features

  • Cessation of heavy, prolonged cannabis use (daily, months)
  • ≥3 signs/symptoms (must include at least 1 physical symptom)

Psychologic

  • Irritability, anger
  • Depressed mood
  • Anxiety, restlessness
  • Decreased appetite/weight loss
  • Sleep disturbance

Physical

  • Abdominal pain
  • Headache
  • Shakiness/tremors
  • Fevers, chills
  • Sweating
Cannabis (marijuana) intoxication

Cannabis (marijuana) intoxication

Manifestations

  • Increased appetite
  • Euphoria
  • Dysphoria/panic
  • Slow reflexes, impaired time perception
  • Dry mouth (xerostomia)
  • Conjunctival irritation

  • ↑ Sympathetic activity (eg, tachycardia)

  • Hyperemesis syndrome*

  • ↓ Spermatogenesis*

Cannabis withdrawal

Clinical features

  • Cessation of heavy, prolonged cannabis use (daily, months)
  • ≥3 signs/symptoms (must include at least 1 physical symptom)

Psychologic

  • Irritability, anger
  • Depressed mood
  • Anxiety, restlessness
  • Decreased appetite/weight loss
  • Sleep disturbance

Physical

  • Abdominal pain
  • Headache
  • Shakiness/tremors
  • Fevers, chills
  • Sweating
Cannabis (marijuana) intoxication

Cannabis (marijuana) intoxication

Manifestations

  • Increased appetite
  • Euphoria
  • Dysphoria/panic
  • Slow reflexes, impaired time perception
  • Dry mouth (xerostomia)
  • Conjunctival irritation

directTables: Screening for unhealthy alcohol use

Screening for unhealthy alcohol use

Single-item screening

  • How many times in the past year have you had 5 (4 for women) or more drinks in a day?

AUDIT-C

  • How often do you drink alcohol?
  • How many drinks do you have on a typical day when you are drinking?
  • How often do you have 6 (4 for women) or more drinks on 1 occasion?

AUDIT

  • 10-item screen assessing frequency, number of drinks & psychosocial consequences

CAGE

  • Have you felt you should cut down on your drinking?
  • Have others annoyed you by criticizing your drinking?
  • Have you ever felt bad or guilty about your drinking?
  • Have you ever taken a drink first thing in the morning (eye-opener) to steady your nerves?
Benefits & risks of alcohol consumption

Benefits & risks of alcohol consumption

Alcohol use

Definition

Clinical effects

Moderate or steady

  • Women: <2 drinks/day
  • Men: <3 drinks/day
  • Possibly ↑ blood pressure
  • ↓ Cardiac events & total mortality
  • ↑ Insulin sensitivity, improved glucose metabolism

Heavy or intermittent

  • Women: >7 drinks/week
    or 3 drinks per occasion
  • Men: >14 drinks/week
    or 4 drinks per occasion
  • ↑ Blood pressure, cardiac events, risk for stroke & total mortality
  • ↑ Risk for atrial fibrillation & dilated cardiomyopathy
  • ↑ Risk for accidents & trauma
  • Unstable glucose levels, potentially severe hypoglycemia in patients taking sulfonylureas
  • ↑ Risk for cirrhosis, acute & chronic pancreatitis

Binge drinking

  • Women: ≥4 drinks per occasion
  • Men: ≥5 drinks per occasion

topics.title: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
topics.subject: path
directTables: Wernicke encephalopathy

Wernicke encephalopathy

Associated conditions

  • Chronic alcohol use (most common)
  • Malnutrition (eg, anorexia nervosa)
  • Hyperemesis gravidarum

Pathophysiology

  • Thiamine deficiency

Clinical features

  • Encephalopathy
  • Oculomotor dysfunction (eg, horizontal nystagmus & bilateral abducens palsy)
  • Postural & gait ataxia

Treatment

  • Intravenous thiamine followed by glucose infusion

directTables: SSRI-associated sexual dysfunction

Features

  • Decreased libido
  • Anorgasmia
  • Delayed ejaculation

topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation

Pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation

Treatment

Indications

Adverse effects/
contraindications

Varenicline

  • More effective than either bupropion or combination NRT
  • Disordered sleep & abnormal dreams

Long-acting NRT
(nicotine patch)

  • ↓ Cravings & daytime withdrawal symptoms
  • Long-acting NRT may be combined with short-acting NRT ("patch plus") to improve efficacy
  • No significant effects, safe in almost all patients

Short-acting NRT
(nasal spray, gum,
lozenge, inhaler)

Bupropion

  • ↓ Postcessation weight gain
  • Good choice for patients with unipolar depression
  • Contraindicated in patients with seizure or eating disorders

NRT = nicotine replacement therapy.
Risks of tobacco cessation & directed interventions

Risks of tobacco cessation & directed interventions

Clinical features

Mitigation

Nicotine withdrawal syndrome

  • Increased appetite
  • Dysphoria/irritability
  • Insomnia & restlessness
  • Behavioral therapy, nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion

Weight gain

  • 1-2 kg (2.2-4.4 lb) in the first several weeks, 4-5 kg (8.8-11 lb) total
  • Behavioral therapy, nicotine replacement, bupropion

Depression

  • Patients with prior psychiatric illness at higher risk
  • Behavioral therapy, bupropion, antidepressant medications

Cough & mouth ulcers

  • Increased symptoms in the first several weeks; typically self-limited
  • Supportive care
Smoking cessation interventions by stage of change

Smoking cessation interventions by stage of change

Not ready to quit

  • Conduct motivational interviewing (4R): relevance, risks, rewards, roadblocks
  • Repeat at every visit
  • Prescribe varenicline* to facilitate reduce-to-quit strategy

Ready to quit

  • Set a firm quit date & discard smoking paraphernalia
  • Provide behavioral counseling & engage support systems
  • Prescribe pharmacotherapy (eg, varenicline, bupropion, NRT)

Struggling to quit

  • Reinforce partial achievements
  • Identify triggers & link them to other (distracting) activities
  • Use biofeedback loops (eg, exhaled CO monitoring, gamification using mobile app)

Recently quit

  • Congratulate & offer continued support
  • Continue pharmacotherapy for 12 weeks
  • Encourage active reflection (anticipated problems, "how has your life changed?")

*2-fold higher rate of durable abstinence.

CO = carbon monoxide; NRT = nicotine replacement therapy.
Behavioral therapy approaches for smoking cessation

Behavioral therapy approaches for smoking cessation

Brief intervention

Brief interaction with a physician in the office

Individual counseling

Formal in-person counseling at least once a week

Group counseling

Group teaching about behavioral techniques & coping skills

Telephone counseling—proactive

Counselor initiates calls to the patient at prearranged times

Telephone counseling—reactive

Patient initiates calls to the counselor when convenient for patient

Text messaging

Automated motivational text messages for support

Self-help material

Pamphlets, audio & video recordings
The 5A

The 5As of smoking cessation

Ask

Ask about tobacco use at every visit

Advise

Provide clear, personalized advice to quit

Assess

Determine readiness to quit

  • If willing, assist (see below)
  • If unwilling, provide motivational intervention

Assist

Assist with quit attempt

  • Provide counseling & refer to a smoking cessation program
  • Recommend medications to reduce nicotine withdrawal symptoms

Arrange

Schedule follow-up to monitor progress

  • Prescribe pharmacotherapy (eg, varenicline, bupropion, NRT)

Struggling to quit

  • Reinforce partial achievements
  • Identify triggers & link them to other (distracting) activities
  • Use biofeedback loops (eg, exhaled CO monitoring, gamification using mobile app)

Recently quit

  • Congratulate & offer continued support
  • Continue pharmacotherapy for 12 weeks
  • Encourage active reflection (anticipated problems, "how has your life changed?")

subs.title: Naltrexone
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Naltrexone

Naltrexone

Mechanism of action

  • Opioid μ receptor antagonist
  • Blocks sedating, analgesic, euphoric effects of opioids

Use & benefits

  • Adjunct therapy for moderate to severe alcohol use disorder
    • Decreases alcohol cravings & frequency of heavy drinking days
    • Can be initiated when a patient is still consuming alcohol
  • Adjunct therapy for opioid use disorder*

Safety & contraindications

  • Should not be prescribed with an opioid (antagonist effect)
  • Can precipitate immediate opioid withdrawal if given to a patient with long-term (>3 weeks) opioid use
  • Avoid in a patient with liver failure or hepatitis

*In the setting of low patient compliance with an oral agent (eg, methadone).

directTables: Mechanism of action

Pharmacotherapy for opioid use disorder

Mechanism of action

Characteristics

Buprenorphine

  • μ opioid receptor partial agonist
  • Lower risk for respiratory suppression/lethal overdose
  • Lower risk for misuse
  • Daily clinic dosing not required

Methadone

  • μ opioid receptor full agonist
  • Greater risk for respiratory suppression/lethal overdose
  • Greater risk for misuse
  • Adverse effects: risk for hyperalgesia, hypogonadism, QTc prolongation
  • Daily clinic dosing required
Treatment of opioid use disorder

Treatment of opioid use disorder

Mechanism

Advantages & disadvantages

Buprenorphine*

Partial μ opioid agonist

  • Lower risk for misuse & lethal overdose
  • Does not require complete withdrawal prior to initiation
  • Slightly less effective at keeping patients in treatment

Methadone

Full μ opioid agonist

  • More effective at patient retention
  • Does not require complete withdrawal prior to initiation
  • Significantly higher risk for misuse & lethal overdose

Naltrexone

Pure opioid antagonist

  • Does not cause physiologic dependence
  • Requires complete opioid withdrawal prior to initiation
  • Increased risk for overdose with noncompliance and relapse

Nonmedication therapy

Psychosocial interventions

  • Helpful adjunct to medication-assisted treatment
  • Used alone in motivated patients who want to avoid medications
  • Less effective than medication-assisted treatment

*Sublingual buprenorphine may sometimes be combined with naloxone (opioid antagonist with poor sublingual bioavailability) to prevent abuse by crushing or dissolving buprenorphine.

Primary ciliary dyskinesia vs cystic fibrosis

Primary ciliary dyskinesia

Cystic fibrosis

Pathogenesis

  • Dynein arm defect → abnormal ciliary motion & impaired mucociliary clearance
  • Mutation in the CFTR gene → impaired ion transport

Respiratory tract features

  • Chronic sinopulmonary infections
  • Nasal polyps
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Digital clubbing
  • Chronic sinopulmonary infections
  • Nasal polyps
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Digital clubbing

Extrapulmonary features

  • Situs inversus (50% of cases)
  • Infertility due to immotile spermatozoa
  • Normal growth
  • Pancreatic insufficiency
  • Infertility due to absent vas deferens (azoospermia)
  • Failure to thrive

Diagnosis

  • Low nasal nitric oxide levels
  • Bronchoscopy & electron microscopic visualization of ciliary abnormalities
  • Genetic testing
  • Elevated sweat chloride levels 
  • Abnormal nasal transepithelial potential difference
  • Genetic testing

directTables: Cystic fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis

Pathogenesis

  • Mutation (ΔF508) of CFTR gene
  • Autosomal recessive  

Clinical features

  • Recurrent sinopulmonary infections
  • Intestinal obstruction (eg, meconium ileus)
  • Pancreatic insufficiency & diabetes
  • Male infertility  

Diagnosis

  • Elevated sweat chloride levels
  • CFTR mutation on genetic testing
  • Abnormal nasal potential difference

Management

  • Nutritional support
  • Airway clearance
  • Antibiotic coverage (Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa)

CFTR = cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator.
Cystic fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis

Clinical features

  • Chronic sinopulmonary disease (eg, bronchiectasis)
  • Gastrointestinal & nutritional abnormalities (eg, pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, failure to thrive)
  • Salt loss syndromes (eg, acute salt depletion, chronic metabolic alkalosis)
  • Male urogenital abnormalities (eg, obstructive azoospermia)

Diagnosis

One or more clinical features

OR

History of cystic fibrosis in a sibling

OR

Positive newborn screening test

PLUS

Increased sweat chloride concentration ≥60 mmol/L on 2 or more occasions

OR

Identification of 2 cystic fibrosis mutations

OR

Abnormal nasal epithelial ion transport (potential difference)

subs.subject: biochem
tables: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)

Pathophysiology

  • Mutation in dystrophin gene on X chromosome
  • Absent dystrophin in muscle cytoskeleton
  • Muscle atrophy → replacement with connective tissue/fat

Clinical findings

  • Proximal muscle weakness (boys age 2-3):
    • Delayed motor milestones, toe-walking, waddling gait
    • Gowers sign
    • Calf pseudohypertrophy
  • Scoliosis, lumbar lordosis
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy & restrictive lung disease

Evaluation

  • ↑ Serum creatine kinase
  • Genetic analysis (diagnostic)

Management

  • Glucocorticoids
  • Serial ECG, echocardiography, PFTs

Prognosis

  • Wheelchair use typical by adolescence
  • Shortened lifespan (age 20-30) from respiratory/heart failure

PFTs = pulmonary function tests.

subs.title: Myotonic dystrophy
subs.subject: biochem
tables: Myotonic dystrophy

Myotonic dystrophy

Pathogenesis

  • Autosomal dominant CTG trinucleotide repeat expansion
  • Longer repeat length correlating with earlier & more severe disease

Presentation

  • Classic (adult): myotonia & weakness (eg, face, hands, ankles)
  • Childhood: cognitive & behavioral difficulties (classic symptoms develop over time)
  • Infantile: hypotonia, respiratory failure, inverted V–shaped upper lip

Associated findings

  • Cardiac: arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy
  • Gastrointestinal: dysphagia, constipation
  • Respiratory: pharyngeal weakness, hypoventilation
  • Nonmuscular: insulin resistance, hypogonadism, cataracts, frontal balding, excessive daytime sleepiness

Diagnosis & treatment

  • Genetic testing
  • Supportive management

CTG = cytosine-thymine-guanine.

  • Cardiac: arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy
  • Gastrointestinal: dysphagia, constipation
  • Respiratory: pharyngeal weakness, hypoventilation
  • Nonmuscular: insulin resistance, hypogonadism, cataracts, frontal balding, excessive daytime sleepiness

Diagnosis & treatment

  • Genetic testing
  • Supportive management

CTG = cytosine-thymine-guanine.

Prognosis

  • Middle-aged life expectancy; reduced mobility, seizures, respiratory difficulties

tables: Vegan diet

Vegan diet

Composition

  • Plant-based foods: fruits, vegetables, legumes, grains
  • No animal-derived foods (eg, meat, dairy, egg)

Potential benefits

  • Lower blood glucose & cholesterol levels
  • Reduced risk for cardiovascular disease (eg, heart disease, stroke)

Potential nutritional deficiencies

  • Common: vitamin B12, vitamin D, calcium
  • Possible*: iron, zinc

*Increased risk: children (rapid growth requires higher zinc/iron) & young women (menstrual blood loss requires higher iron).

subs.subject: biochem
tables: Wernicke encephalopathy

Wernicke encephalopathy

Risk factors

  • Chronic alcohol use (most common)
  • Malnutrition (eg, anorexia, gastric bypass surgery)

Pathophysiology

  • Thiamine deficiency → impaired glucose metabolism & ATP production → neuronal injury/death (eg, mammillary bodies)
  • May be precipitated by high metabolic demand or high glucose load

Clinical
findings

  • Encephalopathy
  • Oculomotor dysfunction
  • Ataxia

Management
& prognosis

  • Thiamine infusion reverses most symptoms.
  • Memory impairment may be chronic/irreversible (Korsakoff syndrome).

directTables: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy)

Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy)

Pathogenesis

  • Insufficient dietary intake (lack of citrus fruits/vegetables)
    • Chronic alcohol/substance use
    • Severe malnutrition (eg, anorexia, restricted diet)
  • Impaired collagen production

Manifestations

  • Cutaneous:
    • Coiled hair, perifollicular hemorrhages
    • Petechiae, ecchymoses
    • Impaired wound healing
  • Mucosal: gingivitis with bleeding
  • Musculoskeletal (eg, periosteal hemorrhage): arthralgia, limp
  • Constitutional: malaise, depression, vasomotor instability

Laboratory findings

  • Anemia (normocytic or microcytic)
  • Normal platelet count & coagulation studies

Treatment

  • Oral/injectable vitamin C (improvement within days to weeks)
  • Toxicity (eg, abdominal pain, diarrhea) with excessive supplementation

directTables: Vitamin D deficiency in children

Vitamin D deficiency in children

Risk factors

  • Exclusive breastfeeding
  • Inadequate sun exposure, heavy skin pigmentation
  • Absence of fortified dairy (dairy alternative) foods

Clinical
manifestations

  • Decreased muscle tone & delayed development
  • Delayed fontanelle closure, frontal bossing
  • Widening of epiphyses
  • Hypertrophy of costochondral joints
  • Short stature, femoral & tibial bowing

Laboratory
findings

  • Low 25-hydroxyvitamin D
  • Elevated alkaline phosphatase
  • Low/normal calcium, low phosphorus
  • Elevated parathyroid hormone
  • Low urine calcium

Histopathology

  • Excess unmineralized osteoid
Vitamin D deficiency

Vitamin D deficiency

topics.title: Protein-energy malnutrition
topics.subject: biochem
directTables: Protein-energy malnutrition

Protein-energy malnutrition

Kwashiorkor
(with edema)

Marasmus
(without edema)

Pathophysiology

Malnutrition due to protein deficiency

  • ↓ Oncotic pressure (edema, ascites)
  • ↓ Carrier lipoproteins (fatty liver)
  • ↓ Immunoglobulins (infections)

Malnutrition due to total calorie deficiency (protein, carbohydrates, fats)

  • ↓ Protein & fat stores (wasting)

Presentation

  • Ascites, edema
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Flaky dermatitis (eg, ↓ keratin)
  • No ascites or edema
  • Emaciation (loose, hanging skin)
  • Disproportionate head size

Management

  • Refeeding (eg, RUTF)
  • Complications:
    • Bacterial infection (eg, empiric antibiotics)
    • Dehydration (eg, ORS)
    • Hypothermia (eg, warm blankets)

Prognosis

Worse prognosis due to higher risk for infection, cardiac failure & refeeding syndrome (eg, ↓ PO4–, ↓ K+, ↓ Mg2+)

Better (but still guarded) prognosis

ORS = oral rehydration solution; RUTF = ready-to-use therapeutic food (eg, provides complete nutrition).

topics.subject: biochem
directTables: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

Epidemiology

  • Hemolytic anemia due to oxidative stress (infection, sulfa drugs, fava beans)
  • X-linked: Asian, African, or Middle Eastern descent

Manifestations

  • Pallor & fatigue
  • Dark urine, jaundice & icterus
  • Abdominal/back pain

Laboratory
findings

  • Hemolysis: ↓ hemoglobin, ↓ haptoglobin,
    ↑ bilirubin & LDH, ↑ reticulocytes
  • Peripheral smear: bite cells & Heinz bodies
  • Negative Coombs test
  • ↓ G6PD activity level (may be normal during attack)

Management

  • Remove or treat responsible agent/condition
  • Provide supportive care

G6PD = glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase.

directTables: Galactosemia

Galactosemia

Etiology

  • GALT deficiency
  • Autosomal recessive
  • Galactose accumulation after lactose or galactose ingestion

Clinical findings

  • Jaundice & hepatomegaly
  • Vomiting & poor feeding/failure to thrive
  • Cataracts
  • Increased risk for Escherichia coli sepsis

Laboratory findings

  • ↑ Bilirubin, AST, ALT
  • ↓ Glucose
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • + Urine reducing substance

Diagnosis

  • May be identified on newborn screening
  • Absent red blood cell GALT activity

Treatment

  • Galactose-free diet (eg, soy-based formula)

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; GALT = galactose 1-phosphate uridylyltransferase.

topics.title: Phenylketonuria
topics.subject: biochem
directTables: Phenylketonuria

Phenylketonuria

Pathophysiology

  • Autosomal recessive mutation in gene for phenylalanine hydroxylase
  • Impaired metabolism of phenylalanine to tyrosine → ↑ phenylalanine causes neurologic injury

Clinical features

  • Neurologic: microcephaly, developmental delay, seizures, severe intellectual disability
  • Nonneurologic: musty body odor, hypopigmentation (eg, skin, hair, eyes), eczema

Diagnosis

  • ↑ Phenylalanine levels:
    • Universal newborn screening
    • Serum amino acid analysis

Treatment

  • Phenylalanine-restricted diet (ie, avoidance of protein-rich foods)
  • Dietary/supplemental tyrosine

Prognosis

  • Preventable disease manifestations with early treatment
  • Delayed diagnosis/treatment → irreversible neurologic injury
Disorders of phenylalanine metabolism

Disorders of phenylalanine metabolism

Phenylketonuria

BH4 deficiency

Enzyme
deficiency

  • Phenylalanine hydroxylase
  • Normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine
  • Dihydropteridine reductase
  • Normally regenerates the cofactor BH4 (essential for reactions involving phenylalanine, tyrosine & tryptophan)

Pathophysiology
of disease

  • ↑ Phenylalanine
    • Neurologic abnormalities (eg, developmental delay, microcephaly, seizures)
    • Hypopigmentation
    • Musty odor
  • ↑ Phenylalanine (same as in PKU)
  • ↓ Neurotransmitters (eg, dopamine, epinephrine, serotonin)
    • Extrapyramidal signs (eg, axial hypotonia, dystonia), feeding difficulties, autonomic dysfunction
    • Dysregulation of appetite/mood/sleep

Treatment

  • Phenylalanine-restricted diet
  • ± Tyrosine supplementation
  • Phenylalanine-restricted diet
  • BH4 supplementation

BH4 = tetrahydrobiopterin.

Features of homocystinuria

 

Pathogenesis

  • Most commonly due to an autosomal recessive mutation causing cystathionine synthase deficiency

Fabry disease

Pathophysiology

Gaucher disease

features

topics.title: Key enzymes in lipid transport
topics.subject: biochem
directTables: Key enzymes involved in cholesterol transport & synthesis

Key enzymes involved in cholesterol transport & synthesis

HMG-CoA reductase

  • Rate-limiting step in endogenous cholesterol production
  • ↑ Cholesterol synthesis

PCSK9

  • Binds to & promotes degradation of LDL-R
  • ↓ LDL-R & ↑ cholesterol levels

LPL

  • Lipolyzes TGs within lipoproteins into FFAs for cellular uptake → catabolizes VLDL & chylomicrons into remnants
  • ↓ Level of FFAs & TG in the blood

CETP

  • Transfers cholesteryl esters from HDL to LDL/VLDL
  • ↑ TG content of HDL → ↓ quality & ↓ levels of HDL

LCAT

  • Esterifies free cholesterol for transport by HDL
  • ↑ Reverse transport of cholesterol to liver

CETP = cholesteryl ester transfer protein; FFA = free fatty acid; LCAT = lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; PCSK9 = proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9; TG = triglyceride.

topics.title: Lipoprotein functions
topics.subject: biochem
directTables: Lipoproteins

Lipoproteins

Structure & synthesis

Function & clearance

VLDL

  • Formed in liver
  • Contains ↑ TGs, ↓ cholesterol
  • Transports TGs
  • Becomes IDL as TG content reduces
  • Requires Apo C-II (LPL co-factor) & ApoE

LDL

  • Formed when IDL is depleted of TGs; also formed in liver
  • Contains ↑ cholesterol, ↓ TG
  • Transports cholesterol
  • Mainly cleared by liver; can be taken up by other tissues
  • Requires LDL-R & apo-B100

HDL

  • Formed in intestine & liver
  • Begins as nascent HDL (↓ TG & ↓ cholesterol); mature HDL has more cholesterol
  • Scavenges excess cholesterol & returns to liver
  • Supports function & clearance of other lipoproteins
  • Requires Apo A-I

Chylomicron

  • Formed in intestines from dietary lipids; ↑↑ TGs & ↓ cholesterol
  • Transports TGs from diet
  • Becomes chylomicron remnants when TG content depleted
  • Requires Apo B-48, ApoE & Apo C-II (LPL cofactor)

Apo B-48 = apolipoprotein B-48; Apo B-100 = apolipoprotein B-100; Apo C-II = apolipoprotein C-II; ApoE = apolipoprotein E; IDL = intermediate-density lipoprotein; LDL-R = low-density lipoprotein receptor; LPL = lipoprotein lipase; TG = triglyceride.

Common patterns of dyslipidemias & their causes

Common patterns of dyslipidemias & their causes

High LDL (eg, >100-130 mg/dL)

  • ↑ LDL formation (eg, excess VLDL or Apo-B hepatic synthesis)
  • ↓ LDL clearance (eg, ↓ LDL-R expression, ↑ PCSK9, ↓ LDL-R binding caused by defective Apo B)

High TGs (eg, >150 mg/dL)

  • ↑ Hepatic VLDL synthesis
  • ↓ Chylomicron or VLDL clearance (eg, defective Apo E)
  • ↓ HDL activity (eg, ↑ CETP activity)
  • ↓ LPL activity (eg, defective Apo C-II → ↓ TG lipolysis)
  • Worsened by metabolic inflammation (eg, insulin resistance)

Low HDL (eg, <40-50 mg/dL)

  • Most commonly a sequela of ↑ LDL & TG
  • Isolated ↓ HDL can occur if ↓ synthesis (eg, defective Apo A-1)

topics.title: Necrosis
topics.subject: path
directTables: Patterns of tissue necrosis

Patterns of tissue necrosis

Type

Etiology

Morphology

Liquefactive necrosis

  • Severe bacterial infections (eg, gangrene)
  • CNS infarcts
  • Necrotic tissue is digested by hydrolytic enzymes into a viscous fluid:
    • Infected abscess fluid is creamy yellow due to dead leukocytes (pus)
    • Brain infarcts resolve into CSF-filled spaces

Fibrinoid necrosis

  • Hypertension
  • Vasculitis
  • Damaged vessels leak fibrin/immune complexes
  • Eosinophilic layer of proteinaceous material in vessel walls

Fat necrosis

  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Trauma (subcutaneous adipose tissue)
  • Free fatty acids released by active enzymes (eg, lipases) or mechanical damage
  • Fatty acids combine with calcium, forming chalky-white deposits (saponification)

Caseous necrosis

  • Mycobacterial infections
  • Fungal infections (eg, Histoplasma, Cryptococcus, Coccidioides)
  • Friable, cheeselike material composed of cell fragments & amorphous proteinaceous debris
  • Surrounded by epithelioid macrophages & giant cells (granuloma)

Coagulative necrosis

  • Irreversible ischemic injury outside CNS
  • Tissue architecture is preserved due to denaturation of lytic enzymes:
    • Cells are anucleate with eosinophilic cytoplasm
    • Leukocytes eventually infiltrate & digest necrotic tissue

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid.

Fat necrosis

  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Trauma (subcutaneous adipose tissue)
  • Free fatty acids released by active enzymes (eg, lipases) or mechanical damage
  • Fatty acids combine with calcium, forming chalky-white deposits (saponification)

Caseous necrosis

  • Mycobacterial infections
  • Fungal infections (eg, Histoplasma, Cryptococcus, Coccidioides)
  • Friable, cheeselike material composed of cell fragments & amorphous proteinaceous debris
  • Surrounded by epithelioid macrophages & giant cells (granuloma)

Coagulative necrosis

  • Irreversible ischemic injury outside CNS
  • Tissue architecture is preserved due to denaturation of lytic enzymes:
    • Cells are anucleate with eosinophilic cytoplasm
    • Leukocytes eventually infiltrate & digest necrotic tissue

CSF = cerebrospinal fluid.

Comparison of tumor grading & staging

Grading

Staging

Describes

  • How closely neoplastic cells resemble normal, mature cells (ie, degree of differentiation)
  • How far the tumor has spread

Assessed by

  • Histopathology
  • Clinical examination (eg, lymphadenopathy)
  • Pathologic examination (eg, gross inspection)
  • Radiologic & nuclear medicine studies (eg, PET/CT)

Criteria*

  • Cellular differentiation
  • Architectural features
  • Mitotic count
  • Tumor size
  • Noninvasive vs invasive
  • Spread to regional lymph nodes
  • Distant metastases

*The specific criteria used vary by tumor type.

tables: Physiologic age-related cardiovascular changes

Physiologic age-related cardiovascular changes

Aortic stiffening

  • Elastin replacement with collagen
  • ↑ Pulse pressure (isolated systolic HTN)

Mild concentric LVH*

  • Response to cardiomyocyte dropout & ↑ afterload
  • Resting EF, SV & cardiac output maintained
  • ↓ Maximal cardiac output

Conduction cell

degeneration

  • Slightly ↓ resting heart rate
  • ↓ Maximal heart rate

Reduced baroreceptor sensitivity & adrenergic responsiveness

  • ↑ Orthostasis
  • ↓ Heart rate & contractility response

*A soft S4 can be a normal finding in the elderly.

EF = ejection fraction; HTN = hypertension; LVH = left ventricular hypertrophy; SV = stroke volume.

subs.title: Gastrointestinal
subs.subject: path
tables: Effect of aging on the liver

Effect of aging on the liver

Anatomic changes

  • Decreased liver size/mass
    • Due to decreased hepatic perfusion

Physiologic changes

  • Decreased regenerative capacity
  • Decreased activity of cytochrome P450 system
  • Decreased protein (eg, albumin, clotting factors) synthesis

Histologic changes

  • Increased hepatocyte size
  • Increased polyploidy
  • Accumulation of lipofuscin (brown atrophy)

subs.title: Special senses
subs.subject: path
tables: Normal age-related ocular changes

Normal age-related ocular changes

Structure

Key changes

Clinical feature

Cornea

  • Flattening of curvature
  • Decreased endothelial cell density
  • Reduced corneal sensitivity
  • Slight reduction in refractive power
  • Clarity maintained
  • Mild risk of dry eye

Lens

  • Lens fibers & proteins accumulate → thicker, less flexible
  • Yellowing or brunescence from pigment deposition & oxidative damage
  • Increased light scatter
  • Presbyopia (loss of near focus)
  • Increase in refractive power
  • Reduced blue light perception
  • Glare, especially at night

Vitreous humor

  • Liquefaction (synchysis)
  • Posterior vitreous detachment common
  • Floaters, flashes of light
  • Predisposition to retinal tears or detachment

Retina

  • Decline in rod photoreceptors (faster than in cones)
  • Lipofuscin accumulation in RPE
  • Slower dark adaptation
  • Reduced night & peripheral vision
  • Slower adjustment to dim light

RPE = retinal pigment epithelium.

topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Medication prescribing in elderly patients

Medication prescribing in elderly patients

Major considerations

  • Increased susceptibility to ADEs
  • Increased polypharmacy risk due to multiple chronic conditions
  • Susceptibility to harms from overtreatment & undertreatment

Principles
of prescribing

  • Limit the number of prescribers
  • Review criteria for geriatric populations (eg, Beers,* START**)
  • Consider time to benefit for drug
  • Tailor regimen to the patient's goals & life expectancy
  • Frequently reassess appropriateness of medication

*Beers criteria: list of medications considered potentially inappropriate or to be used with caution in the elderly.
**START criteria: used to identify potential harm of withholding specific drug in older patients.
ADEs = adverse drug events; START = Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment.

directTables: Mechanisms of drug tolerance

Mechanisms of drug tolerance

Tolerance

Mechanism

Example

Acquired pharmacokinetic

  • ADME: ↓ Absorption, ↑ Distribution, or
    ↑ Metabolism & Excretion (eg, enzyme induction)
  • ↓ Plasma drug concentration relative to naïve state
  • Rifampin (CYP3A4 inducer) accelerates metabolism of warfarin
  • Carbamazepine induces its own metabolism after repeated dosing

Acquired pharmacodynamic

  • ↓ Cellular response to drug (eg, receptor downregulation)
  • Unchanged plasma drug concentration relative to naïve state
  • Chronic opioid use: ↓ expression & responsivity of μ receptor system
  • Frequent albuterol rescue inhaler:
    ↓ expression of airway β2 receptors

Innate

  • Genetic (eg, polymorphisms) & epigenetic (eg, DNA methylation) differences
  • Leads to pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic tolerance
  • Tolerance apparent from first dose
  • Slow metabolizer CYP2C19 allele:
    ↓ clopidogrel activation
    (↓ antiplatelet effect)
  • Slow metabolizer CYP2D6 allele:
    ↓ codeine conversion to morphine
    (↓ analgesic effect)

Behavioral (functional)

  • Ability to compensate for drug-induced impairment through learning & practice
  • Maintaining appearance & mannerisms to appear nonintoxicated at work

topics.subject: pharm
directTables: Organophosphate poisoning

Organophosphate poisoning

Common exposures

  • Pesticide: farmer/field worker, pediatric ingestion, suicide attempt
  • Nerve agent: multiple patients presenting with similar symptoms

Manifestations

  • Muscarinic:
    • Diarrhea/diaphoresis
    • Urination
    • Miosis
    • Bronchospasms, bronchorrhea, bradycardia
    • Emesis
    • Lacrimation
    • Salivation
  • Nicotinic: muscle weakness, paralysis, fasciculations

Management

  • Remove patient's clothes, irrigate skin
  • Atropine reverses muscarinic symptoms
  • Pralidoxime reverses nicotinic and muscarinic symptoms (administer after atropine)

Symptom

Mechanism

"Hot as a hare"

"Dry as a bone"
↓ Secretions (eg, mucous membranes, sweat glands)

  • Superficial vasodilation from ↑ body heat

"Blind as a bat"
Cycloplegia, mydriasis

"Mad as a hatter"
Altered mental status

  • Permeates blood-brain barrier & affects CNS pathways

urinary retention

  • ↓ Intestinal smooth muscle contraction
  • ↓ Detrusor contraction & ↓ internal urethral sphincter relaxation

"Fast as a fiddle"

Tachycardia

  • ↓ Vagal tone at the sinoatrial node

"Red as a beet"
Flushed skin

  • Superficial vasodilation from ↑ body heat

"Blind as a bat"
Cycloplegia, mydriasis

  • Paralysis of ciliary muscle & iris sphincter

"Mad as a hatter"
Altered mental status

  • Permeates blood-brain barrier & affects CNS pathways

"Full as a flask"
Constipation,
urinary retention

  • ↓ Intestinal smooth muscle contraction
  • ↓ Detrusor contraction & ↓ internal urethral sphincter relaxation

"Fast as a fiddle"

Tachycardia

  • ↓ Vagal tone at the sinoatrial node

Physiologic effects

subs.title: Acetaminophen
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Acute acetaminophen toxicity

Acute acetaminophen toxicity

Pathophysiology

  • Depletion of intrahepatic glutathione → accumulation of NAPQI (toxic metabolite of acetaminophen)

Clinical features
(time from ingestion)

  • ≤24 hr
    • Asymptomatic or nonspecific symptoms (eg, nausea, vomiting, fatigue)
  • 24-72 hr
    •  ↑ AST, ALT
  • 72-96 hr
    • AST/ALT levels peak (sometimes >10,000 U/L)
    • Severe cases:  ↑ PT/PTT, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, ↑ bilirubin, acute kidney injury
  • 4-14 days
    • Recovery

Diagnosis

  • Serum acetaminophen level (4-24 hr)
  • Liver function tests, BUN/creatinine, electrolytes

Treatment

  • Activated charcoal (if <4 hr)
  • N-acetylcysteine

ALT = alanine aminotransferase; AST = aspartate aminotransferase; BUN = blood urea nitrogen; NAPQI = N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine.

subs.title: Antimuscarinic, anticholinergic agents
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Anticholinergic toxicity

Anticholinergic toxicity

Etiology

  • Overdose or combination of anticholinergic agent(s)
  • Competitive inhibition of muscarinic ACh receptors in CNS, ciliary body, heart, smooth muscle, secretory glands

Clinical features

  • Agitation, delirium, hallucinations, seizures
  • Mydriasis, blurry vision
  • Tachycardia
  • Urinary retention, ↓ bowel sounds
  • Dry & flushed skin, dry mucous membranes, hyperthermia

Diagnosis

  • Based on clinical findings, no confirmatory laboratory tests

Treatment

  • Supportive care
  • Activated charcoal (awake patients <2 hr of ingestion)
  • Benzodiazepines for agitation & seizures
  • Physostigmine for severe central & peripheral symptoms

ACh = acetylcholine.

subs.title: Arsenic
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Arsenic poisoning

Arsenic poisoning

Mechanism

  • Binds to sulfhydryl groups
  • Disrupts cellular respiration & gluconeogenesis

Sources

  • Pesticides/insecticides
  • Contaminated water (often from wells)
  • Pressure-treated wood

Manifestations

  • Acute: garlic odor to the breath, vomiting, watery diarrhea, QTc prolongation
  • Chronic: hypo-/hyperpigmentation, hyperkeratosis, stocking-glove neuropathy

Treatment

  • Dimercaprol (British anti-Lewisite)
  • DMSA (ie, meso-2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid, succimer)

subs.title: β-blockers
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Beta blocker toxicity

Beta blocker toxicity

Symptom onset

  • 2-6 hr after ingestion

Signs and
symptoms

  • Hypotension
  • Bradycardia
  • Bronchospasm
  • Altered mental status
  • Seizures

Laboratory findings

  • Hypoglycemia

ECG findings

  • Prolonged PR interval
  • Bradycardia

Management

  • Secure airway
  • GI decontamination
  • IV fluid boluses
  • IV atropine
  • IV glucagon

GI = gastrointestinal; IV = intravenous.

subs.title: Cyanide
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Sodium thiosulfate

Treatment of cyanide (CN−) toxicity

Sodium thiosulfate

Sulfur donor that facilitates CN- binding to form thiocyanate, which is excreted in the urine

Hydroxocobalamin

Cobalt binds to CN− to form cyanocobalamin, which is excreted in the urine

Sodium nitrite*

Nitrites promote formation of methemoglobin, which binds CN− with greater affinity than cytochrome c oxidase, reducing CN− toxicity

*Care must be taken with dosing because excessive methemoglobinemia is itself toxic.

Treatment of asymptomatic lead toxicity

Mild

5-44 μg/dL

No medication

Moderate

45-69 μg/dL

subs.title: Mercury
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Chronic mercury toxicity

Chronic mercury toxicity

Exposures

  • Incidental (eg, broken lightbulbs or thermometers)
  • Ingestion (eg, shark, swordfish)
  • Occupational

Clinical features*

  • Neuropsychiatric: tremor, insomnia, personality changes (eg, irritability)
  • Cardiovascular: hypertension, tachycardia
  • Mucocutaneous: gingivitis; diaphoresis; swelling, redness, desquamation of hands/feet
  • Renal: tubular damage/proteinuria

*Some features may mimic pheochromocytoma, including elevated urinary catecholamines.

subs.title: Methanol, ethylene glycol (antifreeze)
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Toxic alcohol ingestion (methanol or ethylene glycol)

Toxic alcohol ingestion (methanol or ethylene glycol)

Typical sources

  • Methanol: windshield wiper fluid, contaminated homemade liquor
  • Ethylene glycol: automotive coolant/antifreeze, brake fluid
  • Industrial solvents & deicing solutions can contain either alcohol

Clinical features

  • Early: CNS sedation & inebriation, osmolar gap
  • Late: AGMA, compensatory tachypnea
    • Ocular toxicity (methanol)
    • Urine oxalate crystals, hypocalcemia, AKI (ethylene glycol)

Management

  • Fomepizole (inhibits ADHase) is preferred therapy
  • Ethanol solution (competes for ADHase) if fomepizole unavailable

ADHase = alcohol dehydrogenase; AGMA = anion gap metabolic acidosis; AKI = acute kidney injury.

directTables: Salicylate toxicity

Salicylate toxicity

Epidemiology

  • Excess ingestion of aspirin or other salicylates (eg, oil of wintergreen)
  • Liver metabolism gets overwhelmed → slower renal excretion → prolonged elevated salicylate levels

Manifestations

  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Hyperventilation
  • Hyperthermia
  • Altered mental status
  • Anion gap metabolic acidosis (elevated lactate)

Diagnosis

  • Serum salicylate level

Treatment

  • Activated charcoal (in alert patients within 2 hr of ingestion)
  • Intravenous sodium bicarbonate (enhances salicylate excretion)
  • Hemodialysis (severe ingestions, pulmonary edema, renal failure)

tables: Causes of QT-interval prolongation

Causes of QT-interval prolongation

Acquired

  • Medications
    • Macrolides & fluoroquinolones
    • Antiemetics (eg, ondansetron)
    • Azoles (eg, fluconazole)
    • Antipsychotics, TCAs & SSRIs
    • Some opioids (eg, methadone, oxycodone)
    • Class Ia antiarrhythmics (eg, quinidine)
    • Class III antiarrhythmics (eg, dofetilide, sotalol)
  • Electrolyte abnormalities
    • ↓ Magnesium, ↓ potassium, ↓ calcium

Congenital

  • Romano-Ward syndrome (autosomal dominant)
  • Jervell & Lange-Nielsen syndrome (autosomal recessive)*

*Associated with sensorineural hearing loss.

SSRIs = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; TCAs = tricyclic antidepressants.

subs.title: Agranulocytosis
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Drug-induced neutropenia

Drug-induced neutropenia

Common triggers

  • Methimazole, propylthiouracil
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
  • Clozapine
  • Sulfasalazine

Mechanism

  • Immune mediated: drug or metabolite binds to neutrophils & triggers a cell-mediated or humoral response
  • Bone marrow toxicity: drug or metabolite directly or indirectly damages granulocyte precursors

Manifestations

  • Usually within 3 months of drug exposure
  • Oropharyngeal ulceration ± fever
  • Other cell lines unaffected

Management

  • Discontinue inciting medication
  • Antibiotics in setting of treatable infection
  • Consider granulocyte colony-stimulating factor

Drug-induced neutropenia

Drug-induced neutropenia

Common triggers

  • Methimazole, propylthiouracil
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
  • Clozapine
  • Sulfasalazine

Mechanism

  • Immune mediated: drug or metabolite binds to neutrophils & triggers a cell-mediated or humoral response
  • Bone marrow toxicity: drug or metabolite directly or indirectly damages granulocyte precursors

Manifestations

  • Usually within 3 months of drug exposure
  • Oropharyngeal ulceration ± fever
  • Other cell lines unaffected

Management

  • Discontinue inciting medication
  • Antibiotics in setting of treatable infection
  • Consider granulocyte colony-stimulating factor

subs.title: Tardive dyskinesia
subs.subject: pharm
tables: Tardive dyskinesia

Tardive dyskinesia

Clinical features

  • Abnormal involuntary movements due to prolonged use of antipsychotics or metoclopramide
  • Orofacial dyskinesia (tongue protrusion, lip smacking, grimacing)
  • Limb dyskinesia (dystonic postures, foot tapping, chorea)
  • Trunk dyskinesia (rocking, thrusting, shoulder shrugging)
  • Greater risk with first-generation antipsychotics

Management

  • Discontinue causative medication if feasible
  • Switch to second-generation antipsychotic (quetiapine, clozapine) if continued antipsychotic is required
  • Treat with valbenazine or deutetrabenazine

topics.title: Quantifying risk
topics.subject: pubh
directTables: Common measures of therapeutic efficacy

Common measures of therapeutic efficacy

Term

Definition

Calculation

Absolute risk reduction (ARR)

Percentage indicating the actual difference in event rate between control & treatment groups

ARR = control rate – treatment rate

Relative risk reduction (RRR)

Percentage indicating relative reduction in the treatment event rate compared to the control group

RRR = ARR / control rate

Relative risk (RR)

Ratio of the probability of an event occurring in the treatment group compared to the control group

RR = treatment rate / control rate

Number needed to treat (NNT)

Number of individuals who need to be treated to prevent a negative outcome in 1 patient

NNT = 1 / ARR

topics.title: Core ethical principles
topics.subject: pubh
directTables: Ethical principles in medicine

Ethical principles in medicine

Principle

Duty

Beneficence

Promote good & act in the best medical interests of the patient

Nonmaleficence

Do no harm to the patient

Autonomy

Protect & facilitate the patient's individual, informed decisions

Justice

Equally distribute health care resources & provide fair & equitable treatment

Proportionality

Ensure that methods used to achieve a worthwhile goal are necessary, appropriate & not excessive

topics.title: Advance directives
topics.subject: pubh
directTables: Advance directives

Advance directives

Definition

  • Legally binding instructions regarding patient's own health care
  • Considered determinative for giving consent/refusal for treatment
  • Takes priority over family's/friends' preferences

Requirements

  • Patient is competent at time directive is prepared
  • Enacted only when patient lacks capacity for decision-making

Types

  • Living will: written document with consent/refusal of specific services
  • Health care proxy: designation of a surrogate decision maker

topics.title: Surrogate decision-maker
topics.subject: pubh
directTables: Next-of-kin surrogate decision maker

Next-of-kin surrogate decision maker

Patient selection

  • Inability to communicate wishes regarding medical decision-making
  • Advance directive not available or applicable
  • No previously designated surrogate decision maker

Surrogate selection

  • Priority to patient's spouse
  • Alternate: adult children, parents, adult siblings, other family members

Implementation

  • Substituted judgment: what the patient, not family, would have wanted
  • Decisions in the patient's best interest

topics.title: Confidentiality
topics.subject: pubh
directTables: HIPAA privacy rule

HIPAA privacy rule

PHI

Information pertaining to:

  • Patient physical or mental health
  • Services provided to patient
  • Payment for services

Provider requirements

  • Maintain physical & device safeguards to protect PHI
  • Establish procedures to prevent unauthorized disclosure
  • Ensure compliance by workforce

Breach of privacy

  • Impermissible use or disclosure of PHI
  • Provider must give written notice to patient regarding details of breach
  • Provider must take steps to mitigate breach & prevent future breach

HIPAA = Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act; PHI = protected health information.

topics.title: Challenging patient and ethical scenarios
topics.subject: pubh
directTables: Intimate partner violence

Intimate partner violence

Risk factors for escalating violence

  • Perpetrator
    • Increasing threats or controlling behavior
    • Violence outside the home/to children
    • Threatening homicide and/or suicide
    • Drug use
    • History of injuring partner/pregnant partner
    • Access to firearms
  • Victim
    • Admitting fear for life
    • Attempting to leave
    • Seeking outside help
    • Threatening or attempting suicide

Management

  • Ensure privacy
  • Do not confront perpetrator
  • Provide nonjudgmental support & validation without pressure
  • Assess for safety & create a safety plan
  • Offer assistance (counseling, resources)
Assessment of intimate partner violence

Assessment of intimate partner violence

Concerning signs

  • Location of injuries (eg, genitals, breasts, abdomen, head, neck, teeth)
  • Inconsistent explanation of injuries
  • Sexually transmitted disease, chronic pelvic pain
  • Nonadherence to visits & treatment/frequent emergency department visits
  • Overly attentive/intrusive partner who resists allowing patient to be seen alone
  • Discomfort/refusal to undress or consent to genital/rectal examination
  • Distressed affect: fearful, tearful, evasive

topics.title: Disease prevention
topics.subject: pubh
directTables: Ideal screening program

Ideal screening program

Disease characteristics

  • Common
  • Serious
  • Long asymptomatic phase
  • Correctable if identified early

Patient characteristics

  • High prevalence in screened population
  • Appropriate age range & gender

Test characteristics

  • Low cost relative to disease severity
  • High sensitivity & specificity
  • Acceptable to broad range of patients

Program characteristics

  • Identifies population to be screened
  • Avoids "overdiagnosis" (detects benign/indolent disease)
  • Avoids "lead-time" bias (detects disease early but does not alter ultimate prognosis)
  • Improves outcomes of screened vs nonscreened population

topics.title: Chemoprophylaxis and post-exposure prophylaxis
topics.subject: pubh
directTables: Occupational HIV postexposure prophylaxis

Occupational HIV postexposure prophylaxis

High-risk contact

(prophylaxis recommended)

Exposure of:

  • Mucous membrane, nonintact skin, or percutaneous exposure

Exposure to:

  • Blood, semen, vaginal secretions, or any body fluid with visible blood (uncertain risk: cerebrospinal fluid, pleural/pericardial fluid, synovial fluid, peritoneal fluid, amniotic fluid)

Low-risk contact

(prophylaxis not recommended)

Exposure to:

  • Urine, feces, nasal secretions, saliva, sweat, tears (with no visible blood)

Timing

  • Initiate urgently, preferably in the first few hours
  • Continue for 4 weeks

Regimen

Treatment with ≥3-drug regimen recommended:

  • Two nucleotide/nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (eg, tenofovir, emtricitabine)

PLUS:

  • Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (eg, raltegravir), protease inhibitor, or nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor
Postexposure prophylaxis for sexual assault

Postexposure prophylaxis for sexual assault

Infection

Medication

Chlamydia

 Doxycycline

Gonorrhea

 Ceftriaxone

Trichomonas vaginalis

Metronidazole

HIV

Multidrug regimen (eg, tenofovir-emtricitabine with raltegravir)

Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B vaccine ± hepatitis B immunoglobulin
Pertussis postexposure prophylaxis

Pertussis postexposure prophylaxis

Indications (regardless of vaccination history)

  • Close contact (eg, household members, direct contact with secretions) with symptomatic patient
  • High-risk patients, even with limited exposure (eg, pregnant, infant, immunodeficient)

Treatment

  • Age <1 month: azithromycin
  • Age ≥1 month: azithromycin, clarithromycin, or erythromycin

AND

directTables: Palliative management of end-of-life symptoms

Palliative management of end-of-life symptoms

Pain

  • Opioids: long acting (scheduled) & short acting
    (as needed)

Dyspnea & respiratory secretions

  • Cooling fan, breathing exercises, suctioning
  • Opioids: codeine, morphine
  • Anticholinergics: scopolamine, glycopyrrolate

Gastrointestinal symptoms

  • Nausea: ondansetron, metoclopramide, chlorpromazine
  • Anorexia: megestrol, mirtazapine

Delirium & anxiety

  • Reorientation, calming, open visitation

directTables: Active vs latent errors

Active vs latent errors

Active error

Latent error

  • Proximal cause
  • Involves actions of frontline personnel
  • Occurs at interface of provider with patient or system
  • "Sharp end" of the scalpel, tip of the iceberg
  • Distal cause
  • Involves organizational vulnerabilities that influence actions of frontline personnel
  • Occurs at level of system, processes & policy
  • "Accident waiting to happen," "blunt end" of the scalpel, below the surface
Preventable adverse drug events

Preventable adverse drug events

Risk factors

Sample corrective strategies

Patient

  • Polypharmacy
  • Low health literacy
  • Very young or advanced age
  • Communication barriers
  • Nonadherence/lack of follow-up
  • Increased checkpoints in medication reconciliation (eg, multiple providers)
  • Plain-language medication counseling
  • Patient "teach-back" (ie, patient describes understanding of treatment in own words)

Provider

  • Vague prescriptions
  • Incorrect medication reconciliation
  • Absence of counseling
  • Illegible handwriting

Medication

  • Look- or sound-alike drugs (eg, prednisone/prednisolone)
Classification of medical errors

Classification of medical errors

Preventable adverse event

  • Event that results from human or systems error
  • Example: wrong diagnosis, wrong drug selection

Negligent adverse event

  • Preventable event caused by clear deviation from standard of care
  • Example: drug administered to patient with known allergy 

Nonpreventable adverse event

  • Unforeseen event not preventable by following established standards of care
  • Example: rare adverse effect of appropriately administered drug

Sentinel event

  • Serious preventable error causing irreversible patient harm or death
  • Example: wrong-site surgery, wrong-patient error

Near-miss event

  • Preventable event that is intercepted before harm reaches patient
  • Example: nurse catches a miscalculated dose of medication before it is administered to the patient

tables: Failure modes & effects analysis (FMEA)

Failure modes & effects analysis (FMEA)

Overview & uses

  • Prospective, systematic assessment for error prevention
  • Identifies potential issues before they occur
  • Informs development of new initiatives

Steps in analysis

  • Form multidisciplinary team
  • Define process to be studied
  • Construct flowchart of process
  • Analyze error risks at each step
  • Identify potential corrective actions
  • Implement plan

directTables: Systems approach to error prevention

Systems approach to error prevention

Overview

  • Address organizational environment & teams
  • Emulate high-reliability organization practices (eg, aviation)

Components

  • Culture of safety: prioritize safety-promoting resources
  • Resilience: systems design to prevent errors
  • Team-based vigilance: safety oversight by entire team
  • Comprehensive analysis: avoid simplistic explanations

Examples

  • Human factors engineering: reduce human effort needed for safe action
  • Swiss-cheese model: multiple overlapping layers to block errors ("holes")
Common tools used in error analysis

Common tools used in error analysis

Root cause analysis (event analysis)

  • Retrospective
  • Identifies all underlying reasons (systems & personnel-related) that an error occurred

Failure modes & effects analysis

  • Prospective
  • Identifies the likelihood & potential sources of system failures before error occurs

Common cause analysis

  • Retrospective
  • Identifies most common themes & trends present among multiple errors

Morbidity & mortality conference

  • Retrospective
  • Identify system-level improvements to address an error through confidential, interdisciplinary, standardized group discussion

directTables: Alert fatigue

Alert fatigue

Definition

  • Health care workers become desensitized to all clinical alarms & alerts, including those of clinical significance 

Causes

  • Exposure to high frequency of alarms
  • Exposure to numerous false alarms (alarms of clinical insignificance)

Examples

  • Alerts (eg, drug-drug interactions) in electronic medical records
  • Automated devices (eg, infusion pumps, telemetry devices)
  • Patient sensors (eg, fall-prevention sensors) 

Prevention strategies

  • Minimize environmental distractions
  • Reduce alarm frequency & false alarm likelihood
  • Examples: decrease sensitivity of fall-prevention sensor to prevent minor patient movement from triggering alarm; minimize low-risk alerts in clinical decision support systems
Common cognitive errors in medicine

Common cognitive errors in medicine

Type of bias

Definition

Example

Anchoring

  • Fixating on initial impressions to make a diagnosis
  • Related to confirmation bias & premature closure
  • Burning throat pain diagnosed as acid reflux despite weight loss
  • Correct diagnosis is lung malignancy

Availability

  • Allowing recently seen or memorable (high-stakes) cases to sway diagnosis
  • Dyspnea diagnosed as influenza during peak influenza season
  • Correct diagnosis is pulmonary embolism

Confirmation

  • Emphasizing evidence that supports presumed diagnosis & overlooking information that supports other diagnoses
  • Related to anchoring bias
  • Burning throat pain after eating spicy food diagnosed as acid reflux despite weight loss
  • Correct diagnosis is malignancy

Framing

  • Allowing diagnostic approach to be influenced by context & presentation of information
  • Abdominal pain diagnosed as opioid withdrawal in patient described as drug seeking
  • Correct diagnosis is bowel obstruction
Features of effective teams

Features of effective teams* in health care

Safety culture

  • Resource commitment to safety

Collaboration

  • Shared understanding & prioritization of goals
  • Distinct roles that avoid a steep hierarchy

Psychologic safety

  • Asking questions & voicing concerns encouraged
  • Avoiding blame or retaliation

Responsiveness

  • Feedback respected & promptly acted on

Situational awareness

  • Persistent mindfulness & safety vigilance
  • Cross-checking of each other's actions

Transparency

  • Prompt disclosure of errors & safety information

*Poor teamwork is a leading root cause of sentinel events; improved communication reduces medical errors & improves patient/clinical outcomes.
Patient safety procedures in the surgical setting

Patient safety procedures in the surgical setting

Preoperative
verification

  • Patient identity, operative site, type of operation, & side (verified/documented by ≥2 providers)
  • Performed in preoperative holding area
  • Should involve patient (or surrogate) and 2 patient identifiers

Site marking

  • Mark (eg, "YES" + initials) on each operative site (do not mark nonoperative sites)
  • Clearly mark using permanent marker

Surgical
time-out

  • Occurs immediately prior to skin incision
  • Repeat verification of patient identity, operative site & side
  • Entire surgical team participates & all concerns addressed
Contributing factors for medical errors

Contributing factors for medical errors

Category

Factors

Examples

Patient

  • Clinical condition
  • Language
  • Cultural or religious beliefs
  • Social support
  • Patient & care provider do not speak the same language.
  • Opposition to blood products prevents transfusion.

Staff

  • Fatigue
  • Language
  • Stress
  • Mental impairment
  • Physician begins task at end of 24-hr call.
  • Nurse is taking opioids for pain when assisting with procedure.

Equipment

  • Unavailability
  • Disrepair
  • Ultrasonographic machine is not available on the floor for central line placement.

Work environment

  • Staffing workloads
  • Error reporting policy & practice
  • Physical design of patient care area
  • There is a high nurse/patient ratio.
  • Anonymous reporting system is not present.
  • Intensive care unit alarms cannot be adjusted.

Education & training

  • Presence of senior staff
  • Unfamiliar task
  • Inexperience
  • Resident is asked to perform lumbar puncture alone after performing only 2 previously.

Task

  • Guidelines & policies
  • Algorithms & protocols
  • Test result availability
  • There is a lack of guidelines on the appropriateness of the procedure.
  • Test results are available only on paper.
